edge_cases.title: Where exactly does a temporary bound to a returned reference die?
edge_cases.explanation:
- Code:
```cpp
std::string create() { return "hello"; }
const std::string& get() { return create(); }   // GCC: returning reference to temporary
const std::string& s = get();
std::cout << s;                                  // UB
```
- A common (and AI-generated) explanation says the temporary "is destroyed at the end of the full expression in the caller". That is wrong. The temporary is created by the `return` statement **inside** `get()`; a temporary bound to the returned value of a function is not extended and is destroyed at the end of the `return` statement's full-expression. By the time `get()` returns, the string is already gone.
- Verified with a tracing type: `~T` prints before the caller's next line runs.
- RVO has nothing to do with it: elision decides where `create()`'s result is built, not how long a reference to it is valid.
- GCC warns (`-Wreturn-local-addr`, on by default). C++26 (P2748) makes binding a returned reference to a temporary ill-formed.
- Deep dive: Topic 1, Object Lifetime and Storage Duration

edge_cases.title: A destructor quietly turns moves into copies
edge_cases.explanation:
- `struct Order { std::string id; ~Order() { log(); } };` looks harmless.
- The user-declared destructor removes the implicit move constructor. `Order b = std::move(a);` compiles and calls the copy constructor: `a.id` keeps its contents, and the string is deep-copied.
- In `std::vector<Order>`, every reallocation copies every element.
- Fix: remove the destructor (logging belongs elsewhere) or add `Order(Order&&) noexcept = default;` and the other defaults.
- The same happens with `~Order() = default;`, which many people add "for clarity".
- Deep dive: Topic 2, Special Member Functions and the Rule of 0/3/5

edge_cases.title: std::move on a const object silently copies
edge_cases.explanation:
- `const std::string s = "..."; std::string t = std::move(s);` compiles without a warning and copies.
- Same with `const` locals returned with `return std::move(x);`, `const` members moved in a constructor, and `const auto&` loop variables: `for (const auto& e : v) out.push_back(std::move(e));` copies every element.
- clang-tidy `performance-move-const-arg` flags these; compilers do not.
- Rule: never move from something declared `const`; drop the `const` when you intend to move.
- Deep dive: Topic 3, Value Categories, std::move and Moved-From State

edge_cases.title: `return std::move(local)` disables NRVO
edge_cases.explanation:
- Output with a tracing type: `ctor move dtor dtor` instead of `ctor dtor`.
- GCC: `warning: moving a local object in a return statement prevents copy elision [-Wpessimizing-move]`.
- Same problem inside `return std::move(cond ? a : b);`: it moves, but a plain `if` would allow implicit move without the cast and keep code clearer.
- Deep dive: Topic 4, Copy Elision, RVO and NRVO

edge_cases.title: An uncaught exception does not guarantee cleanup
edge_cases.explanation:
- `void work() { Guard g; throw std::runtime_error("boom"); }` called from `main` with no `try`.
- No handler exists, so `std::terminate` is called. Whether the stack is unwound first is **implementation-defined**.
- GCC/libstdc++ does not unwind: `~Guard` never runs; the program prints the terminate message and aborts.
- With a `try`/`catch` around the call, `~Guard` runs before the handler.
- Consequence: cleanup that must happen (flush a log, release an OS-wide lock file) needs a top-level `catch (...)` in `main` and in every thread function.
- Deep dive: Topic 5, RAII and Exception Safety

edge_cases.title: unique_ptr<Base> without a virtual destructor
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::unique_ptr<Base> b = std::make_unique<Derived>();` compiles silently.
- `default_delete<Base>` deletes through `Base*`: without `virtual ~Base()`, this is UB. Observed: only `~Base` prints; `Derived`'s `std::string` member is never destroyed (its heap buffer leaks).
- ASan (for a `Base` holding one `int` and a `Derived` adding a `std::string`): `new-delete-type-mismatch: object passed to delete has wrong type: size of the allocated type: 40 bytes; size of the deallocated type: 4 bytes`.
- GCC `-Wall` does not warn here (`-Wdelete-non-virtual-dtor` fires only when the class has other virtual functions).
- Deep dive: Topic 6, std::unique_ptr

edge_cases.title: Two control blocks for one object
edge_cases.explanation:
- `Widget* raw = new Widget; std::shared_ptr<Widget> a(raw); std::shared_ptr<Widget> b(raw);`
- Each constructor that takes a raw pointer creates a **new** control block. `a` and `b` both have `use_count() == 1`; both delete the object: double free (ASan: "attempting double-free").
- Same bug in disguise: `std::shared_ptr<D>(static_cast<D*>(base.get()))`, or `std::shared_ptr<T>(this)` inside a member function (topic 09 shows `enable_shared_from_this`).
- Rule: a raw pointer becomes owned **once**. After that, copy the `shared_ptr`, use the pointer casts, or use the aliasing constructor.
- Deep dive: Topic 7, std::shared_ptr Internals and make_shared

edge_cases.title: Write-once flag publication is safe; republication is not
edge_cases.explanation:
- Producer: `data = d; ready.store(true, release);` Consumer: `while (!ready.load(acquire)) {}` then `data->value`.
- Safe: the only write to `data` happens-before every read of it.
- Add a second producer (or the same producer later) doing `data = std::make_shared<Data>();` while consumers read: TSan reports a data race on `data`.
- A source of confusion: some explanations call even the write-once version a race. It is not; the conflict needs two **unordered** accesses.
- Deep dive: Topic 8, shared_ptr and Thread Safety

edge_cases.title: expired() followed by lock()
edge_cases.explanation:
- `if (!w.expired()) { auto sp = w.lock(); sp->run(); }` looks safe, but another thread can release the last owner between the two calls. `sp` is then empty and `sp->run()` dereferences null (UB, usually a crash).
- `expired()` and `lock()` are each atomic; the sequence of two is not.
- Fix: `if (auto sp = w.lock()) sp->run();`. The test and the acquisition of ownership are one operation.
- Same race with `if (w.use_count() > 0)`.
- Deep dive: Topic 9, weak_ptr, Reference Cycles and enable_shared_from_this

edge_cases.title: Reusing storage and reading through the old pointer
edge_cases.explanation:
- `X* p = new (buf) X{1}; p->~X(); new (buf) X{2}; use(p->n);`
  - If `X` has a `const` (or reference) member: UB in C++17 without `std::launder(p)`; allowed in C++20 (transparent replacement).
  - Through `reinterpret_cast<X*>(buf)`: needs `std::launder` in every version.
- In practice compilers rarely miscompile simple cases, which is why the bug is hard to demonstrate; the rule matters in generic containers with inline storage.
- Fix: keep the pointer returned by the newest placement new.
- Deep dive: Topic 10, new/delete, Placement New and Object Storage

edge_cases.title: The nested type does not use the resource
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::pmr::vector<std::string> v(&res);` allocates its array from `res`, but each long `std::string` element allocates its own buffer with `std::allocator`, i.e. the global heap.
- `std::pmr::vector<std::pmr::string> v(&res);` passes `res` to every element through uses-allocator construction (verified with a counting resource).
- Same trap with `pmr::map<std::string, std::vector<int>>`: use `pmr::string` and `pmr::vector` all the way down.
- Deep dive: Topic 11, Memory Pools and Polymorphic Allocators (PMR)

edge_cases.title: memcmp and hashing over padding
edge_cases.explanation:
- Two objects with equal members can differ in their padding bytes, so `memcmp` says "not equal" and a byte-wise hash puts them in different buckets.
- Zeroed padding is only promised by zero-initialization (statics; value-initialization of a non-aggregate without a user-provided constructor). `T x{}` on a plain aggregate usually zeroes it in practice but does not promise it, and later member assignments and copies do not have to preserve padding values.
- `std::has_unique_object_representations_v<T>` tells you whether byte-wise comparison/hashing is valid for `T`.
- Sending a padded struct over the network or into a file also leaks stale stack or heap bytes.
- Deep dive: Topic 12, Alignment, Padding and Data Layout

- Exact sizes are implementation details; "one vs two allocations" is the portable fact.

code_examples.title: A fixed-size object pool with an intrusive free list
code_examples.explanation:
- Union slots (the object is a union member, so slot size and alignment come for free), O(1) acquire/release, exception-safe construction, and a "fail fast" exhaustion policy.

- Output:

- LIFO reuse: the most recently freed slot is handed out next, which is also the one most likely to be in cache.
- Lifetime: `create` starts an `Order`'s lifetime in existing storage; `destroy` ends it; the storage lives as long as the pool.
- Getting back from `T*` to the slot: because `obj` is a union member, the union and `obj` are pointer-interconvertible, so `reinterpret_cast<Slot*>(p)` is well defined. With a `std::byte` array member instead, the cast relies on layout assumptions the standard does not bless.
- Deep dive: Topic 11, Memory Pools and Polymorphic Allocators (PMR)

interview_qa.question: When exactly is the temporary destroyed here, and what does the caller hold?
interview_qa.answer: The temporary string is created by the `return` statement inside `get()`. A temporary bound to a function's returned reference is not lifetime-extended; it is destroyed at the end of that `return` statement, still inside `get()`. The caller receives a dangling reference, and `std::cout << s` is undefined behaviour.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Verified with a tracing type: the temporary's destructor prints before the caller's next statement.
- A popular explanation ("destroyed at the end of the full expression in the caller") gets the place wrong: it is the callee's full-expression.
- RVO is irrelevant: elision decides where `create()` builds its result, not how long a reference to it lives.
- GCC warns by default: "returning reference to temporary [-Wreturn-local-addr]". C++26 (P2748) makes this ill-formed.
- Observed with GCC 11 `-O0`: the program **segfaults**. Knowing the reference is dangling, GCC returns a null reference (UBSan: "reference binding to null pointer of type 'const struct string'"). Other compilers may print garbage or even "hello".
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`s` is `const&`, so the lifetime is extended." Extension needs the reference to bind directly to the prvalue; `s` binds to whatever `get()` returned.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the fix is to return `std::string` by value, which costs nothing extra with guaranteed elision (topic 04).
- Deep dive: Topic 1, Object Lifetime and Storage Duration
interview_qa.key_takeaway: A temporary in a reference-returning `return` dies inside the callee.

interview_qa.question: What is the static initialization order fiasco and how do you avoid it?
interview_qa.answer: Statics with dynamic initialization in different translation units are initialized in an unspecified order (in practice: link order). If one static's initializer reads another TU's static that is not yet initialized, it sees zero-initialized memory or, for class types, an object whose lifetime has not begun. Fixes: function-local statics (initialized on first use), `constexpr`/`constinit` (constant initialization, no ordering), or no cross-TU global dependencies.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Measured: `int order_port = base_port + 1;` (other file has `int base_port = compute_base_port();`) gave `1` with `g++ main.cpp config.cpp` and `9001` with `g++ config.cpp main.cpp`.
- Initialization phases: zero-initialization, constant initialization (baked into the binary), then dynamic initialization (code before `main`). Only the dynamic phase has the ordering problem.
- `constinit` (C++20) makes the compiler reject a non-constant initializer: "'constinit' variable does not have a constant initializer".
- ASan can detect it at run time: `ASAN_OPTIONS=check_initialization_order=1`.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Globals are initialized in the order they appear in the program."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the mirror problem at shutdown, the destruction order fiasco (Q14).
- Deep dive: Topic 1, Object Lifetime and Storage Duration
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Across files, dynamic static initialization has no order you can rely on.

interview_qa.question: What exactly does the compiler generate if you declare only a destructor? Why does that matter for `std::vector`?
interview_qa.answer: Default constructor, copy constructor and copy assignment are still generated (the copies are deprecated); move constructor and move assignment are not declared. So every move, including `std::vector` growth, silently becomes a copy.
code_examples:
copy copy 
move move
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Do not declare a destructor you do not need; if you need one, default the moves explicitly.

interview_qa.question: Why should move operations be `noexcept`? What happens in `std::vector` if they are not?
interview_qa.answer: `std::vector::push_back` gives the strong guarantee. During reallocation it can only move elements if moving cannot throw; otherwise a failure midway would leave old elements moved-from. So if the move constructor is not `noexcept` and a copy constructor exists, the vector copies every element on growth.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Measured with 1000 `emplace_back` calls (libstdc++): `noexcept` move gave 0 copies and 1023 moves; the identical non-`noexcept` move gave 1023 copies and 0 moves.
- The selection is done with `std::move_if_noexcept` (topic 03).
- If the type is move-only (copy deleted), the vector moves anyway and the guarantee weakens to basic for that operation.
- Implicit and `= default` moves are `noexcept` automatically when all members' moves are.
- Destructors are implicitly `noexcept`; a throwing destructor would break every container.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`vector` requires `noexcept` move." It compiles and works without; it just copies.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`noexcept` makes the move faster." The move itself is the same code; `noexcept` changes which operation the container chooses.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: `static_assert(std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<T>);` next to the class to lock it in.
- Deep dive: Topic 2, Special Member Functions and the Rule of 0/3/5
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `noexcept` on the move constructor is the difference between O(1) and deep-copy relocation in containers.

interview_qa.question: What does `std::move` actually do? Does it move any memory?
interview_qa.answer: `std::move(x)` is a cast, essentially `static_cast<std::remove_reference_t<T>&&>(x)`. It produces an xvalue so that overload resolution can select a move constructor, move assignment or other `T&&` overload. It moves nothing and touches no memory; the selected function does the moving.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `std::move(a);` as a statement has no effect (libstdc++ marks it `[[nodiscard]]`; GCC warns "ignoring return value").
- `Buffer b(std::move(a));`: the cast is followed by overload resolution, which picks `Buffer(Buffer&&)`; the move constructor transfers the pointer.
- It does not change `a` itself or its type: it changes how the **expression** `a` is treated in that one place. After the line, the expression `a` is an lvalue again.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`std::move` changes the variable into an rvalue reference." It produces a new expression; the variable is untouched.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`std::move` guarantees a move." If the only viable overload takes `const T&`, a copy happens.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: "`std::move` is permission, not action: it says *I no longer need this value*; whether anything moves depends on the overload chosen."
- Deep dive: Topic 3, Value Categories, std::move and Moved-From State
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `std::move` is a cast to xvalue; the move constructor or move assignment does the move.

**Explanation:**

- Deep dive: Topic 3, Value Categories, std::move and Moved-From State

interview_qa.question: `const Data a; Data b = std::move(a);` Does this move or copy?
interview_qa.answer: It copies. `std::move(a)` has type `const Data&&`. The move constructor `Data(Data&&)` cannot bind a const rvalue (moving would modify the source), but the copy constructor `Data(const Data&)` can, so it is selected.
code_examples:
copy
move
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `std::move` keeps `const`; const rvalues copy.

interview_qa.question: Why is `return std::move(local);` usually wrong?
interview_qa.answer: `std::move(local)` is not the name of a local object, so NRVO is no longer allowed and a move is forced. `return local;` already gets NRVO or, failing that, an implicit move, so the explicit cast can only make things worse.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Measured with a tracing type: `return t;` prints `ctor dtor`; `return std::move(t);` prints `ctor move dtor dtor`.
- GCC and Clang warn: `-Wpessimizing-move` ("moving a local object in a return statement prevents copy elision"), enabled by `-Wall`.
- For parameters, `return std::move(param);` is merely redundant (`-Wredundant-move`): parameters are moved anyway and never elided.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "It makes sure the object is moved instead of copied." The language already guarantees that.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the cases where `std::move` in a return *is* right: a member (`return std::move(p.first);`), a structured binding, or a data member from an rvalue-qualified member function.
- Deep dive: Topic 4, Copy Elision, RVO and NRVO
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Return locals and parameters by name; reserve `std::move` for sub-objects.
interview_qa.full_content:
**Answer:**
`std::move(local)` is not the name of a local object, so NRVO is no longer allowed and a move is forced. `return local;` already gets NRVO or, failing that, an implicit move, so the explicit cast can only make things worse.

**Explanation:**

interview_qa.question: Can a type with deleted copy and move constructors be returned from a function?
interview_qa.answer: Yes, if it is returned as a prvalue (`return T(args);` or `return {args};`) in C++17 or later. No, if it is returned by name (`T t; return t;`), because NRVO is optional and the code must be valid without it.

interview_qa.question: Is a local object's destructor guaranteed to run if an exception is thrown and never caught?
interview_qa.answer: No. If no matching handler exists, `std::terminate` is called, and whether the stack is unwound before that is implementation-defined. With GCC/libstdc++ the stack is not unwound, so the destructor never runs.
code_examples:
~Guard ran
caught boom
terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::runtime_error'
  what():  boom
interview_qa.key_takeaway: RAII cleanup during exceptions is guaranteed only for exceptions that are caught.
interview_qa.full_content:
**Answer:**
No. If no matching handler exists, `std::terminate` is called, and whether the stack is unwound before that is implementation-defined. With GCC/libstdc++ the stack is not unwound, so the destructor never runs.

**Explanation:**
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <stdexcept>

struct Guard { ~Guard() { std::cout << "~Guard ran" << std::endl; } };

void work() { Guard g; throw std::runtime_error("boom"); }

int main() {
    try { work(); } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        std::cout << "caught " << e.what() << std::endl;   // flush: abort won't
    }
    work();   // no handler anywhere
}
```
- Output (GCC 11, Linux):
```
~Guard ran
caught boom
terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::runtime_error'
  what():  boom
```
- The process then aborts (exit status 134, SIGABRT). The second `~Guard ran` never appears.
- `std::endl` matters here: `abort` does not flush `std::cout`, so with output redirected to a file or pipe, unflushed lines are lost too.
- Not unwinding is useful for debugging: the core dump shows the stack at the throw point.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "RAII guarantees cleanup whenever an exception is thrown."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: put `try { ... } catch (...) { log; return 1; }` in `main` and in every thread entry function when cleanup matters (flushing logs, removing lock files, sending a disconnect).
- Deep dive: Topic 5, RAII and Exception Safety

**Key takeaway:** RAII cleanup during exceptions is guaranteed only for exceptions that are caught.

interview_qa.question: A constructor throws halfway through. Which destructors run?
interview_qa.answer: The object's own destructor does not run, because its lifetime never started. Every base and member that was fully constructed is destroyed in reverse order. If the object was created with `new`, the new-expression also frees the memory.
code_examples:
acquired both
init failed
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Constructor failure destroys finished members, never the object itself: own resources through members, not raw pointers.

interview_qa.question: What is `sizeof(std::unique_ptr<T>)`, and how does a custom deleter change it?
interview_qa.answer: With the default deleter it is the size of a raw pointer (8 bytes on 64-bit). A stateless deleter (empty functor or captureless lambda) adds nothing, thanks to empty-base optimization. interview_qa.explanation:
- Measured on libstdc++ x86-64: default 8, stateless functor 8, lambda 8, function pointer 16, functor with one `int` 16 (padded), `std::function` 40.
- Moving does not change size: a moved-from `unique_ptr` has the same type and size, only the stored pointer is null.
- The size is a property of the **type**, so it is a compile-time constant; nothing is allocated for the deleter.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "A unique_ptr is always 8 bytes." Not with function-pointer or stateful deleters.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "A custom deleter always increases the size."

- Deep dive: Topic 6, std::unique_ptr

interview_qa.question: `std::unique_ptr<Base> b = std::make_unique<Derived>();` compiles. What must be true of `Base` for this to be correct?
interview_qa.answer: `Base` must have a virtual destructor. The converting move turns the deleter into `default_delete<Base>`, which does `delete (Base*)p`; deleting a `Derived` through a `Base*` without a virtual destructor is UB, and in practice `~Derived` (and the destructors of its members) never run.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Polymorphic ownership through `unique_ptr<Base>` requires `virtual ~Base()`.

interview_qa.question: Why is `std::make_shared<T>()` generally preferred over `std::shared_ptr<T>(new T)`?
interview_qa.answer: It performs one allocation for the control block and the object instead of two, which saves an allocator call and per-allocation overhead and keeps the counts next to the object. It also avoids a naked `new`, which historically made it exception-safe in function arguments.
interview_qa.explanation:

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the cases where `make_shared` is wrong (Q7).
- Deep dive: Topic 7, std::shared_ptr Internals and make_shared

interview_qa.question: Is `std::shared_ptr` type-erased? Why can `shared_ptr`s with different deleters live in one vector?
interview_qa.answer: Yes: the deleter (and allocator) are type-erased. - Cost of erasure: indirect (virtual) calls through the control block at destruction time (dispose the object, later destroy the block) and an allocation for the block. `unique_ptr` with a stateless deleter costs nothing extra.
- `std::get_deleter<D>(sp)` recovers the deleter if you name its exact type.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`shared_ptr` is not type-erased; it is fixed-size because it always holds two pointers." The fixed size is a **consequence** of the erasure.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the same mechanism is why `shared_ptr<void>` and `shared_ptr<Base>` still destroy the original concrete type (Q9).
- Deep dive: Topic 7, std::shared_ptr Internals and make_shared

interview_qa.question: What is the aliasing constructor and when would you use it?
interview_qa.answer: `std::shared_ptr<U> q(owner, ptr)` creates a `shared_ptr` that shares `owner`'s control block (count +1) but stores an arbitrary pointer `ptr`, typically a member of the owned object. `q` keeps the whole object alive, and when the count reaches zero the original object is destroyed; `ptr` itself is never deleted.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Aliasing: stored pointer and owned object differ, control block is shared.

interview_qa.question: Is `std::shared_ptr` thread-safe?
interview_qa.answer: It depends on which layer you mean. The control block's reference counting is thread-safe, so different `shared_ptr` objects that share ownership can be copied, reset and destroyed concurrently. The same `shared_ptr` object is not safe if one thread modifies it while another accesses it. And the managed object gets no protection at all.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Three questions to ask:
  - Is the same handle shared between threads with a writer? Needs a mutex or `atomic<shared_ptr>`.
  - Does each thread own a copy? Then lifetime is protected.
  - Is the object's data modified concurrently? Needs its own synchronization or immutability.
- Same rule as any ordinary object for the handle: concurrent `const` access is fine; a writer requires exclusion.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Yes, the counter is atomic." That covers only one of three layers.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "No, so every copy needs a lock." Copies living in different threads are exactly what the atomic count is for.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: "`shared_ptr` answers *when may this be destroyed*, not *who may modify it*."
- Deep dive: Topic 8, shared_ptr and Thread Safety
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Thread-safe ownership, not a thread-safe handle variable, not a thread-safe object.

interview_qa.question: Design a configuration hot-reload with `std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<const Config>>`. What do readers and the writer do, and what does it not protect?
interview_qa.answer: Readers call `auto c = cfg.load();` once per operation and read every field through `c`. The writer builds a complete new `Config`, then `cfg.store(std::move(next));`. Old configs are freed when their last reader drops its snapshot. It protects the handle only: the `Config` objects must be immutable after publication.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `load()` returns an owning `shared_ptr`, so a writer's `store()` can never free a config that a reader still uses.
- Ordering: the default `seq_cst`, or `store(release)` with `load(acquire)`, makes the fields written before publication visible to any reader that obtains the new pointer.
- Rules:
  - One `load()` per operation; two loads may return two versions (`a` from v1, `b` from v2).
  - `shared_ptr<const Config>` so readers cannot mutate.
  - One writer, or serialize writers (Q10).
- Practical notes:
  - Not lock-free (libstdc++ GCC 12+ and MSVC use a lock bit): `is_lock_free()` is `false`.
  - GCC 11 does not provide it; use the mutex version (Q5) there.
  - Basic `atomic<shared_ptr>` facts are in Chapter 4, topic 05, Q20.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Because the pointer is atomic, readers can also update fields of the config." That is a race on the object.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: whichever thread drops the last reference to an old config destroys it; keep heavy destruction off hot reader threads.
- Deep dive: Topic 8, shared_ptr and Thread Safety

interview_qa.question: Two objects hold `shared_ptr`s to each other. What happens? Is it a deadlock?
interview_qa.answer: It is a memory leak, not a deadlock. After the assignments both strong counts are 2; the two `reset()` calls bring each to 1, and nothing can bring them to 0 because each object owns the other. Neither destructor ever runs.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Trace: after `make_shared`: A=1, B=1. `a->b = b`: B=2. `b->a = a`: A=2. `a.reset()`: A=1. `b.reset()`: B=1.
- Both objects are now unreachable from the program but still owned by each other.
- A deadlock needs threads waiting on each other; here nothing waits, nothing runs.
- LeakSanitizer reports such a cycle as "Indirect leak" entries only (each block is referenced by another leaked block).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Deadlock: each waits for the other to be destroyed." Nothing is waiting; it is just reference counting that never reaches zero.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the side effects of the destructors (closing sockets, flushing files, unregistering) are also lost, not just the memory.
- Deep dive: Topic 9, weak_ptr, Reference Cycles and enable_shared_from_this
interview_qa.key_takeaway: A strong cycle is a silent leak; `shared_ptr` is reference counting, not garbage collection.

interview_qa.question: When does `shared_from_this()` fail, and what happens?
interview_qa.answer: Whenever no `shared_ptr` currently owns the object: in the constructor, in the destructor, for stack or `unique_ptr`-owned objects, and when the base is inherited privately. Since C++17 it throws `std::bad_weak_ptr`; before C++17 it was undefined behaviour.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `shared_from_this()` requires an existing owner; enforce it with a factory.

interview_qa.question: What is the difference between the `new` expression and `operator new`?
interview_qa.answer: The `new` expression (`new T(args)`) is a language operation that calls an allocation function to get raw storage and then constructs a `T` in it. `operator new(std::size_t)` is only the allocation function: it returns bytes, like `malloc`, and constructs nothing. You can overload or replace `operator new`; you cannot change what the `new` expression does.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `delete p` is symmetric: destructor first, then `operator delete(p)`.
- Calling `operator new(sizeof(T))` directly gives raw memory with no object in it; you must construct one with placement new before use.
- Customization points are the functions (`operator new/delete` at global or class scope), which is how pools and allocation counters hook in.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "They're the same; `operator new` is just the name of the `new` keyword." Mixing them up leads to "I overloaded `operator new`, why does my constructor still run?" confusion.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: placement new is the new-expression with a non-allocating allocation function (`operator new(std::size_t, void*)` just returns the pointer).
- Deep dive: Topic 10, new/delete, Placement New and Object Storage

interview_qa.question: What is `std::launder` for?
interview_qa.answer: `std::launder(p)` (C++17) returns a pointer to the object that currently lives at address `p`, when the pointer you have cannot legally be used to reach it: the old object was not transparently replaceable (e.g. `const` members in C++17, a base-class subobject), or the pointer was obtained by casting the storage (`reinterpret_cast<T*>(buf)`) rather than from the construction. It generates no code; it stops the optimizer from assuming the old object's values.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Example of the hazard: the compiler may cache a `const int id` read through `p`, or a vtable pointer, across the reconstruction.
- Typical users: implementations of `std::optional`, `std::variant`, small-buffer vectors and pools, which recreate objects in member byte arrays.
- Practical rule that avoids it: store and use the pointer returned by placement new / `construct_at`.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`std::launder` fixes alignment or makes a cast safe." It does not create objects and does not fix alignment, aliasing of a different type, or lifetime problems.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: C++20's relaxation means most reuse-through-old-pointer cases of the same complete type no longer need it.
- Deep dive: Topic 10, new/delete, Placement New and Object Storage

interview_qa.question: What does `monotonic_buffer_resource` do, and for which workloads is it ideal or harmful?
interview_qa.answer: It is an arena: each allocation bumps a pointer forward through a buffer (asking upstream for bigger chunks when full), `deallocate` does nothing, and all memory is reclaimed at once by `release()` or destruction. It is ideal when many allocations share one lifetime (per request, per message, per frame) and harmful when objects have independent lifetimes or containers grow and churn.
interview_qa.explanation:

interview_qa.question: Why does `std::pmr::vector<std::string>` still allocate from the heap, while `std::pmr::vector<std::pmr::string>` does not?
interview_qa.answer: Only the vector's own array uses the resource. A `std::string` element uses `std::allocator`, so each long string allocates its buffer on the global heap. `std::pmr::string` is allocator-aware with a `polymorphic_allocator`, so the vector passes its resource to each element through uses-allocator construction.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `polymorphic_allocator::construct` checks `std::uses_allocator<T, polymorphic_allocator<...>>` and, if true, appends the allocator to the constructor arguments.
- It works recursively: `pmr::map<pmr::string, pmr::vector<pmr::string>>` keeps everything in the same resource.
- Short strings fit the SSO buffer (no allocation at all), so the leak only shows with longer strings: easy to miss in tests.
- Verified with a counting resource: `pmr::vector<std::string>` element allocation did not hit the resource; `pmr::vector<pmr::string>` did, and `v[0].get_allocator().resource()` was the vector's resource.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Once the outer container is pmr, everything inside is in the arena."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: a counting or guard resource in tests is the cheapest way to prove where allocations go.
- Deep dive: Topic 11, Memory Pools and Polymorphic Allocators (PMR)
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Use pmr types all the way down, or nested data escapes the arena.

interview_qa.question: What are `sizeof(A)` and `sizeof(B)` on a typical x86-64 system, and why do they differ?
interview_qa.answer: `sizeof(A)` is 12 and `sizeof(B)` is 8. In `A`, the `int` needs a 4-aligned offset, so 3 padding bytes follow `c`, and 3 bytes of tail padding follow `d` so the size is a multiple of the struct's alignment (4). In `B` the two `char`s share the space after the `int`, leaving only 2 bytes of tail padding.
code_examples:
struct A { char c; int i; char d; };
struct B { int i; char c; char d; };
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Padding depends on member order; `sizeof` includes interior and tail padding.

interview_qa.question: What is a packed struct, and what are the risks of using one?
interview_qa.answer: A packed struct (`#pragma pack(1)` or `__attribute__((packed))`) has no padding: members follow each other byte by byte and the struct's alignment drops to 1. Its members are therefore misaligned, which makes access slower, breaks atomicity and SIMD, can fault on strict-alignment CPUs, and makes pointers or references to members dangerous.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `struct { char c; int i; }` packed: size 5, `i` at offset 1.
- Direct access `p.i` is safe: the compiler knows the member is packed and emits unaligned-safe code.
- `int* q = &p.i;` loses that knowledge. GCC refuses to bind `int&` to an `__attribute__((packed))` member and warns for the pointer (Clang 14 warns for the pointer but accepts the reference); with `#pragma pack` GCC 11 and Clang 14 accepted both silently.
- Arrays of packed structs place most elements at odd addresses.
- Typical legitimate use: describing a wire or file header. Even there, `memcpy`-based parsing into a naturally aligned struct is usually cleaner.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Packing is a free memory optimisation." It trades memory for slower, riskier access.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: reorder members first; pack only when an external byte format forces it.
- Deep dive: Topic 12, Alignment, Padding and Data Layout
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Packing removes padding by creating misaligned members; keep it at the I/O boundary.

practice_tasks.title: Question 1
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Undefined behaviour: m is a dangling reference.
(A plain -O0 build happened to print 5; ASan reports stack-use-after-scope on the read.)
```

**Explanation:**
- `std::max` takes and returns `const int&`. The literal `5` is materialized as a temporary bound to the parameter, and `std::max` returns a reference to it.
- The temporary dies at the end of the full-expression (the `;`). `m` was not bound directly to a prvalue, so there is no lifetime extension.
- GCC 11 gives no warning; GCC 13 adds `-Wdangling-reference`.
- **Key Concept:** Lifetime extension never passes through a function that returns a reference.
- Deep dive: Topic 1, Object Lifetime and Storage Duration

**Fixed Version:**
```cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int limit = 3;
    const int m = std::max(limit, 5);   // copy the value
    std::cout << m << '\n';             // 5
}
```

practice_tasks.title: Question 3
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Compile error (both lines):
error: use of deleted function 'constexpr Buffer::Buffer(const Buffer&)'
note: ... is implicitly declared as deleted because 'Buffer' declares a move
      constructor or move assignment operator
```

**Explanation:**
- Declaring only move assignment deletes the implicit copy constructor and copy assignment, and leaves the move constructor not declared.
- `Buffer b(a);`: the copy constructor is deleted.
- `Buffer c(std::move(a));`: there is no move constructor, so the rvalue falls back to the copy constructor, which is deleted.
- **Key Concept:** Declaring any move operation deletes both copies; it does not give you the other move.
- Deep dive: Topic 2, Special Member Functions and the Rule of 0/3/5

practice_tasks.title: Question 4
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
| copy | copy copy | 
```

**Explanation:**
- `emplace_back` constructs the new element in place: no copy or move for the element being added.
- Growth from capacity 1 to 2 relocates one element; from 2 to 4 relocates two.
- The move constructor is not `noexcept`, and a copy constructor exists, so `std::move_if_noexcept` chooses the **copy** to keep `emplace_back`'s strong guarantee.
- Add `noexcept` to `Msg(Msg&&)` and the output becomes `| move | move move | `.
- **Key Concept:** A move constructor that is not `noexcept` is ignored by vector reallocation whenever copying is possible.
- Deep dive: Topic 2, Special Member Functions and the Rule of 0/3/5

practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
const& const& && && const& 
```

**Explanation:**
- `c.text()`: lvalue object: `const&` (the only overload accepting an lvalue).

practice_tasks.title: Question 6
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
false [] [EURUSD]   (libstdc++)
p is not guaranteed to be valid by the standard.
```

**Explanation:**
- "EURUSD" fits in the small string buffer (SSO, 15 chars in libstdc++), so the characters live inside `s` itself.
- The move constructor copies those characters into `t`'s own inline buffer and makes `s` an empty string. `p` still points into `s`, which now holds `""`.
- No crash and ASan is silent here because `s` is alive; the bug is a wrong value. With a 100-character string libstdc++ transfers the heap buffer and `p == t.data()` is `true`, but [string.require] allows invalidation, so neither case is something to rely on.
- **Key Concept:** Do not hold pointers or `string_view`s into a string across a move of that string.
- Deep dive: Topic 3, Value Categories, std::move and Moved-From State

practice_tasks.answer: Compile error: use of deleted function 'Msg::Msg(Msg&&)' (both return statements)
practice_tasks.explanation:
- The returned names are treated as rvalues. Overload resolution picks the best match for an rvalue, which is the move constructor, deleted or not. Selecting a deleted function is ill-formed; there is no second attempt with the copy constructor.
- If `Msg(Msg&&)` were simply not declared, the copy constructor would be chosen and the program would print `copy`.
- Compiler note: GCC 11 with `-std=c++17` accepts this and prints `copy`; Clang rejects it in every mode, GCC rejects it in C++20.

practice_tasks.title: Question 9
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
+A +B +C -C -B | +A +B +C -A -C -B
```

**Explanation:**
- Early return: locals are destroyed in reverse order: `c` (prints `-C`), then `b` (its destructor deletes B, prints `-B`). The raw pointer `a` is destroyed too, but destroying a raw pointer does nothing: A leaks.
- Normal path: `delete a` runs as a statement (`-A`), then the locals are destroyed at the closing brace (`-C -B`).
- ASan/LeakSanitizer reports one leaked `Resource` from the first call.
- **Key Concept:** Scope exit destroys owners, not pointees; only objects owned by an RAII object are safe on every path.
- Deep dive: Topic 5, RAII and Exception Safety

practice_tasks.title: Question 10
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
working
terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::runtime_error'
  what():  disk full
(then SIGABRT, exit status 134; ~Guard is NOT printed)
```

**Explanation:**
- No handler exists anywhere, so `std::terminate` is called.
- The standard makes stack unwinding in this case **implementation-defined**. GCC/libstdc++ does not unwind, so `~Guard` never runs.
- Adding `try { work(); } catch (const std::exception&) {}` in `main` changes the output to `working`, `~Guard`, `after work`.
- `std::endl` is used because `abort` does not flush `std::cout`; with `'\n'` and redirected output, even `working` could be lost.
- **Key Concept:** RAII cleanup during exceptions is only guaranteed when the exception is caught; put a top-level handler in `main` and in every thread function.
- Deep dive: Topic 5, RAII and Exception Safety

**Answer:**
```
unique holds null
shared holds null
shared deleter called with null
```

**Explanation:**
- `fopen` fails and returns `nullptr` in both cases.

practice_tasks.title: Question 12
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Undefined behaviour: new[] released with scalar delete.
Observed (GCC 11, glibc, stdout on a terminal):
processing
~Sample
munmap_chunk(): invalid pointer      (then SIGABRT)
ASan: attempting free on address which was not malloc()-ed (bad-free).
```

**Explanation:**
- `unique_ptr<Sample>` uses `default_delete<Sample>`, which calls `delete p`. The memory came from `new Sample[3]`.
- For a type with a non-trivial destructor, `new[]` stores the element count in a cookie just before the array, and hands out an address after it. Scalar `delete` runs one destructor (only one `~Sample` line) and passes that interior address to the allocator, which is why glibc and ASan both say the pointer was never allocated.
- With a trivially destructible type (`unique_ptr<int>(new int[10])`) there is no cookie; ASan then reports `alloc-dealloc-mismatch (operator new [] vs operator delete)` and plain glibc happens to run silently. Still UB.
- Fix: `std::unique_ptr<Sample[]> batch(new Sample[3]);`, or `auto batch = std::make_unique<Sample[]>(3);` (then `batch[0].v[0] = 1.0;` and three `~Sample` lines), or simply `std::vector<Sample> batch(3);`.
- **Key Concept:** `unique_ptr<T>` and `unique_ptr<T[]>` choose `delete` vs `delete[]`; the type must match how the memory was allocated.
- Deep dive: Topic 6, std::unique_ptr

practice_tasks.title: Question 13
practice_tasks.answer:
Prints "1 1", then the Session is destroyed twice (UB).
Observed (GCC 11, glibc): "~Session 1", then "~Session <garbage>" (the second destructor reads
freed memory), then "free(): double free detected in tcache 2" and abort.
ASan stops at the second destructor: "heap-use-after-free" while reading id.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- Each constructor that takes a raw pointer allocates a new control block. Two blocks, each with count 1, each believing it is the only owner.
- At the end of `main`, `observer` destroys the object, then `owner` runs the destructor again on freed memory and frees it a second time.
- There is no global table mapping object addresses to control blocks; a `shared_ptr` cannot discover that another one already owns `raw`.
- **Key Concept:** A raw pointer becomes owned once; further owners must be copies of a `shared_ptr`.
- Deep dive: Topic 7, std::shared_ptr Internals and make_shared

practice_tasks.title: Question 15
practice_tasks.answer:
Not race-free: undefined behaviour.
Observed at -O0: "pure virtual method called", "terminate called without an active exception",
abort (the reader called into a control block that the writer had already destroyed).
Other runs print "reader done" normally. ThreadSanitizer reports "data race" between the
copy (reader) and the assignment (writer) of g_cfg.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- Both threads touch the **same** `shared_ptr` object `g_cfg`, and the writer modifies it. The atomic count protects copies of each other, not one handle shared by two threads.
- A copy reads the two pointers and then increments the count; the writer can drop the last reference in between, so the reader may increment a freed control block.
- **Key Concept:** Concurrent read and write of one `shared_ptr` variable needs a mutex or `std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>>`.
- Deep dive: Topic 8, shared_ptr and Thread Safety

practice_tasks.title: Question 16
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Usually prints "42 or 43", but the program has a data race on `data`:
the second assignment is not ordered with the consumer's read. TSan reports "data race".
```

**Explanation:**
- First write: sequenced before the release store, so it happens-before the consumer's read. No race.
- Second write: happens after the release store; nothing orders it with the consumer's read, so a write and a read of the same `shared_ptr` object are concurrent: a race, with the same use-after-free risk as Q1.
- The write-once flag pattern is one-shot publication. For repeated updates, use `std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>>` or a mutex.
- **Key Concept:** Release/acquire orders the accesses it brackets; any later write to the handle is unordered again.
- Deep dive: Topic 8, shared_ptr and Thread Safety

practice_tasks.answer: Prints far less than 40000 (varies; observed 16476 and 17657). No data race (TSan clean): it is a lost update.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- Each access is protected, but the read-modify-write spans two critical sections. Two threads can `get()` the same version, each build `qty + 1`, and the second `set()` overwrites the first.
- Fix: do the whole read-copy-publish under one lock (writers serialize; readers still only lock for the copy), or use `atomic<shared_ptr>` with a `compare_exchange_weak` loop (theory, Example 5).
- **Key Concept:** Protecting each access is not protecting the operation; the invariant "every fill is counted" needs one atomic step.
- Deep dive: Topic 8, shared_ptr and Thread Safety

practice_tasks.title: Question 19
practice_tasks.answer:
~Button, then undefined behaviour when handler() runs: it uses the destroyed local 'button'.
At -O0 it happened to print "ok" from stale memory; ASan: stack-use-after-scope.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `[&button]` captures a reference to the local `shared_ptr` variable, not ownership. The variable dies at the closing brace (and with it the `Button`, which prints `~Button`).
- `handler()` then reads a dead stack object and dereferences whatever pointer it finds there.
- It does avoid the cycle, but by trading a leak for a use-after-free.
- **Key Concept:** To avoid a cycle without dangling, capture a `weak_ptr` by value and `lock()` it.
- Deep dive: Topic 9, weak_ptr, Reference Cycles and enable_shared_from_this

practice_tasks.title: Question 20
practice_tasks.answer:
Undefined behaviour. With GCC + glibc: "~Order 0" (one destructor), then abort with
"munmap_chunk(): invalid pointer". ASan: "attempting free on address which was not malloc()-ed".
GCC 11 also warns: 'operator delete' called on pointer with nonzero offset 8 [-Wfree-nonheap-object].
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `new Order[3]` stores the element count in an 8-byte cookie before the array (Itanium ABI) and returns a pointer just past it.
- Plain `delete` thinks it has one object: it runs one destructor and hands the cookie-shifted address to `operator delete`, which is not the start of any allocation.
- For a trivially destructible type (`new int[3]`) there is no cookie and it may appear to work; ASan still reports `alloc-dealloc-mismatch`.
- **Key Concept:** `new[]` pairs only with `delete[]`; better, use `std::vector` or `std::unique_ptr<T[]>`.
- Deep dive: Topic 10, new/delete, Placement New and Object Storage

practice_tasks.title: Question 23
practice_tasks.answer:
Undefined behaviour: v's elements live in memory owned by arena, which was destroyed when load() returned.
Here (g++ -O0) it crashed with a segmentation fault; ASan reports heap-use-after-free on v[99].
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `return v;` moves the vector out. A moved pmr vector keeps the source's resource, so the returned vector still points into the arena's chunks and still holds `&arena`.
- `arena` is a local: its destructor calls `release()`, returning every chunk to the heap. `v[99]` then reads freed memory, and `v`'s destructor later calls `deallocate` on a destroyed resource.
- The container never owns its resource; it stores a raw pointer.
- **Key Concept:** A pmr object must not outlive its memory resource; never return a container built on a local resource.
- Deep dive: Topic 11, Memory Pools and Polymorphic Allocators (PMR)

practice_tasks.title: Question 24
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
24 16 72 8
```

**Explanation:**
- `Trade`: `side`@0, 7 bytes padding, `px`@8, `flag`@16, 7 bytes tail padding → 24 (a multiple of the alignment 8).
- `Trade2`: `px`@0, `side`@8, `flag`@9, 6 bytes tail padding → 16.
- An array has no extra padding: `3 * 24 = 72`.
- Alignment is the strictest member's: `double` → 8.
- **Key Concept:** Ordering members by decreasing alignment removed 8 of 24 bytes (one third).
- Deep dive: Topic 12, Alignment, Padding and Data Layout

practice_tasks.title: Question 25
practice_tasks.answer: Compile error: cannot bind packed field 'h.Header::length' to 'uint32_t&' {aka 'unsigned int&'}
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `length` sits at offset 1. A `std::uint32_t&` promises a 4-aligned object, which a packed member cannot guarantee, so GCC refuses (taking `&h.length` only warns with `-Waddress-of-packed-member`).
- With `#pragma pack(push, 1)` instead of the attribute, GCC 11 compiled the same code silently: the danger is still there, only the diagnostic is missing.
- Compiler-specific: Clang 14 compiles this exact program (attribute version) without any diagnostic, even with `-Wall -Wextra`, and prints 101. Only GCC rejects it.
- Fix: copy out, modify, copy back: `auto n = h.length; bump(n); h.length = n;`.
- **Key Concept:** References and pointers to packed members are misaligned pointers in disguise.
- Deep dive: Topic 12, Alignment, Padding and Data Layout

quick_reference.content:
#### Object Lifetime and Storage Duration
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Lifetime vs storage? | Storage is memory; lifetime is when the object exists in it |
| Four storage durations? | Automatic, static, thread, dynamic |
| When does a temporary die? | End of the full-expression, unless bound directly to a local reference |
| Temp in `return` of `const T& f()`? | Dies inside `f`; caller gets a dangling reference |
| Does `join()` fix `&local` of the thread? | No; the local died when the function returned |
| Move vs reset on optional? | Move: alive, unspecified; reset: destroyed |
| Member init order? | Declaration order |
| Static init order across files? | Unspecified: use function-local statics or `constinit` |
| Are function-local statics thread-safe? | Initialization yes (C++11), use no |
| Where does `volatile` store a variable? | Wherever its storage duration says; `volatile` only affects accesses |
| Range-for over `temp().member_ref()`? | Dangles before C++23 (P2718 fixes) |

#### Special Member Functions and the Rule of 0/3/5
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Rule of 3? | Destructor, copy ctor, copy assign: need one, need all three |
| Rule of 5? | Rule of 3 plus move ctor and move assign, because the three suppress implicit moves |
| Rule of 0? | Own resources through RAII members and write none of them |
| `Buffer b = a;` with raw pointer, no copy ctor? | Shallow copy, then double delete (UB) |
| `b = a;` with no copy assign? | Old array leaked plus double delete later |
| Dtor + copy ctor + move ctor, then `b = a`? | Compile error: copy assignment deleted |
| Why null the source in a move? | The source's destructor still runs |
| Why `noexcept` on moves? | `vector` growth moves only if the move cannot throw (else copies) |
| Copy-and-swap gives? | Strong guarantee, self-assignment safety, single cleanup path |
| `const` member effect? | Assignment deleted; construction fine |
| fd owner class? | Move-only: delete copies, `noexcept` move with `-1` sentinel |
| Polymorphic base? | Virtual dtor plus the five `= default` (copy often protected) |

#### Value Categories, std::move and Moved-From State
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What does `std::move` do? | `static_cast<T&&>`: makes an xvalue; moves nothing |
| What category is `std::move(x)`? | xvalue (not prvalue) |
| Is a `T&&` parameter an rvalue inside the function? | No, a named variable is an lvalue |
| `std::move` on const? | `const T&&` → copy constructor |
| Moved-from object? | Alive; valid but unspecified; destroy or assign it |
| Moved-from `optional`? | Still engaged |
| Pointer into moved `unique_ptr`'s object? | Still valid |
| Pointer into moved `std::string`? | Not guaranteed (SSO makes it fail in practice) |
| Deleted move ctor? | No fallback to copy: compile error |
| `move_if_noexcept`? | `T&&` if nothrow-movable or not copyable, else `const T&` |
| Ref-qualifiers? | Overload members on `*this` being lvalue (`&`) or rvalue (`&&`) |

#### Copy Elision, RVO and NRVO
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Is RVO guaranteed? | Prvalue elision is guaranteed since C++17; NRVO is not |
| What if NRVO doesn't happen? | Implicit move; copy only if no move constructor is declared |
| Deleted move ctor on `return local;`? | Ill-formed, no fallback to copy |
| Should I `return std::move(local)`? | No: it disables NRVO |
| When is `std::move` in return correct? | Members, structured bindings, sub-objects |
| Can I return a `std::mutex`-like type? | Yes as a prvalue (C++17), never by name |
| Is a parameter NRVO'd? | No, moved |
| Does `x = f()` elide? | No: temporary + move assignment |
| Can elision change output? | Yes, explicitly allowed |
| Sink parameter cost? | lvalue: copy+move; rvalue: move(+move); one extra move vs overloads |
| C++23 change? | Returned local names are xvalues (P2266) |

#### RAII and Exception Safety
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What is RAII? | Acquire in constructor, release in destructor; lifetime equals ownership |
| Only memory? | No: locks, files, sockets, threads, any handle |
| Why does raw `new` leak on throw? | The pointer dies during unwinding, the pointee has no owner |
| Destructors guaranteed on throw? | Only if the exception is caught |
| Constructor throws? | Its destructor never runs; finished members are destroyed |
| Can a destructor throw? | Implicitly `noexcept`: `terminate` |
| `close()` can fail? | Explicit `close()` that reports, destructor swallows |
| Basic vs strong? | Basic: valid but maybe changed; strong: unchanged |
| How to get strong? | Throwing work first, commit with no-throw operations |
| Two objects own one fd? | Double close, and the second close can hit a reused fd |
| Scope guard? | RAII for an ad hoc action; dismiss at the commit point |
| `lock_guard` on throw? | Its destructor unlocks the mutex during unwinding |

#### std::unique_ptr
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What does `std::move(p1)` move? | Nothing; it is a cast. The move constructor transfers the pointer |
| State of `p1` after move? | Guaranteed null |
| Destruction order of `p1`, `p2`? | `p2` first (deletes), then `p1` (empty) |
| Why `unique_ptr` over `shared_ptr` for one owner? | Expresses intent; one pointer, no control block, no atomic counts, cheap move |
| Is the deleter part of the type? | Yes (`shared_ptr`: no, type-erased) |
| Deleter called on null? | Never (for `unique_ptr`) |
| `reset(q)` order? | Store `q`, then delete old |
| Why `make_unique` in C++17? | No naked `new`, type once; the argument-interleaving leak was fixed by C++17 |
| `unique_ptr<int[]>` vs `unique_ptr<int>`? | `delete[]` vs `delete`; mixing is UB |
| How to pass? | `T&`/`T*` to use, by value to sink, `unique_ptr&` to reseat |
| Pimpl needs what? | Out-of-line destructor, constructors and move operations where `Impl` is complete |
| Thread-safe? | Like a raw pointer: distinct objects yes, one object shared with writers no |

#### std::shared_ptr Internals and make_shared
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What is in a `shared_ptr`? | Stored pointer + control-block pointer (16 bytes typical) |
| What is in the control block? | Strong and weak counts, deleter, allocator, the object (make_shared) |
| Copy vs move cost? | Copy: atomic increment; move: no atomic |
| When is the object destroyed? | Strong count 0 |
| When is the control block freed? | Weak count 0 too |
| Main `make_shared` benefit? | One allocation instead of two |
| `make_shared` downsides? | No deleter, needs public ctor, parentheses init, weak_ptr retains memory |
| Is the deleter part of the type? | No (type-erased); for `unique_ptr` it is |
| `shared_ptr<Base>` from `make_shared<Derived>`, no virtual dtor? | Correct `~Derived` runs |
| Aliasing constructor? | Shares ownership, stores a different pointer |
| Does `get()` extend lifetime? | No |
| How to pass to a function that only uses the object? | `T&` or `T*`, not `shared_ptr` |

#### shared_ptr and Thread Safety
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Is `shared_ptr` thread-safe? | Control block yes; same handle with a writer no; object never |
| Two threads reset two copies? | Safe |
| One thread copies `g`, another reassigns `g`? | Data race; mutex or `atomic<shared_ptr>` |
| What does `atomic<shared_ptr>` protect? | The handle (load/store/CAS), not the object |
| Is it lock-free? | Not guaranteed; libstdc++ and MSVC use a lock bit |
| Release/acquire flag + plain `shared_ptr`? | Safe for one write before publication; racy if rewritten |
| Copy-on-write with two writers? | Lost update; serialize writers or CAS loop |
| Why is `shared_ptr` slow under threads? | Atomic RMW on a shared cache line per copy |
| Which thread runs the destructor? | The one that drops the last reference |
| Is `use_count()` reliable? | Only as a hint; `unique()` was removed in C++20 |

#### weak_ptr, Reference Cycles and enable_shared_from_this
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What does `weak_ptr` keep alive? | The control block, never the object |
| Reference cycle: deadlock or leak? | Leak: counts never reach 0, destructors never run |
| How to access through a `weak_ptr`? | `if (auto sp = w.lock())` |
| Why not `expired()` then `lock()`? | Race between the two calls |
| Why does `weak_ptr` have no `->`? | Access without ownership could hit a dead object |
| `lock()` on expired? | Empty `shared_ptr`, no exception |
| Why `enable_shared_from_this`? | `shared_ptr(this)` would create a second control block |
| `shared_from_this()` in constructor? | Throws `bad_weak_ptr` (C++17) |
| Capture in a stored callback? | `weak_ptr`; strong `self` only for external one-shot work |
| `weak_ptr` as a map key? | `std::owner_less<>` comparator |
| Raw pointer always bad? | No: fine for non-owning access with a guaranteed lifetime |
| `shared_ptr` refcount too hot? | Rethink ownership: single owner + observers, pools, explicit reclamation; measure |

#### new/delete, Placement New and Object Storage
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| `new` vs `operator new`? | Expression = allocate + construct; function = bytes only |
| Why `delete[]`? | Cookie and destructor count; mismatch is UB |
| Does `new` return null? | No, throws `bad_alloc` (except `nothrow`) |
| Constructor throws in `new`? | Memory freed automatically, no destructor |
| Does placement new allocate? | No; it constructs in your storage |
| Clean up placement new? | `std::destroy_at(p)`; never `delete p` |
| Same storage, new object: same object? | No, a new lifetime |
| What is `std::launder` for? | Getting a usable pointer to a new object in reused storage |
| Cast recv buffer to struct? | Use `memcpy` / `bit_cast` / C++23 `start_lifetime_as`; mind alignment and endianness |
| Is `malloc` slow? | Usually a fast tcache pop; the problem is unpredictable slow paths (tail latency) |
| RSS grows but no leak? | Retention: heap top pinned, capacity kept, unbounded queues, caches, arenas |
| `destroy_at` / `construct_at`? | C++17 / C++20 |

#### Memory Pools and Polymorphic Allocators (PMR)
- "A pool trades generality for predictability: bounded hot-path work, no surprise page faults, bounded memory."
- "Storage exists is not object exists: construct on acquire, destroy on release, keep the storage."
- "A bounded pool needs an exhaustion policy, and that decision matters more than the free list."
- "PMR separates what a container stores from where its memory comes from, at run time, without changing the type."
- "Monotonic: bump allocation, no individual free, release everything together; perfect when lifetimes are grouped."
- "Pool resources reuse freed blocks per size class; synchronized for sharing, unsynchronized for one thread."
- "Use `null_memory_resource()` upstream if the buffer must be a hard bound."
- "pmr::vector of std::string leaks out of the arena; use pmr types all the way down."
- "Copying a pmr container goes to the default resource; pass the resource explicitly."
- "The resource must outlive every container that uses it: declare it first."

#### Alignment, Padding and Data Layout
- "Members go at multiples of their alignment; the struct's size is rounded to a multiple of its alignment so arrays stay aligned."
- "Alignment is not size: `alignof`, not `sizeof`, decides valid addresses."
- "Sort members by decreasing alignment to cut padding, unless hot/cold grouping or ABI says otherwise."
- "`alignas` only raises alignment; packing lowers it and makes members misaligned."
- "Misaligned access is UB even if x86 tolerates it; copy bytes out with `memcpy`."
- "Padding bytes are unspecified: never `memcmp` or hash a padded struct."
- "Empty members cost a byte plus padding; use a base or `[[no_unique_address]]`."
- "Adjacent bit-fields are one memory location: two threads writing different fields is a data race."
- "`alignas(64)` separates hot variables written by different threads: false sharing is a layout bug."
