subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- Keep four ideas apart; interviewers probe exactly where people blur them:
  - **Storage**: a region of memory that can hold an object (stack slot, heap block, static data, a `std::byte` buffer).
  - **Storage duration**: the rule that says how long the *storage* stays reserved (automatic, static, thread, dynamic).
  - **Lifetime**: the period during which the *object* exists: it starts when initialization completes and ends when its destructor starts (or the storage is released or reused).
  - **Scope**: a compile-time property of a *name* (where it can be used). A `static` local has block scope but program-long lifetime.
- Storage can outlive the object: after `std::optional::reset()`, `std::vector::pop_back()` or an explicit destructor call, the bytes are still there but the object is gone. Using it is undefined behaviour even if the memory "still has the right value".
- A moved-from object is still **alive** (valid but unspecified state, topic 03). A destroyed object is **dead**. Moving does not end lifetime; destruction does.
- Precise vocabulary to use in an interview:
  - "The object's lifetime ended" (destructor ran).
  - "The storage was deallocated" (memory returned to the allocator).
  - "The resource was released" (file closed, heap buffer freed by the owner).
- Every dangling reference, pointer, view or iterator bug is the same bug: a non-owning handle used after the lifetime of the object it refers to ended.

subsections.title: 2. The four storage durations
subsections.content:
| Storage duration | Declared by | Storage obtained | Storage released | Typical implementation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Automatic | Block-scope variable without `static`/`thread_local`/`extern`, parameters | On entry to the block (frame setup) | On exit from the block | Stack slot or register |
| Static | Namespace scope variables, `static` locals, `static` data members | Program start | Program end | `.data` / `.bss` / `.rodata` |
| Thread | `thread_local` | Thread start | Thread end | Per-thread TLS block |
| Dynamic | `new` expression, allocation functions | `operator new` / allocator call | `operator delete` | Heap (free store) |

- Sub-objects (members, base classes, array elements) have the storage duration of the complete object that contains them.
- Temporaries are not a storage duration: a temporary lives until the end of the **full-expression** that created it, unless its lifetime is extended (section 5).
- `int* p = new int(5);` involves two storage durations: `p` itself is automatic, `*p` is dynamic. When `p` goes out of scope the `int` is leaked, not destroyed.
- `std::unique_ptr<int> up = std::make_unique<int>(9);`: the `unique_ptr` object is automatic, the owned `int` is dynamic; the owner's destructor ends the pointee's lifetime (topic 06).

subsections.title: 3. Where things typically live (process layout)
subsections.content:
- The C++ standard defines storage durations, not segments. The layout below is the usual Linux/ELF picture and is implementation behaviour.
```
High addresses
+------------------------------+
| stack (main thread)          |  locals, parameters, return addresses; grows down
| ... thread stacks, mmap,     |  each std::thread gets its own stack (mmap'd)
|     shared libraries, TLS    |  static TLS blocks, large malloc blocks
| heap (brk)                   |  small new/malloc; grows up
| .bss                         |  zero-initialized statics: no bytes in the file
| .data                        |  statics with a non-zero initial value
| .rodata                      |  string literals, many const globals
| .text                        |  machine code
+------------------------------+
Low addresses
```

| Declaration | Storage duration | Typical area |
|---|---|---|
| `int g = 10;` (namespace scope) | Static | `.data` |
| `int g;` (namespace scope) | Static | `.bss` (zero-initialized) |
| `static int s = 10;` (in a function) | Static | `.data` |
| `const int c = 20;` (namespace scope) | Static | `.rodata` or folded away |
| `"hello"` | Static | `.rodata` |
| `int x = 40;` (local) | Automatic | Stack, or only a register |
| `volatile int v = 70;` (local) | Automatic | Stack (`volatile` does not change storage) |
| `new int(80)` | Dynamic | Heap |
| `thread_local int t = 30;` | Thread | Per-thread TLS block |
| function bodies | n/a | `.text` |

- "Local = stack" and "new = heap" are implementation mental models, not guarantees:
  - A local may live only in a register, or be optimized away entirely.
  - Since C++14 the compiler may elide or merge `new`/`delete` pairs (allocation elision), so a `make_unique` may never reach `malloc`.
- Implementation numbers worth knowing (Linux, glibc): main thread stack 8 MB by default (`ulimit -s`), `std::thread` stacks 8 MB of reserved virtual memory each, large `malloc` requests (128 KiB and up by default) go to `mmap` rather than the brk heap.

subsections.title: 4. When lifetime starts and ends
subsections.content:
- **Starts**: when storage is obtained **and** initialization is complete. For a class with a constructor, the object is not "alive" until the constructor finishes. If the constructor throws, the object never existed: its destructor does not run, but fully constructed members and bases are destroyed (topic 05).
- **Ends**:
  - For a class type with a non-trivial destructor: when the destructor call **starts**.
  - Otherwise: when the storage is released or reused.
- During construction and destruction the object is partly alive: members are constructed in declaration order and destroyed in reverse order; virtual calls inside constructors and destructors do not dispatch to more derived classes.
- After lifetime ends, using the object through any old pointer, reference, view or iterator is UB, even if:
  - the memory was not freed (`optional::reset`, `pop_back`, explicit destructor call), or
  - the bytes still contain the old value (very common: the bug "works" in tests).
- Reusing storage with placement new and the rules for pointers to the old object (`std::launder`) are topic 10.

subsections.title: 5. Temporaries and lifetime extension
subsections.content:
- A temporary is destroyed at the end of the full-expression (roughly: at the `;`), in reverse order of creation.
- **Lifetime extension**: binding a temporary (a prvalue, possibly through member access) **directly** to a `const T&` or `T&&` local reference extends the temporary's lifetime to the lifetime of the reference.
- It works through:
  - Plain binding: `const std::string& r = make_string();`
  - Member access on a prvalue: `const auto& levels = make_book().levels;` (the whole `Book` temporary is extended).
  - A conditional of two prvalues: `const T& r = c ? T(1) : T(2);`
  - Brace aggregate initialization of a reference member: `RefAgg a{T(7)};`
  - Array subscript on an array prvalue, casts that preserve the object (`static_cast<const T&>(T{})`).
- It does **not** work (verified with a tracing type, GCC 11):

| Code | Temporary destroyed | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `const T& r = id(T(4));` (function returning its `const T&` argument) | End of full-expression | Dangling |
| `T&& r = std::move(T(5));` | End of full-expression | Dangling: `std::move` returns a reference, not a prvalue |
| `const T& r = T(6).self();` (member returning `*this`) | End of full-expression | Dangling |
| `const std::string& r = get();` where `get` does `return create();` | Inside `get`, at the end of its `return` statement | Dangling (C++26 P2748: ill-formed) |
| `RefAgg a(T(8));` (C++20 parenthesized aggregate init) | End of full-expression | Dangling (brace form extends) |
| `new RefAgg{T(9)}` | End of full-expression | Dangling member |
| `H() : r(T{1}) {}` (reference member in mem-initializer) | When the constructor exits | Ill-formed since C++14; GCC 11 only warns (`-Wextra`), Clang errors |
| `std::string_view sv = std::string("abc");` | End of full-expression | Dangling: a view is not a reference |
| `for (int x : make_book().get())` (before C++23) | Before the loop body runs | Dangling (section 6) |

- Rule: extension only happens when the reference is bound to the temporary itself (or a sub-object of it) in the same declaration. It never passes through a function call that returns a reference, because the compiler cannot know what that reference refers to.
- Extension applies to the reference's lifetime: extending a temporary into a `static const T&` gives it static lifetime; into a function parameter it lasts only until the end of the call's full-expression.

subsections.title: 6. The range-for temporary trap and the C++23 fix
7. Order of construction and destruction
subsections.content:
| Context | Construction order | Destruction order |
|---|---|---|
| Local variables in a block | Order of declaration | Reverse, at block exit (also during stack unwinding) |
| Class: bases and members | Virtual bases, then direct bases left to right, then members in **declaration order** | Exact reverse: members bottom-up, then bases |
| Member initializer list | Ignored for ordering (GCC `-Wreorder` warns) | n/a |
| Array elements | Index 0 upward | Highest index first |
| Temporaries in a full-expression | Order of evaluation | Reverse order of creation, at the end of the full-expression |
| Statics in one translation unit | Order of definition | Reverse order of completed construction, after `main` returns or `exit` |
| Function-local `static` | First time control passes the declaration | Reverse order of completed construction, mixed with globals |
| `thread_local` | Before first use in that thread (implementation: lazily on first odr-use for dynamic initialization) | At thread exit (before `join()` returns); the main thread's at `exit`, before statics |

- Consequence of declaration-order member construction: an initializer that reads another member must refer only to members declared **earlier**. Reading a later member reads an indeterminate value (UB for scalars).
- Destruction order is what makes RAII composable: a member that depends on another member must be declared after it, so it is destroyed first (e.g. a worker thread member declared after the queue it uses).
- `std::exit` runs static destructors; `std::quick_exit` and `std::_Exit` do not; `std::abort` and `std::terminate` do not.

subsections.title: 8. Static initialization and the static initialization order fiasco
subsections.content:
- Statics are initialized in phases:
  1. **Zero-initialization**: all static and thread storage starts as zero (that is why `.bss` costs nothing in the file).
  2. **Constant initialization**: if the initializer is a constant expression, the value is baked into the binary. No code runs, no ordering problem.
  3. **Dynamic initialization**: anything else (calls a non-constexpr function, a constructor that is not constexpr). Runs before `main` in practice.
- Within one translation unit, dynamic initialization follows definition order. Across translation units the order is **unspecified**: in practice it follows link order, which nobody controls deliberately.
- **Static initialization order fiasco (SIOF)**: a static in `a.cpp` whose dynamic initializer reads a static from `b.cpp` that has not been initialized yet; it sees the zero-initialized value (or, for class types, an object whose lifetime has not started: UB).
- Fixes:
  - **Function-local static (Meyers singleton)**: `Config& config() { static Config c = load(); return c; }`. Initialized on first call, so any user triggers it in time.
  - **`constexpr` / `constinit` (C++20)**: guarantees constant initialization, so there is no dynamic phase to order. `constinit` does not imply `const`: the variable can still be modified at run time. If the initializer is not a constant expression, compilation fails ("`constinit` variable does not have a constant initializer").
  - Avoid cross-TU dependencies between globals entirely: pass dependencies explicitly.
- **Destruction order fiasco** (the mirror image): a static's destructor uses another static that was constructed later (so destroyed earlier). Typical: a global object logs in its destructor through a logger singleton that is already gone. Fixes: make the dependency a function-local static accessed during construction (guaranteeing it is constructed first, destroyed last), or intentionally leak it: `static Logger& l = *new Logger;` (never destroyed).
- `std::mutex` has a `constexpr` constructor, so a global mutex is constant-initialized and safe to use from other static initializers.

subsections.title: 9. Magic statics (thread-safe function-local statics)
subsections.content:
- Since C++11, if several threads reach a function-local static's declaration concurrently, exactly one initializes it; the others block until initialization finishes.
- Implementation (Itanium ABI, GCC/Clang): a guard variable checked with an acquire load on every call (fast path: one load and a branch); the slow path calls `__cxa_guard_acquire`/`__cxa_guard_release`.
- If the initializer throws, the static is not considered initialized; the next caller tries again.
- Recursive initialization (the initializer calls the same function again) is UB; GCC throws `__gnu_cxx::recursive_init_error` or deadlocks.
- Only the **initialization** is thread-safe. Later reads and writes to the object need their own synchronization.
- GCC flag `-fno-threadsafe-statics` removes the guard (only for code that is known to be single-threaded).

subsections.title: 10. thread_local: one object per thread
subsections.content:
- Each thread has its own instance; `&tls` differs per thread.
- Initialization:
  - Constant initializer: present from thread start (copied from a TLS template image).
  - Dynamic initializer: guaranteed to happen before the first odr-use in that thread. GCC/Clang initialize namespace-scope `thread_local` lazily through a wrapper function, so a thread that never touches it never constructs it.
- Destruction: at thread exit, in reverse order of construction, before the thread's `join()` returns. For the main thread, at `exit`, before static objects are destroyed.
- Cost: access is a segment-register-relative load (`%fs` on x86-64 Linux) for the executable; in shared libraries it may go through `__tls_get_addr`. Dynamic initialization adds a "initialized yet?" check on each access through the wrapper.
- Lifetime trap: a pointer to a `thread_local` handed to another thread dangles after the owning thread exits.
- A `thread_local` inside a function is also implicitly `static` storage-wise (one per thread, not per call).

subsections.title: 11. `volatile` is not a storage class and not synchronization
subsections.content:
- `volatile` qualifies **accesses**: each read and write of a volatile object is an observable side effect that the compiler must perform and keep in order relative to other volatile accesses.
- It says nothing about **where** the object lives: a `volatile` local is still automatic (typically stack), a `static volatile` is still static storage.
- It does not "force the variable into RAM instead of a register" as a language rule, and it gives **no** atomicity or inter-thread ordering: a data race on a `volatile int` is still UB. Use `std::atomic` for threads.
- Legitimate uses: memory-mapped I/O registers (`*reinterpret_cast<volatile std::uint32_t*>(0x40000000)`: the platform's memory map puts the device there, not `volatile`), signal handlers with `volatile std::sig_atomic_t`, and benchmarks preventing dead-code elimination.
- C++20 deprecated `++`, `--` and compound assignment on volatile objects (`v++`, `v += 1`) because they look atomic but are not; C++23 un-deprecated the bitwise compound forms (`|=`, `&=`, `^=`) used in MMIO code.

subsections.title: 12. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "The temporary returned through a reference is destroyed back in the caller." ✅ A temporary created in a `return` statement of a function returning a reference dies at the end of that `return` statement, inside the callee; the caller receives a dangling reference.
- ❌ "Binding to `const&` always extends lifetime." ✅ Only when binding directly to the prvalue (or its member); not through function calls, `std::move`, views or mem-initializers.
- ❌ "`join()` makes it safe to use a pointer to the thread's local." ✅ The local died when `worker` returned; `join()` only waits for that.
- ❌ "Moving from an object ends its lifetime." ✅ It changes its state; only destruction (`reset`, scope exit, `delete`) ends lifetime.
- ❌ "Static objects are destroyed in declaration order." ✅ Reverse order of completed construction.
- ❌ "Members are initialized in the order of the initializer list." ✅ Declaration order.
- ❌ "`constinit` means `const`." ✅ It only means "statically initialized"; the variable is mutable.
- ❌ "Function-local statics are thread-safe." ✅ Their initialization is; their use is not.
- ❌ "`volatile` puts a variable in RAM / static memory / makes it thread-safe." ✅ None of those.
- ❌ "Local = stack, new = heap, always." ✅ Implementation model: registers, optimized-away locals and elided allocations are allowed.
- ❌ "If the memory still holds the old value, using the object is fine." ✅ Lifetime ended means UB, regardless of the bytes.

- Storage can outlive the object: after `std::optional::reset()`, `std::vector::pop_back()` or an explicit destructor call, the bytes are still there but the object is gone. Using it is undefined behaviour even if the memory "still has the right value".
- A moved-from object is still **alive** (valid but unspecified state, topic 03). A destroyed object is **dead**. Moving does not end lifetime; destruction does.
- Precise vocabulary to use in an interview:
  - "The object's lifetime ended" (destructor ran).
  - "The storage was deallocated" (memory returned to the allocator).
  - "The resource was released" (file closed, heap buffer freed by the owner).
- Every dangling reference, pointer, view or iterator bug is the same bug: a non-owning handle used after the lifetime of the object it refers to ended.

#### 2. The four storage durations
| Storage duration | Declared by | Storage obtained | Storage released | Typical implementation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Automatic | Block-scope variable without `static`/`thread_local`/`extern`, parameters | On entry to the block (frame setup) | On exit from the block | Stack slot or register |
| Static | Namespace scope variables, `static` locals, `static` data members | Program start | Program end | `.data` / `.bss` / `.rodata` |
| Thread | `thread_local` | Thread start | Thread end | Per-thread TLS block |
| Dynamic | `new` expression, allocation functions | `operator new` / allocator call | `operator delete` | Heap (free store) |

- Sub-objects (members, base classes, array elements) have the storage duration of the complete object that contains them.
- Temporaries are not a storage duration: a temporary lives until the end of the **full-expression** that created it, unless its lifetime is extended (section 5).
- `int* p = new int(5);` involves two storage durations: `p` itself is automatic, `*p` is dynamic. When `p` goes out of scope the `int` is leaked, not destroyed.
- `std::unique_ptr<int> up = std::make_unique<int>(9);`: the `unique_ptr` object is automatic, the owned `int` is dynamic; the owner's destructor ends the pointee's lifetime (topic 06).

#### 3. Where things typically live (process layout)
- The C++ standard defines storage durations, not segments. The layout below is the usual Linux/ELF picture and is implementation behaviour.
```
High addresses
+------------------------------+
| stack (main thread)          |  locals, parameters, return addresses; grows down
| ... thread stacks, mmap,     |  each std::thread gets its own stack (mmap'd)
|     shared libraries, TLS    |  static TLS blocks, large malloc blocks
| heap (brk)                   |  small new/malloc; grows up
| .bss                         |  zero-initialized statics: no bytes in the file
| .data                        |  statics with a non-zero initial value
| .rodata                      |  string literals, many const globals
| .text                        |  machine code
+------------------------------+
Low addresses
```

| Declaration | Storage duration | Typical area |
|---|---|---|
| `int g = 10;` (namespace scope) | Static | `.data` |
| `int g;` (namespace scope) | Static | `.bss` (zero-initialized) |
| `static int s = 10;` (in a function) | Static | `.data` |
| `const int c = 20;` (namespace scope) | Static | `.rodata` or folded away |
| `"hello"` | Static | `.rodata` |
| `int x = 40;` (local) | Automatic | Stack, or only a register |
| `volatile int v = 70;` (local) | Automatic | Stack (`volatile` does not change storage) |
| `new int(80)` | Dynamic | Heap |
| `thread_local int t = 30;` | Thread | Per-thread TLS block |
| function bodies | n/a | `.text` |

- "Local = stack" and "new = heap" are implementation mental models, not guarantees:
  - A local may live only in a register, or be optimized away entirely.
  - Since C++14 the compiler may elide or merge `new`/`delete` pairs (allocation elision), so a `make_unique` may never reach `malloc`.
- Implementation numbers worth knowing (Linux, glibc): main thread stack 8 MB by default (`ulimit -s`), `std::thread` stacks 8 MB of reserved virtual memory each, large `malloc` requests (128 KiB and up by default) go to `mmap` rather than the brk heap.

#### 4. When lifetime starts and ends
- **Starts**: when storage is obtained **and** initialization is complete. For a class with a constructor, the object is not "alive" until the constructor finishes. If the constructor throws, the object never existed: its destructor does not run, but fully constructed members and bases are destroyed (topic 05).
- **Ends**:
  - For a class type with a non-trivial destructor: when the destructor call **starts**.
  - Otherwise: when the storage is released or reused.
- During construction and destruction the object is partly alive: members are constructed in declaration order and destroyed in reverse order; virtual calls inside constructors and destructors do not dispatch to more derived classes.
- After lifetime ends, using the object through any old pointer, reference, view or iterator is UB, even if:
  - the memory was not freed (`optional::reset`, `pop_back`, explicit destructor call), or
  - the bytes still contain the old value (very common: the bug "works" in tests).
- Reusing storage with placement new and the rules for pointers to the old object (`std::launder`) are topic 10.

#### 5. Temporaries and lifetime extension
- A temporary is destroyed at the end of the full-expression (roughly: at the `;`), in reverse order of creation.
- **Lifetime extension**: binding a temporary (a prvalue, possibly through member access) **directly** to a `const T&` or `T&&` local reference extends the temporary's lifetime to the lifetime of the reference.
- It works through:
  - Plain binding: `const std::string& r = make_string();`
  - Member access on a prvalue: `const auto& levels = make_book().levels;` (the whole `Book` temporary is extended).
  - A conditional of two prvalues: `const T& r = c ? T(1) : T(2);`
  - Brace aggregate initialization of a reference member: `RefAgg a{T(7)};`
  - Array subscript on an array prvalue, casts that preserve the object (`static_cast<const T&>(T{})`).
- It does **not** work (verified with a tracing type, GCC 11):

| Code | Temporary destroyed | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `const T& r = id(T(4));` (function returning its `const T&` argument) | End of full-expression | Dangling |
| `T&& r = std::move(T(5));` | End of full-expression | Dangling: `std::move` returns a reference, not a prvalue |
| `const T& r = T(6).self();` (member returning `*this`) | End of full-expression | Dangling |
| `const std::string& r = get();` where `get` does `return create();` | Inside `get`, at the end of its `return` statement | Dangling (C++26 P2748: ill-formed) |
| `RefAgg a(T(8));` (C++20 parenthesized aggregate init) | End of full-expression | Dangling (brace form extends) |
| `new RefAgg{T(9)}` | End of full-expression | Dangling member |
| `H() : r(T{1}) {}` (reference member in mem-initializer) | When the constructor exits | Ill-formed since C++14; GCC 11 only warns (`-Wextra`), Clang errors |
| `std::string_view sv = std::string("abc");` | End of full-expression | Dangling: a view is not a reference |
| `for (int x : make_book().get())` (before C++23) | Before the loop body runs | Dangling (section 6) |

- Rule: extension only happens when the reference is bound to the temporary itself (or a sub-object of it) in the same declaration. It never passes through a function call that returns a reference, because the compiler cannot know what that reference refers to.
- Extension applies to the reference's lifetime: extending a temporary into a `static const T&` gives it static lifetime; into a function parameter it lasts only until the end of the call's full-expression.

#### 6. The range-for temporary trap and the C++23 fix
- `for (auto x : range-init) body` expands to roughly:
```cpp
{
    auto&& __range = range-init;          // only THIS binding gets lifetime extension
    auto __begin = __range.begin();
    auto __end = __range.end();
    for (; __begin != __end; ++__begin) { auto x = *__begin; body }
}
```
- `for (int x : load_book().levels)` is fine: `__range` binds to a member of the prvalue, so the whole temporary is extended.
- `for (int x : load_book().get())` where `get()` returns `const std::vector<int>&` dangles: `__range` binds to the reference returned by `get()`, the `Book` temporary dies at the end of the `auto&& __range = ...;` declaration, and the loop iterates freed memory. ASan: `stack-use-after-scope` (or `heap-use-after-free` for heap data).
- Other common forms: `for (char c : get_string().substr(0, 3))` is fine (prvalue), `for (auto& e : std::get<0>(make_tuple_of_vectors()))` dangles, `for (auto& kv : *make_shared_map())` dangles if nothing else owns the map.
- **C++23 (P2718)**: every temporary created in the range-init expression lives until the end of the loop. GCC 15 implements it; GCC 11 (used for the examples here) does not. Code that must build with older compilers still needs the fix: bind the owner to a named variable first, or use the C++20 init-statement `for (auto book = load_book(); int x : book.get())`.

#### 7. Order of construction and destruction
| Context | Construction order | Destruction order |
|---|---|---|
| Local variables in a block | Order of declaration | Reverse, at block exit (also during stack unwinding) |
| Class: bases and members | Virtual bases, then direct bases left to right, then members in **declaration order** | Exact reverse: members bottom-up, then bases |
| Member initializer list | Ignored for ordering (GCC `-Wreorder` warns) | n/a |
| Array elements | Index 0 upward | Highest index first |
| Temporaries in a full-expression | Order of evaluation | Reverse order of creation, at the end of the full-expression |
| Statics in one translation unit | Order of definition | Reverse order of completed construction, after `main` returns or `exit` |
| Function-local `static` | First time control passes the declaration | Reverse order of completed construction, mixed with globals |
| `thread_local` | Before first use in that thread (implementation: lazily on first odr-use for dynamic initialization) | At thread exit (before `join()` returns); the main thread's at `exit`, before statics |

- Consequence of declaration-order member construction: an initializer that reads another member must refer only to members declared **earlier**. Reading a later member reads an indeterminate value (UB for scalars).
- Destruction order is what makes RAII composable: a member that depends on another member must be declared after it, so it is destroyed first (e.g. a worker thread member declared after the queue it uses).
- `std::exit` runs static destructors; `std::quick_exit` and `std::_Exit` do not; `std::abort` and `std::terminate` do not.

#### 8. Static initialization and the static initialization order fiasco
- Statics are initialized in phases:
  1. **Zero-initialization**: all static and thread storage starts as zero (that is why `.bss` costs nothing in the file).
  2. **Constant initialization**: if the initializer is a constant expression, the value is baked into the binary. No code runs, no ordering problem.
  3. **Dynamic initialization**: anything else (calls a non-constexpr function, a constructor that is not constexpr). Runs before `main` in practice.
- Within one translation unit, dynamic initialization follows definition order. Across translation units the order is **unspecified**: in practice it follows link order, which nobody controls deliberately.
- **Static initialization order fiasco (SIOF)**: a static in `a.cpp` whose dynamic initializer reads a static from `b.cpp` that has not been initialized yet; it sees the zero-initialized value (or, for class types, an object whose lifetime has not started: UB).
- Fixes:
  - **Function-local static (Meyers singleton)**: `Config& config() { static Config c = load(); return c; }`. Initialized on first call, so any user triggers it in time.
  - **`constexpr` / `constinit` (C++20)**: guarantees constant initialization, so there is no dynamic phase to order. `constinit` does not imply `const`: the variable can still be modified at run time. If the initializer is not a constant expression, compilation fails ("`constinit` variable does not have a constant initializer").
  - Avoid cross-TU dependencies between globals entirely: pass dependencies explicitly.
- **Destruction order fiasco** (the mirror image): a static's destructor uses another static that was constructed later (so destroyed earlier). Typical: a global object logs in its destructor through a logger singleton that is already gone. Fixes: make the dependency a function-local static accessed during construction (guaranteeing it is constructed first, destroyed last), or intentionally leak it: `static Logger& l = *new Logger;` (never destroyed).
- `std::mutex` has a `constexpr` constructor, so a global mutex is constant-initialized and safe to use from other static initializers.

#### 9. Magic statics (thread-safe function-local statics)
- Since C++11, if several threads reach a function-local static's declaration concurrently, exactly one initializes it; the others block until initialization finishes.
- Implementation (Itanium ABI, GCC/Clang): a guard variable checked with an acquire load on every call (fast path: one load and a branch); the slow path calls `__cxa_guard_acquire`/`__cxa_guard_release`.
- If the initializer throws, the static is not considered initialized; the next caller tries again.
- Recursive initialization (the initializer calls the same function again) is UB; GCC throws `__gnu_cxx::recursive_init_error` or deadlocks.
- Only the **initialization** is thread-safe. Later reads and writes to the object need their own synchronization.
- GCC flag `-fno-threadsafe-statics` removes the guard (only for code that is known to be single-threaded).

#### 10. thread_local: one object per thread
- Each thread has its own instance; `&tls` differs per thread.
- Initialization:
  - Constant initializer: present from thread start (copied from a TLS template image).
  - Dynamic initializer: guaranteed to happen before the first odr-use in that thread. GCC/Clang initialize namespace-scope `thread_local` lazily through a wrapper function, so a thread that never touches it never constructs it.
- Destruction: at thread exit, in reverse order of construction, before the thread's `join()` returns. For the main thread, at `exit`, before static objects are destroyed.
- Cost: access is a segment-register-relative load (`%fs` on x86-64 Linux) for the executable; in shared libraries it may go through `__tls_get_addr`. Dynamic initialization adds a "initialized yet?" check on each access through the wrapper.
- Lifetime trap: a pointer to a `thread_local` handed to another thread dangles after the owning thread exits.
- A `thread_local` inside a function is also implicitly `static` storage-wise (one per thread, not per call).

#### 11. `volatile` is not a storage class and not synchronization
- `volatile` qualifies **accesses**: each read and write of a volatile object is an observable side effect that the compiler must perform and keep in order relative to other volatile accesses.
- It says nothing about **where** the object lives: a `volatile` local is still automatic (typically stack), a `static volatile` is still static storage.
- It does not "force the variable into RAM instead of a register" as a language rule, and it gives **no** atomicity or inter-thread ordering: a data race on a `volatile int` is still UB. Use `std::atomic` for threads.
- Legitimate uses: memory-mapped I/O registers (`*reinterpret_cast<volatile std::uint32_t*>(0x40000000)`: the platform's memory map puts the device there, not `volatile`), signal handlers with `volatile std::sig_atomic_t`, and benchmarks preventing dead-code elimination.
- C++20 deprecated `++`, `--` and compound assignment on volatile objects (`v++`, `v += 1`) because they look atomic but are not; C++23 un-deprecated the bitwise compound forms (`|=`, `&=`, `^=`) used in MMIO code.

#### 12. Misconceptions to unlearn
- ❌ "The temporary returned through a reference is destroyed back in the caller." ✅ A temporary created in a `return` statement of a function returning a reference dies at the end of that `return` statement, inside the callee; the caller receives a dangling reference.
- ❌ "Binding to `const&` always extends lifetime." ✅ Only when binding directly to the prvalue (or its member); not through function calls, `std::move`, views or mem-initializers.
- ❌ "`join()` makes it safe to use a pointer to the thread's local." ✅ The local died when `worker` returned; `join()` only waits for that.
- ❌ "Moving from an object ends its lifetime." ✅ It changes its state; only destruction (`reset`, scope exit, `delete`) ends lifetime.
- ❌ "Static objects are destroyed in declaration order." ✅ Reverse order of completed construction.
- ❌ "Members are initialized in the order of the initializer list." ✅ Declaration order.
- ❌ "`constinit` means `const`." ✅ It only means "statically initialized"; the variable is mutable.
- ❌ "Function-local statics are thread-safe." ✅ Their initialization is; their use is not.
- ❌ "`volatile` puts a variable in RAM / static memory / makes it thread-safe." ✅ None of those.
- ❌ "Local = stack, new = heap, always." ✅ Implementation model: registers, optimized-away locals and elided allocations are allowed.
- ❌ "If the memory still holds the old value, using the object is fine." ✅ Lifetime ended means UB, regardless of the bytes.

edge_cases.title: Where exactly does a temporary bound to a returned reference die?
edge_cases.explanation:
- Code:
```cpp
std::string create() { return "hello"; }
const std::string& get() { return create(); }   // GCC: returning reference to temporary
const std::string& s = get();
std::cout << s;                                  // UB
```
- A common (and AI-generated) explanation says the temporary "is destroyed at the end of the full expression in the caller". That is wrong. The temporary is created by the `return` statement **inside** `get()`; a temporary bound to the returned value of a function is not extended and is destroyed at the end of the `return` statement's full-expression. By the time `get()` returns, the string is already gone.
- Verified with a tracing type: `~T` prints before the caller's next line runs.
- RVO has nothing to do with it: elision decides where `create()`'s result is built, not how long a reference to it is valid.
- GCC warns (`-Wreturn-local-addr`, on by default). C++26 (P2748) makes binding a returned reference to a temporary ill-formed.

edge_cases.title: `std::move` on a temporary kills lifetime extension
edge_cases.explanation:
- `T&& r = T(5);` extends (prints `T5 use ~T5`).
- `T&& r = std::move(T(5));` dangles (prints `T5 ~T5 use`): `std::move` returns `T&&`, the reference is bound to the function's return value, not to the prvalue.
- Same for `const auto& r = std::max(a, b + 1);` when an argument is a temporary: `std::max` returns a reference to one of its arguments.

edge_cases.title: `join()` does not resurrect a dead local
`string_view` to a temporary string
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::string_view getName() { std::string s = build(); return s; }` returns a view into a destroyed local's buffer. The caller "sometimes sees corrupted text later": short strings live inside the dead `std::string` object (SSO), long strings in freed heap memory.
- `std::string_view sv = std::string("abc") + "def";` dangles at the `;`: a view is a class object, not a reference, so no lifetime extension.
- Redesign depends on intent:
  - Ownership needed: return `std::string` (cheap: elision or move, topic 04).
  - Non-owning access: return a view into storage that outlives the call (a member, a static table), and document the lifetime.

edge_cases.title: Lifetime vs state: moving out of an optional vs `reset()`
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::optional<std::string> o = "AAPL..."; std::string& ref = *o;`
  - `std::string s = std::move(*o);`: `o.has_value()` is still `true`; `ref` is **not** dangling (the contained string is alive), but its content is unspecified (topic 03).
  - `o.reset();`: the contained string's destructor runs; `ref` now dangles even though the optional's internal storage still exists.
- Same distinction for `std::variant` (switching alternative destroys the old one) and `std::vector` (`pop_back`, `clear`, reallocation).

edge_cases.title: Range-for over a member of a temporary
edge_cases.explanation:
- `for (int x : load_book().get())` with `get()` returning `const std::vector<int>&`: the `Book` temporary is destroyed before the first iteration (before C++23). ASan reported `stack-use-after-scope`.
- `for (int x : load_book().levels)` (direct member access) is fine because the member access keeps the whole temporary alive.
- The difference is invisible at the call site, which is why C++23 changed the rule (P2718).

edge_cases.title: Member initialization order follows declarations
Static initialization order across translation units
edge_cases.explanation:
- `config.cpp`: `int base_port = compute_base_port();` (dynamic initialization).
- `main.cpp`: `extern int base_port; int order_port = base_port + 1;`
- Result depends on link order: `g++ main.cpp config.cpp` gave `order_port = 1` (it read the zero-initialized `base_port`), `g++ config.cpp main.cpp` gave `9001`.
- For `int` this "only" produces wrong values; for class types (a global `std::string`, `std::map`) it uses an object whose lifetime has not started: UB, often a crash before `main`.
- Fix with a function-local static or `constinit`/`constexpr` (Example 4).

edge_cases.title: Reference members bound in a constructor
edge_cases.explanation:
- `struct H { const T& r; H() : r(T{1}) {} };` and `struct D { const T& r = T{2}; };`: the temporary dies when the constructor exits; every later use of `r` is UB.
- Ill-formed since C++14 (CWG 1696). Clang 14: error "reference member 'r' binds to a temporary object whose lifetime would be shorter than the lifetime of the constructed object". GCC 11 accepts it and only warns with `-Wextra` ("a temporary bound to 'H::r' only persists until the constructor exits").
- More common in real code: a class storing `const std::string&` constructed with a string literal or a temporary: `Order o("AAPL");` with `Order(const std::string& s) : sym_(s) {}`. Prefer storing by value.

interview_qa.question: What is the difference between an object's storage, its storage duration, its lifetime, and its scope?
interview_qa.answer: Storage is the memory that can hold the object; storage duration is the rule for how long that memory stays reserved; lifetime is the period during which the object actually exists (from completed initialization to the start of its destructor); scope is where its *name* is visible in the source.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Storage can outlive the object: after `optional::reset()`, `vector::pop_back()` or an explicit destructor call the bytes remain, the object does not.
- Scope and lifetime differ for `static` locals (block scope, program lifetime) and for heap objects (no name at all, lifetime until `delete`).
- Accessing an object outside its lifetime is UB even if the storage still holds the old bytes.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: using "memory released", "object released" and "resource released" interchangeably. They are three different events.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: a moved-from object is still alive (valid but unspecified); only destruction ends lifetime.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Storage is memory, lifetime is existence, scope is a name: keep them separate.
interview_qa.full_content:
**Answer:**
Storage is the memory that can hold the object; storage duration is the rule for how long that memory stays reserved; lifetime is the period during which the object actually exists (from completed initialization to the start of its destructor); scope is where its *name* is visible in the source.

**Explanation:**
- Storage can outlive the object: after `optional::reset()`, `vector::pop_back()` or an explicit destructor call the bytes remain, the object does not.
- Scope and lifetime differ for `static` locals (block scope, program lifetime) and for heap objects (no name at all, lifetime until `delete`).
- Accessing an object outside its lifetime is UB even if the storage still holds the old bytes.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: using "memory released", "object released" and "resource released" interchangeably. They are three different events.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: a moved-from object is still alive (valid but unspecified); only destruction ends lifetime.

interview_qa.question: What are the four storage durations, and where does each typically live?

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the standard defines durations, not segments; the layout is ELF/Linux convention.

interview_qa.question: Where is a `volatile` variable stored?
interview_qa.answer: Wherever its storage duration puts it: a `volatile` local is automatic (typically stack), a global or `static volatile` has static storage. `volatile` is a qualifier on accesses (each read/write must actually be performed, in order relative to other volatile accesses); it does not choose a location.

interview_qa.question: When exactly is the temporary destroyed here, and what does the caller hold?

interview_qa.question: In what order are class members initialized, and why does it matter?

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the fixed order exists so that destruction can be the exact reverse for every constructor; per-constructor orders would make that impossible.

interview_qa.question: Is a function-local static thread-safe? What does it cost?
interview_qa.answer: Its **initialization** is thread-safe since C++11: if several threads reach the declaration at once, exactly one runs the initializer and the others wait. interview_qa.question: A global object's destructor logs through a logger singleton and the program crashes at exit. Why?
interview_qa.answer: Static objects are destroyed in the reverse order of the completion of their construction. interview_qa.question: When is a `thread_local` object constructed and destroyed?
interview_qa.answer: Each thread has its own instance. If its initializer is constant, it exists from thread start; if dynamic, it is guaranteed to be initialized before its first odr-use in that thread (GCC/Clang do it lazily on first use, so threads that never touch it never construct it). It is destroyed when its thread exits, before `join()` returns; the main thread's instances are destroyed at `exit`, before static objects.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Measured: thread a used `session` → `open t1 ... close t1 after 3 requests`; a thread that never touched it printed no open/close.
- Accessing a `thread_local` is a segment-relative load (`%fs` on x86-64 Linux) in the executable; in a shared library it may call `__tls_get_addr`. Dynamic initialization adds a guard check per access.
- Typical uses: per-thread caches, per-thread memory pools, per-thread random engines, error state like `errno`.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Every thread constructs all `thread_local` objects when it starts."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: a pointer to a `thread_local` handed to another thread dangles after the owner thread exits; thread pools keep threads alive, so per-thread caches there live for the whole program.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: One instance per thread, constructed by first use, destroyed at that thread's exit.

interview_qa.question: A lambda captures a local by reference and is stored for later. What happens?
interview_qa.answer: The closure holds a reference to the local; once the function returns, the local is dead and calling the lambda reads a dangling reference (UB). Capture by value (or move-capture with `[p = std::move(p)]`) anything the callback needs after the scope ends, or capture a `std::shared_ptr`/`std::weak_ptr` when lifetime is shared.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Classic shape: `std::function<int()> make_counter() { int n = 0; return [&] { return ++n; }; }`.
- The same bug with `this`: `[this]` (or `[=]`, which captures `this` in C++17) in a callback registered with a longer-lived component.
- ASan reports `stack-use-after-return` (with `detect_stack_use_after_return=1`) or `stack-use-after-scope`.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`[&]` is fine because the lambda is defined in the same scope." Where it is defined does not matter; where it is **called** does.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: `[&]` is safe for lambdas used immediately (algorithms, `std::thread` joined in the same scope); for stored callbacks, default to explicit by-value captures.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: A stored lambda must own what it uses, or prove the referent outlives it.

practice_tasks.title: Question 2
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Undefined behaviour: m is a dangling reference.
(A plain -O0 build happened to print 5; ASan reports stack-use-after-scope on the read.)
```

**Explanation:**
- `std::max` takes and returns `const int&`. The literal `5` is materialized as a temporary bound to the parameter, and `std::max` returns a reference to it.
- The temporary dies at the end of the full-expression (the `;`). `m` was not bound directly to a prvalue, so there is no lifetime extension.
- GCC 11 gives no warning; GCC 13 adds `-Wdangling-reference`.
- **Key Concept:** Lifetime extension never passes through a function that returns a reference.

**Fixed Version:**
```cpp
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int limit = 3;
    const int m = std::max(limit, 5);   // copy the value
    std::cout << m << '\n';             // 5
}
```

practice_tasks.answer:
Dangling reference member: undefined behaviour in print().

practice_tasks.title: Question 5
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
M0 M2 M1 body | ~M1 ~M2 ~M0 
```

**Explanation:**
- Base class sub-object first (`M0`), then members in **declaration** order: `second` (`M2`), then `first` (`M1`). The initializer list order is ignored (GCC warns with `-Wreorder`).
- Destruction is the exact reverse: members bottom-up (`first`, `second`), then the base.
- **Key Concept:** Declaration order decides construction; destruction is its mirror image.

practice_tasks.title: Question 6
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Reads 1 and 2 are well-defined; read 3 is undefined behaviour.
Observed (GCC 11, libstdc++): "A: 1", "B: 0", "C: 0". Read 3 printed a plausible value and ASan
reported nothing, because the dead string object still sits inside the optional's storage.
```

**Explanation:**
- Moving out of `*o` changes the contained string's **state**; the string is still alive. `has_value()` stays `true` and `ref` is a valid reference. `ref.size()` is allowed (no precondition); its value is unspecified by the standard (libstdc++ gives 0).
- `o.reset()` runs the string's destructor: its **lifetime** ends. `ref` now refers to a dead object even though the optional's internal bytes still exist.
- ASan cannot see this: no memory was freed, only an object destroyed. This is why lifetime bugs survive testing.
- **Key Concept:** Move leaves the object alive in an unspecified state; reset (destruction) ends its lifetime.

Undefined behaviour: v views the buffer of a destroyed std::string.
ASan: heap-use-after-free (the 27-character name is past the SSO limit, so it was heap-allocated).

- `return name;` converts the local `std::string` into a `string_view` of its buffer; then `name` is destroyed and frees that buffer.

practice_tasks.title: Question 12
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
T1 | T2 ~T2 | T3 | ~T3 ~T1 
```

**Explanation:**
- `make(1)` is a prvalue bound directly to `const T& a`: lifetime extended to the end of `main`.
- `make(2);` is a discarded expression: the temporary is materialized and destroyed at the `;`.
- `T&& b = make(3);` also extends (rvalue references extend just like `const&`).
- At the end of `main`, extended temporaries are destroyed like locals, in reverse order: `b`'s object first, then `a`'s.
- **Key Concept:** A prvalue bound directly to a local reference lives as long as the reference; a discarded one dies at the semicolon.

quick_reference.content:
#### Storage durations
| Duration | Begins | Ends | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Automatic | Block entry / declaration | Block exit (reverse order) | `int x;` in a function |
| Static | Before `main` (or first pass for locals) | After `main` (reverse order) | global, `static` local |
| Thread | Thread start / first use | Thread exit | `thread_local` |
| Dynamic | `new` | `delete` | `new T` |
| Temporary | Expression evaluation | End of full-expression (unless extended) | `f(T{})` |

#### Lifetime extension
| Binding | Extended? |
|---|---|
| `const T& r = T{};` / `T&& r = T{};` | Yes |
| `const auto& r = make().member;` | Yes (whole object) |
| `const T& r = c ? T{1} : T{2};` | Yes |
| `RefAgg a{T{}};` | Yes |
| `const T& r = f(T{});` (f returns a reference) | No |
| `T&& r = std::move(T{});` | No |
| `std::string_view sv = std::string{};` | No (not a reference) |
| Reference member in mem-initializer | No (ill-formed) |
| Temporary in `return` of a reference-returning function | No (dies inside the callee) |
| `for (x : temp().get())` | No before C++23, yes in C++23 |

#### Order rules
| What | Rule |
|---|---|
| Members | Declaration order; destroyed in reverse |
| Bases vs members | Bases first; destroyed last |
| Locals | Reverse of declaration |
| Statics (one TU) | Definition order; destroyed in reverse of completion |
| Statics (across TUs) | Unspecified (SIOF) |
| Function-local static | First pass through the declaration; thread-safe init |
| `thread_local` | Before first use in each thread; destroyed at thread exit |

#### Tools
| Problem | Tool |
|---|---|
| Dangling reference/view | ASan (`stack-use-after-scope`, `heap-use-after-free`), `-Wdangling-reference` (GCC 13+), Clang `-Wdangling` |
| Returned reference to a local | `-Wreturn-local-addr` (GCC), `-Wreturn-stack-address` (Clang) |
| Thread local escape | `ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_stack_use_after_return=1` |
| Member order | `-Wreorder` (in `-Wall`) |
| SIOF | `constinit`, ASan `check_initialization_order=1` |

#### Interview one-liners
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Lifetime vs storage? | Storage is memory; lifetime is when the object exists in it |
| Four storage durations? | Automatic, static, thread, dynamic |
| When does a temporary die? | End of the full-expression, unless bound directly to a local reference |
| Temp in `return` of `const T& f()`? | Dies inside `f`; caller gets a dangling reference |
| Does `join()` fix `&local` of the thread? | No; the local died when the function returned |
| Move vs reset on optional? | Move: alive, unspecified; reset: destroyed |
| Member init order? | Declaration order |
| Static init order across files? | Unspecified: use function-local statics or `constinit` |
| Are function-local statics thread-safe? | Initialization yes (C++11), use no |
| Where does `volatile` store a variable? | Wherever its storage duration says; `volatile` only affects accesses |
| Range-for over `temp().member_ref()`? | Dangles before C++23 (P2718 fixes) |

| Lifetime vs storage? | Storage is memory; lifetime is when the object exists in it |
| Four storage durations? | Automatic, static, thread, dynamic |
| When does a temporary die? | End of the full-expression, unless bound directly to a local reference |
| Temp in `return` of `const T& f()`? | Dies inside `f`; caller gets a dangling reference |
| Does `join()` fix `&local` of the thread? | No; the local died when the function returned |
| Move vs reset on optional? | Move: alive, unspecified; reset: destroyed |
| Member init order? | Declaration order |
| Static init order across files? | Unspecified: use function-local statics or `constinit` |
| Are function-local statics thread-safe? | Initialization yes (C++11), use no |
| Where does `volatile` store a variable? | Wherever its storage duration says; `volatile` only affects accesses |
| Range-for over `temp().member_ref()`? | Dangles before C++23 (P2718 fixes) |

topics.topic: Special Member Functions and the Rule of 0/3/5

subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- A class's special member functions define its **value semantics**: what it means to create, duplicate, transfer and destroy one of its objects.
- The compiler writes them for you **memberwise**: copy each member, move each member, destroy each member. That is correct exactly when every member already knows how to copy, move and destroy itself.
- It is wrong when a member is a **handle without ownership semantics**: a raw owning pointer, a file descriptor `int`, a socket, a `HANDLE`. Copying the handle duplicates the *name* of the resource, not the resource, so two objects believe they own it.
- Three rules follow from that one idea:
  - **Rule of 0**: do not own raw resources in ordinary classes; hold RAII members (`std::vector`, `std::string`, `std::unique_ptr`) and write none of the special members.
  - **Rule of 3** (C++98): if you need a user-written destructor, copy constructor or copy assignment, you almost certainly need all three.
  - **Rule of 5** (C++11): the same, plus move constructor and move assignment, because declaring any of the three suppresses the implicit moves.
- The rule is a design check, not a typing exercise: "I wrote a destructor" should trigger the question "what happens when this object is copied, moved, assigned?", and the answer may be `= delete`.

subsections.title: 2. The six special members and when each runs
subsections.content:
| Member | Signature | Runs when |
|---|---|---|
| Default constructor | `T()` | `T a;` `T a{};` `new T` |
| Destructor | `~T()` | End of lifetime (scope exit, `delete`, container erase) |
| Copy constructor | `T(const T&)` | A **new** object is initialized from an lvalue: `T b(a);` `T b = a;` pass/return by value |
| Copy assignment | `T& operator=(const T&)` | An **existing** object is assigned from an lvalue: `b = a;` |
| Move constructor (C++11) | `T(T&&) noexcept` | A new object is initialized from an rvalue: `T b(std::move(a));` |
| Move assignment (C++11) | `T& operator=(T&&) noexcept` | An existing object is assigned from an rvalue: `b = std::move(a);` |

- **Constructor vs assignment** depends on whether the destination already exists. `T b = a;` contains `=` but is initialization, so it calls the copy constructor.
- **Copy vs move** depends on the value category of the source expression (lvalue vs rvalue). Value categories and `std::move` are covered in topic 03.
- `T b = T(100);` calls neither copy nor move in C++17: the prvalue initializes `b` directly (guaranteed copy elision, topic 04).
- Copy assignment has to deal with an **old resource** in the destination; construction does not. That difference is why assignment is the harder function to write.

subsections.title: 3. When the compiler generates what (the Hinnant table)
subsections.content:
- "User-declared" includes `= default` and `= delete`. Only *declaring* matters, not what the body does.

| You declare | Default ctor | Destructor | Copy ctor | Copy assign | Move ctor | Move assign |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nothing | defaulted | defaulted | defaulted | defaulted | defaulted | defaulted |
| Any constructor | not declared | defaulted | defaulted | defaulted | defaulted | defaulted |
| Destructor | defaulted | **yours** | defaulted ⚠️ deprecated | defaulted ⚠️ deprecated | **not declared** | **not declared** |
| Copy ctor | not declared | defaulted | **yours** | defaulted ⚠️ deprecated | **not declared** | **not declared** |
| Copy assign | defaulted | defaulted | defaulted ⚠️ deprecated | **yours** | **not declared** | **not declared** |
| Move ctor | not declared | defaulted | **deleted** | **deleted** | **yours** | not declared |
| Move assign | defaulted | defaulted | **deleted** | **deleted** | not declared | **yours** |

- Read the two asymmetries carefully:
  - Declaring a **copy op or destructor** makes the moves **not declared**. Rvalues then bind to the copy constructor (`const T&` accepts rvalues), so `std::move` silently copies. Correct but slow.
  - Declaring a **move op** makes both copies **deleted**. Copying then fails to compile.
- "Not declared" and "deleted" are different:
  - Not declared: the function does not exist; overload resolution picks something else (the copy).
  - Deleted: the function exists, wins overload resolution, and the call is ill-formed.
- ⚠️ Deprecated (since C++11) means: still generated today, still does a memberwise copy, so a Rule-of-3 violation compiles silently.
  - Destructor-only case (the classic leak/double delete): GCC warns only with `-Wdeprecated-copy-dtor`, Clang with `-Wdeprecated`; neither warns under `-Wall -Wextra` (GCC 11, Clang 14).
  - User-provided copy constructor with an implicit copy assignment (or the reverse): GCC's `-Wextra` includes `-Wdeprecated-copy` and warns when the implicit one is used; Clang 14 is silent under `-Wall -Wextra` if the class also has a user-provided destructor.
- `~T() = default;` written in the class is still **user-declared**: the type stays trivially destructible, but the implicit moves are gone.

subsections.title: 4. The shallow copy problem and the Rule of 3
subsections.content:
- Classic broken class: owns `int* data` from `new int[n]`, has a destructor, no copy control.
- `Buffer b = a;` uses the implicit copy constructor: `b.data = a.data`. Two owners, one allocation.
  - At scope end `~b` frees the array, then `~a` frees it again: **double delete, undefined behaviour** (it *may* crash; ASan reports `attempting double-free`). Do not answer "it segfaults".
  - Any write through `b` is visible through `a`: aliasing bug even before destruction.
- `b = a;` (implicit copy assignment) is worse: `b`'s old array is **leaked** and then double deleted later.
- Rule of 3 fix:
  - **Copy constructor**: allocate a new array, copy the elements (deep copy).
  - **Copy assignment**: produce the new state first, then release the old resource, then commit; return `*this`.
  - **Destructor**: release the resource.
- Copy assignment checklist:
  1. Self-assignment `a = a` must not destroy the source before reading it.
  2. Allocate and copy **before** deleting the old array, so a `std::bad_alloc` leaves `*this` unchanged (strong guarantee).
  3. Release the old resource.
  4. Update all members (pointer and size together), return `*this`.
- The naive order `delete[] data; data = new int[o.size]; copy(...)` fails both 1 (on self-assignment the values are freed before being copied, so the object ends up with garbage) and 2 (a throwing `new` leaves `data` dangling, so the destructor double deletes later).

subsections.title: 5. Copy-and-swap
6. Rule of 5: writing the move operations
7. noexcept moves and std::vector growth
subsections.content:
- When `std::vector` reallocates, it must transfer existing elements to the new buffer. It promises the **strong guarantee** for `push_back`: if an exception happens, the vector is unchanged.
- If the element's move constructor might throw, an exception halfway through would leave some old elements already moved-from, and the original state could not be restored. So the vector uses `std::move_if_noexcept`:
  - Move constructor `noexcept` (or the type is not copyable): **move** the elements.
  - Move constructor may throw and a copy constructor exists: **copy** them.
- Consequence: a correct but non-`noexcept` move constructor makes every growth copy every element: the "copies during reallocation" latency spike seen in profiles.
- Second silent cause: a **user-declared destructor** (even `= default`) removes the implicit move constructor entirely, so growth copies through the copy constructor.
- Implicitly generated and `= default` moves are `noexcept` automatically when all members' moves are `noexcept`. Check with `static_assert(std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<T>);`.
- The mechanism (`move_if_noexcept`, value categories) is covered in topic 03; here the lesson is: **write `noexcept` on moves, and do not add a destructor you do not need**.

subsections.title: 8. Rule of 0 and move-only types
9. = default, = delete, and members that block generation
subsections.content:
- `= default` asks for the compiler's memberwise version. On the first declaration it is not "user-provided": a defaulted copy constructor keeps the type trivially copyable.
- A defaulted special member is **defined as deleted** when some member cannot do the operation:

| Member type | Effect on the containing class |
|---|---|
| `const T` member | Copy/move **assignment** deleted (copy/move constructors fine; default ctor deleted if a `const` scalar member has no initializer) |
| `T&` reference member | Copy/move **assignment** deleted; default ctor deleted (unless the member has a default member initializer) |
| `std::unique_ptr` member | Copy ctor and copy assign deleted |
| `std::mutex` member | All copy and move deleted (mutex is neither) |
| Member without default ctor | Default ctor deleted |

- Containers care: `std::vector<T>` with a `const` member still supports `push_back` (only construction is needed), but `erase`, `insert` in the middle and `std::sort` need assignment and fail to compile.
- If objects must be assignable, hold a pointer (`T*` or `std::reference_wrapper<T>`) instead of a reference member, and a private non-const member with a getter instead of a `const` member.
- `= delete` can delete any function, not only special members (for example `void f(double) = delete;` to block a conversion). A deleted function **participates** in overload resolution; picking it is an error.
- Special rule: a **defaulted** move constructor that is defined as deleted (because a member cannot be moved) is **ignored** by overload resolution, so rvalues fall back to the copy constructor. A move constructor you explicitly write as `= delete` is not ignored (see topic 04 for the `return` case).
- In C++20 any user-declared constructor (even `= default`) stops the class from being an aggregate, so designated initializers `T{.x = 1}` stop working.

subsections.title: 10. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "`T b = a;` calls the assignment operator." ✅ It is initialization: copy constructor.
- ❌ "If I write a destructor the compiler still gives me a move constructor." ✅ It does not; moves silently become copies.
- ❌ "If I write a move constructor I still get the default copy assignment." ✅ Both copy operations become deleted; `b = a` does not compile.
- ❌ "`~T() = default;` changes nothing." ✅ It is user-declared: implicit moves disappear.
- ❌ "Double delete always crashes." ✅ It is undefined behaviour; it may appear to work, corrupt the heap, or crash later.
- ❌ "Move assignment needs a temporary in case allocation throws." ✅ Move assignment does not allocate; that concern belongs to copy assignment.
- ❌ "The default move of a raw pointer member transfers ownership." ✅ Moving a pointer copies it and leaves the source unchanged; only your own move code can null the source. (And with a user destructor there is no implicit move at all.)
- ❌ "Rule of 0 means objects on the stack." ✅ It means resources are owned by RAII members.
- ❌ "Every class with a destructor needs all five written by hand." ✅ It needs all five *decided*: some will be `= delete` or `= default`.
- ❌ "`std::vector` requires `noexcept` moves." ✅ It works without, but copies instead of moving on growth when a copy exists.

| Copy assign | defaulted | defaulted | defaulted ⚠️ deprecated | **yours** | **not declared** | **not declared** |
| Move ctor | not declared | defaulted | **deleted** | **deleted** | **yours** | not declared |

  - **Copy constructor**: allocate a new array, copy the elements (deep copy).

#### 5. Copy-and-swap
- Implement copy assignment in terms of the copy constructor and a non-throwing `swap`:
```cpp
friend void swap(Buffer& a, Buffer& b) noexcept {
    using std::swap;
    swap(a.data_, b.data_);
    swap(a.size_, b.size_);
}
Buffer& operator=(const Buffer& other) {
    Buffer tmp(other);   // may throw: *this untouched
    swap(*this, tmp);    // cannot throw
    return *this;        // tmp's destructor frees the OLD resource
}
```
- Properties:
  - **Strong exception guarantee** for free: the only throwing step happens before `*this` is modified.
  - **Self-assignment safe** without a branch (it makes a wasted copy, which is fine because self-assignment is rare).
  - Releases the old resource through the destructor: no duplicated cleanup code.
- **Unified assignment** variant: `Buffer& operator=(Buffer other) noexcept { swap(*this, other); return *this; }`
  - Takes the parameter **by value**: an lvalue argument is copied, an rvalue argument is moved into the parameter. One function serves as both copy and move assignment.
  - Do not also declare `operator=(Buffer&&)`: `b = std::move(a)` becomes ambiguous.
- Cost: copy-and-swap always allocates. A hand-written copy assignment can reuse existing capacity when sizes match (what `std::vector` does). For a type on a hot path, the strong guarantee may not be worth an allocation per assignment: that is a design choice, say it explicitly in interviews.

#### 6. Rule of 5: writing the move operations
- Move constructor: take the source's resource and leave the source **empty but valid** (destructible and assignable).
```cpp
Buffer(Buffer&& o) noexcept
    : data_(std::exchange(o.data_, nullptr)), size_(std::exchange(o.size_, 0)) {}
```
- `std::exchange(obj, new_value)` (C++14) returns the old value and stores the new one: "steal and reset" in one expression.
- Order matters: copy the pointer **then** null the source. `a.data = nullptr; b.data = a.data;` loses the pointer.
- Why null the source: the moved-from object's destructor still runs. Without the reset, both destructors `delete[]` the same array (double delete). `delete[] nullptr` is a no-op, so null is the natural empty state.
- Move assignment: the destination **already owns** something; release it, take the source's resource, empty the source:
```cpp
Buffer& operator=(Buffer&& o) noexcept {
    if (this != &o) {
        delete[] data_;
        data_ = std::exchange(o.data_, nullptr);
        size_ = std::exchange(o.size_, 0);
    }
    return *this;
}
```
- Move assignment normally does **no allocation**; only copy assignment needs the "allocate first" ordering.
- **Self-move** `a = std::move(a)`: without the check, `delete[] data_` frees the array and then reads it back from the same object: `a` ends up dangling or empty. The standard library only promises that self-move leaves the object in a valid state; your type should at least not corrupt itself. Alternative with no branch (move-and-swap, using the friend `swap` from section 5): `Buffer tmp(std::move(o)); swap(*this, tmp); return *this;`. On self-move `tmp` takes the array, `swap` hands it straight back, and `tmp` dies empty.
- Mark both moves `noexcept` when they cannot throw (pointer and integer copies cannot). Section 7 explains why it matters.

#### 8. Rule of 0 and move-only types
- Rule of 0: let members manage resources; the compiler-generated five are then correct automatically.
```cpp
class Buffer {
    std::vector<int> data_;      // copy = deep copy, move = O(1) transfer
public:
    explicit Buffer(std::size_t n) : data_(n) {}
};                               // no destructor, no copy/move code
```
- "Rule of 0 means everything is on the stack" is wrong: `vector` still allocates on the heap. Rule of 0 is about **who manages** the resource, not where it lives.
- Choose the member by the ownership semantics you want:

| Member | Resulting class semantics |
|---|---|
| `std::vector<T>`, `std::string` | Copyable (deep copy) and movable |
| `std::unique_ptr<T>` / `unique_ptr<T[]>` | Move-only (copy is deleted because the member's copy is deleted) |
| `std::shared_ptr<T>` | Copyable, but copies **share** the object (shallow by design) |
| `std::unique_ptr<FILE, Closer>` | Move-only wrapper for a C resource with custom cleanup |

- **Move-only handle types** (file descriptor, socket, mutex owner): the resource is unique, so copying has no meaning. Delete the copies, implement `noexcept` moves, use a sentinel (`-1`) for "owns nothing", and check the sentinel in the destructor.

- **Rule of 5 defaults** for polymorphic bases: a base needs `virtual ~Base() = default;`, which suppresses implicit moves. Restore them explicitly:
```cpp
struct Base {
    virtual ~Base() = default;
    Base() = default;
    Base(const Base&) = default;              // often protected, to prevent slicing
    Base& operator=(const Base&) = default;
    Base(Base&&) = default;
    Base& operator=(Base&&) = default;
};
```

edge_cases.title: A move constructor deletes copy assignment
edge_cases.explanation:
- Class with destructor, copy constructor and move constructor, but no assignment operators.
- People expect `b = a;` to use the implicit (shallow) copy assignment and leak.
- Reality: declaring the move constructor makes the implicit copy assignment **deleted**, and move assignment is not declared at all. Both `b = a;` and `b = std::move(a);` fail to compile:
```
error: use of deleted function 'constexpr Buffer& Buffer::operator=(const Buffer&)'
note: ... is implicitly declared as deleted because 'Buffer' declares a move
      constructor or move assignment operator
```
- Without the move constructor (destructor + copy constructor only), the deprecated implicit copy assignment *does* exist: `b = a;` compiles, leaks `b`'s array and double deletes later.
- So the Rule-of-5 violation is a compile error in one case and silent UB in the other. Know which.

edge_cases.title: A destructor quietly turns moves into copies
edge_cases.explanation:
- `struct Order { std::string id; ~Order() { log(); } };` looks harmless.
- The user-declared destructor removes the implicit move constructor. `Order b = std::move(a);` compiles and calls the copy constructor: `a.id` keeps its contents, and the string is deep-copied.
- In `std::vector<Order>`, every reallocation copies every element.
- Fix: remove the destructor (logging belongs elsewhere) or add `Order(Order&&) noexcept = default;` and the other defaults.
- The same happens with `~Order() = default;`, which many people add "for clarity".

edge_cases.title: Self-assignment in a naive copy assignment
edge_cases.explanation:
- `Buffer& operator=(const Buffer& o) { delete[] data_; data_ = new int[o.size_]; std::copy(o.data_, o.data_ + o.size_, data_); ... }`
- For `a = a`, `o` and `*this` are the same object: the values are freed, `data_ = new int[...]` also changes `o.data_`, and the copy then copies the new uninitialized array onto itself. The data is silently lost (ASan does not catch it; a variant that saved `o.data_` first would be a use after free).
- Self-assignment happens indirectly: `v[i] = v[j]` with `i == j`, `*p = *q` with aliasing pointers, `std::swap` implementations, sorting algorithms.
- Fixes: `if (this == &o) return *this;`, or allocate-and-copy before deleting (which is also self-safe), or copy-and-swap.

edge_cases.title: Forgetting to null the source in the move constructor
edge_cases.explanation:
- `Buffer(Buffer&& o) noexcept : data_(o.data_), size_(o.size_) {}` compiles and "works" in a quick test.
- The moved-from object still holds the pointer; its destructor frees the array that the new object owns. The new object then uses freed memory and frees it again.
- The bug often shows up only when the moved-from object is a temporary destroyed right away, for example inside `vector` reallocation.
- Rule: a move must leave the source in a state its destructor handles correctly (`nullptr`, `-1`, empty).

edge_cases.title: Defaulted-but-deleted move falls back to copy
edge_cases.explanation:
- `struct Holder { Legacy l; Holder() = default; Holder(const Holder&) = default; Holder(Holder&&) = default; };` where `Legacy` declares `Legacy(Legacy&&) = delete;` and a copy constructor.
- `Holder`'s defaulted move is **defined as deleted** (it would need `Legacy`'s deleted move). A defaulted move constructor that is deleted is ignored by overload resolution, so `Holder b = std::move(a);` compiles and **copies**.
- Contrast: `Legacy b = std::move(la);` does not compile: an explicitly deleted move participates in overload resolution and wins against the copy.
- Lesson: `= default` is a request, not a guarantee. `std::is_move_constructible_v<Holder>` is still `true` (the copy accepts rvalues), but `std::is_nothrow_move_constructible_v<Holder>` is `false` here because `Legacy`'s copy is not `noexcept`: a `static_assert` on the nothrow trait catches it.

edge_cases.title: By-value assignment plus a move assignment is ambiguous
edge_cases.explanation:
- Copy-and-swap with `Buffer& operator=(Buffer other);` handles both lvalues and rvalues.
- Adding `Buffer& operator=(Buffer&& other);` "for speed" makes `b = std::move(a);` ambiguous: both candidates bind an rvalue with the same rank.
```
error: ambiguous overload for 'operator=' (operand types are 'Buffer' and 'std::remove_reference<Buffer&>::type' {aka 'Buffer'})
```
- Pick one design: by-value unified assignment, or the separate `const&` and `&&` pair.

edge_cases.title: const and reference members make the class non-assignable
edge_cases.explanation:
- `struct Trade { const int id; double px; };` can be constructed, copied and moved (construction initializes the `const` member), but `t1 = t2;` does not compile: the implicit copy assignment is deleted.
- `std::vector<Trade>` still allows `push_back` and `emplace_back`, but `std::sort`, `erase` and `insert` in the middle fail to compile because they assign elements.
- Same for `T&` members. Use a private non-const member with a getter, or `std::reference_wrapper<T>` / `T*` instead of `T&`.

edge_cases.title: The deprecated implicit copy hides Rule-of-3 bugs
edge_cases.explanation:
- `-Wall -Wextra` does not warn about a class with a user destructor and an implicit copy. GCC needs `-Wdeprecated-copy-dtor` ("implicitly-declared 'B::B(const B&)' is deprecated"); Clang needs `-Wdeprecated` ("definition of implicit copy constructor for 'B' is deprecated because it has a user-provided destructor").
- Compilers have kept generating these functions for over a decade for compatibility; you cannot rely on the language to stop you.
- Defensive habit: in every class with a destructor, write all five explicitly (`= default`, `= delete` or a body). Linters: clang-tidy `cppcoreguidelines-special-member-functions`.

interview_qa.question: What are the Rule of 3, the Rule of 5 and the Rule of 0? Why did 3 become 5?
