edge_cases.title: expired() followed by lock()
edge_cases.explanation:
- `if (!w.expired()) { auto sp = w.lock(); sp->run(); }` looks safe, but another thread can release the last owner between the two calls. `sp` is then empty and `sp->run()` dereferences null (UB, usually a crash).
- `expired()` and `lock()` are each atomic; the sequence of two is not.
- Fix: `if (auto sp = w.lock()) sp->run();`. The test and the acquisition of ownership are one operation.
- Same race with `if (w.use_count() > 0)`.

edge_cases.title: weak_ptr has no operator->
edge_cases.explanation:
- `child->parent->next` where `parent` is a `weak_ptr` does not compile: "base operand of '->' has non-pointer type 'std::weak_ptr<Node>'".
- This is intentional: there is no moment where you hold a usable pointer without also holding ownership.
- Write `if (auto p = child->parent.lock()) use(p->next);`.

edge_cases.title: lock() vs the shared_ptr(weak_ptr) constructor
edge_cases.explanation:
- `w.lock()` on an expired `weak_ptr` returns an empty `shared_ptr` (no exception).
- `std::shared_ptr<T> sp(w);` on an expired `weak_ptr` throws `std::bad_weak_ptr` (`what()` is "bad_weak_ptr" in libstdc++).
- Choose by intent: `lock()` when "already gone" is a normal outcome (callbacks, caches); the constructor when it indicates a bug and should fail loudly.

edge_cases.title: shared_from_this() in the constructor
edge_cases.explanation:
- During construction no `shared_ptr` owns the object yet; the hidden weak this is still empty.
- C++17 and later: throws `std::bad_weak_ptr`. C++11/14: undefined behaviour.
- Typical bug: `Session() { loop.register(shared_from_this()); }`.
- Fix: two-phase creation: `static std::shared_ptr<Session> create() { auto s = std::shared_ptr<Session>(new Session); s->start(); return s; }` (or `make_shared` with a passkey constructor), and register in `start()`.

edge_cases.title: shared_from_this() on an object nobody shares
edge_cases.explanation:
- Stack object, `unique_ptr`-owned object, or plain `new` without a `shared_ptr`: `shared_from_this()` throws `std::bad_weak_ptr` (C++17).
- Converting `unique_ptr<T>` to `shared_ptr<T>` later does initialize the weak this, because the `shared_ptr` constructor sees the base at that point.
- `weak_from_this()` returns an empty `weak_ptr` instead of throwing: use it when the object may legitimately be unowned.

edge_cases.title: Private inheritance silently disables it
edge_cases.explanation:
- `struct S : std::enable_shared_from_this<S>` with `class` instead of `struct`, or explicit `private`, makes the base inaccessible to `shared_ptr`'s constructor.
- The code compiles, `shared_from_this()` is still callable from inside the class, but the weak this was never set: it throws `bad_weak_ptr` even for an object created with `make_shared`.
- Always write `class X : public std::enable_shared_from_this<X>`.

edge_cases.title: The keep-alive capture that became a cycle
edge_cases.explanation:
- `timer_.on_expire([self = shared_from_this()] { self->tick(); });` where `timer_` is a member of the same object: the object owns the timer, the timer owns the callback, the callback owns the object.
- The object leaks until the timer fires and drops the handler; a periodic timer never drops it.
- The same capture handed to an external executor that runs it once and destroys it is fine and often intended (keeps the session alive until the operation completes).
- Rule: strong self-capture is a cycle exactly when the callback is stored somewhere the object itself owns.

edge_cases.title: weak_ptr in a set or map
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::set<std::weak_ptr<T>>` does not compile when you insert: `weak_ptr` has no `operator<`.
- Use `std::set<std::weak_ptr<T>, std::owner_less<>>`. The ordering uses the control block address, which does not change when the object expires, so the set's invariants stay valid.
- Expired entries remain in the container until you erase them: periodic pruning (`std::erase_if` with `expired()`) is your job.

edge_cases.title: weak observer retains a make_shared block
edge_cases.explanation:
- `auto big = std::make_shared<Buffer4MB>(); cache.push_back(big);` with `cache` holding `weak_ptr`: after `big` dies the destructor runs, but the 4 MB block (object storage + control block, one allocation) is freed only when the last `weak_ptr` dies.
- Long-lived weak observers of large objects: use `std::shared_ptr<T>(new T)` (separate allocations), or prune expired weak pointers promptly. Measurement in topic 07.

interview_qa.question: What is `std::weak_ptr`, and why not just use a raw pointer as the non-owning link?
interview_qa.answer: A `weak_ptr` is a non-owning observer of an object managed by `shared_ptr`. It does not keep the object alive, but because it participates in the same control block it can always tell whether the object still exists, and `lock()` turns it into a temporary owner safely. A raw pointer cannot tell you whether its target has been destroyed.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `weak_ptr` increments the **weak** count only; the object's lifetime is governed solely by the **strong** count.
- The control block outlives the object while weak references exist, which is what makes `expired()` / `lock()` answerable after destruction.
- A raw pointer to a destroyed object looks exactly like a valid one; using it is a use-after-free.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`weak_ptr` is just a non-owning pointer." That is also true of `T*`; the point is **lifetime awareness** through the control block.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: raw pointers remain the right choice when the lifetime is guaranteed by structure (owner outlives every use); `weak_ptr` is for when the observer cannot know the owner's schedule.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `weak_ptr` = non-owning + can detect death + can temporarily acquire ownership.

interview_qa.question: After `p.reset()`, does the `42` still exist? Does the control block? What does `w.lock()` do?
interview_qa.answer: The `int` object is destroyed at `p.reset()` (strong count 1 → 0). The control block survives because `w` still references it (weak count 1). `w.lock()` sees strong count 0 and returns an empty `shared_ptr`; it cannot bring the object back.

interview_qa.question: Why does `weak_ptr` have no `operator->`, and what exactly does `lock()` return?
interview_qa.answer: Because the object may already be destroyed, there must be no way to access it without first becoming an owner. `lock()` returns a `std::shared_ptr<T>`: a real co-owner (strong count +1) if the object is alive, or an empty `shared_ptr` if it has expired.

interview_qa.question: What is wrong with `if (!w.expired()) w.lock()->process();`?
interview_qa.answer: It is a check-then-act race: another thread can release the last `shared_ptr` between `expired()` and `lock()`. `lock()` then returns an empty `shared_ptr` and `->` dereferences null (undefined behaviour). Use `if (auto sp = w.lock()) sp->process();`.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Each call is atomic; the pair is not.
- `lock()` is implemented with a compare-and-swap that increments the strong count only if it is not 0, so it can never return a pointer to a dying object.
- `expired() == true` is final and safe to act on (e.g. prune a dead observer). `expired() == false` is stale as soon as it is read.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "It's fine because `expired()` is thread-safe." Thread-safe calls do not make a sequence of calls atomic.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the same race exists with `w.use_count() > 0`; and single-threaded code can hit it too if a callback between the two calls releases the owner.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Test and acquire in one step: the result of `lock()` is the check.

interview_qa.question: What is the difference between `w.lock()` and `std::shared_ptr<T>(w)`?

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: `bad_weak_ptr::what()` returns "bad_weak_ptr" in libstdc++.

interview_qa.question: Two objects hold `shared_ptr`s to each other. What happens? Is it a deadlock?
interview_qa.answer: It is a memory leak, not a deadlock. After the assignments both strong counts are 2; the two `reset()` calls bring each to 1, and nothing can bring them to 0 because each object owns the other. Neither destructor ever runs.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Trace: after `make_shared`: A=1, B=1. `a->b = b`: B=2. `b->a = a`: A=2. `a.reset()`: A=1. `b.reset()`: B=1.
- Both objects are now unreachable from the program but still owned by each other.
- A deadlock needs threads waiting on each other; here nothing waits, nothing runs.
- LeakSanitizer reports such a cycle as "Indirect leak" entries only (each block is referenced by another leaked block).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Deadlock: each waits for the other to be destroyed." Nothing is waiting; it is just reference counting that never reaches zero.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the side effects of the destructors (closing sockets, flushing files, unregistering) are also lost, not just the memory.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: A strong cycle is a silent leak; `shared_ptr` is reference counting, not garbage collection.

interview_qa.question: In a parent/child structure, which link should be `weak_ptr`? What goes wrong if you pick the other one?
interview_qa.answer: The parent owns the child (`shared_ptr` down) and the child observes the parent (`weak_ptr` up). Making the parent's child link weak instead also breaks the cycle, but then the parent no longer keeps its child alive: the child dies as soon as its other owners go, even though the parent still refers to it.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Rule: strong edges must form a tree (or DAG) following ownership; every back edge is weak (or a raw pointer with guaranteed lifetime).
- Correct version:
```cpp
struct Order {
    std::weak_ptr<Order> parent;    // observe
    std::shared_ptr<Order> child;   // own
};
```
- With that: `parent->child = child; child->parent = parent;` gives parent strong 1, child strong 2. `parent.reset()` destroys the parent, which releases the child (2 → 1); `child.reset()` destroys the child.
- Same rule elsewhere: list `next` strong, `prev` weak; object owns its callback, callback observes the object.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Any link, as long as one is weak." It compiles and stops the leak, but encodes the wrong ownership.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: for genuinely cyclic graphs, let a container/arena own all nodes and use indices or raw pointers between them.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Weak goes on the edge that does not mean ownership.

interview_qa.question: A button stores an `onClick` lambda that captures the button's own `shared_ptr` by value. Why does `~Button` never print?

interview_qa.question: What problem does `enable_shared_from_this` solve, and why not `std::shared_ptr<T>(this)`?
interview_qa.answer: A member function sometimes needs a `shared_ptr` to its own object, for example to keep it alive during an async operation. `shared_ptr<T>(this)` creates a second, independent control block for an object already owned elsewhere, leading to a double delete. `enable_shared_from_this<T>` stores a hidden `weak_ptr` to the owning control block, so `shared_from_this()` returns a `shared_ptr` that shares the existing ownership.

interview_qa.question: When does `shared_from_this()` fail, and what happens?
interview_qa.answer: Whenever no `shared_ptr` currently owns the object: in the constructor, in the destructor, for stack or `unique_ptr`-owned objects, and when the base is inherited privately. Since C++17 it throws `std::bad_weak_ptr`; before C++17 it was undefined behaviour.

interview_qa.question: In async code, when should a handler capture `shared_from_this()` and when `weak_from_this()`?
interview_qa.answer: Capture a strong `self` when the handler is held by an external executor that runs it once and then destroys it: the session should stay alive until the operation completes, and there is no cycle. interview_qa.question: How would you implement an observer pattern with `weak_ptr`, and why is it safer than raw observer pointers?
interview_qa.answer: The subject stores `std::vector<std::weak_ptr<Observer>>`. On each notification it `lock()`s every entry, calls the live observers and erases the expired ones. Observers can die without unsubscribing; with raw pointers a forgotten unsubscribe means the subject calls into freed memory.
interview_qa.explanation:
- The subject must not hold `shared_ptr<Observer>` unless it is supposed to keep observers alive; and if observers also hold the subject strongly, that is a cycle.
- Pruning with `std::erase_if(obs, [](auto& w) { return w.expired(); })` (C++20) is fine: an expired answer never becomes wrong.
- Thread-safety: the vector itself still needs a lock (or a copy-on-write snapshot) if subscribe and notify run on different threads (topic 08).

interview_qa.question: How do you use `weak_ptr` as a key in `std::set` or `std::map`?
interview_qa.answer: `weak_ptr` has no `operator<` (or `==` or hash), so supply `std::owner_less<>`: `std::set<std::weak_ptr<T>, std::owner_less<>>`. It orders by control block (owner), which stays stable after the object expires, so the container's ordering invariant never breaks.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Value comparison would be meaningless: an expired `weak_ptr` has no meaningful pointer value to compare.

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: a typical use is a "seen" set of observers or sessions, keyed by identity, that must not keep them alive.

interview_qa.question: A cache returns raw pointers to its entries; another thread may evict entries. What is the bug and how do you fix it?
interview_qa.answer: The cache owns the objects, but callers keep raw pointers after the cache may evict and destroy them: use-after-free. The access was separated from the lifetime. Fix by returning `shared_ptr` (eviction drops only the cache's ownership; the object lives until the last user finishes), or keep raw access and add an explicit deferred reclamation scheme if refcount cost matters.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Sequence: worker gets `Object*` → cache evicts and destroys → worker dereferences freed memory.
- `shared_ptr` fix: cache stores `shared_ptr<const Object>`, `get()` returns a copy; eviction is just `erase`.
- Alternatives at high rates: epoch-based reclamation, hazard pointers, pinning/leasing an entry for the duration of use, or single-owner handoff.
- A `weak_ptr`-valued cache is the inverse design: the cache never keeps entries alive, users do (flyweight).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Raw pointers are the bug; never use them." The raw pointer is fine when the lifetime is guaranteed; here it is not.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the mutex around the map does not help: it protects the map, not the lifetime of objects after `get()` returns.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Returning a non-owning pointer requires a lifetime guarantee; eviction breaks it.

interview_qa.question: A child's destructor calls `parent.lock()` to tell the parent it is going away. Why is the parent never notified at shutdown?
interview_qa.answer: When the children are destroyed as members of the parent, the parent's strong count is already 0: `~Parent` is running, so `lock()` on a `weak_ptr` to it returns empty. The notification works when a child dies on its own while the parent is alive, and silently does nothing during the parent's own teardown.
code_examples:
parent notified: child 2
-- reset parent --
~Parent, live=1
child 1: parent.lock() is empty
interview_qa.key_takeaway: During the owner's destruction, every `weak_ptr` to it is already expired; do teardown work in the owner, not through `lock()` from its members.

interview_qa.question: Is `weak_ptr::lock()` thread-safe?
interview_qa.answer: Yes, with the usual handle rule: calling `lock()` on a `weak_ptr` while other threads release or copy other `shared_ptr`/`weak_ptr` instances to the same object is safe and atomic. Modifying the **same** `weak_ptr` instance from two threads (or reading it while another thread assigns it) is a data race.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `lock()` atomically increments the strong count only if it is non-zero (a CAS loop in libstdc++). It either wins and returns a live owner, or sees 0 and returns empty; it never returns a pointer to an object being destroyed.
- The object itself gets no protection: two threads that both `lock()` successfully still need synchronization to modify it.
- C++20 `std::atomic<std::weak_ptr<T>>` exists for sharing one `weak_ptr` variable between threads.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`lock()` is just `expired()` plus a copy, so it races." The standard requires it to execute atomically.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the control block is always thread-safe; the handle and the pointee are not (three layers, topic 08).
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `lock()` is atomic against concurrent release; the same `weak_ptr` object is not shared-writable.

interview_qa.question: How would you find a `shared_ptr` reference cycle in a large codebase?
interview_qa.answer: Run tests under LeakSanitizer (ASan): a cycle shows up as "Indirect leak" entries with allocation stacks pointing at `make_shared` calls. In production look for steady RSS growth with heap profilers, and for destructors that never run (log or count them). Then draw the ownership graph of the types involved and find the back edge.
interview_qa.explanation:
- LSan finds memory unreachable from roots at exit; a pure cycle has no direct leak because every node is still pointed to by another leaked node.
- Usual suspects: `std::function` members capturing `shared_ptr` to the owner, parent/child pointers both strong, observers holding the subject while the subject holds them, timers and completion handlers stored on the session.
- Instrumentation: count live instances (static atomic counter in ctor/dtor) and assert it returns to zero after a test scenario.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`shared_ptr` cannot leak." Cycles are exactly the case it cannot handle.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: prevent rather than detect: code review rule "every `shared_ptr` member must name its owner direction"; prefer `unique_ptr` + raw/weak back links.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Cycles hide as indirect leaks; find the strong back edge.

interview_qa.question: What does `weak_ptr` cost?
interview_qa.answer: Each `weak_ptr` is two pointers (16 bytes on typical x86-64); creating, copying and destroying one is an atomic update of the weak count; every `lock()` is an atomic CAS on the strong count plus a later decrement. With `make_shared`, outstanding `weak_ptr`s also keep the whole object-plus-control-block allocation from being freed after the object dies.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Observer-style designs that `lock()` per event pay two atomic RMWs per observer per event, on a cache line shared with every other owner.
- `enable_shared_from_this` adds a hidden `weak_ptr` to every object.
- Large objects with long-lived weak observers: allocate with `shared_ptr<T>(new T)` so the object's storage can be freed separately from the control block.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`weak_ptr` is free because it doesn't own anything." It still maintains a count and pins the control block.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: in single-threaded hot paths a generation-checked handle (index + generation counter) gives the same "is it still alive?" check without atomics.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `weak_ptr` is cheap, not free: atomics per lock, and it pins memory with `make_shared`.

practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**

```
0 1
```

**Explanation:**

**Answer:**

**Explanation:**

- **Key Concept:** Destruction cascades along owning members, stopping at any node that still has another owner.

#### weak_ptr operations
| Expression | Result | Throws? |
|---|---|---|
| `w.lock()` | `shared_ptr` or empty | No |
| `std::shared_ptr<T>(w)` | `shared_ptr` | `bad_weak_ptr` if expired |
| `w.expired()` | `use_count() == 0` | No |
| `w.use_count()` | Strong count | No |
| `w->x`, `*w`, `w.get()` | Compile error | n/a |
| `w.owner_before(v)` / `std::owner_less<>` | Ordering by control block | No |
| `sizeof(std::weak_ptr<T>)` | 16 (typical x86-64) | n/a |

#### Counts and lifetimes
| Event | Strong | Weak | Object | Control block |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `auto p = make_shared<T>()` | 1 | 0 | alive | alive |
| `weak_ptr w = p` | 1 | 1 | alive | alive |
| `auto q = w.lock()` | 2 | 1 | alive | alive |
| `q.reset(); p.reset()` | 0 | 1 | **destroyed** | alive (make_shared memory kept) |
| `w.reset()` | 0 | 0 | gone | **freed** |

#### enable_shared_from_this rules
| Situation | `shared_from_this()` |
|---|---|
| Object owned by `shared_ptr`, public base | Works, shares control block |
| Inside constructor or destructor | Throws `bad_weak_ptr` (C++17) |
| Stack / `unique_ptr` / raw `new` object | Throws `bad_weak_ptr` (C++17); UB before |
| Private or ambiguous base | Throws `bad_weak_ptr` even with `make_shared` |
| Need a non-throwing version | `weak_from_this()` (C++17) |

#### Which link is weak?
| Relationship | Strong edge | Weak edge |
|---|---|---|
| Tree | parent → child | child → parent |
| Doubly linked list | `next` | `prev` |
| Object with stored callback | object → callback | callback → object |
| Subject / observer | (observers owned elsewhere) | subject → observers |
| Cache | users → object | cache → object |

#### Interview one-liners
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| What does `weak_ptr` keep alive? | The control block, never the object |
| Reference cycle: deadlock or leak? | Leak: counts never reach 0, destructors never run |
| How to access through a `weak_ptr`? | `if (auto sp = w.lock())` |
| Why not `expired()` then `lock()`? | Race between the two calls |
| Why does `weak_ptr` have no `->`? | Access without ownership could hit a dead object |
| `lock()` on expired? | Empty `shared_ptr`, no exception |
| Why `enable_shared_from_this`? | `shared_ptr(this)` would create a second control block |
| `shared_from_this()` in constructor? | Throws `bad_weak_ptr` (C++17) |
| Capture in a stored callback? | `weak_ptr`; strong `self` only for external one-shot work |
| `weak_ptr` as a map key? | `std::owner_less<>` comparator |
| Raw pointer always bad? | No: fine for non-owning access with a guaranteed lifetime |
| `shared_ptr` refcount too hot? | Rethink ownership: single owner + observers, pools, explicit reclamation; measure |

topics.topic: new/delete, Placement New and Object Storage

subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- Two separate things always exist: **storage** (bytes with an address) and an **object** (a typed thing whose **lifetime** begins when construction completes and ends when its destructor starts).
- Storage can exist without an object (a raw buffer), and many objects can live in the same storage one after another.
- `new T(args)` (the **new-expression**) does two steps:
  1. Calls an **allocation function** `operator new(sizeof(T))` to get raw storage.
  2. Constructs a `T` in that storage.
- `delete p` (the **delete-expression**) does the reverse:
  1. Calls `p->~T()` (destructor).
  2. Calls a **deallocation function** `operator delete(p)` to return the storage.
- `operator new` / `operator delete` are just functions that hand out and take back bytes, like `malloc` / `free`. They know nothing about types or constructors.
- Placement new is the new-expression **without step 1**: you supply the storage, it only constructs. The matching manual cleanup is an explicit destructor call **without** deallocation.
- Everything in this topic (pairing rules, pools, `std::launder`, wire buffers) follows from keeping storage and object lifetime apart.

subsections.title: 2. new/delete pairing rules
subsections.content:
| Acquired with | Release with | Mismatch |
|---|---|---|
| `new T` | `delete p` | UB |
| `new T[n]` | `delete[] p` | UB (`delete` on array, or `delete[]` on single) |
| `malloc` / `calloc` / `realloc` | `free` | UB with `delete` |
| `new (buf) T` (placement) | `p->~T()` / `std::destroy_at(p)` only | `delete p` is UB |
| `operator new(n)` (raw call) | `operator delete(p)` | No constructors or destructors run |

- Why `delete[]` must match `new[]`:
  - For a type with a non-trivial destructor, `new T[n]` asks for **extra bytes** (an "array cookie", 8 bytes in the Itanium ABI used by GCC/Clang) and stores `n` there so `delete[]` knows how many destructors to run.
  - Measured: `new D[3]` for a 1-byte class with a destructor requested 11 bytes (3 + 8).
  - `delete` on that pointer runs one destructor and passes the wrong address to the deallocator: heap corruption or a crash. For trivially destructible types it often "works", which is why the bug survives code review. ASan reports `alloc-dealloc-mismatch`.
- Mixing `malloc` and `delete` (or `new` and `free`) is UB even if the default `operator new` happens to call `malloc`: a replaced `operator new`, a different allocator, or a cookie breaks it. And `malloc` never runs constructors.
- `delete nullptr` and `delete[] nullptr` are no-ops: never write `if (p) delete p;`.
- Deleting twice, or deleting a pointer not from `new`, is UB (ASan: `double-free`, `bad-free`).
- In modern code you rarely write `delete` at all: `std::make_unique`, containers and RAII (topics 05, 06) do it. Knowing the rules still matters for pools, custom allocators and reviewing legacy code.

subsections.title: 3. Initialization forms and failure
subsections.content:
- `new T` default-initializes: for `int` or a class with a trivial default constructor, members are **indeterminate**; reading them is UB.
- `new T()` and `new T{}` value-initialize: zero for scalars and for members of classes whose default constructor is not user-provided.
- `new int[5]()` zeroes the array; `new int[5]` does not.
- On failure, the ordinary `operator new` **throws `std::bad_alloc`**; it never returns `nullptr`. So `if (!p)` after a plain `new` is dead code.
- `new (std::nothrow) T` returns `nullptr` on failure instead (but a throwing constructor still throws).
- `new T[n]` with a negative or absurd `n` throws `std::bad_array_new_length` (derived from `bad_alloc`).
- **new_handler**: `std::set_new_handler(h)`. When allocation fails, `operator new` calls `h()` and retries, in a loop. The handler must do one of: free some memory (e.g. release a reserve block), install a different handler, throw `bad_alloc`, or terminate. With no handler installed, `bad_alloc` is thrown.
- Linux reality: with overcommit (the default), `new` of a few GB usually **succeeds**; physical pages are assigned on first touch, and real exhaustion is handled by the OOM killer, not by `bad_alloc`. Only impossible requests (larger than the address space or overcommit heuristics allow) fail immediately.
- If the constructor throws, the new-expression calls the **matching** `operator delete` automatically, so no memory leaks; the object never existed, so no destructor runs.

subsections.title: 4. Overloading and replacing operator new
subsections.content:
- **Class-specific** `static void* operator new(std::size_t)` / `operator delete(void*)` (implicitly `static`): used by `new T` / `delete p` for that class and its derived classes (which pass their own, larger size).
  - Typical use: route a hot type to a pool or free list (pool design in topic 11).
  - Not used by `new T[n]` unless you also define `operator new[]`; not used by `::new T` (global scope qualifier); **not used by `std::make_shared` / `std::allocate_shared`**, which allocate the control block plus object through `std::allocator` (verified: the class `operator new` was not called).
  - If you define `operator new`, define the matching `operator delete`: when a constructor throws, the new-expression looks for the matching deallocation function.
- **Global replacement**: define `void* operator new(std::size_t)` and `void operator delete(void*) noexcept` (and preferably the sized, array and aligned forms) in one translation unit. The linker uses yours for the whole program, including the standard library.
  - Uses: counting allocations in tests ("this hot path performs zero allocations"), routing to jemalloc/tcmalloc/mimalloc, adding guards or statistics.
  - Rules: must not return `nullptr` (throw `bad_alloc`), must handle size 0 (return a unique non-null pointer), must not use `std::cout` or anything that allocates before it is set up.
- **Placement forms with extra arguments**: `void* operator new(std::size_t, Arena&)`, called as `new (arena) T(args)`. If the constructor throws, the compiler calls the matching `operator delete(void*, Arena&)`; if none exists, the memory leaks silently.
- **Sized deallocation (C++14)**: `operator delete(void*, std::size_t)` receives the object size, so the allocator can skip a size lookup. With a virtual destructor, deleting through `Base*` passes the **dynamic** type's size.
- **Destroying delete (C++20)**: `void operator delete(T*, std::destroying_delete_t)` takes over both destruction and deallocation (used for variable-sized objects); rare in interviews.

subsections.title: 5. Over-aligned types and aligned new (C++17)
subsections.content:
- `__STDCPP_DEFAULT_NEW_ALIGNMENT__` (16 on x86-64 GCC/Clang) is the alignment ordinary `operator new` guarantees.
- Before C++17, `new` of `struct alignas(64) Line { ... };` was **not** guaranteed to be 64-byte aligned: a silent bug for cache-line-padded structures and SIMD types.
- C++17: for types with alignment above that value, the new-expression calls `operator new(std::size_t, std::align_val_t)`, and `delete` calls `operator delete(void*, std::align_val_t)`. `std::allocator` (so `std::vector<Line>`) does the same.
- If you replace or overload `operator new` for such types, provide the `align_val_t` overloads too.
- Raw aligned buffers: `alignas(T) std::byte buf[sizeof(T)]`, or `std::aligned_alloc(align, size)` (release with `free`; C11 required `size` to be a multiple of `align`, C17 (DR 460) relaxed that, but rounding `size` up is still the portable choice). `std::aligned_storage` is deprecated in C++23: use `alignas` on a byte array.

subsections.title: 6. Placement new and explicit destruction
subsections.content:
- Syntax: `T* p = ::new (static_cast<void*>(addr)) T(args);` (the plain `new (addr) T(args)` form is fine for ordinary types; the `::` and `void*` cast guard against class overloads in generic code).
- It performs **no allocation**; the standard `operator new(std::size_t, void*)` just returns `addr`.
- Requirements on the storage: at least `sizeof(T)` bytes, aligned to `alignof(T)`, and not holding a live object you still need (constructing over a live non-trivial object without destroying it first skips its destructor: leaks).
- Use the **pointer returned** by placement new to access the object (see section 7 for why).
- Ending the lifetime: `p->~T();` or `std::destroy_at(p);` (C++17). Never `delete p`: the storage did not come from `operator new(sizeof(T))` (stack buffer: ASan `bad-free`; pool slot: corrupts the pool).
- For trivially destructible types the destructor call is optional, but writing `std::destroy_at` keeps generic code correct.
- Standard helpers in `<memory>`:

| Helper | Since | Does |
|---|---|---|
| `std::destroy_at(p)` | C++17 | `p->~T()` (arrays: destroys elements, C++20) |
| `std::destroy(first, last)`, `std::destroy_n(first, n)` | C++17 | Destroy a range |
| `std::construct_at(p, args...)` | C++20 | `::new (voidify(p)) T(args...)`, usable in `constexpr` |
| `std::uninitialized_copy/move/fill(_n)` | C++98/17 | Construct into raw memory; destroy what was built if one constructor throws |
| `std::uninitialized_default_construct(_n)`, `std::uninitialized_value_construct(_n)` | C++17 | Default/value-construct a range in raw memory |

- `std::construct_at` exists mostly for `constexpr` (placement new is not allowed in constant evaluation until C++26) and for allocator-aware generic code.
- Array placement new `new (buf) T[n]` historically allowed an unspecified extra overhead (a cookie) beyond `n * sizeof(T)`, so `buf` could overflow; CWG 2382 removed this for the non-allocating form. Prefer a loop or `std::uninitialized_value_construct_n` anyway.
- Exception safety when constructing several objects manually: if the k-th constructor throws, destroy the first k-1. The `uninitialized_*` algorithms do this for you.

subsections.title: 7. Storage reuse and std::launder (C++17)
subsections.content:
- After `p->~T(); new (buf) T(...);`, the new object is a **different object** in the same storage, even if the address and type are the same. Same address does not mean same object (relevant to ABA reasoning too).
- When may the **old** pointer `p` be used to reach the new object? Only if the new object **transparently replaces** the old one ([basic.life]): same storage, same type (ignoring cv), the old object was not a `const` complete object, and neither is a base-class subobject or `[[no_unique_address]]` member.
  - C++17 also excluded types with `const` or reference **members**: reusing a `struct { const int id; }` through the old pointer was UB, and `std::launder(p)` was required. C++20 removed that restriction.
- `reinterpret_cast<T*>(buf)` where `buf` is a byte array does **not** give a pointer to the `T` that placement new created there: it is a pointer to the bytes with a different type. Formally you need `std::launder(reinterpret_cast<T*>(buf))`. Practical rule: keep and use the pointer returned by placement new (or `construct_at`).
- `std::launder(p)` returns a pointer to the object that currently lives at address `p`. It changes no bits; it tells the optimizer not to assume the old object's values (for example a cached `const` member or vtable pointer).
- Where it matters in practice: containers with inline storage (`optional`, `variant`, small-buffer vectors) that recreate objects in a member byte array.

subsections.title: 8. Implicit-lifetime types and wire buffers
subsections.content:
- **Implicit-lifetime types** (C++20, P0593; [class.prop]): scalars, arrays, and implicit-lifetime classes, which are either aggregates (whose destructor is not user-provided, per CWG 2605) or classes with at least one trivial eligible constructor and a trivial, non-deleted destructor (e.g. a plain `struct Header { std::uint32_t seq; std::uint16_t len; };`).
- Some operations **implicitly create** such objects in storage if that gives the program defined behaviour: `std::malloc`, `operator new`, `std::allocator::allocate`, `std::memcpy`/`memmove`, and starting the lifetime of an `unsigned char` or `std::byte` array. This blessed the long-standing C idiom `auto* h = static_cast<Header*>(std::malloc(sizeof(Header))); h->seq = 1;` (it was technically UB before; applied as a defect report).
- Network or file bytes are a different matter: `reinterpret_cast<const Header*>(rx_buf + offset)` has several problems at once:
  - Object model: no `Header` object was created there by the C++ program (formally UB).
  - Strict aliasing: reading `char` bytes as `uint32_t` violates the aliasing rules unless an object of that type lives there (only `char`, `unsigned char` and `std::byte` may alias anything).
  - Alignment: `offset` may be odd; misaligned access is UB (traps on some CPUs; UBSan reports it).
  - Layout: padding and endianness must match the wire format exactly.
- Correct options:
  - `std::memcpy(&h, rx_buf + offset, sizeof h);`: well defined, alignment-free; compilers turn it into a plain load (no call) at `-O2`.
  - `std::bit_cast<To>(from)` (C++20): reinterpret the bytes of one trivially copyable value as another of the same size (`float` ↔ `uint32_t`, `std::array<std::byte, 8>` → `double`). `constexpr`, compile error if sizes differ.
  - `std::start_lifetime_as<T>(p)` (C++23): explicitly starts the lifetime of an implicit-lifetime `T` over existing bytes, keeping their values, with no copy. Library support is still limited (not in GCC 11's libstdc++ used for this chapter).
- Still convert byte order (`std::byteswap` in C++23, `ntohl`, or `std::endian` checks in C++20) and validate lengths before trusting any field.

subsections.title: 9. What malloc really costs (glibc, typical Linux)
subsections.content:
- C++ says nothing about speed; everything below is implementation behaviour (glibc 2.35, x86-64).
- `new` → `operator new` → `malloc`. The path a call takes is not predictable from the call site:

| Path | When | Cost (order of magnitude) |
|---|---|---|
| **tcache** hit | Small sizes (up to 1032 bytes by default), per-thread cache of up to 7 freed chunks per size class | Tens of ns, no lock |
| Arena bins (fastbins, small/large bins) | tcache empty or full | Lock on the arena, bin search, possible coalescing |
| Grow heap with `brk`/`sbrk` (main arena) | No suitable free chunk | System call |
| `mmap` a dedicated region | Request ≥ mmap threshold (128 KiB default, adapts upward to 32 MiB) | System call; `free` does `munmap` immediately |
| First touch of a new page | After any of the growth paths | Page fault + kernel zeroes the page (µs level per page) |

- Threads: glibc creates additional **arenas** under contention (up to 8 × cores on 64-bit) so threads rarely share one lock, at the cost of more memory spread across arenas.
- Cross-thread free (allocate in producer, free in consumer) pushes chunks into another thread's arena or tcache: more locking and worse locality.
- `free` is not free either: coalescing neighbours, trimming the top of the heap, `munmap` (which on multi-threaded processes may need TLB shootdowns across cores).
- Low-latency conclusion: the problem is **variance** (tail latency), not the average. A hot path that is fast 99.9 % of the time and occasionally hits a syscall plus page faults ruins p99.9. Remedies: preallocate and reuse (reserve, pools, arenas, `std::pmr`, topic 11), pre-fault memory at startup (touch pages, `mlock`), replace the allocator (jemalloc, tcmalloc, mimalloc), and verify with an allocation-counting `operator new` in tests.
- ❌ "Every `new` takes a lock and makes a system call." ✅ The common small-allocation path is a user-space tcache pop; the expensive paths are rare but unpredictable.

subsections.title: 10. Fragmentation and RSS growth without a leak
subsections.content:
- **External fragmentation**: plenty of free bytes in total, but split into holes too small or badly placed to satisfy a request (or to give back to the OS).
- **Internal fragmentation**: the allocator hands out more than requested (size classes, 16-byte alignment, chunk headers: a 24-byte request uses a 32-byte chunk).
- Why RSS stays high after `free` (glibc): the heap can only shrink from the top. One live block near the top pins everything below it; freed chunks inside the heap stay mapped (and counted in RSS) until `malloc_trim` or reuse. Measured: 200 000 × 256 B blocks (about 55 MB RSS), all freed except the last one: RSS unchanged; after `malloc_trim(0)` it dropped back to about 5 MB.
- Other causes of "growing memory, no leak":
  - Containers keep their capacity: a `vector` that once held 10 million elements keeps that buffer after `clear()` (`shrink_to_fit` or swap with an empty vector).
  - Unbounded queues/backlogs during bursts, caches without eviction, pools that grow to their high-water mark and never shrink.
  - Objects still reachable but retained longer than intended (a `shared_ptr` held in a map, a `weak_ptr` pinning a `make_shared` block: topic 07/09).
  - Per-thread arenas each holding their own free memory.
- Investigation: track RSS over time against workload; heap profilers (heaptrack, massif, jemalloc/tcmalloc profiling); `malloc_info`/`malloc_stats`; container sizes and capacities; pool high-water marks. Valgrind/LSan find leaks, not retention.

subsections.title: 11. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "`new` and `operator new` are the same thing." ✅ The new-expression allocates via `operator new` **and** constructs; `operator new` only allocates.
- ❌ "`new` returns `nullptr` when memory runs out." ✅ It throws `std::bad_alloc`; only `new (std::nothrow)` returns null. On Linux it often succeeds and the OOM killer acts later.
- ❌ "`delete` on an array just leaks the other elements." ✅ It is UB: wrong destructor count and wrong address passed to the deallocator.
- ❌ "Placement new allocates in the buffer." ✅ It allocates nothing; it constructs in storage you own.
- ❌ "After placement new, `delete p` cleans up." ✅ Call the destructor (`std::destroy_at`); the storage owner releases the storage.
- ❌ "Same address, same type: it's the same object." ✅ A new lifetime is a new object; old pointers are only valid under the transparent-replacement rules.
- ❌ "Casting the receive buffer to a struct pointer is fine." ✅ Aliasing, alignment, object lifetime and endianness all bite; use `memcpy`, `bit_cast` or `start_lifetime_as`.
- ❌ "Class `operator new` controls every allocation of that class." ✅ Not `make_shared`, not `::new`, not arrays without `operator new[]`.
- ❌ "`destroy_at` is C++20." ✅ `destroy_at` is C++17; `construct_at` is C++20.
- ❌ "RSS growing means a leak." ✅ Retention, fragmentation, capacity and unbounded queues grow RSS with every allocation correctly freed.

- `new (std::nothrow) T` returns `nullptr` on failure instead (but a throwing constructor still throws).
- `new T[n]` with a negative or absurd `n` throws `std::bad_array_new_length` (derived from `bad_alloc`).
- **new_handler**: `std::set_new_handler(h)`. When allocation fails, `operator new` calls `h()` and retries, in a loop. The handler must do one of: free some memory (e.g. release a reserve block), install a different handler, throw `bad_alloc`, or terminate. With no handler installed, `bad_alloc` is thrown.
- Linux reality: with overcommit (the default), `new` of a few GB usually **succeeds**; physical pages are assigned on first touch, and real exhaustion is handled by the OOM killer, not by `bad_alloc`. Only impossible requests (larger than the address space or overcommit heuristics allow) fail immediately.
- If the constructor throws, the new-expression calls the **matching** `operator delete` automatically, so no memory leaks; the object never existed, so no destructor runs.

#### 4. Overloading and replacing operator new
- **Class-specific** `static void* operator new(std::size_t)` / `operator delete(void*)` (implicitly `static`): used by `new T` / `delete p` for that class and its derived classes (which pass their own, larger size).
  - Typical use: route a hot type to a pool or free list (pool design in topic 11).
  - Not used by `new T[n]` unless you also define `operator new[]`; not used by `::new T` (global scope qualifier); **not used by `std::make_shared` / `std::allocate_shared`**, which allocate the control block plus object through `std::allocator` (verified: the class `operator new` was not called).
  - If you define `operator new`, define the matching `operator delete`: when a constructor throws, the new-expression looks for the matching deallocation function.
- **Global replacement**: define `void* operator new(std::size_t)` and `void operator delete(void*) noexcept` (and preferably the sized, array and aligned forms) in one translation unit. The linker uses yours for the whole program, including the standard library.
  - Uses: counting allocations in tests ("this hot path performs zero allocations"), routing to jemalloc/tcmalloc/mimalloc, adding guards or statistics.
  - Rules: must not return `nullptr` (throw `bad_alloc`), must handle size 0 (return a unique non-null pointer), must not use `std::cout` or anything that allocates before it is set up.
- **Placement forms with extra arguments**: `void* operator new(std::size_t, Arena&)`, called as `new (arena) T(args)`. If the constructor throws, the compiler calls the matching `operator delete(void*, Arena&)`; if none exists, the memory leaks silently.
- **Sized deallocation (C++14)**: `operator delete(void*, std::size_t)` receives the object size, so the allocator can skip a size lookup. With a virtual destructor, deleting through `Base*` passes the **dynamic** type's size.
- **Destroying delete (C++20)**: `void operator delete(T*, std::destroying_delete_t)` takes over both destruction and deallocation (used for variable-sized objects); rare in interviews.

#### 5. Over-aligned types and aligned new (C++17)
- `__STDCPP_DEFAULT_NEW_ALIGNMENT__` (16 on x86-64 GCC/Clang) is the alignment ordinary `operator new` guarantees.
- Before C++17, `new` of `struct alignas(64) Line { ... };` was **not** guaranteed to be 64-byte aligned: a silent bug for cache-line-padded structures and SIMD types.
- C++17: for types with alignment above that value, the new-expression calls `operator new(std::size_t, std::align_val_t)`, and `delete` calls `operator delete(void*, std::align_val_t)`. `std::allocator` (so `std::vector<Line>`) does the same.
- If you replace or overload `operator new` for such types, provide the `align_val_t` overloads too.
- Raw aligned buffers: `alignas(T) std::byte buf[sizeof(T)]`, or `std::aligned_alloc(align, size)` (release with `free`; C11 required `size` to be a multiple of `align`, C17 (DR 460) relaxed that, but rounding `size` up is still the portable choice). `std::aligned_storage` is deprecated in C++23: use `alignas` on a byte array.

#### 6. Placement new and explicit destruction
- Syntax: `T* p = ::new (static_cast<void*>(addr)) T(args);` (the plain `new (addr) T(args)` form is fine for ordinary types; the `::` and `void*` cast guard against class overloads in generic code).
- It performs **no allocation**; the standard `operator new(std::size_t, void*)` just returns `addr`.
- Requirements on the storage: at least `sizeof(T)` bytes, aligned to `alignof(T)`, and not holding a live object you still need (constructing over a live non-trivial object without destroying it first skips its destructor: leaks).
- Use the **pointer returned** by placement new to access the object (see section 7 for why).
- Ending the lifetime: `p->~T();` or `std::destroy_at(p);` (C++17). Never `delete p`: the storage did not come from `operator new(sizeof(T))` (stack buffer: ASan `bad-free`; pool slot: corrupts the pool).
- For trivially destructible types the destructor call is optional, but writing `std::destroy_at` keeps generic code correct.
- Standard helpers in `<memory>`:

| Helper | Since | Does |
|---|---|---|
| `std::destroy_at(p)` | C++17 | `p->~T()` (arrays: destroys elements, C++20) |
| `std::destroy(first, last)`, `std::destroy_n(first, n)` | C++17 | Destroy a range |
| `std::construct_at(p, args...)` | C++20 | `::new (voidify(p)) T(args...)`, usable in `constexpr` |
| `std::uninitialized_copy/move/fill(_n)` | C++98/17 | Construct into raw memory; destroy what was built if one constructor throws |
| `std::uninitialized_default_construct(_n)`, `std::uninitialized_value_construct(_n)` | C++17 | Default/value-construct a range in raw memory |

- `std::construct_at` exists mostly for `constexpr` (placement new is not allowed in constant evaluation until C++26) and for allocator-aware generic code.
- Array placement new `new (buf) T[n]` historically allowed an unspecified extra overhead (a cookie) beyond `n * sizeof(T)`, so `buf` could overflow; CWG 2382 removed this for the non-allocating form. Prefer a loop or `std::uninitialized_value_construct_n` anyway.
- Exception safety when constructing several objects manually: if the k-th constructor throws, destroy the first k-1. The `uninitialized_*` algorithms do this for you.

#### 7. Storage reuse and std::launder (C++17)
- After `p->~T(); new (buf) T(...);`, the new object is a **different object** in the same storage, even if the address and type are the same. Same address does not mean same object (relevant to ABA reasoning too).
- When may the **old** pointer `p` be used to reach the new object? Only if the new object **transparently replaces** the old one ([basic.life]): same storage, same type (ignoring cv), the old object was not a `const` complete object, and neither is a base-class subobject or `[[no_unique_address]]` member.
  - C++17 also excluded types with `const` or reference **members**: reusing a `struct { const int id; }` through the old pointer was UB, and `std::launder(p)` was required. C++20 removed that restriction.
- `reinterpret_cast<T*>(buf)` where `buf` is a byte array does **not** give a pointer to the `T` that placement new created there: it is a pointer to the bytes with a different type. Formally you need `std::launder(reinterpret_cast<T*>(buf))`. Practical rule: keep and use the pointer returned by placement new (or `construct_at`).
- `std::launder(p)` returns a pointer to the object that currently lives at address `p`. It changes no bits; it tells the optimizer not to assume the old object's values (for example a cached `const` member or vtable pointer).
- Where it matters in practice: containers with inline storage (`optional`, `variant`, small-buffer vectors) that recreate objects in a member byte array.

#### 8. Implicit-lifetime types and wire buffers
- **Implicit-lifetime types** (C++20, P0593; [class.prop]): scalars, arrays, and implicit-lifetime classes, which are either aggregates (whose destructor is not user-provided, per CWG 2605) or classes with at least one trivial eligible constructor and a trivial, non-deleted destructor (e.g. a plain `struct Header { std::uint32_t seq; std::uint16_t len; };`).
- Some operations **implicitly create** such objects in storage if that gives the program defined behaviour: `std::malloc`, `operator new`, `std::allocator::allocate`, `std::memcpy`/`memmove`, and starting the lifetime of an `unsigned char` or `std::byte` array. This blessed the long-standing C idiom `auto* h = static_cast<Header*>(std::malloc(sizeof(Header))); h->seq = 1;` (it was technically UB before; applied as a defect report).
- Network or file bytes are a different matter: `reinterpret_cast<const Header*>(rx_buf + offset)` has several problems at once:
  - Object model: no `Header` object was created there by the C++ program (formally UB).
  - Strict aliasing: reading `char` bytes as `uint32_t` violates the aliasing rules unless an object of that type lives there (only `char`, `unsigned char` and `std::byte` may alias anything).
  - Alignment: `offset` may be odd; misaligned access is UB (traps on some CPUs; UBSan reports it).
  - Layout: padding and endianness must match the wire format exactly.
- Correct options:
  - `std::memcpy(&h, rx_buf + offset, sizeof h);`: well defined, alignment-free; compilers turn it into a plain load (no call) at `-O2`.
  - `std::bit_cast<To>(from)` (C++20): reinterpret the bytes of one trivially copyable value as another of the same size (`float` ↔ `uint32_t`, `std::array<std::byte, 8>` → `double`). `constexpr`, compile error if sizes differ.
  - `std::start_lifetime_as<T>(p)` (C++23): explicitly starts the lifetime of an implicit-lifetime `T` over existing bytes, keeping their values, with no copy. Library support is still limited (not in GCC 11's libstdc++ used for this chapter).
- Still convert byte order (`std::byteswap` in C++23, `ntohl`, or `std::endian` checks in C++20) and validate lengths before trusting any field.

#### 9. What malloc really costs (glibc, typical Linux)
- C++ says nothing about speed; everything below is implementation behaviour (glibc 2.35, x86-64).
- `new` → `operator new` → `malloc`. The path a call takes is not predictable from the call site:

| Path | When | Cost (order of magnitude) |
|---|---|---|
| **tcache** hit | Small sizes (up to 1032 bytes by default), per-thread cache of up to 7 freed chunks per size class | Tens of ns, no lock |
| Arena bins (fastbins, small/large bins) | tcache empty or full | Lock on the arena, bin search, possible coalescing |
| Grow heap with `brk`/`sbrk` (main arena) | No suitable free chunk | System call |
| `mmap` a dedicated region | Request ≥ mmap threshold (128 KiB default, adapts upward to 32 MiB) | System call; `free` does `munmap` immediately |
| First touch of a new page | After any of the growth paths | Page fault + kernel zeroes the page (µs level per page) |

- Threads: glibc creates additional **arenas** under contention (up to 8 × cores on 64-bit) so threads rarely share one lock, at the cost of more memory spread across arenas.
- Cross-thread free (allocate in producer, free in consumer) pushes chunks into another thread's arena or tcache: more locking and worse locality.
- `free` is not free either: coalescing neighbours, trimming the top of the heap, `munmap` (which on multi-threaded processes may need TLB shootdowns across cores).
- Low-latency conclusion: the problem is **variance** (tail latency), not the average. A hot path that is fast 99.9 % of the time and occasionally hits a syscall plus page faults ruins p99.9. Remedies: preallocate and reuse (reserve, pools, arenas, `std::pmr`, topic 11), pre-fault memory at startup (touch pages, `mlock`), replace the allocator (jemalloc, tcmalloc, mimalloc), and verify with an allocation-counting `operator new` in tests.
- ❌ "Every `new` takes a lock and makes a system call." ✅ The common small-allocation path is a user-space tcache pop; the expensive paths are rare but unpredictable.

#### 10. Fragmentation and RSS growth without a leak
- **External fragmentation**: plenty of free bytes in total, but split into holes too small or badly placed to satisfy a request (or to give back to the OS).
- **Internal fragmentation**: the allocator hands out more than requested (size classes, 16-byte alignment, chunk headers: a 24-byte request uses a 32-byte chunk).
- Why RSS stays high after `free` (glibc): the heap can only shrink from the top. One live block near the top pins everything below it; freed chunks inside the heap stay mapped (and counted in RSS) until `malloc_trim` or reuse. Measured: 200 000 × 256 B blocks (about 55 MB RSS), all freed except the last one: RSS unchanged; after `malloc_trim(0)` it dropped back to about 5 MB.
- Other causes of "growing memory, no leak":
  - Containers keep their capacity: a `vector` that once held 10 million elements keeps that buffer after `clear()` (`shrink_to_fit` or swap with an empty vector).
  - Unbounded queues/backlogs during bursts, caches without eviction, pools that grow to their high-water mark and never shrink.
  - Objects still reachable but retained longer than intended (a `shared_ptr` held in a map, a `weak_ptr` pinning a `make_shared` block: topic 07/09).
  - Per-thread arenas each holding their own free memory.
- Investigation: track RSS over time against workload; heap profilers (heaptrack, massif, jemalloc/tcmalloc profiling); `malloc_info`/`malloc_stats`; container sizes and capacities; pool high-water marks. Valgrind/LSan find leaks, not retention.

#### 11. Misconceptions to unlearn
- ❌ "`new` and `operator new` are the same thing." ✅ The new-expression allocates via `operator new` **and** constructs; `operator new` only allocates.
- ❌ "`new` returns `nullptr` when memory runs out." ✅ It throws `std::bad_alloc`; only `new (std::nothrow)` returns null. On Linux it often succeeds and the OOM killer acts later.
- ❌ "`delete` on an array just leaks the other elements." ✅ It is UB: wrong destructor count and wrong address passed to the deallocator.
- ❌ "Placement new allocates in the buffer." ✅ It allocates nothing; it constructs in storage you own.
- ❌ "After placement new, `delete p` cleans up." ✅ Call the destructor (`std::destroy_at`); the storage owner releases the storage.
- ❌ "Same address, same type: it's the same object." ✅ A new lifetime is a new object; old pointers are only valid under the transparent-replacement rules.
- ❌ "Casting the receive buffer to a struct pointer is fine." ✅ Aliasing, alignment, object lifetime and endianness all bite; use `memcpy`, `bit_cast` or `start_lifetime_as`.
- ❌ "Class `operator new` controls every allocation of that class." ✅ Not `make_shared`, not `::new`, not arrays without `operator new[]`.
- ❌ "`destroy_at` is C++20." ✅ `destroy_at` is C++17; `construct_at` is C++20.
- ❌ "RSS growing means a leak." ✅ Retention, fragmentation, capacity and unbounded queues grow RSS with every allocation correctly freed.

edge_cases.title: delete on memory from new[]
edge_cases.explanation:
- `auto* p = new Order[3]; delete p;` compiles silently.
- For types with destructors the pointer returned by `new[]` is 8 bytes past the real allocation (after the cookie), so `delete` runs one destructor and passes a wrong address to `operator delete`. Measured: glibc aborted with "munmap_chunk(): invalid pointer"; ASan: "attempting free on address which was not malloc()-ed". GCC 11 even warns at compile time: "'operator delete' called on pointer with nonzero offset 8 [-Wfree-nonheap-object]".
- For `new int[3]; delete p;` there is no cookie and it may appear to work: still UB, and ASan reports `alloc-dealloc-mismatch (operator new [] vs operator delete)`.
- Fix: `delete[]`, or better `std::vector` / `std::unique_ptr<T[]>`.

edge_cases.title: delete on a placement-new object
edge_cases.explanation:
- `alignas(T) std::byte buf[sizeof(T)]; T* p = new (buf) T; delete p;` runs the destructor, then frees a stack address: crash. ASan: "attempting free on address which was not malloc()-ed".
- In a pool the same mistake hands a slot inside the pool's block to `free`, corrupting the heap.
- Fix: `std::destroy_at(p);` and let the owner of `buf` manage the storage.

edge_cases.title: Forgetting the destructor after placement new
edge_cases.explanation:
- Constructing a `std::string` (or any resource owner) in a buffer and later just reusing or discarding the buffer leaks whatever the object owned.
- A long string's heap buffer is reported by LeakSanitizer as a direct leak; a short (SSO) string leaks nothing visible, which hides the bug in tests with short data.
- Constructing a second object over a live one has the same effect: the first destructor never runs.

edge_cases.title: Misaligned storage
edge_cases.explanation:
- `unsigned char buf[sizeof(T)];` has alignment 1. Placement new into it (or into `buf + 1`) can create a misaligned object: UB. UBSan: "constructor call on misaligned address ... which requires 4 byte alignment".
- On x86 most misaligned loads work (slower, and not atomic); on other architectures, or with SIMD/atomic instructions, they trap.
- Fix: `alignas(T) std::byte buf[sizeof(T)];`, or align offsets inside a pool to `alignof(T)`.

edge_cases.title: A throwing constructor and custom placement forms
edge_cases.explanation:
- With ordinary `new T`, a throwing constructor causes `operator delete` to be called automatically: no leak.
- With `new (arena) T` using a custom `operator new(std::size_t, Arena&)`, the compiler calls `operator delete(void*, Arena&)` only if you declared it. Without it, nothing is called (the memory leaks from the arena) and there is no warning.
- The non-allocating `new (void*) T` needs nothing: there is no memory to give back.

edge_cases.title: Class operator new is bypassed
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::make_shared<T>()` allocates control block + object through `std::allocator`: `T::operator new` is not called.
- `new T[n]` uses `T::operator new[]` if declared, otherwise the global one.
- `::new T` explicitly selects the global allocation function.
- If the class allocator exists for correctness (e.g. shared memory, a special heap), these bypasses are bugs: use `std::allocate_shared` with a matching allocator, or `= delete` the array forms.

edge_cases.title: Reusing storage and reading through the old pointer
edge_cases.explanation:
- `X* p = new (buf) X{1}; p->~X(); new (buf) X{2}; use(p->n);`
  - If `X` has a `const` (or reference) member: UB in C++17 without `std::launder(p)`; allowed in C++20 (transparent replacement).
  - Through `reinterpret_cast<X*>(buf)`: needs `std::launder` in every version.
- In practice compilers rarely miscompile simple cases, which is why the bug is hard to demonstrate; the rule matters in generic containers with inline storage.
- Fix: keep the pointer returned by the newest placement new.

edge_cases.title: if (p == nullptr) after new
edge_cases.explanation:
- `int* p = new int[n]; if (!p) return error;` never takes the error branch: plain `new` throws.
- The opposite mistake: `new (std::nothrow) T` and no null check.
- On Linux, `new char[8ULL << 30]` (8 GiB) typically succeeds on a 16 GB machine because of overcommit; failure shows up later as an OOM kill when pages are touched.

edge_cases.title: Implicit object creation is not a license for any cast
edge_cases.explanation:
- `malloc` then use as `Header*` is fine (C++20 implicit object creation for implicit-lifetime types).
- `malloc` then use as `std::string*` is not: `std::string` is not an implicit-lifetime type; its constructor must run (placement new).
- A `char` array (not `unsigned char` / `std::byte`) does not provide storage for implicit object creation.

interview_qa.question: What is the difference between the `new` expression and `operator new`?
interview_qa.answer: The `new` expression (`new T(args)`) is a language operation that calls an allocation function to get raw storage and then constructs a `T` in it. `operator new(std::size_t)` is only the allocation function: it returns bytes, like `malloc`, and constructs nothing. You can overload or replace `operator new`; you cannot change what the `new` expression does.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `delete p` is symmetric: destructor first, then `operator delete(p)`.
- Calling `operator new(sizeof(T))` directly gives raw memory with no object in it; you must construct one with placement new before use.
- Customization points are the functions (`operator new/delete` at global or class scope), which is how pools and allocation counters hook in.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "They're the same; `operator new` is just the name of the `new` keyword." Mixing them up leads to "I overloaded `operator new`, why does my constructor still run?" confusion.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: placement new is the new-expression with a non-allocating allocation function (`operator new(std::size_t, void*)` just returns the pointer).
interview_qa.key_takeaway: New-expression = allocate + construct; `operator new` = allocate only.

interview_qa.question: Walk through `new Order(5)` when the constructor throws. Is anything leaked?
interview_qa.answer: `operator new(sizeof(Order))` allocates, the constructor runs and throws, and the new-expression itself calls the matching `operator delete` on that storage before the exception propagates. Nothing leaks, and no destructor runs because the object's lifetime never began.
interview_qa.explanation:

interview_qa.question: Why is heap allocation considered a source of latency jitter? Does every `new` take a lock and make a system call?
interview_qa.answer: No. In glibc most small allocations are a per-thread tcache pop with no lock and no syscall. The jitter comes from the slow paths you cannot predict at the call site: arena bin searches and locks, coalescing on free, growing the heap with `brk`/`mmap`, and page faults when fresh pages are first touched. Low-latency code removes these from the hot path by preallocating.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Fast: tcache (up to 7 chunks per size class, sizes up to 1032 bytes by default).
- Slower: arena bins under a lock; glibc spreads threads over up to 8 × cores arenas.
- Slowest: `mmap` for blocks ≥ 128 KiB (threshold adapts), `brk` growth, page faults on first touch (kernel zeroes each page).
- Cross-thread free (producer allocates, consumer frees) adds contention and poor locality.
- Remedies: `reserve`, object pools, arenas / `std::pmr` (topic 11), pre-faulting memory at startup, faster allocators (jemalloc, tcmalloc, mimalloc), and an allocation-counting test.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`new` always takes a lock and goes to the kernel." That overstates the common case and loses credibility.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: "The issue is the tail (p99/p99.9), not the average; you don't know which path a given allocation takes."
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Allocation is usually cheap but unpredictable; predictability is what pools buy.

interview_qa.question: What is the difference between internal and external fragmentation?
interview_qa.answer: External fragmentation: free memory exists in total but is split into holes that cannot satisfy a request (or cannot be returned to the OS). Internal fragmentation: the allocator gives a block bigger than requested (size classes, alignment, headers), wasting space inside each allocation.
interview_qa.explanation:
- External example: `USED | free 32 | USED | free 16 | USED | free 64 | USED`: 112 bytes free, no 100-byte block.
- Internal example: glibc rounds a 24-byte request into a 32-byte chunk with header overhead; a pool of 256-byte slots storing 70-byte objects wastes 186 bytes per slot.
- Long-running processes with mixed lifetimes and sizes suffer external fragmentation most; fixed-size pools and arenas by lifetime avoid it.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Fragmentation means memory is leaked." Nothing is leaked; it is unusable or unreturnable.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: fragmentation is one reason RSS stays high after frees (Q16).
interview_qa.key_takeaway: External = unusable holes between blocks; internal = waste inside blocks.

interview_qa.question: Memory usage keeps growing but every allocation is eventually freed. What could cause it, and how do you investigate?
interview_qa.answer: Retention rather than a leak: containers keeping their capacity, unbounded queues or backlogs during bursts, caches without eviction, pools that grow to a high-water mark, objects reachable longer than intended, and allocator behaviour (heap top pinned by one live block, fragmentation, per-thread arenas). Investigate with RSS over time against load, heap profiling, container sizes and capacities, pool high-water marks and allocator statistics.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Measured (glibc): 200 000 × 256-byte blocks, all freed except the last: RSS stayed at about 58 MB; `malloc_trim(0)` brought it back to about 5 MB (theory Example 7).
- `vector::clear()` keeps the buffer; `shrink_to_fit()` (non-binding) or swapping with an empty vector releases it.
- Deep copies instead of moves cost CPU and temporary memory, but if the copies are destroyed they do not explain persistent growth.
- Tools: heaptrack, massif, jemalloc/tcmalloc heap profiles, `malloc_info`, `/proc/<pid>/smaps`.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "If valgrind reports no leaks, memory can't grow." Leak checkers find unreachable memory, not retained memory.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: bound every queue and cache explicitly, and decide the overflow policy (drop, block, shed load).
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Growing RSS without leaks means retention; find where memory is held, not where `delete` is missing.

interview_qa.question: Is `delete this` legal?
interview_qa.answer: Yes, if the object was allocated with plain `new` (not `new[]`, not placement, not on the stack or as a member), and after `delete this` the function touches no members, `this`, or virtual functions, and no caller uses the object again.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Classic use: intrusive reference counting (`void release() { if (--refs_ == 0) delete this; }`) and COM-style objects.
- Any member access after the `delete` is a use-after-free.
- Forcing heap allocation: make the destructor private/protected so stack instances fail to compile.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Never legal, an object can't delete itself." It is legal; it is just easy to misuse.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: with an atomic refcount, use `fetch_sub(1, std::memory_order_acq_rel) == 1` before `delete this` so all prior writes are visible to the deleting thread.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `delete this` is fine for `new`-allocated objects if nothing touches the object afterwards.

interview_qa.question: What is the difference between `new T`, `new T()` and `new T{}`?
interview_qa.answer: `new T` default-initializes: scalars and members of classes with a trivial (or defaulted, non-initializing) default constructor are left indeterminate. `new T()` and `new T{}` value-initialize: they zero those members first if the default constructor is not user-provided, then run it. With a user-provided constructor all three just call it.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `new int` → indeterminate; `new int()` / `new int{}` → 0.
- `struct P { int x; };`: `new P` leaves `x` indeterminate, `new P()` zeroes it.
- `struct Q { int x; Q() {} };`: `new Q()` does not zero `x`: the constructor is user-provided.
- Arrays: `new int[5]` indeterminate, `new int[5]()` and `new int[5]{}` zero.
- Reading an indeterminate value is UB; MemorySanitizer (Clang) or Valgrind memcheck catch it, ordinary tests often do not. (`-ftrivial-auto-var-init` only initializes stack variables; it does nothing for heap objects.)
- Pedantic detail: for an aggregate such as `P`, `new P{}` is formally aggregate initialization rather than value-initialization; the effect on `x` (zero) is the same.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Heap memory is always zeroed." Fresh pages from the OS are zero, recycled chunks are not.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: `std::make_unique<T>()` value-initializes; `std::make_unique_for_overwrite<T>()` (C++20) default-initializes deliberately to skip zeroing large buffers.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Parentheses or braces value-initialize; bare `new T` may leave garbage.

interview_qa.question: How would you guarantee that a latency-critical path performs no heap allocation?
interview_qa.answer: Design it in (preallocate everything at startup: `reserve`d containers, fixed-capacity buffers, object pools or arenas, no `std::function` or `std::string` growth on the path), then enforce it with a test that replaces global `operator new` with a counter and asserts zero allocations across many iterations after warm-up.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Hidden allocators: `std::string` beyond SSO, `std::function` with large captures, `std::shared_ptr` creation, `std::map`/`unordered_map` inserts, exceptions (`__cxa_allocate_exception`), logging/formatting, `std::vector` growth.
- Pre-fault memory (touch every page, optionally `mlock`) so the first real message does not pay page faults.
- `std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource` with `null_memory_resource()` upstream turns an unexpected allocation into a `bad_alloc` you see in testing (topic 11).
- Production monitoring: allocator statistics or eBPF uprobes on `malloc` for the hot thread.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Use `new` carefully." Without a test, allocations creep back in through library calls.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: allocation-free is a property you regression-test, like correctness.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Preallocate by design, prove it with an allocation-counting test.

practice_tasks.title: Question 2
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
operator new
Member()
Widget() body
~Member
operator delete
caught init failed
```

**Explanation:**
- The new-expression allocates first, then constructs: members, then the constructor body.
- The body throws: already-constructed members are destroyed (`~Member`), but `~Widget` does not run because the `Widget` lifetime never began.
- The new-expression then calls the matching `operator delete`, so the memory does not leak, and only then does the exception reach the `catch`.
- **Key Concept:** A throwing constructor in `new` gives back the memory automatically; only fully constructed subobjects are destroyed.

practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
caught std::bad_alloc
nothrow returned nullptr
```

**Explanation:**
- Plain `new` never returns `nullptr`; on failure it throws `std::bad_alloc`. The `if (p == nullptr)` branch is dead code.
- `new (std::nothrow)` reports failure by returning `nullptr`.
- 64 TiB exceeds what Linux will reserve even with overcommit, so the failure is immediate. A merely "too large for RAM" request (say 8 GiB on a 16 GB box) would typically succeed and fail later as an OOM kill when touched.
- Under ASan the program aborts instead ("requested allocation size exceeds maximum supported size"), unless `ASAN_OPTIONS=allocator_may_return_null=1`.
- **Key Concept:** Know which form you call: throwing `new` needs `try`, `nothrow` needs a null check.

practice_tasks.title: Question 8
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
handler call 1
handler call 2
handler call 3
bad_alloc after 3 handler calls
```

**Explanation:**
- On failure `operator new` calls the current new_handler and retries, in a loop, as long as a handler is installed.
- A handler must make progress: free memory (e.g. release a reserve block), install another handler, uninstall itself, throw `bad_alloc`, or terminate. A handler that does none of these loops forever.
- Here the third call uninstalls the handler, so the next failed attempt throws.
- Run without sanitizers (ASan's allocator aborts on this size instead).
- **Key Concept:** The new_handler is a retry loop, not a notification.

practice_tasks.title: Question 10
practice_tasks.answer:
Prints "2 250" with GCC at -O0, but:
C++17: undefined behaviour. Fill has a const member, so the new object does not transparently
replace the old one; p must be laundered: std::launder(p)->id.
C++20: well-defined (the const/reference-member restriction was removed).
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `p` pointed to the first `Fill`, whose lifetime ended at `p->~Fill()`. Whether `p` can reach the second `Fill` depends on the transparent replacement rules.
- In C++17, a `const` member let the compiler assume `p->id` never changes, so it could legally print a cached `1`.
- Simplest code that is correct in every version: keep the pointer returned by the second placement new.
- Accessing through `reinterpret_cast<Fill*>(buf)` would need `std::launder` in every version.
- **Key Concept:** Reused storage holds a new object; use the pointer from its construction (or `std::launder`).

caught bad leg
then LeakSanitizer: "Direct leak of 62 byte(s) in 2 object(s)": legs 0 and 1 were constructed
but never destroyed (their strings' heap buffers).

- The failing `Leg(2)` itself is fine: its `name` member was already constructed and is destroyed during unwinding.

practice_tasks.title: Question 12
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
0 0 0
5
```

**Explanation:**
- `new Plain()` value-initializes: `Plain` has no user-provided constructor, so `x` is zeroed. `new Plain{}` is aggregate initialization (`Plain` is an aggregate); a member with no initializer is initialized from `{}`, so `x` is also 0.
- `new int[4]()` value-initializes every element to 0.
- `new UserCtor()` calls the user-provided constructor, which initializes nothing: `x` is indeterminate, and reading it before assignment would be undefined behaviour (it may well print 0 on a fresh heap page, which hides the bug).
- `new Plain` (no parentheses) would also leave `x` indeterminate.
- **Key Concept:** Parentheses/braces zero-initialize only when the class has no user-provided default constructor.

quick_reference.content:
#### Expression vs function
| You write | Allocation | Construction | Destruction | Deallocation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `new T(a)` | `operator new(sizeof(T))` | yes | | |
| `delete p` | | | `~T()` | `operator delete(p)` |
| `new T[n]` | `operator new[](n*sizeof(T) + cookie)` | n times | | |
| `delete[] p` | | | n times (reverse) | `operator delete[]` |
| `new (buf) T(a)` | none | yes | | |
| `std::destroy_at(p)` (C++17) | | | `~T()` | none |
| `std::construct_at(p, a)` (C++20) | none | yes | | |
| `operator new(n)` | yes | no | | |

#### Failure behaviour
| Form | On failure |
|---|---|
| `new T` | throws `std::bad_alloc` (after calling the new_handler in a loop) |
| `new (std::nothrow) T` | returns `nullptr` |
| `new T[bad_n]` | throws `std::bad_array_new_length` |
| Constructor throws | memory released via matching `operator delete`, no destructor |
| Linux overcommit | big `new` may succeed; OOM killer later |

#### Standard versions
| Feature | Since |
|---|---|
| Sized `operator delete(void*, size_t)` | C++14 |
| Aligned new (`std::align_val_t`) | C++17 |
| `std::launder`, `std::destroy_at`, `std::destroy(_n)`, `uninitialized_*_construct` | C++17 |
| `std::construct_at`, `std::bit_cast`, implicit object creation, destroying delete | C++20 |
| `std::start_lifetime_as`, `std::byteswap`; `std::aligned_storage` deprecated | C++23 |

#### glibc malloc facts (not guaranteed by C++)
| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| Default `new` alignment | 16 bytes |
| tcache | per thread, up to 7 chunks per size class, sizes up to 1032 bytes |
| mmap threshold | 128 KiB default, adapts upward (max 32 MiB) |
| Arenas | up to 8 × cores (64-bit) |
| Array cookie | 8 bytes for types with non-trivial destructors (Itanium ABI) |
| Heap trimming | Only from the top; `malloc_trim(0)` also releases free pages inside |

#### Interview one-liners
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| `new` vs `operator new`? | Expression = allocate + construct; function = bytes only |
| Why `delete[]`? | Cookie and destructor count; mismatch is UB |
| Does `new` return null? | No, throws `bad_alloc` (except `nothrow`) |
| Constructor throws in `new`? | Memory freed automatically, no destructor |
| Does placement new allocate? | No; it constructs in your storage |
| Clean up placement new? | `std::destroy_at(p)`; never `delete p` |
| Same storage, new object: same object? | No, a new lifetime |
| What is `std::launder` for? | Getting a usable pointer to a new object in reused storage |
| Cast recv buffer to struct? | Use `memcpy` / `bit_cast` / C++23 `start_lifetime_as`; mind alignment and endianness |
| Is `malloc` slow? | Usually a fast tcache pop; the problem is unpredictable slow paths (tail latency) |
| RSS grows but no leak? | Retention: heap top pinned, capacity kept, unbounded queues, caches, arenas |
| `destroy_at` / `construct_at`? | C++17 / C++20 |
