subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- A general-purpose allocator (`operator new` / `malloc`) must serve any size, any lifetime, any thread. That generality costs bookkeeping and makes the cost of one call **unpredictable**.
- A **pool** or **arena** exploits something you know about the workload:
  - **Fixed size**: all objects are the same type (orders, messages) → a fixed-size object pool with a free list.
  - **Grouped lifetime**: everything allocated while handling one request/packet/frame dies together → an arena (bump allocator), freed in one step.
  - **Known thread ownership**: one thread allocates and frees → no synchronization at all.
- Two separate things are managed, and every design must keep them apart:
  - **Storage**: raw bytes owned by the pool for its whole life.
  - **Object lifetime**: starts at construction in a slot (placement new, see topic 10) and ends at the explicit destructor call. "Storage exists" is not "object exists".
- `std::pmr` (C++17, header `<memory_resource>`) standardizes the "where does the memory come from" part:
  - `std::pmr::memory_resource`: an abstract class with virtual allocate/deallocate.
  - `std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<T>`: an allocator that holds a `memory_resource*` and forwards to it.
  - `std::pmr::vector`, `std::pmr::string`, `std::pmr::map`, ...: ordinary containers whose allocator is `polymorphic_allocator`.
- The container's algorithm stays the same; only its allocation policy changes, chosen at **run time** without changing the container's type.
- The headline benefit is **predictability** (tail latency), not "faster on average". Always measure.

subsections.title: 2. Why general-purpose allocation hurts a hot path
subsections.content:
- The fast path of a modern allocator is cheap (glibc per-thread tcache: tens of ns). The problem is that you cannot tell which path a call will take:
  - tcache/fastbin hit (user space, cheap),
  - arena search, splitting and coalescing of free chunks,
  - lock contention on a shared arena,
  - growing the heap (`brk`/`mmap`) and first-touch **page faults**,
  - `free` that consolidates or returns memory to the OS (`munmap`, trim).
- Result: good median, bad p99/p99.9. A pool moves the expensive work (getting and touching memory) to startup, so the hot path does a bounded amount of work.
- Other wins: fewer cache misses on allocator metadata, objects packed contiguously (locality), no fragmentation from mixed lifetimes, memory use bounded and visible.
- Do not overstate it: "every `new` is a system call" is false. Most allocations never enter the kernel. The argument is variance, not average cost.
- Allocator internals (tcache, arenas, RSS growth) are covered in topic 10.

subsections.title: 3. Designing a fixed-size object pool
subsections.content:
- **Storage**: one block sized for N slots, allocated up front and suitably aligned:
  - `alignas(T) std::byte buf[N * sizeof(T)]`, or `::operator new(bytes, std::align_val_t{alignof(T)})` for over-aligned `T` (C++17).
  - Not `new T[N]`: that constructs N objects (runs N constructors) and ties slot lifetime to the array.
- **Slot address**: slot `i` is at `base + i * slot_size` bytes, not `base + i`. `slot_size` must be a multiple of `alignof(T)` (it is if you use `sizeof(T)`, which is always a multiple of `alignof(T)`).
- **Free list**:
  - Index-based: an array/stack of free indices (extra memory, simple).
  - **Intrusive**: a free slot stores the pointer to the next free slot inside its own bytes. No extra memory. Requires `slot_size >= sizeof(void*)` and pointer alignment; a `union Slot { Slot* next; alignas(T) std::byte obj[sizeof(T)]; };` gives both automatically.
- **Acquire** = pop free-list head + construct (placement new or `std::construct_at`); **release** = run `~T()` + push the slot. Both O(1), no search, no system call.
- **Release must not `delete`**: the storage belongs to the pool. `delete p` on a pooled object is UB (it was not allocated by a matching `new`).
- **Exception safety**: if the constructor throws after the slot was popped, push it back, otherwise the pool leaks a slot per failure.
- **Debug aids**: fill freed slots with a pattern, keep an in-use count, assert on double release, poison free slots under ASan (`ASAN_POISON_MEMORY_REGION`), assert all slots are free in the pool's destructor.
- **Handle type**: return `std::unique_ptr<T, PoolDeleter>` so release happens automatically (custom deleter, see topic 06). Raw `T*` handles invite leaks and double release.

subsections.title: 4. Sizing and the exhaustion policy
subsections.content:
- A bounded pool is only a design once you answer: **what happens when all slots are in use?** Interviewers ask this more than they ask about the free list.

| Policy | Behaviour | When it fits |
|---|---|---|
| Fail fast | `create()` returns `nullptr` / error code; caller rejects the request | Order entry: reject and alert instead of slowing everything down |
| Drop | Discard the new item (or the oldest) and count drops | Market data you can recover by snapshot, telemetry |
| Block | Wait until a slot is released (condition variable) | Producer may be slowed down safely (back-pressure) |
| Fallback to heap | Allocate from `new`, mark it as "not pooled" | Correctness matters more than latency; spikes stay visible in metrics |
| Grow | Allocate another chunk of slots (never move existing ones) | Unknown peak; growth happens off the hot path or rarely |

- Size from **measured peak + headroom**, and export the high-water mark as a metric.
- Pre-fault the memory at startup (touch every page, or `mlock`) so the first use on the hot path does not take page faults.
- Silent fallback to the heap is the worst choice in a latency-critical path: the system "works" while p99 quietly degrades.

subsections.title: 5. Pools and threads
subsections.content:
- A single shared free list touched by several threads:
  - With a mutex: correct, but every acquire/release serializes on one lock.
  - With an atomic head (CAS): lock-free, but the head's cache line bounces between cores, and a naive CAS pop suffers from **ABA** (see Chapter 4, lock-free and ABA). Still a contention hotspot.
- Usual answer: **per-thread pools** (`thread_local` pool or one pool per worker). No synchronization, no shared cache line.
- Per-thread pools raise the **cross-thread free** problem: object allocated by thread A and released by thread B. Options:
  - Ownership rule: only the owning thread releases (B sends the pointer back through a queue).
  - Remote-free list: B pushes onto A's lock-free "returned" stack; A drains it during its own acquires.
- **Reuse safety**: a slot may only be reused once no reader can still access it. With several consumers this is solved by **deferred reclamation** (per-consumer progress counters, epochs, hazard pointers): covered in Chapter 4.
- Pool bookkeeping (in-use counters per thread) should live on separate cache lines to avoid false sharing (topic 12 and the Systems chapter).
- PMR mirror: `unsynchronized_pool_resource` (one thread, no locking) vs `synchronized_pool_resource` (thread-safe).

subsections.title: 6. The PMR model
subsections.content:
- `std::pmr::memory_resource` (non-virtual interface pattern):

| Public, non-virtual | Private virtual you override |
|---|---|
| `void* allocate(size_t bytes, size_t align = alignof(max_align_t))` | `do_allocate(bytes, align)` |
| `void deallocate(void* p, size_t bytes, size_t align = alignof(max_align_t))` | `do_deallocate(p, bytes, align)` |
| `bool is_equal(const memory_resource& other) const noexcept` | `do_is_equal(other)` |

  - `deallocate` receives the size and alignment again, so a resource needs no per-block header.
  - `is_equal` answers "can memory allocated by one be freed by the other?". Containers use it to decide whether a move can steal buffers.
- `std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<T>`:
  - Holds only a `memory_resource*` (8 bytes on x86-64). Implicitly constructible from `memory_resource*`, so `std::pmr::vector<int> v(&res);` works.
  - Default-constructed: uses `std::pmr::get_default_resource()` at that moment.
  - C++20 adds `polymorphic_allocator<>` (= `<std::byte>`) and `allocate_bytes`, `allocate_object<T>`, `new_object<T>(args...)`, `delete_object(p)`.
  - Its copy assignment is **deleted**: the resource of a container is fixed at construction.
- Aliases: `std::pmr::vector<T>` = `std::vector<T, std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<T>>`; same for `string`, `deque`, `list`, `map`, `unordered_map`, `set`, ...
- Why runtime polymorphism instead of an allocator template parameter:
  - `std::vector<int, ArenaAlloc>` and `std::vector<int>` are different types, so every function taking them must be a template (type infection).
  - All `std::pmr::vector<int>` objects have the same type, whatever resource they use.
- Costs: a virtual call per allocation (often devirtualized or negligible next to the saving), one extra pointer per container (libstdc++ x86-64: `pmr::vector<int>` 32 vs 24 bytes, `pmr::string` 40 vs 32), and allocator-propagation rules that surprise people (section 9).

subsections.title: 7. Standard memory resources
subsections.content:
| Resource | Strategy | Frees individual blocks? | Thread-safe |
|---|---|---|---|
| `new_delete_resource()` | Calls global `operator new/delete` | Yes | Yes |
| `null_memory_resource()` | Every `allocate` throws `std::bad_alloc` | n/a | Yes |
| `monotonic_buffer_resource` | Bump pointer through a buffer, then upstream chunks | No (`deallocate` is a no-op) | No |
| `unsynchronized_pool_resource` | Pools of fixed-size blocks per size class | Yes, back to its pool for reuse | No |
| `synchronized_pool_resource` | Same, with internal locking | Yes | Yes |

- There is **no** `std::pmr::pool_resource`: the two pool classes are `synchronized_pool_resource` and `unsynchronized_pool_resource` (`std::pmr::pool_resource` is a compile error).
- Resources form chains through an **upstream** resource: when a resource runs out, it asks its upstream for more. The default upstream is `get_default_resource()` (normally `new_delete_resource()`).
- `null_memory_resource()` as upstream turns "a buffer with heap fallback" into "a hard bound": exhaustion throws instead of allocating.
- The standard resource classes (`monotonic_buffer_resource`, the two pool resources) are neither copyable nor movable (deleted copy constructor and assignment). Containers refer to resources by pointer.

subsections.title: 8. monotonic_buffer_resource and the pool resources in detail
subsections.content:
- **monotonic_buffer_resource** (arena):
  - Allocation: align the current pointer, bump it forward. Very cheap.
  - `deallocate`: does nothing. Memory comes back only on `release()` or destruction, all at once.
  - Initial buffer: optional; give it a stack or static buffer to avoid touching the heap at all. Ownership of that buffer stays with you.
  - When the current buffer is full it requests a new chunk from upstream, larger each time (geometric growth, factor implementation-defined; libstdc++ about 1.5x: 1088, 1600, 2368, 3520 bytes for 1000-byte requests). Large requests get a chunk big enough for them.
  - `release()`: returns all upstream chunks and resets to the initial buffer, so the next allocation reuses the stack buffer.
  - Ideal for: per-request / per-message / per-frame scratch data, parse trees, building a result that is discarded together.
  - Bad for: long-lived containers that grow or churn (each `vector` reallocation leaves the old buffer as dead space), mixed lifetimes (one long-lived object pins the whole arena).
- **unsynchronized_pool_resource / synchronized_pool_resource**:
  - Keep a set of pools, one per block-size class; each pool carves chunks from upstream into blocks and keeps freed blocks on a free list for reuse.
  - Freed blocks go back to the pool, **not** to the OS or upstream. Chunks are returned only on `release()` or destruction.
  - Requests larger than `largest_required_pool_block` bypass the pools: allocated directly from upstream and freed back immediately.
  - `std::pmr::pool_options{max_blocks_per_chunk, largest_required_pool_block}` tunes chunk growth and the size limit; the implementation may adjust them (`options()` returns the values actually used; libstdc++ default 16384 / 4096).
  - `synchronized_pool_resource` is safe for concurrent use (libstdc++ keeps per-thread pools plus a shared lock); `unsynchronized` must be used by one thread at a time.
- Choosing:

| Workload | Resource |
|---|---|
| Many small allocations, all freed together at the end of a unit of work | `monotonic_buffer_resource` (+ `release()` per unit) |
| Independent lifetimes, mixed sizes, one thread | `unsynchronized_pool_resource` |
| Same, shared between threads | `synchronized_pool_resource` (or one unsynchronized pool per thread) |
| Hard upper bound, never touch the heap | any of the above with `null_memory_resource()` upstream and a pre-sized buffer |
| One type, fixed count, special policies | your own object pool (section 3) |

subsections.title: 9. Allocator propagation: where pmr surprises people
subsections.content:
- **Uses-allocator construction**: when a `pmr` container constructs an element whose type "uses an allocator" (`pmr::string`, `pmr::vector`, `pair` of them), `polymorphic_allocator::construct` passes the container's resource down. Nested data lives in the same arena.
  - `std::pmr::vector<std::pmr::string>`: string buffers come from the resource.
  - `std::pmr::vector<std::string>`: only the vector's array comes from the resource; each long `std::string` still allocates from the global heap.
- `polymorphic_allocator` does **not** propagate on copy, move-assignment or swap (`propagate_on_container_*` are false, `select_on_container_copy_construction` returns a default-constructed allocator):

| Operation | Resource of the result |
|---|---|
| `pmr::vector<int> b(a);` copy construction | **default resource**, not `a`'s |
| `pmr::vector<int> b(a, &res);` allocator-extended copy | `res` |
| `pmr::vector<int> b(std::move(a));` move construction | `a`'s resource (buffer stolen) |
| `b = a;` copy assignment | `b` keeps its own resource |
| `b = std::move(a);` same resource (`is_equal`) | buffer stolen, O(1) |
| `b = std::move(a);` different resources | element-wise move into `b`'s resource: allocates, O(n) |
| `swap(a, b)` with different resources | **undefined behaviour** (precondition: equal allocators) |

- Returning a `pmr` container by value moves it: the result still points at the original resource (which may be about to die, see section 10).
- Rule: decide the resource at construction and pass it explicitly everywhere (`v(other, &res)`, `pmr::string s(&res)`); do not rely on assignment to "move data into the arena".

subsections.title: 10. Lifetime rules, custom resources, and pmr vs a custom pool
subsections.content:
- **The resource must outlive every object that uses it.** A container holds a raw `memory_resource*` and does not own the resource (same relationship as `string_view` to a string).
  - Declare the resource **before** the containers in a scope or class: destruction is in reverse order, so containers release their memory first.
  - Do not return a container that uses a local resource.
  - In a class, member order matters: a container member declared before its resource member is constructed with a pointer to an unconstructed resource and destroyed after the resource died.
- **Custom memory_resource**: derive, override the three private virtuals, forward to an upstream. Typical custom resources:
  - Counting / tracking resource (tests, metrics, "no allocation in the hot path" assertions).
  - A fixed-size slab tuned to one block size.
  - A resource over shared memory or a huge-page region.
  - `do_is_equal`: usually `this == &other` (or a `dynamic_cast` and compare state).
- **Default resource**: `std::pmr::set_default_resource(r)` replaces it process-wide (atomic, returns the old one). Pointing it at a counting resource in tests catches `pmr` objects created without an explicit resource. It does not affect `std::vector`/`std::string` or `new`.
- **pmr vs a hand-written pool**:
  - pmr: standard, composable, works with all containers and nested data, no free-list code to get wrong.
  - Custom pool: exact capacity, explicit exhaustion policy, known thread ownership, cache-line layout, no virtual call, objects rather than bytes.
  - Many systems use both: pmr arenas for request-scoped scratch data, custom pools/rings for the core message objects.

subsections.title: 11. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "A pool makes allocation faster." ✅ Its main value is bounded, predictable cost; measure average and tail separately.
- ❌ "Every `new` goes to the kernel." ✅ Most allocations are served in user space; the problem is the occasional slow path you cannot predict.
- ❌ "`new T[N]` is a good way to create the pool's storage." ✅ It constructs N objects; a pool needs raw aligned storage and constructs on acquire.
- ❌ "Releasing a pooled object means `delete p`." ✅ Run the destructor and return the slot; the storage belongs to the pool.
- ❌ "A monotonic resource over a 4096-byte buffer never touches the heap." ✅ Only if its upstream is `null_memory_resource()`; by default it falls back to the heap.
- ❌ "Monotonic memory is reused after `deallocate`." ✅ `deallocate` is a no-op; reuse only after `release()`.
- ❌ "`std::pmr::pool_resource` is the pool allocator." ✅ It does not exist: use `unsynchronized_pool_resource` or `synchronized_pool_resource`.
- ❌ "`pmr::vector<std::string>` keeps everything in my arena." ✅ Only the vector's array; use `pmr::vector<pmr::string>`.
- ❌ "Copying a pmr container keeps the resource." ✅ Copy construction uses the default resource; copy assignment keeps the target's resource.
- ❌ "The container owns its memory resource." ✅ It stores a pointer; the resource must outlive it.
- ❌ "A pool freeing a block returns memory to the OS." ✅ It returns the block to the pool for reuse; chunks go back only on `release()`/destruction.
- ❌ "PMR replaces custom object pools." ✅ It replaces a lot of allocator plumbing; specialised pools still win when capacity, policy and threading are fixed.

theory.full_text:
#### 1. Mental model
- A general-purpose allocator (`operator new` / `malloc`) must serve any size, any lifetime, any thread. That generality costs bookkeeping and makes the cost of one call **unpredictable**.
- A **pool** or **arena** exploits something you know about the workload:
  - **Fixed size**: all objects are the same type (orders, messages) → a fixed-size object pool with a free list.
  - **Grouped lifetime**: everything allocated while handling one request/packet/frame dies together → an arena (bump allocator), freed in one step.
  - **Known thread ownership**: one thread allocates and frees → no synchronization at all.
- Two separate things are managed, and every design must keep them apart:
  - **Storage**: raw bytes owned by the pool for its whole life.
  - **Object lifetime**: starts at construction in a slot (placement new, see topic 10) and ends at the explicit destructor call. "Storage exists" is not "object exists".
- `std::pmr` (C++17, header `<memory_resource>`) standardizes the "where does the memory come from" part:
  - `std::pmr::memory_resource`: an abstract class with virtual allocate/deallocate.
  - `std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<T>`: an allocator that holds a `memory_resource*` and forwards to it.
  - `std::pmr::vector`, `std::pmr::string`, `std::pmr::map`, ...: ordinary containers whose allocator is `polymorphic_allocator`.
- The container's algorithm stays the same; only its allocation policy changes, chosen at **run time** without changing the container's type.
- The headline benefit is **predictability** (tail latency), not "faster on average". Always measure.

#### 2. Why general-purpose allocation hurts a hot path
- The fast path of a modern allocator is cheap (glibc per-thread tcache: tens of ns). The problem is that you cannot tell which path a call will take:
  - tcache/fastbin hit (user space, cheap),
  - arena search, splitting and coalescing of free chunks,
  - lock contention on a shared arena,
  - growing the heap (`brk`/`mmap`) and first-touch **page faults**,
  - `free` that consolidates or returns memory to the OS (`munmap`, trim).
- Result: good median, bad p99/p99.9. A pool moves the expensive work (getting and touching memory) to startup, so the hot path does a bounded amount of work.
- Other wins: fewer cache misses on allocator metadata, objects packed contiguously (locality), no fragmentation from mixed lifetimes, memory use bounded and visible.
- Do not overstate it: "every `new` is a system call" is false. Most allocations never enter the kernel. The argument is variance, not average cost.
- Allocator internals (tcache, arenas, RSS growth) are covered in topic 10.

#### 3. Designing a fixed-size object pool
- **Storage**: one block sized for N slots, allocated up front and suitably aligned:
  - `alignas(T) std::byte buf[N * sizeof(T)]`, or `::operator new(bytes, std::align_val_t{alignof(T)})` for over-aligned `T` (C++17).
  - Not `new T[N]`: that constructs N objects (runs N constructors) and ties slot lifetime to the array.
- **Slot address**: slot `i` is at `base + i * slot_size` bytes, not `base + i`. `slot_size` must be a multiple of `alignof(T)` (it is if you use `sizeof(T)`, which is always a multiple of `alignof(T)`).
- **Free list**:
  - Index-based: an array/stack of free indices (extra memory, simple).
  - **Intrusive**: a free slot stores the pointer to the next free slot inside its own bytes. No extra memory. Requires `slot_size >= sizeof(void*)` and pointer alignment; a `union Slot { Slot* next; alignas(T) std::byte obj[sizeof(T)]; };` gives both automatically.
- **Acquire** = pop free-list head + construct (placement new or `std::construct_at`); **release** = run `~T()` + push the slot. Both O(1), no search, no system call.
- **Release must not `delete`**: the storage belongs to the pool. `delete p` on a pooled object is UB (it was not allocated by a matching `new`).
- **Exception safety**: if the constructor throws after the slot was popped, push it back, otherwise the pool leaks a slot per failure.
- **Debug aids**: fill freed slots with a pattern, keep an in-use count, assert on double release, poison free slots under ASan (`ASAN_POISON_MEMORY_REGION`), assert all slots are free in the pool's destructor.
- **Handle type**: return `std::unique_ptr<T, PoolDeleter>` so release happens automatically (custom deleter, see topic 06). Raw `T*` handles invite leaks and double release.

#### 4. Sizing and the exhaustion policy
- A bounded pool is only a design once you answer: **what happens when all slots are in use?** Interviewers ask this more than they ask about the free list.

| Policy | Behaviour | When it fits |
|---|---|---|
| Fail fast | `create()` returns `nullptr` / error code; caller rejects the request | Order entry: reject and alert instead of slowing everything down |
| Drop | Discard the new item (or the oldest) and count drops | Market data you can recover by snapshot, telemetry |
| Block | Wait until a slot is released (condition variable) | Producer may be slowed down safely (back-pressure) |
| Fallback to heap | Allocate from `new`, mark it as "not pooled" | Correctness matters more than latency; spikes stay visible in metrics |
| Grow | Allocate another chunk of slots (never move existing ones) | Unknown peak; growth happens off the hot path or rarely |

- Size from **measured peak + headroom**, and export the high-water mark as a metric.
- Pre-fault the memory at startup (touch every page, or `mlock`) so the first use on the hot path does not take page faults.
- Silent fallback to the heap is the worst choice in a latency-critical path: the system "works" while p99 quietly degrades.

#### 5. Pools and threads
- A single shared free list touched by several threads:
  - With a mutex: correct, but every acquire/release serializes on one lock.
  - With an atomic head (CAS): lock-free, but the head's cache line bounces between cores, and a naive CAS pop suffers from **ABA** (see Chapter 4, lock-free and ABA). Still a contention hotspot.
- Usual answer: **per-thread pools** (`thread_local` pool or one pool per worker). No synchronization, no shared cache line.
- Per-thread pools raise the **cross-thread free** problem: object allocated by thread A and released by thread B. Options:
  - Ownership rule: only the owning thread releases (B sends the pointer back through a queue).
  - Remote-free list: B pushes onto A's lock-free "returned" stack; A drains it during its own acquires.
- **Reuse safety**: a slot may only be reused once no reader can still access it. With several consumers this is solved by **deferred reclamation** (per-consumer progress counters, epochs, hazard pointers): covered in Chapter 4.
- Pool bookkeeping (in-use counters per thread) should live on separate cache lines to avoid false sharing (topic 12 and the Systems chapter).
- PMR mirror: `unsynchronized_pool_resource` (one thread, no locking) vs `synchronized_pool_resource` (thread-safe).

#### 6. The PMR model
- `std::pmr::memory_resource` (non-virtual interface pattern):

| Public, non-virtual | Private virtual you override |
|---|---|
| `void* allocate(size_t bytes, size_t align = alignof(max_align_t))` | `do_allocate(bytes, align)` |
| `void deallocate(void* p, size_t bytes, size_t align = alignof(max_align_t))` | `do_deallocate(p, bytes, align)` |
| `bool is_equal(const memory_resource& other) const noexcept` | `do_is_equal(other)` |

  - `deallocate` receives the size and alignment again, so a resource needs no per-block header.
  - `is_equal` answers "can memory allocated by one be freed by the other?". Containers use it to decide whether a move can steal buffers.
- `std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<T>`:
  - Holds only a `memory_resource*` (8 bytes on x86-64). Implicitly constructible from `memory_resource*`, so `std::pmr::vector<int> v(&res);` works.
  - Default-constructed: uses `std::pmr::get_default_resource()` at that moment.
  - C++20 adds `polymorphic_allocator<>` (= `<std::byte>`) and `allocate_bytes`, `allocate_object<T>`, `new_object<T>(args...)`, `delete_object(p)`.
  - Its copy assignment is **deleted**: the resource of a container is fixed at construction.
- Aliases: `std::pmr::vector<T>` = `std::vector<T, std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<T>>`; same for `string`, `deque`, `list`, `map`, `unordered_map`, `set`, ...
- Why runtime polymorphism instead of an allocator template parameter:
  - `std::vector<int, ArenaAlloc>` and `std::vector<int>` are different types, so every function taking them must be a template (type infection).
  - All `std::pmr::vector<int>` objects have the same type, whatever resource they use.
- Costs: a virtual call per allocation (often devirtualized or negligible next to the saving), one extra pointer per container (libstdc++ x86-64: `pmr::vector<int>` 32 vs 24 bytes, `pmr::string` 40 vs 32), and allocator-propagation rules that surprise people (section 9).

#### 7. Standard memory resources
| Resource | Strategy | Frees individual blocks? | Thread-safe |
|---|---|---|---|
| `new_delete_resource()` | Calls global `operator new/delete` | Yes | Yes |
| `null_memory_resource()` | Every `allocate` throws `std::bad_alloc` | n/a | Yes |
| `monotonic_buffer_resource` | Bump pointer through a buffer, then upstream chunks | No (`deallocate` is a no-op) | No |
| `unsynchronized_pool_resource` | Pools of fixed-size blocks per size class | Yes, back to its pool for reuse | No |
| `synchronized_pool_resource` | Same, with internal locking | Yes | Yes |

- There is **no** `std::pmr::pool_resource`: the two pool classes are `synchronized_pool_resource` and `unsynchronized_pool_resource` (`std::pmr::pool_resource` is a compile error).
- Resources form chains through an **upstream** resource: when a resource runs out, it asks its upstream for more. The default upstream is `get_default_resource()` (normally `new_delete_resource()`).
- `null_memory_resource()` as upstream turns "a buffer with heap fallback" into "a hard bound": exhaustion throws instead of allocating.
- The standard resource classes (`monotonic_buffer_resource`, the two pool resources) are neither copyable nor movable (deleted copy constructor and assignment). Containers refer to resources by pointer.

#### 8. monotonic_buffer_resource and the pool resources in detail
- **monotonic_buffer_resource** (arena):
  - Allocation: align the current pointer, bump it forward. Very cheap.
  - `deallocate`: does nothing. Memory comes back only on `release()` or destruction, all at once.
  - Initial buffer: optional; give it a stack or static buffer to avoid touching the heap at all. Ownership of that buffer stays with you.
  - When the current buffer is full it requests a new chunk from upstream, larger each time (geometric growth, factor implementation-defined; libstdc++ about 1.5x: 1088, 1600, 2368, 3520 bytes for 1000-byte requests). Large requests get a chunk big enough for them.
  - `release()`: returns all upstream chunks and resets to the initial buffer, so the next allocation reuses the stack buffer.
  - Ideal for: per-request / per-message / per-frame scratch data, parse trees, building a result that is discarded together.
  - Bad for: long-lived containers that grow or churn (each `vector` reallocation leaves the old buffer as dead space), mixed lifetimes (one long-lived object pins the whole arena).
- **unsynchronized_pool_resource / synchronized_pool_resource**:
  - Keep a set of pools, one per block-size class; each pool carves chunks from upstream into blocks and keeps freed blocks on a free list for reuse.
  - Freed blocks go back to the pool, **not** to the OS or upstream. Chunks are returned only on `release()` or destruction.
  - Requests larger than `largest_required_pool_block` bypass the pools: allocated directly from upstream and freed back immediately.
  - `std::pmr::pool_options{max_blocks_per_chunk, largest_required_pool_block}` tunes chunk growth and the size limit; the implementation may adjust them (`options()` returns the values actually used; libstdc++ default 16384 / 4096).
  - `synchronized_pool_resource` is safe for concurrent use (libstdc++ keeps per-thread pools plus a shared lock); `unsynchronized` must be used by one thread at a time.
- Choosing:

| Workload | Resource |
|---|---|
| Many small allocations, all freed together at the end of a unit of work | `monotonic_buffer_resource` (+ `release()` per unit) |
| Independent lifetimes, mixed sizes, one thread | `unsynchronized_pool_resource` |
| Same, shared between threads | `synchronized_pool_resource` (or one unsynchronized pool per thread) |
| Hard upper bound, never touch the heap | any of the above with `null_memory_resource()` upstream and a pre-sized buffer |
| One type, fixed count, special policies | your own object pool (section 3) |

#### 9. Allocator propagation: where pmr surprises people
- **Uses-allocator construction**: when a `pmr` container constructs an element whose type "uses an allocator" (`pmr::string`, `pmr::vector`, `pair` of them), `polymorphic_allocator::construct` passes the container's resource down. Nested data lives in the same arena.
  - `std::pmr::vector<std::pmr::string>`: string buffers come from the resource.
  - `std::pmr::vector<std::string>`: only the vector's array comes from the resource; each long `std::string` still allocates from the global heap.
- `polymorphic_allocator` does **not** propagate on copy, move-assignment or swap (`propagate_on_container_*` are false, `select_on_container_copy_construction` returns a default-constructed allocator):

| Operation | Resource of the result |
|---|---|
| `pmr::vector<int> b(a);` copy construction | **default resource**, not `a`'s |
| `pmr::vector<int> b(a, &res);` allocator-extended copy | `res` |
| `pmr::vector<int> b(std::move(a));` move construction | `a`'s resource (buffer stolen) |
| `b = a;` copy assignment | `b` keeps its own resource |
| `b = std::move(a);` same resource (`is_equal`) | buffer stolen, O(1) |
| `b = std::move(a);` different resources | element-wise move into `b`'s resource: allocates, O(n) |
| `swap(a, b)` with different resources | **undefined behaviour** (precondition: equal allocators) |

- Returning a `pmr` container by value moves it: the result still points at the original resource (which may be about to die, see section 10).
- Rule: decide the resource at construction and pass it explicitly everywhere (`v(other, &res)`, `pmr::string s(&res)`); do not rely on assignment to "move data into the arena".

#### 10. Lifetime rules, custom resources, and pmr vs a custom pool
- **The resource must outlive every object that uses it.** A container holds a raw `memory_resource*` and does not own the resource (same relationship as `string_view` to a string).
  - Declare the resource **before** the containers in a scope or class: destruction is in reverse order, so containers release their memory first.
  - Do not return a container that uses a local resource.
  - In a class, member order matters: a container member declared before its resource member is constructed with a pointer to an unconstructed resource and destroyed after the resource died.
- **Custom memory_resource**: derive, override the three private virtuals, forward to an upstream. Typical custom resources:
  - Counting / tracking resource (tests, metrics, "no allocation in the hot path" assertions).
  - A fixed-size slab tuned to one block size.
  - A resource over shared memory or a huge-page region.
  - `do_is_equal`: usually `this == &other` (or a `dynamic_cast` and compare state).
- **Default resource**: `std::pmr::set_default_resource(r)` replaces it process-wide (atomic, returns the old one). Pointing it at a counting resource in tests catches `pmr` objects created without an explicit resource. It does not affect `std::vector`/`std::string` or `new`.
- **pmr vs a hand-written pool**:
  - pmr: standard, composable, works with all containers and nested data, no free-list code to get wrong.
  - Custom pool: exact capacity, explicit exhaustion policy, known thread ownership, cache-line layout, no virtual call, objects rather than bytes.
  - Many systems use both: pmr arenas for request-scoped scratch data, custom pools/rings for the core message objects.

#### 11. Misconceptions to unlearn
- ❌ "A pool makes allocation faster." ✅ Its main value is bounded, predictable cost; measure average and tail separately.
- ❌ "Every `new` goes to the kernel." ✅ Most allocations are served in user space; the problem is the occasional slow path you cannot predict.
- ❌ "`new T[N]` is a good way to create the pool's storage." ✅ It constructs N objects; a pool needs raw aligned storage and constructs on acquire.
- ❌ "Releasing a pooled object means `delete p`." ✅ Run the destructor and return the slot; the storage belongs to the pool.
- ❌ "A monotonic resource over a 4096-byte buffer never touches the heap." ✅ Only if its upstream is `null_memory_resource()`; by default it falls back to the heap.
- ❌ "Monotonic memory is reused after `deallocate`." ✅ `deallocate` is a no-op; reuse only after `release()`.
- ❌ "`std::pmr::pool_resource` is the pool allocator." ✅ It does not exist: use `unsynchronized_pool_resource` or `synchronized_pool_resource`.
- ❌ "`pmr::vector<std::string>` keeps everything in my arena." ✅ Only the vector's array; use `pmr::vector<pmr::string>`.
- ❌ "Copying a pmr container keeps the resource." ✅ Copy construction uses the default resource; copy assignment keeps the target's resource.
- ❌ "The container owns its memory resource." ✅ It stores a pointer; the resource must outlive it.
- ❌ "A pool freeing a block returns memory to the OS." ✅ It returns the block to the pool for reuse; chunks go back only on `release()`/destruction.
- ❌ "PMR replaces custom object pools." ✅ It replaces a lot of allocator plumbing; specialised pools still win when capacity, policy and threading are fixed.

edge_cases.title: "The buffer is 4096 bytes, so the heap is never used"
edge_cases.explanation:
- `monotonic_buffer_resource r(buf.data(), buf.size());` silently falls back to `get_default_resource()` (the heap) when the buffer is exhausted.
- Verified (libstdc++): a 1000-byte request fits the buffer; a following 5000-byte request makes the resource call upstream `allocate(6208)`.
- For a hard bound pass `std::pmr::null_memory_resource()` as upstream: the same 5000-byte request then throws `std::bad_alloc`, which you can catch and handle as an explicit exhaustion policy.

edge_cases.title: Vector growth wastes a monotonic arena
edge_cases.explanation:
- `deallocate` is a no-op, so every reallocation of a growing `pmr::vector` leaves the old array as dead space.
- With a 4096-byte buffer and `null_memory_resource()` upstream, pushing 1000 `int`s (4000 bytes) throws `bad_alloc` at size 512: the capacities 1, 2, 4, ..., 512 already consumed 4092 bytes and 1024 more `int`s do not fit.
- After `v.reserve(1000)` the same 1000 elements fit easily.
- Same effect with `erase`/`insert` churn, rehashing `pmr::unordered_map`, string concatenation in a loop.

edge_cases.title: The nested type does not use the resource
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::pmr::vector<std::string> v(&res);` allocates its array from `res`, but each long `std::string` element allocates its own buffer with `std::allocator`, i.e. the global heap.
- `std::pmr::vector<std::pmr::string> v(&res);` passes `res` to every element through uses-allocator construction (verified with a counting resource).
- Same trap with `pmr::map<std::string, std::vector<int>>`: use `pmr::string` and `pmr::vector` all the way down.

edge_cases.title: Copy construction leaves the arena
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::pmr::vector<pmr::string> copy = v;` uses the **default** resource, not `v`'s (`select_on_container_copy_construction` returns a default `polymorphic_allocator`). Verified: `copy.get_allocator().resource() == &res` is false.
- Hidden copies (passing by value, `auto x = container;`, returning a member by value) silently move data to the heap.
- Fix: allocator-extended copy `pmr::vector<pmr::string> copy(v, &res);`.

edge_cases.title: Move assignment between different resources is a copy
edge_cases.explanation:
- `b = std::move(a);` steals `a`'s buffer only if `a` and `b` use equal resources. With different resources, `b` keeps its own resource and moves elements one by one into newly allocated memory: O(n) and allocating (verified: `b.data()` differs from `a`'s old buffer).
- `swap(a, b)` with unequal resources is undefined behaviour.
- Move construction always takes the source's resource, so it is O(1) but carries the (maybe short-lived) resource with it.

edge_cases.title: The resource dies before the container
edge_cases.explanation:
- A container holds a raw pointer to its resource. Three common ways to break that:
  - Returning a `pmr` container from a function that owns the resource as a local.
  - Class members in the wrong order: `struct S { pmr::vector<int> v{&res}; monotonic_buffer_resource res; };` constructs `v` with a pointer to a not-yet-constructed `res`, and destroys `res` before `v`.
  - Storing a `pmr` container in a longer-lived structure (cache, queue) while the per-request arena is released.
- Symptoms: use-after-free (ASan reports heap-use-after-free on the chunks the resource freed), or a call through a destroyed object's vtable.

edge_cases.title: Unsynchronized resources shared by threads
edge_cases.explanation:
- `monotonic_buffer_resource` and `unsynchronized_pool_resource` have no internal locking. Two threads allocating from the same instance is a data race even if each thread uses its own container.
- Fix: one resource per thread (`thread_local` arena), or `synchronized_pool_resource`, or an external lock.
- `new_delete_resource()`, `null_memory_resource()` and `synchronized_pool_resource` are safe to share.

edge_cases.title: The pooled object is released twice or to the wrong pool
edge_cases.explanation:
- An intrusive free list has no protection: releasing the same pointer twice puts one slot on the free list twice, and two later `create()` calls return the **same** address. Two live objects share storage; corruption appears far from the bug.
- Releasing a pointer that was never from this pool links a foreign address into the free list.
- `delete` on a pooled object: UB (not from `new`).
- Defences: `unique_ptr` with a pool deleter as the only handle, debug-mode "in use" bitmap, address-range checks, ASan poisoning of free slots.

edge_cases.title: Slot too small or misaligned for the free list
edge_cases.explanation:
- An intrusive free list stores a pointer inside each free slot. If `sizeof(T) < sizeof(void*)` (e.g. a pool of `char` or `short`), the link overwrites the neighbouring slot.
- If slot storage is not aligned for `T` (`std::byte buf[N * sizeof(T)]` without `alignas(T)`), objects are misaligned: UB, slow or faulting loads on some CPUs, broken atomics.
- A `union Slot { Slot* next; alignas(T) std::byte obj[sizeof(T)]; };` fixes both: the slot is at least pointer-sized and aligned for both members.

code_examples.title: A fixed-size object pool with an intrusive free list
code_examples.explanation:
- Union slots (the object is a union member, so slot size and alignment come for free), O(1) acquire/release, exception-safe construction, and a "fail fast" exhaustion policy.

- Output:

- LIFO reuse: the most recently freed slot is handed out next, which is also the one most likely to be in cache.
- Lifetime: `create` starts an `Order`'s lifetime in existing storage; `destroy` ends it; the storage lives as long as the pool.
- Getting back from `T*` to the slot: because `obj` is a union member, the union and `obj` are pointer-interconvertible, so `reinterpret_cast<Slot*>(p)` is well defined. With a `std::byte` array member instead, the cast relies on layout assumptions the standard does not bless.

interview_qa.question: What is a memory pool, and why would a low-latency system use one?
interview_qa.answer: A memory pool preallocates a block of storage and hands out reusable slots from it instead of calling the general-purpose allocator for every object. Allocation and release become a bounded, O(1) operation on the pool's own free list, which makes hot-path latency predictable.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Startup: allocate (and pre-touch) storage for N objects. Hot path: pop a slot, construct the object in it; on release destroy the object and push the slot back.
- Benefits: no allocator bookkeeping or locking on the hot path, no surprise page faults, memory bounded and measurable, objects packed together (locality), no fragmentation from mixed lifetimes.
- Costs: fixed capacity, an exhaustion policy to design, manual lifetime management, thread-ownership rules.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Because `new` is slow and always calls the kernel." Most allocations are served in user space in tens of nanoseconds.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the win is variance (p99/p99.9), so prove it with latency percentiles, not just an average benchmark.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: A pool replaces "unknown allocator path" with "bounded free-list operation" on the hot path.

interview_qa.question: malloc's fast path is only tens of nanoseconds. What exactly does a pool change that removes allocation jitter?
interview_qa.answer: A pool replaces "usually fast, occasionally slow" with "always the same few instructions". All memory is obtained and touched at startup; on the hot path acquire and release are a pop and a push on a free list, with no searching, no lock, no system call and no first-touch page fault. Why general-purpose `malloc` has a slow tail (bins, arena locks, `brk`/`mmap`, page faults) is covered in topic 10 Q14.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Why the tail matters at all: at 500k messages/s, a 1-in-10,000 slow allocation still happens 50 times a second, and each one lands on some message's latency.
- What the pool removes from the hot path:
  - Variable work: no size-class lookup, no splitting or coalescing; every slot has the same size.
  - Kernel involvement: memory is allocated and pre-faulted (written once) at startup, so no `brk`/`mmap` and no page faults later.
  - Contention: a per-thread (or single-threaded) pool needs no lock and no atomic.
  - Poor locality: slots are contiguous, and LIFO reuse hands out the slot that was freed most recently, which is likely still in cache.
- What it does not remove:
  - Allocations inside the object (a `std::string` or `std::vector` member still uses the heap unless it is a pmr type or fixed-capacity).
  - Constructor and destructor cost.
  - The exhaustion decision: a pool makes capacity explicit, so running out needs a policy (Q6).
  - Cross-thread release: a slot freed on another thread needs a return path (Q7).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Pools are faster because malloc always takes a lock." The average gain can be small; the win is the bounded worst case.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: prove it with a latency histogram (p99/p99.9) before and after, not with an average (Q20).
interview_qa.key_takeaway: A pool trades flexibility for a bounded, constant-time hot path; it fixes variance, not just the mean.

interview_qa.question: A candidate creates the pool with `new Order[10000]`. What is wrong with that?
interview_qa.answer: `new Order[10000]` constructs 10,000 `Order` objects up front, requires a default constructor, and ties all their lifetimes to the array. A pool needs raw, suitably aligned storage, constructs an object only when a slot is acquired and destroys it when the slot is released.
interview_qa.explanation:
- "Storage exists" is not "object exists": the pool owns bytes; each object's lifetime starts at placement new (or `std::construct_at`) and ends at `p->~Order()` (topic 10).
- Raw storage options: `alignas(Order) std::byte buf[N * sizeof(Order)]`, or `::operator new(bytes, std::align_val_t{alignof(Order)})` for over-aligned types (C++17).
- With an array of live objects you would have to "reset" objects instead of constructing them, and `delete[]` would run 10,000 destructors at shutdown.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "It's fine, placement new on top of an existing object is the same thing." Constructing over a live non-trivial object without destroying it first skips its destructor and leaks its resources.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: slot `i` lives at `base + i * sizeof(Order)` bytes, not `base + i`.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Allocate raw aligned bytes once; construct on acquire, destroy on release.

interview_qa.question: How do you make acquire and release O(1), and what constraints does an intrusive free list put on the slot?
interview_qa.answer: Keep the free slots in a singly linked list whose "next" pointer is stored inside the free slot itself. Acquire pops the head, release pushes onto the head: both O(1) with no search. The slot must be at least `sizeof(void*)` bytes and aligned for both a pointer and `T`.
interview_qa.explanation:
- A union does both for free:
```cpp
union Slot {
    Slot* next;                                // meaningful while free
    alignas(T) std::byte storage[sizeof(T)];   // meaningful while in use
};
```
- Alternatives: a stack of free indices (extra memory, but works for tiny `T` and makes double-free checks easy), or a bitmap (needs a search).
- LIFO reuse returns the most recently freed (cache-warm) slot.
- If the constructor throws after popping, push the slot back or the pool slowly leaks.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Scan the array for a free slot." O(N) and unpredictable, which defeats the purpose.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: a pool of `char` with an intrusive list would let the link overwrite neighbouring slots; the union's size and alignment prevent that.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Intrusive free list = zero extra memory and O(1), provided the slot can hold an aligned pointer.

interview_qa.question: How must a pooled object be released? What happens if someone calls `delete` on it?
interview_qa.answer: Call the destructor explicitly (`p->~T()` or `std::destroy_at(p)`) and return the slot to the pool's free list. `delete p` is undefined behaviour: the pointer did not come from a matching `new`, so the global allocator would try to free memory it never handed out. The symptom varies with where the pool storage lives (observed with glibc 2.35): "free(): invalid pointer" for a slot inside a heap block, "double free or corruption (out)" for stack-backed storage, or no message at all when the slot happens to be the first byte of the pool's own heap block (that `delete` frees the entire pool, and the crash comes later, far from the bug).
interview_qa.explanation:
- The storage belongs to the pool for the pool's whole life; only the object's lifetime ends at release.
- Make the right thing automatic: hand out `std::unique_ptr<T, PoolDeleter>` where the deleter calls `pool.destroy(p)`. Stateful deleter: 16 bytes per handle (topic 06).
- Releasing twice puts one slot on the free list twice; two later acquires get the same address. Debug builds should track in-use slots.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Just skip the destructor, the memory is reused anyway." Fine only for trivially destructible types; otherwise strings, vectors and file handles inside leak.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: in debug builds, poison freed slots (fill pattern, ASan poisoning) so use-after-release is caught.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Release = destroy the object + return the slot; never `delete`, and wrap it in a deleter.

interview_qa.question: Your pool has 10,000 slots and all are in use. What should happen on the next acquire?
interview_qa.answer: It depends on the domain, but it must be an explicit decision: fail fast (return an error and reject the request), drop (and count drops), block until a slot frees (back-pressure), fall back to the heap visibly, or grow by another chunk. Silent fallback in a latency-critical path is the worst choice.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Order entry: rejecting a new order with an alert is often better than slowing every order down.
- Recoverable market data: dropping and resynchronizing from a snapshot can be acceptable.
- Back-pressure: blocking the producer is safe only if the producer can afford to wait.
- Growth: allocate a new chunk (never move live objects); do it off the hot path or accept a rare spike.
- Sizing: measured peak plus headroom, export the high-water mark, alert well before exhaustion.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Make the pool big enough so it never happens." Load is bounded by the outside world, not by your estimate.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: exhaustion is usually a symptom of a stuck consumer or a leak of handles; the metric matters as much as the policy.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: A bounded pool is only a design once the exhaustion policy is defined.

interview_qa.question: Several threads acquire and release from one pool. What problems appear, and how do you design around them?
interview_qa.answer: A shared free list needs synchronization: a mutex serializes every acquire, and an atomic CAS head is lock-free but its cache line bounces between cores and a naive pop suffers from ABA. The usual design is per-thread pools, which then need a rule for objects freed by a thread other than the one that allocated them.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Per-thread pools: `thread_local` or one pool per worker; no locks, no shared cache line.
- Cross-thread free: either only the owner releases (send the pointer back through a queue), or the freeing thread pushes onto the owner's lock-free "remote free" stack that the owner drains.
- Multiple readers of one pooled message: a slot can be reused only when no reader can still see it; use deferred reclamation (progress counters, epochs, hazard pointers: Chapter 4).
- Keep per-thread counters and pool headers on separate cache lines (false sharing, topic 12).
- PMR equivalent: `synchronized_pool_resource` (shared) vs `unsynchronized_pool_resource` per thread.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Make the head atomic and it's solved." Correctness needs ABA protection (tagged pointer or similar), and performance still suffers from contention.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: ownership design first (who allocates, who frees), synchronization second.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Prefer partitioning (one pool per thread) over sharing; then solve cross-thread frees explicitly.

interview_qa.question: What is `std::pmr`, and why use polymorphic allocators instead of a custom allocator template parameter?
interview_qa.answer: `std::pmr` (C++17, `<memory_resource>`) separates a container from its allocation strategy: containers use `polymorphic_allocator`, which forwards to a `memory_resource*` chosen at run time. Unlike a template allocator, the strategy is not part of the type, so `std::pmr::vector<int>` objects using a heap, an arena or a pool are all the same type.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `std::vector<int, ArenaAlloc<int>>` and `std::vector<int>` are different types: every function that accepts them must be a template, and you cannot store them in the same container.
- `memory_resource` is an abstract class: public `allocate`/`deallocate`/`is_equal`, private virtual `do_*` functions.
- Standard resources: `new_delete_resource()`, `null_memory_resource()`, `monotonic_buffer_resource`, `unsynchronized_pool_resource`, `synchronized_pool_resource`.
- Resources chain through an upstream resource used when they run out.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "pmr is a faster allocator." It is a framework; speed depends on the resource and workload.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: nested allocator-aware types (pmr strings inside a pmr vector) receive the same resource automatically through uses-allocator construction.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: PMR = runtime-selected allocation strategy without changing the container's type.

interview_qa.question: What does `monotonic_buffer_resource` do, and for which workloads is it ideal or harmful?
interview_qa.answer: It is an arena: each allocation bumps a pointer forward through a buffer (asking upstream for bigger chunks when full), `deallocate` does nothing, and all memory is reclaimed at once by `release()` or destruction. It is ideal when many allocations share one lifetime (per request, per message, per frame) and harmful when objects have independent lifetimes or containers grow and churn.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Very cheap allocation: align, bump, bounds check.
- Grouped lifetime pattern: build scratch structures for one message, process, `release()`.
- Harmful cases:
  - A long-lived object in the arena pins all the dead space around it.
  - A growing `pmr::vector` leaves every old array as dead space (reserve first).
  - Long-running containers with insert/erase churn grow without bound.
- Not thread-safe: one arena per thread.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "When an object is freed its memory is reused by the next allocation." Not until `release()`.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: "monotonic" (not "monolithic") refers to the allocation pointer only moving forward.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Monotonic = bump allocate, never free individually, release everything together.

interview_qa.question: I gave a monotonic resource a 4096-byte stack buffer. Can it still touch the heap?
interview_qa.answer: Yes. When the buffer is exhausted it asks its upstream resource, which defaults to `get_default_resource()` (normally `new_delete_resource()`, the heap). To make the buffer a hard bound, pass `std::pmr::null_memory_resource()` as upstream; exhaustion then throws `std::bad_alloc`.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Buffer + default upstream = soft limit; buffer + `null_memory_resource()` = hard limit.

interview_qa.question: How do `monotonic_buffer_resource`, `unsynchronized_pool_resource` and `synchronized_pool_resource` differ?
interview_qa.answer: Monotonic never reuses individual blocks and frees all at once. The pool resources keep per-size-class pools of blocks and reuse freed blocks, so they suit independent lifetimes; `unsynchronized` has no locking and must be used by one thread at a time, `synchronized` is safe to share between threads.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Pool resources carve chunks from upstream into fixed-size blocks; `deallocate` returns a block to its pool (not to the OS). Chunks go back on `release()` or destruction.
- Requests above `largest_required_pool_block` bypass the pools and go directly to upstream.
- `std::pmr::pool_options{max_blocks_per_chunk, largest_required_pool_block}` tunes them; `options()` returns the effective values (libstdc++ defaults 16384 and 4096).
- Typical combination: per-thread `unsynchronized_pool_resource` with a `monotonic_buffer_resource` upstream for a fully preallocated region.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Use `std::pmr::pool_resource`." There is no such class; it is a compile error.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: `synchronized` is not free; one unsynchronized pool per thread avoids lock traffic entirely.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Grouped lifetimes → monotonic; independent lifetimes → pool (unsynchronized per thread, synchronized when shared).

interview_qa.question: Why does `std::pmr::vector<std::string>` still allocate from the heap, while `std::pmr::vector<std::pmr::string>` does not?
interview_qa.answer: Only the vector's own array uses the resource. A `std::string` element uses `std::allocator`, so each long string allocates its buffer on the global heap. `std::pmr::string` is allocator-aware with a `polymorphic_allocator`, so the vector passes its resource to each element through uses-allocator construction.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `polymorphic_allocator::construct` checks `std::uses_allocator<T, polymorphic_allocator<...>>` and, if true, appends the allocator to the constructor arguments.
- It works recursively: `pmr::map<pmr::string, pmr::vector<pmr::string>>` keeps everything in the same resource.
- Short strings fit the SSO buffer (no allocation at all), so the leak only shows with longer strings: easy to miss in tests.
- Verified with a counting resource: `pmr::vector<std::string>` element allocation did not hit the resource; `pmr::vector<pmr::string>` did, and `v[0].get_allocator().resource()` was the vector's resource.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Once the outer container is pmr, everything inside is in the arena."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: a counting or guard resource in tests is the cheapest way to prove where allocations go.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Use pmr types all the way down, or nested data escapes the arena.

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: a counting or guard resource in tests is the cheapest way to prove where allocations go.

**Key takeaway:** Use pmr types all the way down, or nested data escapes the arena.

interview_qa.question: Which memory resource does a copy of a pmr container use? What about copy assignment and move construction?
interview_qa.answer: Copy construction uses the default resource, not the source's (`polymorphic_allocator::select_on_container_copy_construction` returns a default-constructed allocator). Copy and move assignment keep the target's own resource. Move construction takes the source's resource. To copy into a specific resource use the allocator-extended constructor `T copy(src, &res)`.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Copy construct → default resource; assign → keep own; move construct → source's. Pass the resource explicitly.

interview_qa.question: What does `b = std::move(a)` cost when `a` and `b` are pmr vectors on different resources? And `swap(a, b)`?
interview_qa.answer: If the resources compare equal (`is_equal`), the buffer is stolen in O(1). If they differ, `b` must keep its own resource, so it allocates in its resource and moves the elements one by one: O(n) and allocating. `swap` with unequal allocators is undefined behaviour.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Verified: after `b = std::move(a)` with different monotonic resources, `b.data()` was not `a`'s old buffer and `b` still used its own resource.
- With the same resource, `b.data()` was exactly `a`'s old buffer.
- `is_equal` is the hook: two resource objects can declare themselves interchangeable (e.g. two handles to the same arena).
- Consequence: "moving data into the arena" by assignment is a copy in disguise; construct the data in the right resource from the start.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Move assignment is always O(1) and noexcept for vectors." That holds for `std::allocator` (always equal), not for stateful allocators.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the same rule explains why `noexcept` on move assignment of pmr containers is conditional.

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: a tracking resource with `set_default_resource` is a cheap way to enforce "no allocation after warm-up" in tests.

interview_qa.question: What is the default memory resource, and how can `set_default_resource` help in testing?

interview_qa.question: What does PMR cost compared with `std::allocator`?
interview_qa.answer: A virtual call per allocation and deallocation, one extra pointer per container (libstdc++ x86-64: `pmr::vector<int>` is 32 bytes vs 24, `pmr::string` 40 vs 32), and non-propagating allocator semantics that can make copies and moves allocate. In return, allocations can be far cheaper (bump or pool) and more predictable than the general heap.
interview_qa.explanation:
- The virtual call is a few nanoseconds and often devirtualized when the compiler sees the concrete resource; it is small next to a heap allocation it replaces.
- The extra pointer matters in large arrays of small containers (cache footprint).
- Move assignment between unequal resources is O(n) and may throw; `std::allocator` moves are always O(1).
- Resource lifetime becomes a correctness concern that `std::allocator` never has.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "PMR is zero-cost." It is cheap, not free.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: measure both the allocator cost and the change in tail latency; the virtual call is rarely the bottleneck.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: PMR costs a virtual call and a pointer; it pays off when the resource beats the general heap.

interview_qa.question: When would you write your own object pool instead of using a pmr pool resource?
interview_qa.answer: When the workload has fixed properties a general resource cannot exploit: one object type with a known maximum count, a specific exhaustion policy, a strict "no heap after startup" rule, known thread ownership (SPSC hand-off), cache-line layout of slots, or handing out objects and handles rather than raw bytes. Otherwise a standard resource is less code and less risk.
interview_qa.explanation:
- pmr strengths: standard, composable (resources chain), works with every allocator-aware container and nested data, no free-list code to debug.
- Custom pool strengths: exact capacity and metrics, no virtual calls, pre-faulted memory, policy-specific behaviour (drop/reject), objects constructed in place with typed handles.
- Common split: pmr arenas for per-message scratch data; a custom pool or ring buffer for the core message/order objects.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "PMR replaces object pools entirely" or "always write your own for performance."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: you can implement the custom pool as a `memory_resource` and get both.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: pmr for general allocation policy; a custom pool when capacity, policy and ownership are fixed and known.

interview_qa.question: How would you prove that a pool actually improved your system?
interview_qa.answer: Measure latency distributions (p50, p99, p99.9, max) under realistic load before and after, and confirm the mechanism: count allocations on the hot path (should be zero after warm-up), count page faults, and check memory usage. An improved average with an unchanged tail means the pool did not fix the real problem.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Allocation counting: a guard/counting `memory_resource`, a replaced `operator new` in tests, or heap profilers (heaptrack, jemalloc stats).
- Page faults: `perf stat -e page-faults,minor-faults` on the process; pre-faulting should move them to startup.
- Compare with a realistic workload: microbenchmarks in a tight loop make `malloc` look perfect because its caches stay hot.
- Watch for regressions: a too-small pool falling back to the heap, or a monotonic arena growing because of container churn.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Run a loop of a million allocations and compare the time."
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: monitor the pool's high-water mark and exhaustion events in production.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Prove it with tail percentiles plus zero hot-path allocations, not with an average.

practice_tasks.title: Question 1
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
bad_alloc at size 512
```

**Explanation:**
- `push_back` grows capacity 1, 2, 4, ..., 512 (libstdc++ doubles). Each growth allocates a new array; the monotonic resource's `deallocate` is a no-op, so every old array stays as dead space.
- Arrays of 1 + 2 + ... + 512 ints = 1023 × 4 = 4092 bytes are consumed. The next growth needs 1024 × 4 = 4096 bytes, which does not fit, and the upstream is `null_memory_resource()`, so it throws.
- With `v.reserve(1000)` first, one 4000-byte allocation fits and all 1000 elements are stored.
- With the default upstream it would not throw; it would quietly allocate from the heap.
- **Key Concept:** In a monotonic arena, container growth wastes memory; reserve up front or size the arena for the sum of all growth steps.

practice_tasks.answer:
Undefined behaviour: v's elements live in memory owned by arena, which was destroyed when load() returned.
Here (g++ -O0) it crashed with a segmentation fault; ASan reports heap-use-after-free on v[99].
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `return v;` moves the vector out. A moved pmr vector keeps the source's resource, so the returned vector still points into the arena's chunks and still holds `&arena`.

practice_tasks.title: Question 7
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
same slot: 1
x->id = 3
```
(The double release is a bug. The second `p->~Order()` is itself formally undefined behaviour, since the object's lifetime already ended ([class.dtor]); with a non-trivial destructor it would also do real damage, e.g. a double free.)

**Explanation:**
- The second `destroy(a)` pushes the same slot again: the free list becomes `a → a → ...` (the slot's `next` now points to itself).
- `create(2)` pops `a`, and because `a->next == a` the head is still `a`; `create(3)` returns the same address and overwrites order 2.
- Two "live" objects now share one slot: silent data corruption far from the bug.
- Defences: hand out `std::unique_ptr<Order, PoolDeleter>` only, track in-use slots in debug builds, assert on double release.
- **Key Concept:** An intrusive free list trusts its callers; a double release creates aliasing objects.

practice_tasks.title: Question 8
practice_tasks.answer:
log: 0 100
log: 9 300
(GCC 11 at `-O0`, and the same under ASan/UBSan, which report nothing. At `-O2` the first line printed `log: 0` followed by a garbage `qty`. Reading `*a` after `destroy(a)` is undefined behaviour.)
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `destroy(a)` ends the order's lifetime and pushes its slot on the free list. The link pointer is stored in the slot's first 8 bytes, exactly where `id` was: the free list was empty, so `next` is `nullptr` and `id` reads as `0`. `qty` is untouched, so the log looks half right.
- The next `create` takes the most recently freed slot (LIFO), so `a` now aliases `c`: the handler "sees" order 9. In production this shows up as wrong orders in logs or, worse, a stale handler modifying someone else's order.
- ASan is silent because the slots are part of a live object (`pool` on the stack); it only knows about `malloc`/`new` boundaries, not about the pool's internal free list.
- Debug-build defence: poison a slot when it goes on the free list (`ASAN_POISON_MEMORY_REGION` from `<sanitizer/asan_interface.h>`) and unpoison it when it is handed out. With that pool the buggy `main` stops at the first stale read with `AddressSanitizer: use-after-poison`.
- Ownership fix: hand out `std::unique_ptr<Order, PoolDeleter>` (theory Example 2) so release and the end of use are tied together, and keep no raw copies past the release.
- **Key Concept:** A pool recycles slots immediately; a pointer kept after release reads the free-list link or the next tenant, and only explicit poisoning lets ASan see it.

- `a(1000, 7, &r1)`: one allocation from `r1`.
- `b = std::move(a)`: resources differ (`r2` vs `r1`), `polymorphic_allocator` does not propagate, so `b` allocates in `r2` and moves the elements one by one: `r2` +1.
- `c = std::move(b)`: `c` uses `r1`, `b` uses `r2`: again element-wise into a new `r1` allocation: `r1` +1.
- `d(std::move(c))`: move **construction** takes `c`'s allocator and steals its buffer: no allocation.
- **Key Concept:** Move assignment between unequal resources is a copy with allocation; only same-resource moves and move construction are O(1).

practice_tasks.title: Question 11
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
before uses arena: 0
after uses arena:  1
old was new_delete: 1
after still arena: 1
```

**Explanation:**
- A default-constructed `polymorphic_allocator` reads `get_default_resource()` once, at construction. Changing the default later does not affect existing objects.
- `set_default_resource` returns the previous default, initially `new_delete_resource()`.
- Assigning a string from another resource copies the characters into `after`'s own resource: the resource is fixed at construction.
- Order matters at the end too: `after` and `arena` are destroyed in reverse order (`after` first), so it frees into a live arena.
- **Key Concept:** The resource is chosen once, at construction; the default resource is only a construction-time fallback.

practice_tasks.title: Question 12
practice_tasks.answer:
Not correct: data race inside the shared resource (undefined behaviour).
TSan (GCC 11): "WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race" in std::construct_at<int>: one thread writes an int into pool
memory that the other thread wrote without synchronization (inside the shared pool's chunk), then "done".
practice_tasks.explanation:
- The containers are separate, but both allocate from one `unsynchronized_pool_resource`, which has no internal locking. Concurrent `allocate`/`deallocate` race on its internal free lists and chunk bookkeeping, which can hand the same block to both threads or corrupt the lists; TSan flags the unsynchronized accesses to the shared chunk.
- Same rule for `monotonic_buffer_resource`: not thread-safe.
- Fixes: `std::pmr::synchronized_pool_resource` (TSan clean), or better for latency, one `unsynchronized_pool_resource` per thread (`thread_local`).
- **Key Concept:** Thread safety of a pmr setup is a property of the resource, not of the containers.

practice_tasks.title: Question 13
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Compile error: use of deleted function 'std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<_Tp>& std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<_Tp>::operator=(const std::pmr::polymorphic_allocator<_Tp>&) [with _Tp = int]'
```

**Explanation:**
- `polymorphic_allocator` is copy-constructible but its copy assignment is deleted: once an allocator (and therefore a container) is bound to a resource, it never switches to another.
- This is why pmr containers never propagate the allocator on assignment, and why assignment between containers on different resources copies or moves elements instead of stealing buffers.
- **Key Concept:** A pmr object's resource is fixed for its lifetime; choose it at construction.

quick_reference.content:
#### Object pool checklist
| Item | Rule |
|---|---|
| Storage | Raw, aligned for `T`, allocated once at startup; not `new T[N]` |
| Slot | `union { Slot* next; alignas(T) std::byte obj[sizeof(T)]; }` |
| Acquire | Pop head, placement new; push back if the constructor throws |
| Release | `p->~T()`, push slot; never `delete p` |
| Handle | `unique_ptr<T, PoolDeleter>` |
| Exhaustion | Decide: fail fast, drop, block, fallback (visible), grow |
| Threads | Per-thread pools; cross-thread free via queue or remote-free list |
| Reuse with many readers | Deferred reclamation (Chapter 4) |

#### Standard resources
| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Heap, through the pmr interface | `std::pmr::new_delete_resource()` |
| Fail every allocation | `std::pmr::null_memory_resource()` |
| Bump arena, free all at once | `std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource` + `release()` |
| Reusable blocks, one thread | `std::pmr::unsynchronized_pool_resource` |
| Reusable blocks, many threads | `std::pmr::synchronized_pool_resource` |
| Hard memory bound | Any resource with `null_memory_resource()` upstream |
| Pool tuning | `std::pmr::pool_options{max_blocks_per_chunk, largest_required_pool_block}` |
| Change default | `std::pmr::set_default_resource(&r)` (returns old) |

#### Propagation table (polymorphic_allocator)
| Operation | Resulting resource |
|---|---|
| Copy construct | Default resource |
| `T b(a, &r)` | `r` |
| Move construct | Source's resource |
| Copy assign | Target keeps its own |
| Move assign, equal resources | Target, buffer stolen |
| Move assign, different resources | Target, element-wise move (allocates) |
| Swap, different resources | UB |

#### Interview one-liners
- "A pool trades generality for predictability: bounded hot-path work, no surprise page faults, bounded memory."
- "Storage exists is not object exists: construct on acquire, destroy on release, keep the storage."
- "A bounded pool needs an exhaustion policy, and that decision matters more than the free list."
- "PMR separates what a container stores from where its memory comes from, at run time, without changing the type."
- "Monotonic: bump allocation, no individual free, release everything together; perfect when lifetimes are grouped."
- "Pool resources reuse freed blocks per size class; synchronized for sharing, unsynchronized for one thread."
- "Use `null_memory_resource()` upstream if the buffer must be a hard bound."
- "pmr::vector of std::string leaks out of the arena; use pmr types all the way down."
- "Copying a pmr container goes to the default resource; pass the resource explicitly."
- "The resource must outlive every container that uses it: declare it first."
