subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- A mutex is a single key to a room (the **critical section**). Whoever holds the key is the **owner**; everyone else waits.
- It protects data only through a **protocol**: every access to the shared state, reads included, must hold the **same** mutex. One unprotected access anywhere breaks the guarantee.
- Three properties to keep apart:
  - **Mutual exclusion**: at most one owner at a time.
  - **Ownership**: the thread that locked it is the one that must unlock it.
  - **Synchronization**: an `unlock()` synchronizes with the next successful `lock()` of the same mutex, so everything written before the unlock is visible after the lock (happens-before).
- What a mutex does **not** give: an execution order between threads, fairness, or protection for data accessed outside the lock.
- Lock objects (`lock_guard`, `unique_lock`, `scoped_lock`, `shared_lock`) are RAII wrappers: their lifetime represents ownership. Never make the programmer remember to unlock.

subsections.title: 2. std::mutex: the exact contract
subsections.content:
- `lock()`: blocks until the calling thread owns the mutex.
- `try_lock()`: returns immediately, `true` if acquired. It is allowed to **fail spuriously** even if the mutex is free.
- `unlock()`: precondition: the calling thread owns the mutex.
- Undefined behaviour cases (each is a classic interview trap):

| Action | Result |
|---|---|
| Locking a `std::mutex` you already own (`lock` or `try_lock`) | UB (glibc: blocks forever) |
| Unlocking from a thread that is not the owner | UB |
| Unlocking a mutex that is not locked | UB |
| Destroying a mutex while it is locked | UB |
| Owner thread exits while holding the lock | Undefined behaviour; in practice (glibc) it stays locked forever |

- Other properties:
  - Not copyable, not movable: a class containing a mutex is non-copyable by default.
  - `constexpr` default constructor: a global `std::mutex` is constant-initialized, so it is safe to use from other static initializers.
  - No fairness: a thread arriving later can "barge" ahead of threads already waiting.
  - `lock()` may throw `std::system_error`. An implementation is permitted (not required) to report `resource_deadlock_would_occur` when it detects relocking; glibc's default mutex does not check, it just blocks.
- Locking for reading in a `const` member function needs `mutable std::mutex m_;`.

subsections.title: 3. RAII lock wrappers
subsections.content:
| Wrapper | Since | Locks on construction | Manual unlock/relock | Movable | Multiple mutexes | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `std::lock_guard<M>` | C++11 | Yes (or `adopt_lock`) | No | No | No | Simple scope |
| `std::unique_lock<M>` | C++11 | Optional (`defer_lock`, `try_to_lock`, `adopt_lock`, timeout) | Yes | Yes | No | Condition variables, early unlock, handing a lock out of a function |
| `std::scoped_lock<Ms...>` | C++17 | Yes, deadlock-avoiding for 2+ | No | No | Yes | Default choice; any number of mutexes |
| `std::shared_lock<M>` | C++14 | Shared (read) ownership | Yes | Yes | No | Readers on a `shared_mutex` |

- All four acquire **exclusive** ownership except `shared_lock`. The difference between `lock_guard` and `unique_lock` is flexibility, not exclusivity.
- `unique_lock` has two independent states: the **object exists**, and it **may or may not own** the mutex (`owns_lock()`). After `unlock()` the object still exists but owns nothing; its destructor then does nothing.
- `unique_lock::lock()` on a lock that already owns its mutex throws `std::system_error` (`resource_deadlock_would_occur`); `unlock()` when not owning throws `operation_not_permitted`.
- `condition_variable::wait` requires `std::unique_lock<std::mutex>` because it must release the mutex while sleeping and reacquire it before returning.
- Tags:
  - `std::defer_lock`: associate, do not lock yet (lock later, often via `std::lock`).
  - `std::try_to_lock`: call `try_lock`, check `owns_lock()`.
  - `std::adopt_lock`: the thread already owns it; only take over the unlock.
- Size and cost (libstdc++ x86-64): `lock_guard` holds one reference (8 bytes); `unique_lock` holds a pointer plus an owns flag (16 bytes) and checks the flag in its destructor. Negligible next to the lock itself.

subsections.title: 4. The other mutex types
subsections.content:
| Type | Recursive | Timed (`try_lock_for/until`) | Shared (reader) mode |
|---|---|---|---|
| `std::mutex` | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| `std::timed_mutex` | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ |
| `std::recursive_mutex` | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| `std::recursive_timed_mutex` | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| `std::shared_mutex` (C++17) | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |
| `std::shared_timed_mutex` (C++14) | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ |

- **Recursive mutex**: the owner may lock again; it must unlock the same number of times. Usually a design smell: it hides re-entrancy and lets a nested call see half-updated invariants. Prefer a private `do_x_locked()` helper that assumes the lock is held.
- **Timed mutex**: `try_lock_for(50ms)` waits up to the duration. Useful for "give up and degrade" paths and for diagnostics (log when a lock is held suspiciously long). Plain `std::mutex` has no timed API: calling `try_lock_for` on it does not compile.

subsections.title: 5. Reader-writer locks (shared_mutex)
subsections.content:
- Readers take `std::shared_lock` (many at once); writers take `std::unique_lock` or `std::lock_guard` (exclusive).
- Fairness is **implementation-defined**:
  - The standard does not say whether a waiting writer blocks newly arriving readers.
  - libstdc++ on Linux wraps glibc `pthread_rwlock_t`, whose default policy prefers readers. With overlapping readers, a writer can starve: in a test with 4 overlapping readers a writer waited about 1 s, until the readers stopped.
- Not automatically faster than `std::mutex`:
  - Every reader still performs an atomic RMW on the shared lock word, so the lock's cache line bounces between reader cores.
  - For tiny critical sections (a map lookup), a plain mutex is often as fast or faster.
  - Wins appear when read sections are long relative to lock overhead and writes are rare.
- No upgrade: holding a `shared_lock` and then requesting `unique_lock` on the same mutex in the same thread is UB (in practice a self-deadlock). Release, take the exclusive lock, and re-check the condition.
- Low-latency view: unpredictable writer waits become tail-latency spikes. Alternatives: plain mutex, sharding, copy-on-write snapshots behind an atomic pointer, RCU, seqlocks, single-writer designs.

subsections.title: 6. What a blocked thread actually does
subsections.content:
- C++ only says `lock()` "blocks". Everything below is implementation behaviour (shown for glibc/Linux, the most common interview target).
- **Fast path (uncontended)**: one atomic compare-and-swap in user space (0 to 1). No system call, no kernel.
- **Slow path (contended)**: the waiter marks the lock word "locked with waiters" (2) and calls `futex(FUTEX_WAIT)`. The kernel puts the thread to sleep on a wait queue keyed by the lock's address, with no CPU used while sleeping.
- **Unlock**: atomic store/exchange back to 0. Only if the old value said "waiters exist" does it call `futex(FUTEX_WAKE, 1)`. Uncontended unlock is pure user space.
- **Wake-up**: the woken thread must compete for the lock again; a running thread may grab it first (barging). No FIFO guarantee.
- **Spin-then-sleep** is an implementation choice:
  - glibc's default mutex type does not spin: after a failed fast path it goes straight to the futex wait.
  - glibc's `PTHREAD_MUTEX_ADAPTIVE_NP`, and many other runtimes, spin briefly first, betting the owner releases within a few hundred nanoseconds.
  - A pure spinlock never sleeps: it burns a core for the entire wait.
- "Waiting" is not the same as "blocking": a waiter may spin (active) or sleep (passive). Under contention a thread *may* enter the kernel; it does not *have to*.
- The kernel's futex queue is not "a counter the kernel maintains"; the lock word lives in user memory and the kernel is only involved for sleeping and waking.

subsections.title: 7. Cost: uncontended vs contended
subsections.content:
| Situation | What happens | Rough cost (modern x86, order of magnitude) |
|---|---|---|
| Uncontended, same thread keeps the line hot | Two atomic RMWs (lock + unlock), cache-local | A few ns to ~25 ns per lock/unlock pair |
| Uncontended, lock last used on another core | Same, plus cache-line transfer | ~50 to 150 ns |
| Contended, owner releases quickly | Cache-line ping-pong between cores, possible brief spin | ~50 to a few hundred ns per acquisition |
| Contended, waiter must sleep | `FUTEX_WAIT` + `FUTEX_WAKE` syscalls + context switch + scheduler wake-up | Several µs to tens of µs per hand-off, worse under load |

- Measured on one 20-core Linux box (GCC 11, glibc): uncontended `lock_guard` increment about 3 ns; 2 threads fighting over one mutex about 50 ns per increment; 8 threads about 100 ns per increment; the same counter as a relaxed `std::atomic` about 13 ns.
- The real cost of contention is not the syscall; it is **serialization** (only one core does useful work) and **tail latency** (an unlucky request waits for a sleeping/waking cycle or for a long critical section).
- Rule: an uncontended mutex is cheap; contention is what you design against.

subsections.title: 8. Lock granularity and holding locks across slow work
subsections.content:
- **Critical section length** dominates contention. Never hold a lock across: I/O, logging to a file or socket, memory allocation in hot paths, waiting on another thread, callbacks, or expensive computation.
- **Snapshot pattern**: copy the needed shared state under the lock, release, do the slow work on the private copy. Moving code outside the lock is only safe if that code no longer touches shared mutable state.
- **Granularity trade-off**:
  - Too coarse (one global mutex): unrelated operations serialize; CPU stays low while latency climbs.
  - Too fine (many small locks): more lock/unlock overhead, lock-ordering rules, and invariants that span two locks become race conditions.
- **Sharding / lock striping**: split the data by key (`hash(key) % N`), one mutex per shard. Contention drops roughly by N if keys are spread; watch for hot shards.
- **Single-owner sharding**: route each key to one owning thread; inside a shard no lock is needed at all, and per-key ordering is preserved.
- **False sharing between locks**: an array of `{std::mutex, data}` structs packs several mutexes into one 64-byte line, so unrelated shards still bounce the same cache line. Pad each shard with `alignas(64)` (or `std::hardware_destructive_interference_size`).
- **Mutex vs atomic**: a mutex protects a multi-variable invariant; an atomic protects one variable. A single contended atomic also bounces its cache line, so "atomic is always faster" is false under heavy contention.

subsections.title: 9. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "Every mutex lock is a system call." ✅ Uncontended lock and unlock are user-space atomics; the kernel is only used to sleep and wake waiters.
- ❌ "Under contention the kernel must get involved." ✅ It may; spinning implementations can hand over without a syscall.
- ❌ "Thread 2 sees the update because the store buffer was flushed." ✅ Unlock synchronizes-with the next lock, which establishes happens-before. Fences are how hardware implements it.
- ❌ "The thread that started first gets the mutex first." ✅ No ordering, no FIFO, no fairness.
- ❌ "A waiting thread spins and burns CPU." ✅ A `std::mutex` waiter normally sleeps (possibly after a short spin).
- ❌ "When a thread finishes, its mutexes are released." ✅ Nothing is released automatically; destroying a locked mutex is UB.
- ❌ "Any thread can unlock a mutex." ✅ Only the owner; use a semaphore for cross-thread signaling.
- ❌ "`unique_lock` is the exclusive one, `lock_guard` is not." ✅ Both are exclusive; `unique_lock` is the flexible one.
- ❌ "`shared_mutex` is faster for reads." ✅ Only when read sections are long enough to amortize its overhead; fairness is implementation-defined.
- ❌ "Once a writer waits, new readers queue behind it." ✅ Not guaranteed; glibc prefers readers by default.
- ❌ "Producer/consumer on one mutex means constant contention." ✅ Contention happens only when critical sections overlap; it grows with throughput and section length.
- ❌ "Sharding removes the need for mutexes." ✅ Only if each shard has exactly one owner thread.

theory.full_text:
#### 1. Mental model
- A mutex is a single key to a room (the **critical section**). Whoever holds the key is the **owner**; everyone else waits.
- It protects data only through a **protocol**: every access to the shared state, reads included, must hold the **same** mutex. One unprotected access anywhere breaks the guarantee.
- Three properties to keep apart:
  - **Mutual exclusion**: at most one owner at a time.
  - **Ownership**: the thread that locked it is the one that must unlock it.
  - **Synchronization**: an `unlock()` synchronizes with the next successful `lock()` of the same mutex, so everything written before the unlock is visible after the lock (happens-before).
- What a mutex does **not** give: an execution order between threads, fairness, or protection for data accessed outside the lock.
- Lock objects (`lock_guard`, `unique_lock`, `scoped_lock`, `shared_lock`) are RAII wrappers: their lifetime represents ownership. Never make the programmer remember to unlock.

#### 2. std::mutex: the exact contract
- `lock()`: blocks until the calling thread owns the mutex.
- `try_lock()`: returns immediately, `true` if acquired. It is allowed to **fail spuriously** even if the mutex is free.
- `unlock()`: precondition: the calling thread owns the mutex.
- Undefined behaviour cases (each is a classic interview trap):

| Action | Result |
|---|---|
| Locking a `std::mutex` you already own (`lock` or `try_lock`) | UB (glibc: blocks forever) |
| Unlocking from a thread that is not the owner | UB |
| Unlocking a mutex that is not locked | UB |
| Destroying a mutex while it is locked | UB |
| Owner thread exits while holding the lock | Undefined behaviour; in practice (glibc) it stays locked forever |

- Other properties:
  - Not copyable, not movable: a class containing a mutex is non-copyable by default.
  - `constexpr` default constructor: a global `std::mutex` is constant-initialized, so it is safe to use from other static initializers.
  - No fairness: a thread arriving later can "barge" ahead of threads already waiting.
  - `lock()` may throw `std::system_error`. An implementation is permitted (not required) to report `resource_deadlock_would_occur` when it detects relocking; glibc's default mutex does not check, it just blocks.
- Locking for reading in a `const` member function needs `mutable std::mutex m_;`.

#### 3. RAII lock wrappers
| Wrapper | Since | Locks on construction | Manual unlock/relock | Movable | Multiple mutexes | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `std::lock_guard<M>` | C++11 | Yes (or `adopt_lock`) | No | No | No | Simple scope |
| `std::unique_lock<M>` | C++11 | Optional (`defer_lock`, `try_to_lock`, `adopt_lock`, timeout) | Yes | Yes | No | Condition variables, early unlock, handing a lock out of a function |
| `std::scoped_lock<Ms...>` | C++17 | Yes, deadlock-avoiding for 2+ | No | No | Yes | Default choice; any number of mutexes |
| `std::shared_lock<M>` | C++14 | Shared (read) ownership | Yes | Yes | No | Readers on a `shared_mutex` |

- All four acquire **exclusive** ownership except `shared_lock`. The difference between `lock_guard` and `unique_lock` is flexibility, not exclusivity.
- `unique_lock` has two independent states: the **object exists**, and it **may or may not own** the mutex (`owns_lock()`). After `unlock()` the object still exists but owns nothing; its destructor then does nothing.
- `unique_lock::lock()` on a lock that already owns its mutex throws `std::system_error` (`resource_deadlock_would_occur`); `unlock()` when not owning throws `operation_not_permitted`.
- `condition_variable::wait` requires `std::unique_lock<std::mutex>` because it must release the mutex while sleeping and reacquire it before returning.
- Tags:
  - `std::defer_lock`: associate, do not lock yet (lock later, often via `std::lock`).
  - `std::try_to_lock`: call `try_lock`, check `owns_lock()`.
  - `std::adopt_lock`: the thread already owns it; only take over the unlock.
- Size and cost (libstdc++ x86-64): `lock_guard` holds one reference (8 bytes); `unique_lock` holds a pointer plus an owns flag (16 bytes) and checks the flag in its destructor. Negligible next to the lock itself.

#### 4. The other mutex types
| Type | Recursive | Timed (`try_lock_for/until`) | Shared (reader) mode |
|---|---|---|---|
| `std::mutex` | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| `std::timed_mutex` | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ |
| `std::recursive_mutex` | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| `std::recursive_timed_mutex` | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| `std::shared_mutex` (C++17) | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |

edge_cases.title: The lock that locks nothing
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::lock_guard<std::mutex>{m};` creates a temporary that locks and unlocks immediately, at the end of the full expression.
- `std::unique_lock<std::mutex>(m);` is parsed as a **declaration** of a new default-constructed `unique_lock` named `m`, shadowing the mutex. It locks nothing. GCC warns: "unnecessary parentheses in declaration of 'm'".
- `std::lock_guard<std::mutex>(m);` is also a declaration, but `lock_guard` has no default constructor, so it fails to compile (the lucky case).
- `std::scoped_lock lk;` with no arguments compiles and locks nothing.
- Rule: always name the guard: `std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(m);`.

edge_cases.title: A finished thread keeps its lock
edge_cases.explanation:
- If the owner returns without unlocking (exception caught but unlock forgotten), the thread terminates normally and `join()` succeeds.
- Undefined behaviour by the standard. In practice (glibc) the mutex stays locked forever: other threads block indefinitely, and the owner can no longer unlock it because it no longer exists.
- At program exit the locked mutex is destroyed, which is UB.
- RAII fixes all of it: the guard's destructor runs on normal return, early return and exception unwinding.

edge_cases.title: Locking twice in one thread
No upgrade from shared to exclusive
edge_cases.explanation:
- People assume: "I hold a read lock and found the key missing, so I'll take the write lock to insert it."
- `std::shared_mutex` has no upgrade operation. Calling `lock()` while the same thread holds `lock_shared()` waits for all readers to leave, including itself: self-deadlock (UB).
- Two readers trying to upgrade at the same time would deadlock each other even on a lock type that allowed it, which is why upgrades are not offered.
- Correct pattern: release the shared lock, acquire the exclusive lock, then **re-check** (another writer may have inserted in between).

edge_cases.title: Returning a reference escapes the lock
edge_cases.explanation:
- A getter that locks and returns `const T&` (or a pointer, iterator, or `string_view`) into protected data releases the lock on return; the caller then reads unprotected memory that another thread may be modifying or freeing.
- Same leak via callbacks that receive a reference to internal state and store it.
- Fix: return by value (copy under the lock), or provide a `with_locked(f)` method that runs `f` while the lock is held.

edge_cases.title: try_lock is immediate, may fail spuriously, and is not timed
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::mutex::try_lock()` never waits. It may return `false` even if nobody holds the mutex, so never use its result as a "is anyone holding it?" query.
- `m.try_lock_for(10ms)` on a plain `std::mutex` does not compile; use `std::timed_mutex` (or `recursive_timed_mutex`, `shared_timed_mutex`).
- Timed waits use `steady_clock` for `try_lock_for` durations; `try_lock_until` with `system_clock` can be affected by wall-clock adjustments.

edge_cases.title: A mutex member changes the class
edge_cases.explanation:
- `std::mutex` is neither copyable nor movable, so a class with a mutex member loses its implicit copy and move operations. Containers that need to relocate elements (e.g. `std::vector<Account>` growth) stop compiling.
- If copying is needed, write the copy constructor yourself: lock the source, copy the data, give the new object its own fresh mutex.
- `const` getters need `mutable std::mutex`; locking is not a logical modification of the object.

edge_cases.title: Sharded locks that still contend
edge_cases.explanation:
- Splitting one mutex into 64 shard mutexes should cut contention, but `struct Shard { std::mutex m; long v; };` is 48 bytes on glibc x86-64, so neighbouring shards share cache lines.
- Threads on different shards still invalidate each other's cache line on every lock and update (false sharing): correct, but much slower than expected.
- Fix: `struct alignas(64) Shard { ... };`. Also check that keys spread evenly; one hot key makes sharding useless.

code_examples.explanation:
- One mutex guards two members that must change together; `const` readers use a `mutable` mutex.

- Output: `40000 true`.
- Two atomics instead of one mutex would make each member race-free but would let a reader see `qty_` updated and `notional_` not yet: the invariant needs one critical section.

- Each key maps to one of N shards; each shard has its own mutex and sits on its own cache line.

- An operation that needs two keys in different shards now needs two locks: use `std::scoped_lock` or a fixed shard order.
- The next step up is single-owner sharding: each shard is touched by one thread only, and the mutexes disappear.

interview_qa.question: What does a `std::mutex` guarantee, and what does it not guarantee?
interview_qa.answer: It guarantees mutual exclusion (one owner at a time), ownership (only the locking thread may unlock), and synchronization (an unlock happens before the next successful lock). It does not guarantee which thread gets it first, fairness, or protection for unlocked accesses.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Protection is a protocol: every access to the shared data, including reads, must hold the same mutex.
- The synchronization part is what makes writes visible: writes before `unlock()` are visible after the next `lock()` of the same mutex.
- No FIFO: a newly arriving thread can acquire the mutex ahead of threads that have been waiting.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "A mutex makes the variable thread-safe." The mutex knows nothing about the variable. One code path that touches it without the lock reintroduces the data race.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the UB list: relocking in the owner thread, unlocking from a non-owner, destroying while locked.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: A mutex is exclusion + ownership + synchronization, and it only works if everyone follows the same protocol.
interview_qa.full_content:

interview_qa.key_takeaway: Mutex = exclusion, not ordering and not fairness.

interview_qa.question: A thread holds a mutex for 10 minutes and other threads are waiting for it. Are the waiters burning CPU for those 10 minutes?

- Waiting is not the same as blocking: a waiter can spin (active) or sleep (passive).

- ❌ Common wrong answer: "A thread waiting on a mutex keeps checking it in a loop." That describes a spinlock.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: low-latency systems sometimes choose busy polling on dedicated cores on purpose, trading CPU for avoiding wake-up latency and jitter.

**Key takeaway:** Mutex waiters sleep (maybe after a short spin); spinlock waiters burn CPU.

interview_qa.question: What is lock contention? In a producer/consumer queue protected by one mutex, is the mutex always contended?
interview_qa.answer: Contention means a thread tries to acquire a mutex that another thread currently holds. A shared mutex is not contended by default: if producer and consumer critical sections do not overlap, both acquire it on the fast path. Contention grows with throughput and critical-section length.
interview_qa.explanation:
- No overlap: `[lock push unlock] ... [lock pop unlock]`: synchronized, zero contention.
- High throughput with both threads hammering the queue: overlaps become frequent and some acquisitions must wait, possibly sleep, adding latency and jitter.
- Even "uncontended" hand-offs between two cores move the mutex's cache line back and forth (~50 to 150 ns), which is not free.
- An SPSC ring buffer removes **mutex** contention (no lock, one owner per index) but not **cache-coherence** traffic on the shared indices; that is why head and tail live on separate cache lines.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Producer/consumer with a mutex means 99% contention, so the kernel is always involved." Contention depends on overlap, and even contended waits do not necessarily enter the kernel.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: "SPSC has no contention" is imprecise; say "no lock contention, but the producer and consumer still share cache lines".
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Contention = overlapping acquisition attempts; sharing a lock does not imply it.

interview_qa.question: With `std::shared_mutex` and 100 active readers, what happens to an arriving writer? Do new readers queue behind it?
interview_qa.answer: The writer must wait until all current readers release. Whether new readers are held back once a writer waits is implementation-defined; with a reader-preferring implementation (glibc's default rwlock) overlapping readers can starve the writer indefinitely.
interview_qa.explanation:
- libstdc++ on Linux builds `std::shared_mutex` on `pthread_rwlock_t` with glibc's default reader-preferring policy. Observed: with 4 overlapping readers, a writer waited about 1 s, exactly until the readers stopped.
- Other implementations may prefer writers or alternate phases; portable code must not rely on either.
- Low-latency consequence: even without full starvation, writer waits are unpredictable, so p99/p99.9 latency spikes on the write path (and on readers queued behind a writer, under writer-preferring policies).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Once a writer is waiting, new readers queue after it, so the writer gets in next." That is one possible policy, not a guarantee.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: choose the lock from the latency requirements, not just the read/write ratio: plain mutex for short sections, copy-on-write snapshots for wait-free reads, or a single-writer design.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `shared_mutex` fairness is unspecified; writers can starve and tail latency suffers.

interview_qa.question: A reader holds a `shared_lock`, finds the key missing, and wants to insert it. Can it upgrade to an exclusive lock?
interview_qa.answer: No. `std::shared_mutex` has no upgrade. Requesting `lock()` while the same thread holds a shared lock waits for all readers including itself: undefined behaviour, a self-deadlock in practice. Release the shared lock, take the exclusive lock, then re-check.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: No upgrade: release, lock exclusively, re-check.

interview_qa.question: Roughly how expensive is an uncontended lock versus a contended one, and where does the cost come from?
interview_qa.answer: Uncontended: two atomic RMWs, a few to ~25 ns when the line is cache-local. Contended but short: cache-line ping-pong, roughly 50 to a few hundred ns per acquisition. Contended with sleeping: futex syscalls plus context switch and wake-up latency, several µs or more.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Measured on one 20-core Linux machine (GCC 11, glibc): uncontended `lock_guard` + increment about 3 ns; 2 threads competing about 50 ns per increment; 8 threads about 100 ns; a relaxed `std::atomic` increment with 8 threads about 13 ns. Numbers vary a lot by CPU; quote orders of magnitude, not exact values.
- Deeper costs of contention:
  - Serialization: only one core makes progress in the critical section (Amdahl's law).
  - Tail latency: the unlucky request waits for a full critical section or a sleep/wake cycle.
  - Lock convoys: if the owner is preempted, every waiter waits for it to be rescheduled.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Atomics are always faster than mutexes." A single atomic hammered by many cores also bounces its cache line; per-thread counters or sharding beat both.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the fix for contention is structural (shorter critical sections, sharding, single owner), not a "faster lock".
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Uncontended locks are cheap; contention costs serialization and tail latency.

interview_qa.question: Tail latency spikes because a reporting thread holds the order-book mutex too long. What do you do?
interview_qa.answer: Shrink the critical section: copy only the needed state under the lock, release it, and build the report from the private snapshot. Better, decouple completely: have the hot path publish snapshots or events to the reporting thread through a queue, so reporting can never block it.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Fix lock-induced tail latency by shortening hold time, not by changing the lock type.

interview_qa.question: 12 threads share one `unordered_map` behind a global mutex. CPU is 50% but latency is high. How do you redesign it?
interview_qa.answer: The global mutex serializes unrelated keys. Partition by key: either one mutex per shard (lock striping), or better, route each shard to a single owning worker so it needs no lock at all. Then check for hot shards and pad shard locks to separate cache lines.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Low CPU plus high latency is the classic sign of threads waiting on a lock rather than working.
- Striping: `shard = hash(key) % N`, each shard `{alignas(64) mutex, map}`. Contention drops roughly by N if keys are evenly spread.
- Single-owner: requests for key K always go to worker `hash(K) % 12`. No lock, preserved per-key ordering, better cache locality.
- Costs: cross-shard operations (multi-key transactions, global iteration) need multiple locks in a fixed order or a coordination step; a hot key still bottlenecks one shard.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Sharding means no mutex is needed." Only true if each shard has exactly one owner thread; if several workers can touch a shard, each shard still needs its lock.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: an array of unpadded `{mutex, data}` shards puts several mutexes on one cache line, so "independent" shards still false-share.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Split by key; prefer single-owner shards over lock-per-shard when routing allows it.

practice_tasks.title: Question 1
practice_tasks.answer: Nothing is locked: data race on counter (undefined behaviour). The output is unpredictable: with -O2 it often prints 200000 anyway (the unlocked loop is folded into one += 100000); at -O0 it printed about 100000.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `std::unique_lock<std::mutex>(mtx);` is parsed as a declaration: a new default-constructed `unique_lock` named `mtx`, which shadows the global mutex inside the loop body. A default-constructed `unique_lock` owns nothing.
- GCC warns: "unnecessary parentheses in declaration of 'mtx' [-Wparentheses]". Read that warning as "this is a declaration, not a lock".
- The `lock_guard` version of the same mistake does not compile (no default constructor), which is one more reason to prefer it.
- **Key Concept:** Always give the guard a name: `std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock(mtx);`.
practice_tasks.key_concept: Always give the guard a name: `std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lock(mtx);`.

practice_tasks.title: Question 2
practice_tasks.answer: Not protected: data race on total (undefined behaviour). Typically prints less than 200000.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `std::lock_guard<std::mutex>{m};` creates an unnamed temporary. A temporary is destroyed at the end of the full expression, the semicolon, so the mutex is locked and immediately unlocked.
- `total += v;` then runs with no lock held.
- Compilers do not warn here; code review and `-Wthread-safety` annotations (Clang) catch it.
- **Key Concept:** The lock lasts as long as the guard object; an unnamed guard lasts one statement.

practice_tasks.title: Question 3
practice_tasks.answer: Compile error: 'class std::lock_guard<std::mutex>' has no member named 'unlock'
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `lock_guard` is deliberately minimal: lock in the constructor, unlock in the destructor, no other operations.
- To release early either use a nested scope `{ std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m); value = 42; }` or switch to `std::unique_lock`, which has `unlock()` and `lock()`.
- **Key Concept:** `lock_guard` = scope-bound ownership; `unique_lock` = controllable ownership.

practice_tasks.title: Question 4
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
owns: 1
error: Resource deadlock avoided
owns: 0
error: Operation not permitted
```

**Explanation:**
- `unique_lock` keeps an "owns" flag. `lock()` while owning throws `std::system_error` with `errc::resource_deadlock_would_occur`; `unlock()` while not owning throws with `errc::operation_not_permitted`.
- The exact `what()` text is the library's (shown for libstdc++); the error codes are standard.
- Calling `m.lock()` twice on the raw `std::mutex` would instead be UB (a silent hang with glibc). The wrapper protects you only because it checks its own flag.
- After `unlock()` the `unique_lock` object still exists, it just owns nothing; its destructor then does nothing.
- **Key Concept:** Object lifetime and lock ownership are separate states in `unique_lock`.

practice_tasks.title: Question 5
practice_tasks.answer:
caught: boom
other thread acquired: false
practice_tasks.explanation:
- The exception skips `m.unlock()`. Stack unwinding only runs destructors, and a raw mutex has no owner object to destroy.
- The main thread still owns `m` after catching the exception, so another thread cannot acquire it. With `lock()` instead of `try_lock()` the other thread would block forever.
- The final `m.unlock()` is legal only because `main` is the owning thread.
- Fix: `std::lock_guard<std::mutex> g(m);` in `process()`; its destructor unlocks during unwinding.
- **Key Concept:** Manual lock/unlock is not exception safe; RAII is.

practice_tasks.title: Question 6
practice_tasks.answer:
worker: handled error, returning
main: try_lock -> false
Not well-defined overall: at exit the global mutex is destroyed while still locked (undefined behaviour).
practice_tasks.explanation:
- The worker thread terminates normally and `join()` returns: holding a lock does not keep a thread alive.
- Thread termination releases nothing. The mutex stays locked with an owner that no longer exists, so no thread can ever legally unlock it.
- If `main` had called `m.lock()` instead of `try_lock()`, it would hang forever.
- Destroying a locked `std::mutex` is UB. With glibc nothing visible happens, which is why this bug is easy to miss.
- **Key Concept:** A thread's exit does not unlock its mutexes; only RAII or an explicit unlock by the owner does.

practice_tasks.title: Question 7
practice_tasks.answer:
Undefined behaviour: unlock() requires the calling thread to own the mutex.
Observed with glibc (default mutex type does not check the owner):
worker: unlocked main's mutex
main: try_lock -> 1
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `std::mutex` has ownership semantics. Unlocking from another thread violates the precondition of `unlock()`.
- It "works" on glibc because the default mutex type does not record or check the owner on unlock. An error-checking mutex, another platform, or a debug runtime may fail or abort. Code that relies on this is broken but passes tests.
- If you need "thread A blocks until thread B says go", that is signaling, not mutual exclusion: use `std::binary_semaphore`, a condition variable with a predicate, or an atomic flag with `wait/notify`.
- **Key Concept:** Mutexes have owners; semaphores do not.

practice_tasks.title: Question 8
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
enter depth 1
enter depth 2
enter depth 3
unlocked: 1
```

**Explanation:**
- A `recursive_mutex` keeps an owner and a lock count. Each nested `lock_guard` increments the count; each destructor decrements it. The mutex is free only when the count returns to zero.
- After `visit(2)` returns all three guards are gone, so `try_lock` succeeds (by the owner thread, which is allowed for a recursive mutex).
- With `std::mutex`, the second `lock()` inside the recursion is UB; with glibc the thread blocks on itself forever after printing `enter depth 1`.
- Design note: prefer a public function that locks once and a private recursive helper that assumes the lock is held.
- **Key Concept:** Recursive mutexes count; ordinary mutexes self-deadlock.

practice_tasks.title: Question 9
practice_tasks.answer: Yes, always (even single-threaded). Prints "reader: key missing, upgrading" and then hangs: undefined behaviour, self-deadlock.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- The exclusive lock must wait until all shared owners release. The thread itself is a shared owner and is now blocked, so it waits for itself forever.
- `std::shared_mutex` offers no upgrade. Even if it did, two readers upgrading at the same time would deadlock each other.
- Correct pattern: drop the shared lock, take the exclusive lock, re-check (another writer may have inserted the key in the gap).
- **Key Concept:** Shared to exclusive is release-then-acquire-then-recheck, never an in-place upgrade.

practice_tasks.title: Question 10
practice_tasks.answer: Compile error: 'class std::mutex' has no member named 'try_lock_for'
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `std::mutex` supports only `lock`, `try_lock` and `unlock`. `try_lock` returns immediately; it never waits.
- Timed acquisition (`try_lock_for`, `try_lock_until`) exists only on `std::timed_mutex`, `std::recursive_timed_mutex` and `std::shared_timed_mutex`.
- With a `unique_lock`, the timed calls are also available on the wrapper (`lk.try_lock_for(10ms)`) when the underlying mutex is timed.
- **Key Concept:** "Try for a while" needs a timed mutex type.

practice_tasks.title: Question 11
practice_tasks.answer:
Undefined behaviour plus a race condition. In test runs it crashed (segmentation fault) every time.
Orders get processed twice, others never, and near the end pop_front() runs on an already-empty deque.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- The intent (do slow work outside the lock) is right, but the reference `o` escapes the critical section.
- Both consumers can read the same `front()` before either pops it: the same order is processed twice, and each `pop_front` then removes a different element, so another order is never processed.
- While one consumer reads `o.id`, the other can `pop_front()` and destroy that element: use-after-free.
- With one order left, both consumers see it, both unlock, and both later pop: the second `pop_front()` on an empty deque is UB (here, the crash).
- `++processed[o.id]` from two threads on the same index is also a data race.
- Fix: take ownership under the lock (copy or move the element out and pop it), then release and process the private copy.
- **Key Concept:** Releasing early is only safe if nothing you use afterwards still points into shared state.
practice_tasks.key_concept: Releasing early is only safe if nothing you use afterwards still points into shared state.

practice_tasks.title: Question 12
practice_tasks.answer:
total=8000000 sizeof(Shard)=48
Correct, but shards share cache lines (48-byte shards in 64-byte lines), so "independent" threads false-share and slow each other down.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- Correctness: each shard's counter is only touched under that shard's mutex, and `main` reads after `join()`. No data race. (`sizeof` is 48 with glibc on x86-64: a 40-byte `pthread_mutex_t` plus a `long`.)
- Performance: neighbouring shards straddle the same 64-byte line. Every lock, unlock and increment by one thread invalidates the line in the other core's cache, so the threads contend in hardware even though they never contend for a mutex.
- Fix: `struct alignas(64) Shard` (or `std::hardware_destructive_interference_size` where available). In this extreme case each thread owns its shard, so no mutex is needed at all: per-thread counters summed after `join()`.
- **Key Concept:** Lock striping needs cache-line separation, and single ownership beats any lock.

practice_tasks.title: Question 13
practice_tasks.answer: Compile error: use of deleted function 'Account::Account(Account&&)'
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `std::mutex` is neither copyable nor movable, so `Account`'s implicit copy and move constructors are deleted.
- `push_back` needs to move the temporary into the vector and to relocate elements when it grows.
- Options:
  - Construct in place in a container that never relocates: `std::deque<Account>` with `emplace_back()`, or `std::list`.
  - Store `std::unique_ptr<Account>` in the vector.
  - Write a copy/move constructor that locks the source and gives the new object a fresh mutex (only if copying an account makes sense).
- **Key Concept:** A mutex member makes the class non-copyable and non-movable unless you define those operations yourself.

practice_tasks.answer:
Not safe: data race (undefined behaviour). The lock is released when name() returns, and the caller reads name_ through the reference while rename() may be modifying or reallocating it.
Often prints 1, but can read garbage sizes or crash.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- The guard protects only the time between lock and `return`. Returning a reference (or pointer, iterator, `string_view`) hands out access to the protected data with no lock held.
- `rename` can reallocate the string's buffer; the reader may then use freed memory.
- ThreadSanitizer reports this as a data race between `rename` and the caller's `size()`.
- Fix: return by value (the copy is made while the lock is held), or offer `with_name(f)` that calls `f` under the lock.
- **Key Concept:** Never let references to guarded data escape the critical section.

quick_reference.content:
#### Which lock wrapper?
| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| Lock for a whole scope | `std::scoped_lock lk(m);` or `std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(m);` |
| Two or more mutexes | `std::scoped_lock lk(m1, m2);` |
| Condition variable wait | `std::unique_lock<std::mutex> lk(m);` |
| Unlock early / relock | `std::unique_lock` |
| Return or move a held lock | `std::unique_lock` |
| Try without waiting | `std::unique_lock lk(m, std::try_to_lock); if (lk.owns_lock())` |
| Wait with a timeout | `std::timed_mutex` + `try_lock_for` |
| Many readers, rare writers | `std::shared_mutex` + `std::shared_lock` (read) / `std::unique_lock` (write) |

#### UB and surprises
| Action | Result |
|---|---|
| Relock `std::mutex` in the owner thread | UB, hangs in practice |
| `unique_lock::lock()` while owning | Throws `system_error` (resource deadlock) |
| Unlock from non-owner | UB |
| Destroy locked mutex | UB |
| Owner thread exits holding the lock | UB (glibc: stays locked forever) |
| `shared_lock` then `unique_lock` in one thread | UB, self-deadlock |

subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- A condition variable (CV) is a **doorbell**, not a mailbox.
  - It lets a thread sleep until someone says "something may have changed, go and look".
  - It does **not** store the condition, and it does **not** remember rings that nobody heard.
- Three separate pieces, three separate jobs:

| Piece | Example | Job |
|---|---|---|
| Shared state (the predicate) | `ready`, `!queue.empty()`, `stopping` | The actual condition. The only thing that is "remembered". |
| Mutex | `std::mutex m` | Protects the shared state and orders reads/writes of it (happens-before). |
| Condition variable | `std::condition_variable cv` | Lets a thread block efficiently and be woken when the state may have changed. |

- One sentence to keep: **wait for the state, not for the notification.**
- Why not just poll?
  - `while (queue.empty()) {}` without a lock burns a full core and is a data race on `queue`.
  - The same loop while **holding** the mutex is worse: the producer can never get the mutex to push, so it never ends.
  - A CV blocks the thread, so the scheduler runs other work, and wakes it when a producer signals.

subsections.title: 2. The canonical pattern
3. What `cv.wait(lock)` does, step by step
subsections.content:
- Precondition: the calling thread owns `lock` (calling `wait` with an unlocked lock is undefined behaviour).
- Contract in three lines:

| Phase | Mutex owned by caller? |
|---|---|
| Before calling `wait` | Yes |
| While blocked inside `wait` | No (released so producers can change the state) |
| When `wait` returns (for any reason) | Yes, always reacquired first |

- Inside `wait(lock)`:
  1. **Atomically** release the mutex and register as a waiter on the CV (no gap between the two).
  2. Block.
  3. Unblock because of `notify_one`, `notify_all`, a spurious wakeup, or (timed waits) a timeout.
  4. Reacquire the mutex. This may itself block if another thread holds it.
  5. Return to the caller.
- Only step 1 needs to be atomic for correctness. Step 3 + 4 ("wake then relock") is **not** one atomic operation; another thread can grab the mutex in between.
- `wait` needs a lock it can unlock and relock: that is why it takes `std::unique_lock<std::mutex>&`. `std::lock_guard` has no `unlock()`/`lock()` and does not compile here.
- If reacquiring the mutex fails with an exception, `std::terminate` is called: `wait` never returns without the lock.

subsections.title: 4. The predicate overload and why the loop is mandatory
subsections.content:
- `cv.wait(lock, pred)` is specified as exactly:

```cpp
while (!pred())
    wait(lock);
```

- Consequences:
  - The predicate is checked **before** blocking: if it is already true, `wait` returns immediately and never sleeps. No notification is needed.
  - The predicate is re-checked after **every** wakeup, always with the mutex held.
- Three reasons a plain `if (!ready) cv.wait(lock);` is wrong:
  - **Spurious wakeup:** the standard permits `wait` to return with no notification at all. The cause (signals, futex races, implementation details) does not matter, only that it is allowed.
  - **Stolen wakeup:** you were notified, but another consumer reacquired the mutex first and consumed the item.
  - **Shared CV:** the notification was about a different condition (for example "space available" instead of "data available").
- The CV never inspects your predicate. It does not know what `ready` or `queue.empty()` means; your lambda does.

subsections.title: 5. Lost wakeups: the check-then-sleep gap
subsections.content:
- A notification with no current waiter is simply dropped. CVs keep no count (unlike a semaphore).
- The classic broken hand-rolled wait:

```text
Consumer                         Producer
lock(m)
check ready == false
unlock(m)              <- gap
                                 lock(m); ready = true; unlock(m)
                                 notify_one()   (nobody waiting yet: dropped)
go to sleep            <- sleeps forever, although ready == true
```

- How the real `wait` closes the gap:
  - The consumer checks the predicate while holding `m`.
  - `wait` releases `m` and becomes a waiter as one atomic step.
  - The producer must take `m` to change the state, so its change and its notify can only happen **after** the consumer is registered. The notify is guaranteed to find it.
- The protocol only works if **both** sides use the mutex for the state:
  - Plain `bool` written without the mutex: data race, undefined behaviour.
  - `std::atomic<bool>` written without the mutex: no data race, but the lost wakeup is back. The store and the `notify_one` can both land between the consumer's predicate check and its registration as a waiter.
  - Fix: modify the state under the mutex (or at minimum lock and unlock the mutex between the store and the notify).

subsections.title: 6. `notify_one` vs `notify_all`, and where to notify
subsections.content:
- `notify_one`: unblocks one waiting thread, if any (which one is unspecified).
- `notify_all`: unblocks all current waiters. They then **compete for the mutex one at a time**; each rechecks the predicate.
  - One item + `notify_all` to N consumers: one gets it, the rest wake, find the queue empty, and sleep again. This is the **thundering herd**.
  - Woken threads that are waiting for the mutex are no longer CV waiters. When the mutex is released they proceed **without a second notification**.
- Use `notify_all` when:
  - the state change can satisfy several waiters (shutdown flag, batch of items, "barrier released");
  - different waiters on the same CV wait for **different** predicates (otherwise `notify_one` may wake the wrong kind of waiter and the right one sleeps forever).
- Notify while holding the lock, or after unlocking?
  - **Both are correct.** The state change is what must be under the mutex, not the notify.
  - After unlock is usually more efficient: the woken thread does not immediately block on a mutex the notifier still holds ("hurry up and wait").
  - Notify under the lock when the waiter might destroy the CV as soon as it sees the state (for example a CV inside an object the waiter frees). After unlock, the notifier could touch a destroyed CV.
- A notification does **not**:
  - make the predicate true,
  - run the woken thread immediately,
  - hand it the mutex.

subsections.title: 7. Timed waits
subsections.content:
- `wait_for(lock, rel)` and `wait_until(lock, abs)` are **blocking** waits with a deadline, not polling loops.
  - They release the mutex, block, and return on notify, spurious wakeup, or timeout, always with the mutex reacquired.
- Return values:

| Call | Returns | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `wait_for(lock, d)` | `std::cv_status` | `timeout` if the time elapsed, else `no_timeout`. `no_timeout` does **not** mean the condition is true (spurious wakeups). |
| `wait_for(lock, d, pred)` | `bool` | The final value of `pred()`. `false` means it timed out with the predicate still false. |
| `wait_until(lock, t, pred)` | `bool` | Same, against an absolute time point. |

- The predicate overload of `wait_for` is specified as `wait_until(lock, steady_clock::now() + d, pred)`: one fixed deadline for the whole wait.
- A hand-written loop `while (!ready) cv.wait_for(lock, d);` restarts the timeout on every wakeup, so a stream of unrelated notifications can postpone the "timeout" forever.
- Prefer `steady_clock` deadlines. A `system_clock` deadline moves when the wall clock is adjusted.

subsections.title: 8. Shutdown and stop flags
subsections.content:
- A worker waiting with `!queue.empty()` as its only predicate cannot be woken for shutdown: there is no state change it accepts.
- Standard worker pool design:

```cpp
cv.wait(lk, [&] { return !q.empty() || stopping; });
if (q.empty() && stopping) return;   // drain first, then exit
```

- Decisions to state explicitly in an interview:
  - **Drain vs abandon:** `if (q.empty() && stopping)` finishes queued work; `if (stopping)` drops it. Pick one on purpose.
  - Set `stopping` **under the mutex**, then `notify_all` (every worker must see it, so `notify_one` is a bug).
  - Reject or ignore new pushes after `stopping` is set.
  - Join the threads after notifying.
- C++20: `std::condition_variable_any::wait(lock, stop_token, pred)` integrates with `std::jthread` cancellation. A stop request wakes the waiter and the wait returns `pred()`.

subsections.title: 9. `condition_variable` vs `condition_variable_any` vs alternatives
subsections.content:
| Tool | Waits on | Remembers signals? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `std::condition_variable` | `unique_lock<std::mutex>` only | No | Fastest CV; maps to the native condvar (pthread/futex on Linux). |
| `std::condition_variable_any` | Any BasicLockable (`shared_lock`, custom locks, `scoped_lock`) | No | Usually bigger and slower (holds its own internal mutex). C++20 adds `stop_token` overloads. |
| `std::atomic<T>::wait/notify` (C++20) | Value of one atomic | Value is the state | `wait(old)` blocks while value == old; spurious wakeups are hidden. Good for a single flag or counter. |
| `std::counting_semaphore` (C++20) | Internal counter | Yes (count) | `release()` before `acquire()` is not lost. |
| `std::latch` / `std::barrier` (C++20) | Countdown / phases | Yes | One-shot or cyclic rendezvous. |

- Rules for `std::condition_variable`:
  - All threads concurrently waiting on one CV must use the **same** mutex (otherwise undefined behaviour).
  - Destroying the CV is allowed once every waiter has been **notified**, even if they have not yet reacquired the mutex. Destroying it while a thread is still blocked on it is undefined behaviour.
  - `std::notify_all_at_thread_exit(cv, std::move(lk))` notifies after thread-local destructors run (useful for detached threads).
- Typical implementation (glibc, Linux): a userspace sequence counter plus `futex` wait/wake. Waking does not transfer the mutex; the woken thread competes for it like anyone else.
- Bounded queues (a second CV for "not full", ring buffers) are a design topic of their own; here only the signalling rules matter.

subsections.title: 10. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "`wait` unlocks the mutex when the predicate is false." ✅ `wait(lock)` (no predicate) always releases the mutex while blocked; the predicate only decides whether to call it again.
- ❌ "The CV checks the condition." ✅ The CV knows nothing about your state; your predicate checks it under the mutex.
- ❌ "If I hold the mutex, how can another thread change `ready`?" ✅ You do not hold it while blocked in `wait`; that is the whole point.
- ❌ "A spurious wakeup is a notification that happened by mistake." ✅ It is a return from `wait` with no matching notification; the standard allows it.
- ❌ "The CV remembers a notify that happened before I waited." ✅ It is dropped; only the predicate remembers.
- ❌ "Wake-up plus mutex reacquisition is one atomic step." ✅ Only release-and-register is atomic; reacquisition is a normal lock that can block.
- ❌ "After `notify_all`, the threads stuck on the mutex need another notify." ✅ They are already woken; they just wait for the mutex.
- ❌ "`notify_one` means the predicate is now true / the thread runs now / it gets the mutex." ✅ None of these is guaranteed.
- ❌ "Notifying while holding the lock is a bug." ✅ It is correct, sometimes slower, and sometimes required for lifetime reasons.
- ❌ "`wait_for` is active polling." ✅ It blocks like `wait`, with a deadline.
- ❌ "`cv_status::no_timeout` means my condition is true." ✅ It only means the time did not run out.
- ❌ "Making the flag `std::atomic` lets me skip the mutex." ✅ It removes the data race but reintroduces the lost wakeup.
- ❌ "Waiting for a mutex means spinning and burning CPU." ✅ Implementation-defined; mainstream mutexes block in the kernel after a short (or no) spin.

- ❌ "A spurious wakeup is a notification that happened by mistake." ✅ It is a return from `wait` with no matching notification; the standard allows it.
- ❌ "The CV remembers a notify that happened before I waited." ✅ It is dropped; only the predicate remembers.
- ❌ "Wake-up plus mutex reacquisition is one atomic step." ✅ Only release-and-register is atomic; reacquisition is a normal lock that can block.
- ❌ "After `notify_all`, the threads stuck on the mutex need another notify." ✅ They are already woken; they just wait for the mutex.
- ❌ "`notify_one` means the predicate is now true / the thread runs now / it gets the mutex." ✅ None of these is guaranteed.
- ❌ "Notifying while holding the lock is a bug." ✅ It is correct, sometimes slower, and sometimes required for lifetime reasons.
- ❌ "`wait_for` is active polling." ✅ It blocks like `wait`, with a deadline.
- ❌ "`cv_status::no_timeout` means my condition is true." ✅ It only means the time did not run out.
- ❌ "Making the flag `std::atomic` lets me skip the mutex." ✅ It removes the data race but reintroduces the lost wakeup.
- ❌ "Waiting for a mutex means spinning and burning CPU." ✅ Implementation-defined; mainstream mutexes block in the kernel after a short (or no) spin.

edge_cases.title: The notification happened before anyone waited
An atomic flag set outside the mutex still loses wakeups
edge_cases.explanation:
- What people assume: "`ready` is `std::atomic<bool>`, so no lock is needed in the producer".
- What happens:
  - Consumer holds `m`, evaluates `ready` (false), and is about to enter `wait`.
  - Producer stores `ready = true` and calls `notify_one()` without touching `m`. No waiter is registered yet, so the notify is dropped.
  - Consumer then releases `m` and blocks. Nobody will notify again: hang.
- Why: the gap-closing guarantee of `wait` only holds if the state changes while the waiter cannot be between "checked" and "registered", and only the mutex enforces that.
- Fix: write the flag under the mutex, or do `{ std::lock_guard lk(m); }` between the store and the notify.

edge_cases.title: `notify_one` wakes the wrong kind of waiter
edge_cases.explanation:
- Setup: one CV shared by threads waiting for **different** predicates (producers waiting for "not full", consumers waiting for "not empty", or threads waiting for "my turn").
- What happens: `notify_one` wakes a thread whose predicate is still false. It goes back to sleep, and the thread that could have progressed is never woken. The system stalls although work is possible.
- Fix: `notify_all`, or one CV per predicate (the usual "not_full" + "not_empty" pair).

edge_cases.title: Woken by `notify_all`, then stuck on the mutex
edge_cases.explanation:
- Setup: three consumers, one item, `notify_all()`. C1 gets the mutex and holds it for 40 seconds.
- What happens: C2 and C3 have already been unblocked from the CV. They are now blocked **on the mutex**, not on the CV.
- When C1 unlocks, one of them acquires the mutex, sees an empty queue, and waits again. No second notification is needed.
- Lesson: keep the critical section short. Pop the item, unlock, then process.

edge_cases.title: Notify after unlock, but the CV is already gone
edge_cases.explanation:
- Setup: a waiter owns an object containing the CV and destroys it as soon as it observes `done == true`.

```cpp
{ std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lk(s->m); s->done = true; }
// waiter may wake (spuriously or otherwise), see done, and delete s here
s->cv.notify_one();   // ❌ use after free
```

- Fix: notify while still holding the mutex, so the waiter cannot return from `wait` before the notify completes, or tie the object lifetime to both sides (for example `shared_ptr`).

edge_cases.title: Timeout is not "condition false", and loops restart the timer
edge_cases.explanation:
- `wait_for` returning `cv_status::timeout` does not prove the condition is false: the state can change between the timeout and the mutex reacquisition. Always re-read the state.
- `while (!ready) if (cv.wait_for(lk, 1s) == std::cv_status::timeout) return false;` restarts the 1 s budget on every wakeup. If unrelated notifications arrive every 200 ms, it never times out.
- Fix: `cv.wait_for(lk, 1s, pred)` or `cv.wait_until(lk, deadline, pred)` with a fixed deadline.

edge_cases.title: Undefined behaviour in the API itself
edge_cases.explanation:
- Calling `wait` when the `unique_lock` does not own the mutex.
- Two threads waiting concurrently on the same `std::condition_variable` with **different** mutexes.
- Destroying a CV while a thread is still blocked on it (not yet notified).
- Passing `std::lock_guard` to `wait`: not UB, simply a compile error.

edge_cases.title: Shutdown that drops work or never wakes anyone
edge_cases.explanation:
- `if (stopping) return;` right after the wait exits even when items are queued. If the pool must finish accepted work, use `if (q.empty() && stopping) return;`.
- Setting `stopping = true` and calling `notify_one()` wakes one worker; the others sleep forever and `join()` hangs. Use `notify_all()`.
- Setting `stopping` without the mutex (plain `bool`) is a data race; as an atomic it reopens Edge Case 2.

code_examples.title: One-shot "data ready" signal
code_examples.explanation:
- The minimal correct pattern: state under the mutex, notify after unlock, predicate wait.

- Output: `consumer got: market snapshot`, regardless of which thread runs first.
- The mutex unlock in `producer` synchronizes-with the lock in `consumer`, so `payload` is visible without being atomic.

code_examples.title: Worker pool with graceful (draining) shutdown
code_examples.explanation:
- Multiple consumers, `notify_one` per item, `notify_all` for shutdown, work processed outside the lock.

- Output: `processed=1000 sum=333833500` on every run: shutdown drains the queue before workers exit.
- Swap the exit test for `if (stopping_) return false;` and the count becomes nondeterministic.

- `wait_for` with a predicate returns the predicate's value, so timeout handling is one `if`.

- The second wait returns after about 20 ms, not 5 s: the deadline is only an upper bound.

interview_qa.question: What problem does a condition variable solve, and why is busy-waiting on a queue a bad alternative?
interview_qa.answer: It lets a thread block until shared state may have changed, instead of polling. Busy-waiting burns a core (and is a data race without a lock); polling while holding the mutex is worse, because the producer can never get the lock to make progress.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Polling without a lock: `while (q.empty()) {}`
  - wastes a full CPU while doing nothing useful;
  - reads `q` concurrently with the producer's writes: a data race, undefined behaviour.
- Polling while holding the mutex:
  - the producer needs the same mutex to push, so the loop can never end;
  - the program livelocks or hangs.
- With a CV, the waiting thread is descheduled; the scheduler runs other runnable threads until a producer notifies.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "A condition variable is a faster mutex." It is not a lock at all; it is always used **together** with a mutex.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the CV is only the wake-up mechanism. The condition itself is ordinary shared state protected by the mutex, and the CV never stores it.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: A CV replaces polling with blocking; it does not replace the mutex.

interview_qa.question: What is a spurious wakeup, and why must `wait` be called in a loop?
interview_qa.answer: A spurious wakeup is a return from `wait` with no matching notification; the standard explicitly allows it. Because returning from `wait` says nothing about the condition, the condition must be rechecked under the mutex: `while (!pred) cv.wait(lk);` or `cv.wait(lk, pred)`.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `if (!ready) cv.wait(lk); use(data);` can proceed with `ready == false` after a spurious wakeup.
- The loop also covers two non-spurious cases:
  - **stolen wakeup:** you were notified, but another consumer got the mutex first and took the item;

interview_qa.question: What does `cv.wait(lock, pred)` do internally, and what happens if `pred` is already true when you call it?

interview_qa.question: Does a condition variable remember a notification sent when nobody was waiting? Why does correct code not care?

interview_qa.question: What is a lost wakeup, and how does `condition_variable::wait` prevent it?

  - or use `std::promise`/`std::future` for one-shot completion.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Always notify after unlocking, it is the best practice." It is a performance default, not a rule.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the same hazard exists for the mutex inside the object; the safest one-shot primitives are designed so the signaller touches nothing after publishing.

**Key takeaway:** Lifetime can override the "notify after unlock" performance habit.

practice_tasks.title: Question 1
practice_tasks.answer: Undefined behaviour: the second woken consumer calls front()/pop() on an empty queue.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- Both consumers block on the CV. `notify_all` unblocks **both**.
- They reacquire the mutex one at a time. The first takes `10`.
- The second returns from `wait` too, never rechecks `q.empty()` (it used `if`), and calls `front()` on an empty `std::queue`: undefined behaviour (often garbage or a crash).
- The same `if` also breaks on a spurious wakeup with a single consumer.
- Using `notify_one` for the first push would only hide the bug; stolen and spurious wakeups still exist.
- **Key Concept:** Returning from `wait` never proves the condition; always re-check it in a loop (or use the predicate overload).
practice_tasks.key_concept: Returning from `wait` never proves the condition; always re-check it in a loop (or use the predicate overload).
additional_code: Undefined behaviour: the second woken consumer calls front()/pop() on an empty queue.

practice_tasks.title: Question 2
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
timeout ready=1
```

**Explanation:**
- `notify_one` ran when nobody was waiting, so it was dropped. CVs do not remember notifications.
- The raw `wait_for` therefore blocks for the full 200 ms and reports `timeout`, although `ready` has been `true` the whole time.
- With a plain `cv.wait(lk)` this program would hang forever.
- (A spurious wakeup could in theory print `no_timeout`; that would not mean anything was signalled either.)
- `cv.wait_for(lk, 200ms, [] { return ready; })` returns `true` immediately without blocking.
- **Key Concept:** Wait for the state, not for the notification.

practice_tasks.title: Question 3
practice_tasks.answer: Data race on `ready` (and `data`): undefined behaviour. It usually prints data=42, but nothing is guaranteed (it can also hang).
practice_tasks.explanation:
- The consumer reads `ready` (in the predicate) and `data` under `m`; the producer writes both **without** `m`. Conflicting non-atomic accesses with no happens-before = data race.
- `notify_one` does not synchronize memory; only the mutex unlock/lock pair does.
- Independently of the UB, the write and the notify can fall between the consumer's predicate check and its registration as a waiter: a lost wakeup and a hang.
- ThreadSanitizer (`-fsanitize=thread`) reports "data race" on `ready` and `data` for this program.
- **Key Concept:** Both sides must use the mutex for the shared state; the CV only wakes threads.
practice_tasks.key_concept: Both sides must use the mutex for the shared state; the CV only wakes threads.
additional_code: Data race on `ready` (and `data`): undefined behaviour. It usually prints data=42, but nothing is guaranteed (it can also hang).

practice_tasks.title: Question 4
practice_tasks.answer: Yes. It hangs and prints nothing (here deterministically; in real code, rarely and randomly).
practice_tasks.explanation:
- t = 0 ms: consumer holds `m`, reads `ready == false`, then stalls inside the predicate.
- t = 50 ms: producer stores `true` and calls `notify_one`. The consumer is not yet a waiter, so the notify is dropped.
- t = 100 ms: predicate returns `false`; `wait` releases `m` and blocks. No one will ever notify again.
- `std::atomic` fixed the data race, not the protocol: the CV's "no lost wakeup" guarantee relies on the producer needing the mutex to change the state.
- With the fix, the producer's `lock_guard` blocks until the consumer has released `m` inside `wait`, i.e. until it is a registered waiter, so the notify cannot be missed.
- **Key Concept:** Change CV-guarded state under the same mutex, even if the variable is atomic.
practice_tasks.key_concept: Change CV-guarded state under the same mutex, even if the variable is atomic.
additional_code: Yes. It hangs and prints nothing (here deterministically; in real code, rarely and randomly).

practice_tasks.title: Question 5
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
took 42
exited=3
```

**Explanation:**
- `notify_all` unblocks all three consumers, but they reacquire `m` one at a time.
- The first one takes `42`; the other two find `q.empty() && !stopping`, so the predicate loop puts them back to sleep. No duplicate "took" line is possible.
- The second `notify_all` wakes everyone with `stopping == true` and an empty queue, so all three exit.
- The output is the same no matter which consumer wins; only the thread that printed "took" differs.
- Had shutdown used `notify_one`, only one consumer would exit and `join()` would hang.
- **Key Concept:** `notify_all` wakes everybody, the mutex serializes them, and the predicate filters them.

practice_tasks.title: Question 6
practice_tasks.answer: processed 0 of 5
practice_tasks.explanation:
- The worker cannot take `m` until `main` unlocks it, and by then the queue has 5 items **and** `stopping == true`.
- The predicate is true, `wait` returns, and `if (stopping) return;` exits immediately: all five accepted tasks are silently dropped.
- In a real pool the same happens whenever shutdown races with recently queued work.
- If abandoning work is not intended, exit only when there is nothing left: `if (q.empty() && stopping) return;` This prints `processed 5 of 5`.
- **Key Concept:** Decide explicitly between "drain then stop" and "stop now"; `if (stopping)` silently chooses the latter.
practice_tasks.key_concept: Decide explicitly between "drain then stop" and "stop now"; `if (stopping)` silently chooses the latter.
additional_code: processed 0 of 5

practice_tasks.title: Question 7
practice_tasks.answer: Compile error: no matching function for call to 'std::condition_variable::wait(std::lock_guard<std::mutex>&, ...)'
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `std::condition_variable::wait` takes `std::unique_lock<std::mutex>&` only.
- `wait` must unlock the mutex while blocked and relock it before returning; `lock_guard` has no `unlock()`/`lock()`, so there is no conversion.
- Even though `ready` is already `true` (so no blocking would happen), the type requirement is checked at compile time.
- `std::condition_variable_any` would accept `std::unique_lock`, `std::shared_lock`, or any type with `lock()`/`unlock()`, but still not a `lock_guard` (no `unlock()`).
- **Key Concept:** `wait` = temporary unlock + relock, which needs `std::unique_lock`.
practice_tasks.key_concept: `wait` = temporary unlock + relock, which needs `std::unique_lock`.
additional_code: Compile error: no matching function for call to 'std::condition_variable::wait(std::lock_guard<std::mutex>&, ...)'

practice_tasks.title: Question 8
practice_tasks.answer: Yes, it can hang (nondeterministic; in practice it usually hangs within a few runs). When it completes it prints moves=30000.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- Three threads wait on one CV for **different** predicates (`turn == 0`, `1`, `2`).
- Player 0 sets `turn = 1` and calls `notify_one`, which may wake player 2. Player 2's predicate is false, so it sleeps again.
- Player 1 was never notified and sleeps forever; nobody else can advance `turn`. All three are blocked.
- It is a lost wakeup caused by `notify_one` choosing the wrong waiter, not by a missing mutex.
- Fix: `notify_all` (everyone rechecks, exactly one proceeds), or one CV per player and notify the next player's CV.
- **Key Concept:** `notify_one` is only safe if every waiter on that CV can use the state change.
practice_tasks.key_concept: `notify_one` is only safe if every waiter on that CV can use the state change.
additional_code: Yes, it can hang (nondeterministic; in practice it usually hangs within a few runs). When it completes it prints moves=30000.

practice_tasks.title: Question 9
practice_tasks.answer: ready=0 after 4 s
practice_tasks.explanation:
- Each unrelated `notify_all` wakes `wait_ready` with `no_timeout`; `ready` is still false, so it calls `wait_for(lk, 1s)` again with a **fresh** 1 s budget.
- The ticker notifies every 200 ms for 3 s; the timeout can only fire 1 s after the last tick, at about 4 s total.
- With a continuous stream of notifications (or frequent spurious wakeups) it would never time out.
- The fixed version uses one absolute deadline and prints `ready=0 after 1 s`.
- **Key Concept:** A timeout belongs to the whole wait: use `wait_for(lk, d, pred)` or `wait_until(lk, deadline, pred)`.
practice_tasks.key_concept: A timeout belongs to the whole wait: use `wait_for(lk, d, pred)` or `wait_until(lk, deadline, pred)`.
additional_code: ready=0 after 4 s

practice_tasks.title: Question 10
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
returned, predicate calls=1, owns lock=1
```

**Explanation:**
- `wait(lk, pred)` is `while (!pred()) wait(lk);`. The predicate is evaluated once, before any blocking.
- It is already `true`, so the thread never blocks and no notification is needed.
- The lock is still owned on return (it was never released).
- This is exactly why "notify before wait" is harmless with the predicate form.
- **Key Concept:** The predicate is checked first; a CV wait on an already-true condition costs one function call.

practice_tasks.title: Question 11
practice_tasks.answer: Use-after-free (undefined behaviour). It usually prints "ok", which hides the bug.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- After the signaller unlocks, the waiter can observe `done == true` without blocking at all (or after a spurious wakeup), return, and `delete c`.
- The signaller then calls `c->cv.notify_one()` on a destroyed object.
- The CV rule: you may destroy it once all waiters were notified, but the **notifier** must not touch it afterwards.
- ThreadSanitizer flags this program: a data race between the CV destructor (`pthread_cond_destroy`) in `main` and `notify_one` in the signalling thread.
- Options:
  - notify while holding `c->m` (the waiter cannot get past `wait` until the signaller unlocks);
  - or give both sides ownership, as in the fixed version (most robust: the signaller never touches freed memory);
  - or use `std::promise<void>`/`std::future<void>` for one-shot completion.
- **Key Concept:** "Notify after unlock" is a performance habit; object lifetime can overrule it.
practice_tasks.key_concept: "Notify after unlock" is a performance habit; object lifetime can overrule it.
additional_code: Use-after-free (undefined behaviour). It usually prints "ok", which hides the bug.

practice_tasks.title: Question 12
practice_tasks.answer: elapsed ~400 ms
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `wait` returns with the mutex held, and the 50 ms "processing" happens **before** the lock is released (the `unique_lock` destructor runs at the end of the loop body).
- So only one worker runs at a time: 8 tasks × 50 ms ≈ 400 ms. The other three workers are blocked on the mutex the whole time.
- Moving the work out of the critical section lets the 4 workers run in parallel: 2 rounds × 50 ms ≈ 100 ms (the fixed version prints `elapsed ~100 ms`).
- Producers would also be blocked during processing in a real system.
- **Key Concept:** `wait` gives you the lock back; release it before doing the actual work.
practice_tasks.key_concept: `wait` gives you the lock back; release it before doing the actual work.
additional_code: elapsed ~400 ms

quick_reference.content:
#### Wait API at a glance
| Call | Blocks? | Returns | Mutex on return |
|---|---|---|---|
| `wait(lk)` | Yes | `void`, any reason (notify / spurious) | Held |
| `wait(lk, pred)` | Only while `!pred()` | `void`, `pred()` is true | Held |
| `wait_for(lk, d)` | Yes, max `d` | `cv_status` | Held |
| `wait_for(lk, d, pred)` | While `!pred()`, max `d` total | `bool` = `pred()` | Held |
| `wait_until(lk, t, pred)` | Same, absolute deadline | `bool` = `pred()` | Held |
| `cv_any.wait(lk, stoken, pred)` (C++20) | Until `pred()` or stop request | `bool` = `pred()` | Held |

#### Why `wait` can return
| Reason | Predicate guaranteed true? |
|---|---|
| `notify_one` / `notify_all` | No (another thread may have consumed it, or it was for another predicate) |
| Spurious wakeup | No |
| Timeout | No (and not guaranteed false either) |
| Stop request (`condition_variable_any` + `stop_token`) | No |

#### Notification rules
| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| One item added, waiters are interchangeable | `notify_one` |
| Shutdown / broadcast / batch / several items | `notify_all` |
| Waiters on one CV wait for different predicates | `notify_all` or separate CVs |
| Waiter may destroy the CV right after waking | Notify while holding the mutex |
| Otherwise | Unlock, then notify (fewer wasted wakeups) |

#### Interview one-liners
| Question | One-liner |
|---|---|
| What is a CV? | A way to block until shared state may have changed; the predicate is the state, the CV is only the doorbell. |
| Why a mutex? | It protects the predicate and lets `wait` release-and-register atomically, closing the lost-wakeup gap. |
| Why `unique_lock`? | `wait` must unlock while blocked and relock before returning; `lock_guard` cannot. |
| Why a loop / predicate? | Spurious wakeups, stolen wakeups, and notifications meant for other predicates. |
| Lost wakeup? | A notify that happens between "checked the state" and "started waiting"; it is dropped because CVs keep no memory. |
| Notify under lock? | Correct either way; after unlock is usually cheaper. |
| `notify_all` cost? | Thundering herd: all wake, serialize on the mutex, most go back to sleep. |
| `wait_for`? | Blocking wait with a deadline; use the predicate overload; timeout is not "condition false". |
| Shutdown? | Predicate `!q.empty() || stopping`, set `stopping` under the lock, `notify_all`, drain or abandon on purpose. |
| Atomic flag without lock? | No data race, but lost wakeup returns; lock the mutex between the store and the notify. |
| CV vs semaphore? | A semaphore remembers releases as a count; a CV forgets notifications. |
