subsections.title: 1. Mental model
subsections.content:
- `std::atomic<T>` is a **contract from the C++ memory model**, not a hardware recipe.
- The contract has three separate parts. Keep them apart in interviews:

| Property | Question it answers | Controlled by |
|---|---|---|
| **Atomicity** | Can anyone observe a half-done (torn) operation? Can two RMWs lose an update? | `std::atomic` itself, for every memory order |
| **Modification order** | In what single order did the writes to *this one object* happen? | Every atomic object has its own total order of modifications |
| **Ordering / synchronization** | What does this operation say about *other* memory (non-atomic data, other atomics)? | The `memory_order` argument (covered in topic 06) |

- Default memory order for every operation is `std::memory_order_seq_cst`. This topic uses the default everywhere; the ordering details live in topic 06.
- The hardware (lock-prefixed instructions, cache-coherence protocols such as MESI, store buffers, fences) is **how an implementation keeps the contract**, not what the contract is.
- One-line summary: an atomic makes **each individual operation** on **one object** indivisible. It does not make a sequence of operations, or several objects, indivisible.

subsections.title: 2. What `std::atomic<T>` guarantees (and what it does not)
subsections.content:
- ✅ **No data race:** concurrent reads and writes of the same atomic object from different threads are well-defined. The same accesses on a plain `int` or `bool` are a data race, which is undefined behaviour.
- ✅ **No torn values:** a load returns some value that was actually stored (or the initial value), never a mix of bytes from two stores. This holds for `relaxed` too.
- ✅ **RMW operations never lose updates:** `fetch_add`, `exchange`, `compare_exchange_*`, `++`, `+=` each read the latest value in the object's modification order and write the new one as one indivisible step.
- ✅ **Single modification order per object:** all threads agree on the order of writes to that one atomic.
- ❌ **Not "everyone sees the newest value instantly":** a value you loaded is a snapshot that can be stale one instruction later. A plain load (unlike an RMW) is not required to return the very latest value.
- ❌ **Not a transaction:** `x.load()` followed by `x.store()` is two atomic operations with a gap in between.
- ❌ **Not lock-free by definition:** `std::atomic<T>` may be implemented with an internal lock (see section 6).
- Requirements on `T` for the primary template: trivially copyable, and copy/move constructible and assignable. `std::atomic<std::string>` does not compile (`static_assert` fires).
- `std::atomic` is **not copyable or movable**: `std::atomic<int> b = a;` is ill-formed. `std::atomic<int> a = 0;` is fine since C++17 (guaranteed copy elision, uses the `T` constructor).
- Since C++20 the default constructor value-initializes (`std::atomic<int> x;` holds 0). Before C++20 it was left uninitialized; always write `std::atomic<int> x{0};` to be portable.

subsections.title: 3. The operation catalogue
subsections.content:
| Operation | Kind | Returns | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `load()` | read | current value | snapshot only |
| `store(v)` | write | `void` | blind overwrite |
| `exchange(v)` | RMW | **old** value | atomic swap |
| `fetch_add / fetch_sub` | RMW | **old** value | integers, pointers (scaled by `sizeof(T)`), floating point since C++20 |
| `fetch_and / fetch_or / fetch_xor` | RMW | **old** value | integers only |
| `++x`, `x++`, `--x`, `x--` | RMW | **value**, not a reference | `++x` returns new value, `x++` returns old; not available for `atomic<bool>` or floating point |
| `x += v`, `x -= v`, `x |= v` ... | RMW | new value (by value) | same as the matching `fetch_*` plus the operand |
| `x = v` | write | `v` (by value) | same as `store(v)` |
| `compare_exchange_weak / strong` | conditional RMW | `bool` | updates `expected` on failure |
| `wait(old) / notify_one / notify_all` | C++20 | `void` | block until value differs from `old` |

- ⚠️ `x = x + 1` is **not** an RMW: it is `load`, add, `store`. No data race (both halves are atomic), but updates can be lost.
- `x += 1` **is** a single RMW.
- Signed atomic arithmetic **wraps** (two's complement) with no undefined behaviour, unlike plain signed `int` overflow.
- `atomic<bool>` has no arithmetic. Integer `fetch_max/fetch_min` arrive in C++26; before that, write a CAS loop.

subsections.title: 4. Compare-and-swap (`compare_exchange_*`) precisely
subsections.content:
- Signature: `bool compare_exchange_strong(T& expected, T desired);` (same for `_weak`).
- Semantics, performed atomically:
```text
if (current == expected) { current = desired; return true;  }   // success
else                     { expected = current; return false; }  // failure: expected is OVERWRITTEN
```
- `expected` is passed **by reference** and is written on failure. This is the most asked detail:
  - value 15, expected 10, CAS to 20: fails, value stays 15, expected becomes 15.
- Comparison is **bitwise** (value representation, like `memcmp`), not `operator==`:
  - `double` `+0.0` and `-0.0` compare equal with `==` but CAS treats them as different.
  - A NaN can match itself in CAS even though `NaN == NaN` is false.
  - For structs, C++20 says padding bits do not participate; older implementations could fail forever on garbage padding.
- **weak vs strong:**
  - `compare_exchange_weak` may **fail spuriously**: return `false` even though `current == expected`. On a spurious failure `expected` is written with the current value, which equals what it already held.
  - `compare_exchange_strong` fails only if the values really differed.
- Why spurious failure exists: on LL/SC architectures (ARM `ldxr/stxr` without LSE, POWER `lwarx/stwcx.`, RISC-V `lr/sc`) the store-conditional fails if the reservation was lost (interrupt, context switch, cache-line eviction, a write to a neighbouring variable in the same reservation granule). `weak` maps to one LL/SC attempt; `strong` must wrap it in an internal retry loop.
- On x86-64 both compile to the same `lock cmpxchg`; there is no spurious failure there and no speed difference.
- Rule of thumb:
  - ✅ Already in a retry loop that recomputes `desired`: use `weak`.
  - ✅ One-shot decision ("did I win the claim?"), or a loop where retrying is expensive: use `strong`.
- Two-order overload `compare_exchange_weak(expected, desired, success_order, failure_order)` exists; the failure order cannot be `release` or `acq_rel` (details in topic 06).

subsections.title: 5. The CAS loop: building any RMW
subsections.content:
- Template for an arbitrary atomic update `x = f(x)`:
```cpp
T expected = x.load();
T desired;
do {
    desired = f(expected);                      // recompute from the fresh expected
} while (!x.compare_exchange_weak(expected, desired));
```
- Two reasons the loop is needed:
  1. Another thread changed the value between our read and our CAS (real failure; `expected` now holds the new value).
  2. `weak` can fail spuriously.
- Rules for a correct loop:
  - Recompute `desired` from `expected` **inside** the loop. A `desired` computed once outside can write a stale value (counter can go backwards).
  - Keep the loop body short and side-effect free: it may run many times.
  - Add an early exit when no write is needed (e.g. atomic max: stop if `expected >= v`).
- Progress: a CAS loop is **lock-free** (some thread always succeeds) but **not wait-free** (one unlucky thread can retry indefinitely). See topic 08.
- Prefer a dedicated RMW (`fetch_add`, `fetch_or`, `exchange`) when one exists: no retry, and on x86 `fetch_add` is a single `lock xadd`.

subsections.title: 6. Lock-freedom of atomics
subsections.content:
- `std::atomic<T>` is allowed to use a lock internally. The only type **guaranteed** lock-free is `std::atomic_flag`.
- Queries:

| API | When evaluated | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `a.is_lock_free()` | runtime | this object's operations are lock-free |
| `std::atomic<T>::is_always_lock_free` | compile time (C++17) | lock-free on every execution of this program |
| `ATOMIC_INT_LOCK_FREE` etc. | preprocessor | 0 never, 1 sometimes, 2 always |

- There is no standard `is_atomic_lock_free()` function.
- Typical x86-64 / GCC behaviour (not guaranteed by the standard):
  - 1, 2, 4, 8-byte trivially copyable types: lock-free.
  - 16-byte types: `is_lock_free()` reports `false` with GCC (the operations go through `libatomic`, and you must link `-latomic`), even though the CPU has `cmpxchg16b`.
  - Larger types: a lock from a hashed lock table inside `libatomic`.
- Consequence: an "algorithm made only of atomics" is not lock-free if one of those atomics is not lock-free.
- Lock-free atomics are also **address-free**, which is why only they are safe to use across processes in shared memory.

subsections.title: 7. Special atomic types
subsections.content:
- **`std::atomic_flag`:** a boolean flag, guaranteed lock-free.
  - Pre-C++20: only `test_and_set()` and `clear()`, initialize with `ATOMIC_FLAG_INIT`.
  - C++20: default constructs to clear, adds `test()`, `wait()`, `notify_one()`, `notify_all()`.
  - Classic use: the building block of a spinlock.
- **`std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>>` (C++20, in `<memory>`):**
  - Solves: one `shared_ptr` *object* being read by one thread and reassigned by another. With a plain `shared_ptr` that is a data race even though the reference count is thread-safe.
  - Replaces the C++11 free functions `std::atomic_load(&sp)` / `std::atomic_store(&sp, ...)`, deprecated in C++20.
  - Not required to be lock-free; mainstream implementations (libstdc++ from GCC 12, MSVC) use an internal spin lock, so `is_lock_free()` is `false`.
  - Typical use: read-mostly configuration snapshot (readers `load()` a `shared_ptr<const Config>`, a writer `store()`s a new one).
- **`std::atomic_ref<T>` (C++20):** atomic operations on an existing non-atomic object (must satisfy `atomic_ref<T>::required_alignment`). While any `atomic_ref` to it exists, all accesses must go through `atomic_ref`.
- **`wait` / `notify` (C++20):** `x.wait(old)` blocks until the value is observed to differ from `old` (on Linux typically a futex for 4-byte types). Avoids hand-written spin loops and condition variables for simple flags.

subsections.title: 8. What it costs: the hardware view (typical x86-64)
subsections.content:
- Real GCC 11 `-O2` codegen for `std::atomic<int> x` with default `seq_cst`:

| C++ | x86-64 instruction | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `x.load()` | `mov` | plain load; x86 loads already have acquire semantics |
| `x.store(v)` | `xchg` | seq_cst store needs a full barrier; `xchg` with memory is implicitly locked |
| `x.store(v, release)` | `mov` | cheap |
| `x.fetch_add(1)` | `lock xadd` | |
| `x.fetch_add(1)` (result unused) | `lock add` | |
| `x.fetch_or(m)` (result used) | `lock cmpxchg` loop | no single x86 instruction returns the old value of an OR |
| `x.exchange(v)` | `xchg` | |
| `x.compare_exchange_*` | `lock cmpxchg` | weak and strong identical |

- The `lock` prefix makes the RMW atomic by holding the **cache line** in the Modified/Exclusive state for the duration (cache locking). It does not lock the bus or RAM for normal aligned operations, and does not stop other cores.
- Every RMW (and every store) needs **exclusive ownership of the cache line** (a read-for-ownership). If another core owns it, the line must be transferred and other copies invalidated.
- Typical costs (order of magnitude, vary by CPU):
  - Uncontended locked RMW on a line already owned: roughly 10 to 20+ cycles, plus it acts as a full barrier that drains the store buffer.
  - Contended: the line ping-pongs between cores; each transfer costs tens of ns on one socket and more across sockets. Throughput of a single hot counter can **drop** as you add threads.
- Loads of a line that nobody writes are cheap: every core keeps a Shared copy. **Writes** are what scale badly.
- False sharing: two *independent* hot variables (atomic or not) in the same 64-byte line cause the same ping-pong. Fix with `alignas(64)` (or `std::hardware_destructive_interference_size`) or per-thread counters.
- ❌ Do not define atomics as "flush the store buffer" or "works because of MESI". Those are mechanisms one implementation may use; the C++ guarantee is the contract in section 1.

subsections.title: 9. Atomic or mutex?
subsections.content:
| Use an atomic when | Use a mutex when |
|---|---|
| The shared state is **one** independent value | An **invariant spans several variables** (balance and active flag, head and size) |
| The update is a single RMW (`fetch_add`, `exchange`) or a short CAS loop | The critical section is several steps or complex logic |
| You need a flag, counter, sequence number, pointer swap | Correctness with atomics would need a clever lock-free algorithm |
| Readers vastly outnumber writers on a small value | You need to block waiting threads instead of burning CPU |

- An uncontended `std::mutex` on Linux is also cheap: lock is one atomic CAS in user space, unlock is one atomic RMW; the kernel (futex) is entered **only under contention**.
- Under heavy contention both suffer from cache-line transfer; atomics just avoid sleeping. A hot CAS loop can burn more CPU than a mutex that puts waiters to sleep.
- Strong answer pattern: pick by **what must be protected** (one value vs an invariant), then measure.

subsections.title: 10. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "Another core cannot load the atomic into a register while I modify it." ✅ It can; a loaded copy is a private snapshot. Atomicity is about operations on the atomic object, not about blocking readers.
- ❌ "Atomic means the store buffer is flushed." ✅ Not a C++ guarantee; some orders on some CPUs emit a fence, a `relaxed` store on x86 is a plain `mov`.
- ❌ "`std::atomic` works because MESI makes the line exclusive." ✅ The implementation may use coherence plus locked instructions to satisfy the C++ contract; the contract is atomicity plus modification order plus ordering.
- ❌ "Only `load` and `store` of an atomic are atomic; `++counter` is not." ✅ `++`, `--`, `+=`, `fetch_*`, `exchange`, CAS are all atomic RMWs.
- ❌ "`counter = counter + 4` is atomic because `counter` is atomic." ✅ It is a load plus a store: no data race, but lost updates.
- ❌ "`load(); +1; store();` loses updates because the local variable is not atomic." ✅ The local is thread-private and fine; the gap between the two atomic operations is the problem.
- ❌ "`relaxed` atomics can tear." ✅ Atomicity does not depend on memory order. `relaxed` only drops ordering/synchronization of other memory.
- ❌ "Relaxed load guarantees I see the store from the other thread." ✅ No synchronization is created; it will eventually observe it, but nothing about other data is published (topic 06).
- ❌ "On failure CAS leaves `expected` alone." ✅ It overwrites `expected` with the current value.
- ❌ "`weak` is faster than `strong`." ✅ Identical on x86; can be cheaper on LL/SC CPUs. Choose by whether you already loop.
- ❌ "A CAS loop is wait-free." ✅ It is lock-free; one thread can starve.
- ❌ "Atomics are generally lock-free, `is_atomic_lock_free()` tells you." ✅ Only `atomic_flag` is guaranteed; use `is_lock_free()` / `is_always_lock_free`.
- ❌ "Atomic is always faster than a mutex, and a mutex always enters the kernel." ✅ Uncontended mutexes stay in user space; contended atomics bounce cache lines.
- ❌ "It is only a `bool`, the CPU writes it atomically, so no `atomic` needed." ✅ Concurrent plain read and write is a data race (UB); the compiler may hoist the load out of the loop and spin forever.
- ❌ "Atomics cause false sharing." ✅ False sharing comes from independent hot variables sharing a cache line; atomics just make it more visible.
- ❌ "`std::atomic` is an application-level construct." ✅ It is a language/library abstraction implemented with compiler and hardware support.

theory.full_text:
#### 1. Mental model
- `std::atomic<T>` is a **contract from the C++ memory model**, not a hardware recipe.
- The contract has three separate parts. Keep them apart in interviews:

| Property | Question it answers | Controlled by |
|---|---|---|
| **Atomicity** | Can anyone observe a half-done (torn) operation? Can two RMWs lose an update? | `std::atomic` itself, for every memory order |
| **Modification order** | In what single order did the writes to *this one object* happen? | Every atomic object has its own total order of modifications |
| **Ordering / synchronization** | What does this operation say about *other* memory (non-atomic data, other atomics)? | The `memory_order` argument (covered in topic 06) |

- Default memory order for every operation is `std::memory_order_seq_cst`. This topic uses the default everywhere; the ordering details live in topic 06.
- The hardware (lock-prefixed instructions, cache-coherence protocols such as MESI, store buffers, fences) is **how an implementation keeps the contract**, not what the contract is.
- One-line summary: an atomic makes **each individual operation** on **one object** indivisible. It does not make a sequence of operations, or several objects, indivisible.

#### 2. What `std::atomic<T>` guarantees (and what it does not)
- ✅ **No data race:** concurrent reads and writes of the same atomic object from different threads are well-defined. The same accesses on a plain `int` or `bool` are a data race, which is undefined behaviour.
- ✅ **No torn values:** a load returns some value that was actually stored (or the initial value), never a mix of bytes from two stores. This holds for `relaxed` too.
- ✅ **RMW operations never lose updates:** `fetch_add`, `exchange`, `compare_exchange_*`, `++`, `+=` each read the latest value in the object's modification order and write the new one as one indivisible step.
- ✅ **Single modification order per object:** all threads agree on the order of writes to that one atomic.
- ❌ **Not "everyone sees the newest value instantly":** a value you loaded is a snapshot that can be stale one instruction later. A plain load (unlike an RMW) is not required to return the very latest value.
- ❌ **Not a transaction:** `x.load()` followed by `x.store()` is two atomic operations with a gap in between.
- ❌ **Not lock-free by definition:** `std::atomic<T>` may be implemented with an internal lock (see section 6).
- Requirements on `T` for the primary template: trivially copyable, and copy/move constructible and assignable. `std::atomic<std::string>` does not compile (`static_assert` fires).
- `std::atomic` is **not copyable or movable**: `std::atomic<int> b = a;` is ill-formed. `std::atomic<int> a = 0;` is fine since C++17 (guaranteed copy elision, uses the `T` constructor).
- Since C++20 the default constructor value-initializes (`std::atomic<int> x;` holds 0). Before C++20 it was left uninitialized; always write `std::atomic<int> x{0};` to be portable.

#### 3. The operation catalogue
| Operation | Kind | Returns | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `load()` | read | current value | snapshot only |
| `store(v)` | write | `void` | blind overwrite |
| `exchange(v)` | RMW | **old** value | atomic swap |
| `fetch_add / fetch_sub` | RMW | **old** value | integers, pointers (scaled by `sizeof(T)`), floating point since C++20 |
| `fetch_and / fetch_or / fetch_xor` | RMW | **old** value | integers only |
| `++x`, `x++`, `--x`, `x--` | RMW | **value**, not a reference | `++x` returns new value, `x++` returns old; not available for `atomic<bool>` or floating point |
| `x += v`, `x -= v`, `x |= v` ... | RMW | new value (by value) | same as the matching `fetch_*` plus the operand |
| `x = v` | write | `v` (by value) | same as `store(v)` |
| `compare_exchange_weak / strong` | conditional RMW | `bool` | updates `expected` on failure |
| `wait(old) / notify_one / notify_all` | C++20 | `void` | block until value differs from `old` |

- ⚠️ `x = x + 1` is **not** an RMW: it is `load`, add, `store`. No data race (both halves are atomic), but updates can be lost.
- `x += 1` **is** a single RMW.
- Signed atomic arithmetic **wraps** (two's complement) with no undefined behaviour, unlike plain signed `int` overflow.
- `atomic<bool>` has no arithmetic. Integer `fetch_max/fetch_min` arrive in C++26; before that, write a CAS loop.

#### 4. Compare-and-swap (`compare_exchange_*`) precisely
- Signature: `bool compare_exchange_strong(T& expected, T desired);` (same for `_weak`).
- Semantics, performed atomically:
```text
if (current == expected) { current = desired; return true;  }   // success
else                     { expected = current; return false; }  // failure: expected is OVERWRITTEN
```
- `expected` is passed **by reference** and is written on failure. This is the most asked detail:
  - value 15, expected 10, CAS to 20: fails, value stays 15, expected becomes 15.
- Comparison is **bitwise** (value representation, like `memcmp`), not `operator==`:
  - `double` `+0.0` and `-0.0` compare equal with `==` but CAS treats them as different.
  - A NaN can match itself in CAS even though `NaN == NaN` is false.
  - For structs, C++20 says padding bits do not participate; older implementations could fail forever on garbage padding.
- **weak vs strong:**
  - `compare_exchange_weak` may **fail spuriously**: return `false` even though `current == expected`. On a spurious failure `expected` is written with the current value, which equals what it already held.
  - `compare_exchange_strong` fails only if the values really differed.
- Why spurious failure exists: on LL/SC architectures (ARM `ldxr/stxr` without LSE, POWER `lwarx/stwcx.`, RISC-V `lr/sc`) the store-conditional fails if the reservation was lost (interrupt, context switch, cache-line eviction, a write to a neighbouring variable in the same reservation granule). `weak` maps to one LL/SC attempt; `strong` must wrap it in an internal retry loop.
- On x86-64 both compile to the same `lock cmpxchg`; there is no spurious failure there and no speed difference.
- Rule of thumb:
  - ✅ Already in a retry loop that recomputes `desired`: use `weak`.
  - ✅ One-shot decision ("did I win the claim?"), or a loop where retrying is expensive: use `strong`.
- Two-order overload `compare_exchange_weak(expected, desired, success_order, failure_order)` exists; the failure order cannot be `release` or `acq_rel` (details in topic 06).

#### 5. The CAS loop: building any RMW
- Template for an arbitrary atomic update `x = f(x)`:
```cpp
T expected = x.load();
T desired;
do {
    desired = f(expected);                      // recompute from the fresh expected
} while (!x.compare_exchange_weak(expected, desired));
```
- Two reasons the loop is needed:
  1. Another thread changed the value between our read and our CAS (real failure; `expected` now holds the new value).
  2. `weak` can fail spuriously.
- Rules for a correct loop:
  - Recompute `desired` from `expected` **inside** the loop. A `desired` computed once outside can write a stale value (counter can go backwards).
  - Keep the loop body short and side-effect free: it may run many times.
  - Add an early exit when no write is needed (e.g. atomic max: stop if `expected >= v`).
- Progress: a CAS loop is **lock-free** (some thread always succeeds) but **not wait-free** (one unlucky thread can retry indefinitely). See topic 08.
- Prefer a dedicated RMW (`fetch_add`, `fetch_or`, `exchange`) when one exists: no retry, and on x86 `fetch_add` is a single `lock xadd`.

#### 6. Lock-freedom of atomics
- `std::atomic<T>` is allowed to use a lock internally. The only type **guaranteed** lock-free is `std::atomic_flag`.

|---|---|---|
| `a.is_lock_free()` | runtime | this object's operations are lock-free |
| `std::atomic<T>::is_always_lock_free` | compile time (C++17) | lock-free on every execution of this program |
| `ATOMIC_INT_LOCK_FREE` etc. | preprocessor | 0 never, 1 sometimes, 2 always |

- There is no standard `is_atomic_lock_free()` function.
- Typical x86-64 / GCC behaviour (not guaranteed by the standard):
  - 1, 2, 4, 8-byte trivially copyable types: lock-free.
  - 16-byte types: `is_lock_free()` reports `false` with GCC (the operations go through `libatomic`, and you must link `-latomic`), even though the CPU has `cmpxchg16b`.

edge_cases.title: `x = x + 1` is not `x += 1`
edge_cases.explanation:
- People assume: "`x` is atomic, so any expression on it is atomic."
- What happens: `x = x + 1` calls `load()`, adds in a register, then `store()`. Two threads can both load 5 and both store 6.
- Not undefined behaviour (each access is atomic), but a **logic bug: lost updates**.
- `x += 1`, `++x`, `x.fetch_add(1)` are each one RMW and never lose increments.
```cpp
#include <atomic>
std::atomic<int> x{0};
void bad()  { x = x + 1; }        // load, add, store: can lose updates
void good() { x += 1; }           // one atomic RMW (lock add on x86)
int main() { bad(); good(); return x.load() == 2 ? 0 : 1; }
```

edge_cases.title: A plain `bool` stop flag can spin forever
CAS overwrites `expected` on failure
CAS compares bits, not `operator==`
edge_cases.explanation:
- People assume: CAS uses `==`.
- What happens: comparison is on the value representation (like `memcmp`).
  - `std::atomic<double>` holding `-0.0`, expected `0.0`: `0.0 == -0.0` is true, but the CAS **fails** and `expected` becomes `-0.0`.
  - A NaN loaded from the atomic **matches** in CAS although `NaN == NaN` is false.
  - Structs with padding: C++20 excludes padding bits; pre-C++20 implementations could fail repeatedly because of uninitialized padding.
- See Code Example 2, line 4 of its output: `ok=0 d=-0 expected=-0`.

edge_cases.title: `std::atomic<BigStruct>` compiles but may hide a lock
edge_cases.explanation:
- People assume: wrapping anything in `std::atomic` gives fast lock-free access.
- What happens:
  - Non-trivially-copyable `T` (e.g. `std::string`, `std::vector`): compile error from a `static_assert`. (`std::shared_ptr` works only through its dedicated C++20 specialization.)
  - Trivially copyable but large `T`: compiles, but uses a lock inside `libatomic`; with GCC you may also get a **link error** (`undefined reference to __atomic_load`/`__atomic_is_lock_free`) until you add `-latomic`.
  - 16-byte types on x86-64 with GCC: `is_lock_free()` returns `false`.
- Check with `static_assert(std::atomic<T>::is_always_lock_free);` when your design depends on it.

edge_cases.title: Two atomics do not make one invariant atomic
A loaded value is stale immediately
edge_cases.explanation:
- People assume: `if (x.load() == 0) x.store(1);` means "set to 1 only if it was 0".
- What happens: the load is a snapshot; another thread can store between the load and the store. Both threads can "win".
- Fix: `int e = 0; x.compare_exchange_strong(e, 1);` makes the test and the set one atomic step.
- Same reason `if (!q.empty()) q.pop();` is broken on concurrent containers.

edge_cases.title: `volatile` is not `atomic`
edge_cases.explanation:
- People assume: `volatile` makes a variable thread-safe (it does in Java/C#).
- What happens in C++: `volatile` only forbids the compiler from removing or merging accesses (meant for memory-mapped I/O and signal handlers with `volatile sig_atomic_t`).
  - No atomicity of `++` (still load, add, store).
  - No inter-thread ordering.
  - Concurrent access is still a data race (UB).
- Use `std::atomic` for inter-thread communication. `volatile std::atomic<T>` exists but is almost never what you want.

code_examples.title: Lost updates vs atomic RMW
code_examples.explanation:
- `load` + `store` loses increments (without UB), `fetch_add` never does.

- `fetch_add:` always prints `800000`.
- `load + store:` prints a smaller, run-dependent number (a typical run printed around half). No sanitizer reports a data race: it is a **race condition** (logic bug), not a **data race** (UB).

code_examples.explanation:

interview_qa.question: What does std::atomic<int> guarantee that a plain int does not?
interview_qa.answer: Concurrent access to a std::atomic is not a data race, every operation is indivisible (no torn values, no lost read-modify-write updates), and all threads agree on one modification order for that object. Ordering of other memory is a separate knob: the memory_order argument.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Plain `int` accessed by two threads with at least one write and no synchronization is a **data race**, which is undefined behaviour, even if the CPU happens to load and store `int` atomically.
- `std::atomic<int>` makes every access well-defined:
  - a load returns a value that some store actually wrote (never half of one),
  - RMWs (`fetch_add`, `++`, `exchange`, CAS) never lose an update,
  - each atomic object has a single total order of modifications that every thread observes consistently.
- Three separate ideas: **atomicity** (this answer), **modification order** (per object), **ordering/synchronization** of other data (topic 06).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "It makes the variable thread-safe." Only each individual operation is atomic; a sequence of operations or several variables are not protected as a unit.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the default order is `seq_cst`; `std::atomic<T>` is not guaranteed lock-free; the guarantee is a C++ contract that the implementation satisfies with locked instructions and cache coherence, not "the cache gets flushed".
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Atomic = no data race + indivisible operations + one modification order per object; it is not a transaction.

interview_qa.question: Given std::atomic<int> counter, is ++counter atomic? What about counter = counter + 1?

interview_qa.question: Is incrementing with a separate load and store equivalent to `fetch_add(1)`?
interview_qa.answer: No. Another thread can modify counter between the load and the store, and the store then overwrites that update with a stale value. fetch_add performs the read, the add and the write as one indivisible operation, so no increment is lost.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Interleaving with two threads:
```text
T1: load -> 0        T2: load -> 0
T1: store 1          T2: store 1      final 1, expected 2
```
- With N threads doing many iterations the final value can be far below the expected total (in a test with 4 threads x 200000, about half was lost). The theoretical minimum for 2 threads doing k iterations each is 2.

interview_qa.question: While one thread is doing fetch_add on an atomic, can another thread load it into a register?
interview_qa.answer: Yes. Any thread can load the atomic at any time and gets a value from the object's modification order, either before or after the fetch_add, never a torn one. The loaded copy is a private snapshot that may be stale immediately; atomicity does not block readers.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Atomicity means the RMW is indivisible relative to **other operations on that atomic**: a load sees the value before or after it, and a concurrent RMW cannot base its result on a value already consumed by another RMW.
- Registers are not coherent. If thread B loaded 10 into a register and thread A then incremented to 11, B's register still says 10. That is fine; B's copy is just a local value.
- What prevents lost updates is that two **RMWs** each operate on the latest value in modification order (hardware: the core must own the cache line exclusively during a locked RMW).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "The other core cannot load the atomic variable into its register while it is being modified." Readers are never excluded.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the contract is atomicity plus modification order; the mechanism on x86 is a `lock`-prefixed instruction holding the cache line in M/E state for the duration, not a global lock, and unrelated cores keep running.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Atomics prevent torn and lost operations on the object, not other threads from reading it.

interview_qa.question: With memory_order_relaxed, can a load ever see a torn value? Is the reader guaranteed to see the writer's latest store?
interview_qa.answer: It can never be torn: atomicity holds for every memory order, including relaxed. But relaxed creates no synchronization: the reader is not guaranteed to see the latest store at that moment, and it says nothing about other memory written before the store.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Torn read = seeing some bytes from the old value and some from the new. `std::atomic<T>` rules this out for every order.

- If the writer also wrote non-atomic `data` before the relaxed store of `ready`, the reader seeing `ready == true` does **not** make reading `data` safe (data race). That needs release/acquire (topic 06).

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: plain non-atomic `int64_t` on 32-bit platforms, or misaligned data, can genuinely tear; that is one reason plain shared variables are not an option.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Memory order never affects whether a single atomic operation is atomic.

interview_qa.question: Why does a simple bool stop flag need to be `std::atomic<bool>`?
interview_qa.answer: Because concurrent unsynchronized read and write of a plain bool is a data race, which is undefined behaviour regardless of what the CPU does. The compiler may assume no other thread changes it and hoist the load out of the loop, so the worker can spin forever.
interview_qa.explanation:
- The C++ rule: same memory location, two threads, at least one write, no synchronization, not atomic: **data race, UB**.
- Concrete failure (verified with GCC 11 at `-O2`): `while (running) { ++work; }` is compiled as "read `running` once, then loop forever". The program hangs; at `-O0` it terminates. ThreadSanitizer reports the data race.
- `std::atomic<bool> running{true};` tells the compiler the location is shared: every iteration performs a real atomic load.
- For a pure stop flag that publishes no other data, `relaxed` is enough. Join the worker before destroying what it uses (`join()` provides the synchronization).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "After one or two iterations it will see `false`, so a plain bool is fine." There is no such guarantee; the loop may never re-read it.
- ❌ Another wrong answer: "Use `volatile bool`." `volatile` forces re-reads in practice but is still a data race in C++ and gives no ordering.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: hardware atomicity of a load/store is not the same as C++ synchronization; the language model is what the optimizer reasons about.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Any variable written by one thread and read by another needs an atomic or a lock, even a bool.

interview_qa.question: What does compare_exchange_strong(expected, desired) do, and what happens to expected when it fails?
interview_qa.answer: Atomically: if the current value equals expected, it stores desired and returns true. Otherwise it returns false, leaves the atomic unchanged, and writes the current value into expected (passed by reference). Example: value 15, expected 10, desired 20 gives false, value 15, expected 15.
code_examples:
- The update of `expected` is what makes retry loops cheap: no extra `load()` is needed before the next attempt.
- Comparison is bitwise (value representation): for `double`, `+0.0` vs `-0.0` fail to match even though `==` says equal.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: CAS failure returns false and refreshes `expected` with what is actually there.

interview_qa.question: In a CAS increment loop, why is the while loop necessary?
interview_qa.answer: Two reasons: another thread may have changed the value since we read it, so the CAS fails and we must retry from the refreshed expected; and compare_exchange_weak may fail spuriously even when the values match. The loop repeats until our CAS wins against the value we based desired on.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: The loop handles both competing writers and spurious failure; always recompute `desired` from the fresh `expected`.

interview_qa.question: What is the difference between compare_exchange_weak and compare_exchange_strong, and when do you pick each?
interview_qa.answer: weak may fail spuriously (return false although current == expected); strong fails only when the values really differ. Use weak inside a retry loop that recomputes desired anyway; use strong for a one-shot decision where a false failure would be wrong or a retry is expensive.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Why spurious failure exists: LL/SC architectures (ARM without LSE `ldxr/stxr`, POWER, RISC-V `lr/sc`) lose the reservation on an interrupt, context switch, cache-line eviction, or a write to a neighbouring variable. `weak` maps to one LL/SC attempt; `strong` must loop internally until it gets a real answer.
- On x86-64 both compile to the same `lock cmpxchg`; there is no spurious failure and no speed difference. (ARMv8.1 LSE also has a native `cas` instruction.)
- One-shot example: "exactly one thread claims initialization": `if (state.compare_exchange_strong(e, 1)) init();`. With `weak`, every thread could fail and nobody initializes.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "weak is faster, strong is slower." Not guaranteed; identical on x86, potentially slightly cheaper on LL/SC in a loop because it avoids a nested loop.
- ❌ Another imprecise answer: "Use strong when you need a single snapshot." The real distinction is: with strong, a failure means the value actually changed.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: on a spurious failure, `expected` is rewritten with the current value, which equals what it already held, so the loop just retries.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Weak in loops, strong for one-shot decisions; performance difference is architecture-specific.

interview_qa.question: Is a CAS retry loop wait-free?
interview_qa.answer: No. It is lock-free: whenever a CAS fails, some other thread's CAS succeeded, so the system makes progress. But a particular thread can lose every race and retry without bound, so there is no per-thread step bound, which wait-free requires.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Lock-free: system-wide progress; individual starvation possible.
- Wait-free: every thread finishes its operation within a bounded number of its own steps.
- The CAS loop is lock-free only if the atomic itself is lock-free (`is_always_lock_free`).
- `fetch_add` on x86 is a single `lock xadd` with no retry, so it is commonly treated as wait-free; on LL/SC CPUs without LSE it is itself a retry loop. The standard does not promise wait-freedom for any operation.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "CAS is wait-free because no thread waits on a lock." Not holding a lock is not the definition; the progress guarantee is.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: under heavy contention a CAS loop burns CPU and generates cache-line traffic; exponential back-off or a different design (sharding, `fetch_add`) helps. Topic 08 covers progress guarantees in depth.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: CAS loop = lock-free, not wait-free.

interview_qa.question: When would you choose std::atomic over std::mutex, and when is a mutex the better choice?
interview_qa.answer: Use an atomic when the shared state is one independent value and the update is a single RMW or a short CAS loop (counter, flag, pointer swap). Use a mutex when an invariant spans several variables or several steps, because separate atomics cannot make the compound operation atomic.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Mutex example: `if (active && balance >= amt) balance -= amt;`. Making `active` and `balance` separate atomics still allows two threads to pass the check and overdraw.
- A single CAS loop on `balance` that re-checks `expected >= amt` works only because the invariant then lives in one word.
- Think in terms of **what is protected**: an atomic protects one operation on one object; a mutex protects a critical section over any amount of state.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Atomic is a lightweight mutex, always use it when possible." It cannot protect multi-variable invariants, and lock-free multi-step logic is notoriously error-prone.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: choose by correctness requirement first, then contention and latency profile, then measure. Mutexes block waiters (no wasted CPU); atomics never block but can spin and bounce cache lines.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Atomic for one value, mutex for an invariant.

interview_qa.question: Is an atomic increment always faster than a mutex-protected increment? Does locking a mutex always enter the kernel?
interview_qa.answer: Usually faster for a single counter, but not always. An uncontended Linux mutex stays in user space (one atomic CAS to lock, one atomic RMW to unlock, futex syscall only when contended). Under contention both pay for cache-line transfers; atomics avoid sleeping but are not contention-free.
interview_qa.explanation:
- glibc `pthread_mutex_lock` fast path: one `lock cmpxchg`. Unlock: one atomic RMW, plus a `futex(FUTEX_WAKE)` syscall only if there are waiters.
- So an uncontended mutex increment is roughly two atomic RMWs plus the increment; an atomic increment is one RMW.
- Contended case:
  - Atomic: every `fetch_add` needs exclusive ownership of the line; with many cores the line ping-pongs and throughput can fall as threads are added (measured: 4 threads on one counter about 7x slower than per-thread padded counters).
  - Mutex: waiters may spin briefly, then sleep (context switches, scheduler latency).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Mutex always does a kernel transition, atomic is handled at application level, so atomic is always faster." Both claims are wrong.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the real fix for a hot counter is to remove sharing (per-thread or per-core counters, batching), not to pick a different primitive.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Contention, not the primitive, dominates the cost; uncontended mutexes are cheap.

- So an uncontended mutex increment is roughly two atomic RMWs plus the increment; an atomic increment is one RMW.
- Contended case:
  - Atomic: every `fetch_add` needs exclusive ownership of the line; with many cores the line ping-pongs and throughput can fall as threads are added (measured: 4 threads on one counter about 7x slower than per-thread padded counters).
  - Mutex: waiters may spin briefly, then sleep (context switches, scheduler latency).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Mutex always does a kernel transition, atomic is handled at application level, so atomic is always faster." Both claims are wrong.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the real fix for a hot counter is to remove sharing (per-thread or per-core counters, batching), not to pick a different primitive.

**Key takeaway:** Contention, not the primitive, dominates the cost; uncontended mutexes are cheap.

interview_qa.question: Is std::atomic<T> always lock-free? How do you check?
interview_qa.answer: No. Only std::atomic_flag is guaranteed lock-free; other specializations may use an internal lock. Check at runtime with a.is_lock_free(), at compile time with std::atomic<T>::is_always_lock_free (C++17), or with the ATOMIC_xxx_LOCK_FREE macros (0, 1, 2).
interview_qa.explanation:
- Typical x86-64 GCC results: `int`, pointers, 8-byte structs are always lock-free; a 24-byte struct is not; 16-byte types report `false` (operations go through `libatomic`, link with `-latomic`).
- When not lock-free, the implementation still provides full atomic semantics, typically with a lock taken from a hashed lock table.
- Why it matters:
  - A "lock-free algorithm" built on a non-lock-free atomic is not lock-free.
  - Only lock-free atomics are address-free, so only they are safe in memory shared between processes.
  - Not lock-free means not async-signal-safe.
- Guard design assumptions: `static_assert(std::atomic<Node*>::is_always_lock_free);`
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Atomics are generally lock-free; use `is_atomic_lock_free()`." There is no such function, and "generally" does not hold for arbitrary `T`.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: "atomic" describes indivisibility; "lock-free" is a progress guarantee. They are different properties.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Atomic does not imply lock-free; `static_assert(is_always_lock_free)` when it matters.

interview_qa.question: What does fetch_add compile to on x86-64, and why does it cost more than a plain increment?
interview_qa.answer: lock xadd (or lock add if the result is unused). The lock prefix makes the core hold the cache line exclusively for the whole read-modify-write and acts as a full memory barrier. If another core owns the line, it must be transferred first, which is the expensive part under contention.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Verified GCC 11 `-O2` codegen for `std::atomic<int>`:

| C++ (seq_cst) | x86-64 |
|---|---|
| `fetch_add(1)` | `lock xadd` |
| `fetch_add(1)`, result unused | `lock add` |
| `fetch_or(m)`, result used | `lock cmpxchg` loop |
| `exchange(v)`, `store(v)` | `xchg` |
| `load()` | `mov` |

- Cost components:
  - Read-for-ownership: other cores' copies are invalidated (MESI-family protocol).
  - Cache locking: the line is held for the duration; other cores are not stopped, the bus is not locked for aligned data.
  - Full barrier: the store buffer must drain before the locked op completes, so it also serializes this core's memory operations.
- Order of magnitude: about 10 to 20+ cycles uncontended; with contention, each operation may wait for a cross-core line transfer (tens of ns, more across sockets).
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "The lock prefix locks the whole bus/RAM and other cores stop." Modern CPUs lock only the cache line; unrelated work continues.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: `fetch_or` returning the old value has no single x86 instruction, so it becomes a CAS loop (not wait-free on x86); if only one bit is needed, compilers may use `lock bts`.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Atomic RMW cost is cache-line ownership plus a full barrier; contention multiplies it.

interview_qa.question: Is it accurate to say std::atomic works by flushing the store buffer, or because MESI makes the cache line exclusive?
interview_qa.answer: No. Those are possible hardware mechanisms, not the definition. C++ specifies a contract (atomicity, a modification order per object, and ordering per memory_order); the compiler and CPU choose instructions, fences and coherence actions to satisfy it, and they differ by architecture and order.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Counter-examples to "atomic = store buffer flush":
  - A `relaxed` or `release` store on x86 is a plain `mov`; nothing is flushed.
  - A `seq_cst` store on x86 is `xchg`, which does drain the store buffer; on ARMv8 it is `stlr`.
- Counter-example to "atomic = MESI": coherence alone keeps single-location reads/writes consistent, but it does not make load-add-store indivisible; that requires a locked instruction or LL/SC.
- Modification order does not mean the newest value is instantly in every core's register.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Atomic flushes the cache and store buffer so other cores see the value." It mixes implementation with specification and is wrong for relaxed/release operations.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: answer at the C++ level first (atomicity, modification order, happens-before), then say "on x86 this compiles to `lock xadd`, which holds the line in M state", clearly labelled as implementation.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Explain the contract first, the hardware second, and never confuse the two.

interview_qa.question: Many threads increment one std::atomic<long> metrics counter and it does not scale. Why, and how would you fix it?
interview_qa.answer: Every fetch_add needs exclusive ownership of the same cache line, so the line ping-pongs between cores and operations serialize on line transfers. Fix by removing sharing: per-thread or per-core counters on separate cache lines (alignas(64)), summed on read, or batching local increments.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Scale writes by not sharing them; pad per-thread state to separate cache lines.

interview_qa.question: Which types can you put in std::atomic<T>? Can you write std::atomic<std::string> or copy an atomic?
interview_qa.answer: T must be trivially copyable (and copy/move constructible and assignable), so std::atomic<std::string> does not compile. std::atomic itself is neither copyable nor movable; std::atomic<int> b = a; is ill-formed. Use b(a.load()) to copy the value.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Built-in specializations: integral types, pointers, `bool`, floating point (with `fetch_add/fetch_sub` since C++20), plus `std::shared_ptr` / `std::weak_ptr` (C++20).
- User structs work if trivially copyable; whether they are lock-free depends on size and alignment.
- Why not copyable: a copy would be a load from one object and a store to another, two operations that cannot be one atomic step; deleting the copy constructor prevents pretending otherwise.
- `std::atomic<int> a = 0;` compiles since C++17 (guaranteed elision).
- C++20: `std::atomic<int> x;` value-initializes to 0; earlier standards left it uninitialized.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "Any type can be made atomic." Non-trivially-copyable types fail a `static_assert`.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: CAS on floating point compares bits (`-0.0` vs `+0.0` mismatch, NaN can match), and padding in user structs matters for CAS on pre-C++20 implementations.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `std::atomic<T>` needs trivially copyable `T`, and the atomic object itself is non-copyable.

interview_qa.question: How would you implement an atomic "update maximum" operation, and what mistakes are common?
interview_qa.answer: Use a CAS loop: load expected; while expected < v, try compare_exchange_weak(expected, v); on failure expected refreshes and the condition is re-checked. Stop as soon as the stored value is already >= v, so no write happens. C++26 adds fetch_max for integers.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: CAS loop with the condition re-evaluated on every refreshed `expected`.

interview_qa.question: What is std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>> for, and is it lock-free?
interview_qa.answer: It makes reading and replacing one shared_ptr object from several threads safe (C++20), e.g. readers load a config snapshot while a writer stores a new one. A plain shared_ptr only makes the reference count thread-safe, not the object itself. It is not required to be lock-free and usually is not.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Thread-safe refcount is not thread-safe pointer object; `atomic<shared_ptr>` fixes the latter, usually with a lock.
interview_qa.full_content:
**Answer:**
It makes reading and replacing one shared_ptr object from several threads safe (C++20), e.g. readers load a config snapshot while a writer stores a new one. A plain shared_ptr only makes the reference count thread-safe, not the object itself. It is not required to be lock-free and usually is not.

**Explanation:**
- With plain `std::shared_ptr<Config> g;`, one thread doing `g = make_shared<Config>()` while another does `auto c = g;` is a data race: the copy reads the pointer pair while it is being replaced.
- C++20 usage (not compiled here: needs GCC 12+, MSVC 19.27+):
```cpp
std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<const Config>> cfg;
// reader
std::shared_ptr<const Config> snap = cfg.load();   // keeps old config alive while used
// writer
cfg.store(std::make_shared<const Config>(new_values));
```
- Replaces the C++11 free functions `std::atomic_load(&sp)` / `std::atomic_store(&sp, p)`, deprecated in C++20.
- Implementations: libstdc++ uses a lock bit inside the control-block pointer, MSVC a spin lock; `is_lock_free()` is `false`.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`shared_ptr` is already thread-safe, so no atomic needed." Only the control block's count is; concurrent access to the same `shared_ptr` instance is not.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: readers still do an atomic refcount increment per load (a contended cache line for hot configs); RCU or epoch schemes avoid that on the read path (topic 08).

**Key takeaway:** Thread-safe refcount is not thread-safe pointer object; `atomic<shared_ptr>` fixes the latter, usually with a lock.

interview_qa.question: Why is volatile not a substitute for std::atomic in C++?
interview_qa.answer: volatile only prevents the compiler from removing or merging accesses; it gives no atomicity (volatile ++ is still load, add, store), no inter-thread ordering, and concurrent access is still a data race. It is for memory-mapped I/O and signal handlers, not threads.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `volatile int c; ++c;` from two threads loses updates and is UB.
- `volatile bool` as a stop flag "works" on many compilers because loads are not hoisted, but the program still has a data race and other data published before the flag is not ordered.
- In Java and C#, `volatile` does imply visibility/ordering; that is a frequent source of confusion for engineers switching languages.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "`volatile` makes it read from memory every time, so threads see the latest value." Re-reading is not synchronization.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: C++20 deprecated many compound `volatile` operations (`++`, `+=` on volatile) precisely because people assumed atomicity.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: For threads use `std::atomic`; `volatile` is for hardware and signals.

interview_qa.question: What do C++20 atomic wait and notify give you over a spin loop?
interview_qa.answer: x.wait(old) blocks the thread until it observes a value different from old after a notify (it re-checks, so spurious wakeups are hidden), without burning CPU. notify_one/notify_all wake waiters. It is a lightweight futex-style alternative to a mutex plus condition variable for simple state changes.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: `wait`/`notify` turn a spin on an atomic into an efficient block, but only observe value changes.

practice_tasks.title: Question 1
practice_tasks.answer: Any value from 2 to 200000; typically well below 200000. No data race (no UB): it is a race condition that loses updates.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `load` and `store` are each atomic, so there is no data race and no torn value.
- The increment as a whole is not atomic: both threads can load the same value and both store `v + 1`.
- Why the minimum is 2: A loads 0 and pauses; B does 99999 increments; A stores 1; B loads 1 and pauses; A finishes its remaining 99999 iterations; B stores 2.
- The local `v` is not the problem: it is private to each thread. The gap between the two atomic operations is.
- **Key Concept:** Two atomic operations are not one atomic operation.

practice_tasks.title: Question 3
practice_tasks.answer: No data race, but updates can be lost: any multiple of 4 from 8 to 8000. Run-dependent (eight test runs printed 8000, 4368, 6320, 8000, 7516, 8000, 7584, 8000).
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `counter = counter + 4` is `operator int()` (atomic load), an addition in a register, then `operator=` (atomic store).
- Two threads can both load 40 and both store 44: one increment of 4 is lost.
- Because each half is atomic, there is no UB; the bug is a lost update (race condition).
- With only 1000 iterations one thread may finish before the other starts, so 8000 appears in some runs. A passing run proves nothing about correctness.
- `counter += 4` is a single atomic RMW and always gives 8000.
- **Key Concept:** `x += 4` is atomic; `x = x + 4` is load plus store.

practice_tasks.title: Question 4
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
failed: value=15 expected=15
retry success: value=20 expected=15
```

**Explanation:**
- First CAS: `15 != 10`, so it fails. The atomic is unchanged (15), and `expected` is overwritten with the current value (15).
- Second CAS: `expected` is now 15, which matches, so `value` becomes 20. On success `expected` is not modified.
- This automatic refresh of `expected` is exactly what makes CAS retry loops work without an extra `load()`.
- **Key Concept:** CAS failure writes the current value into `expected`.

practice_tasks.title: Question 5
practice_tasks.answer: Bug: desired is computed once, outside the loop. The program prints a run-dependent value below 400000 (and the counter can even move backwards during the run).
practice_tasks.explanation:
- Suppose a thread reads 5, so `desired = 6`. Other threads push the counter to 9.
- The CAS fails and refreshes `expected = 9`, but `desired` is still 6.
- Next attempt: CAS(9 to 6) succeeds. The counter **goes backwards**, erasing 3 increments.
- No data race and no UB; the CAS loop is just computing the new value from stale data.
- In a test run with 4 threads it printed well below 400000.
- **Key Concept:** In a CAS loop, recompute `desired` from the refreshed `expected` on every iteration.

practice_tasks.title: Question 6
practice_tasks.answer: Data race on running: undefined behaviour. With GCC 11 at -O2 it hangs forever (nothing printed); at -O0 it happens to print "stopped".
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `running` is written by `main` and read by `worker` with no synchronization, and it is not atomic: data race, UB.
- The optimizer may assume no other thread modifies `running` during the loop, so it reads it once and turns the loop into `if (running) for (;;) ++work;`. Verified: the `-O2` binary never stops.
- "A bool store is atomic on the CPU, it will be seen after a few iterations" is the classic wrong intuition: the C++ memory model, not the CPU, decides what the compiler may do.
- `volatile bool` would usually stop the hoisting but is still a data race in C++.
- `relaxed` is enough here because the flag publishes no other data; `join()` synchronizes the final read of `work`.
- **Key Concept:** Shared flags must be `std::atomic`, even a single `bool`.

practice_tasks.title: Question 7
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
true
false -0 -0
```

**Explanation:**
- `0.0 == -0.0` is `true` under IEEE comparison.
- `compare_exchange_strong` compares the **value representation** (bitwise, like `memcmp`), not `operator==`. `+0.0` and `-0.0` have different sign bits, so the CAS fails.
- On failure, `expected` receives the current value `-0.0`; `d` is unchanged.
- The reverse surprise also exists: a NaN loaded from the atomic matches itself in CAS although `NaN == NaN` is false.
- **Key Concept:** CAS is bitwise; floating point and padded structs can surprise you.

practice_tasks.title: Question 8
practice_tasks.answer: 1 on x86-64, but the code is wrong: compare_exchange_weak may fail spuriously, so on LL/SC CPUs (ARM without LSE, POWER, RISC-V) the initialization can be skipped entirely (prints 0).

- `weak` may return `false` even though `initialized == false`. There is no retry loop, so a spurious failure means nobody ever initializes.
- x86 `lock cmpxchg` never fails spuriously, which is why tests on a laptop pass and the bug appears on ARM servers or phones.
- Use `compare_exchange_strong` for one-shot decisions.
- Second design issue: other threads that lose the CAS return immediately, possibly before the winner has finished initializing. If callers must wait for initialization, use `std::call_once` or a static local.

**Explanation:**
- Pointers and 8-byte trivially copyable structs fit a native 8-byte atomic instruction: lock-free.
- A 24-byte struct cannot be updated by one instruction, so `std::atomic<Large>` is implemented with a lock (in GCC's `libatomic`). It is still fully atomic, just not lock-free.
- Doing actual operations on `std::atomic<Large>` with GCC requires linking `-latomic`.
- Platform-specific: the standard only guarantees `std::atomic_flag` is lock-free.
- A "lock-free" algorithm built on `std::atomic<Large>` would silently contain a lock.
- **Key Concept:** `std::atomic<T>` does not imply lock-free; check `is_always_lock_free`.

practice_tasks.title: Question 10
practice_tasks.answer: Not thread-safe. Prints 20 (one withdrawal) or -60 (both threads passed the check before either subtracted).
practice_tasks.explanation:
- Every individual operation is atomic, so there is no data race.
- The invariant "never go negative" needs check and act to be one atomic step. Both threads can read 100, both pass `>= 80`, both subtract.
- Making more variables atomic does not help; the problem is the compound operation.
- Fix options: a mutex around the whole check-and-update (needed if `active` must be part of the decision), or a CAS loop on `balance` that re-checks the condition against each refreshed `expected`.
- **Key Concept:** Atomics protect single operations; invariants spanning several steps or variables need a mutex or a single-word CAS loop.

practice_tasks.title: Question 11
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Compile error on line B: use of deleted copy constructor std::atomic<int>::atomic(const std::atomic<int>&). Line A is fine in C++17 and later.
```

**Explanation:**
- `std::atomic` deletes its copy constructor and copy assignment. A copy would be a load from `a` and a store to `b`: two operations that cannot be one atomic step, so the library refuses to pretend.
- Line A uses the `atomic(int)` constructor; with C++17 guaranteed copy elision no copy/move constructor is needed. (In C++11/14 line A was ill-formed.)
- Confirmed with GCC 11: `error: use of deleted function 'std::atomic<int>::atomic(const std::atomic<int>&)'`.
- To copy the value: `std::atomic<int> b{a.load()};`.
- **Key Concept:** Atomics are non-copyable, non-movable objects; copy the value explicitly.

**Fixed Version:**
```cpp
#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::atomic<int> a = 5;
    std::atomic<int> b{a.load()};   // explicit load of the value
    std::cout << b << '\n';         // 5
}
```

practice_tasks.title: Question 12
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
5 7 7 20 20 0
```

**Explanation:**
- `x++` returns the old value (5), `x` becomes 6.
- `++x` returns the new value (7).
- `fetch_add(10)` returns the **old** value (7), `x` becomes 17.
- `x += 3` returns the **new** value (20), by value, not a reference.
- `exchange(0)` returns the old value (20) and stores 0.
- All `fetch_*` and `exchange` return the previous value; compound assignment operators return the result.
- **Key Concept:** Know which atomic operations return old vs new values.

practice_tasks.title: Question 13
practice_tasks.answer: No mutual exclusion: data race on shared (undefined behaviour). Typically prints less than 200000.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `test_and_set()` returns the **previous** value. The lock is acquired when it returns `false`.
- With the inverted condition `while (!flag.test_and_set())`:
  - If the flag was clear, the call returns `false`, the loop continues, the next call returns `true` and the loop exits: the thread "acquires" a lock it set itself.
  - If another thread holds the lock, the call returns `true` and the loop exits immediately: the thread enters anyway.
- So two threads can be inside the critical section at once, and `++shared` on a plain `long` is a data race.
- **Key Concept:** `test_and_set` returns the old value: spin while it returns `true`.

practice_tasks.title: Question 14
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
-2147483648
4294967295
```

**Explanation:**
- For a plain `int`, `INT_MAX + 1` is undefined behaviour.
- For atomic signed integers the standard defines arithmetic as if performed on the corresponding unsigned type and converted back: two's complement wraparound, **no UB**.
- Unsigned atomics wrap as usual (`0 - 1` gives `UINT_MAX` = 4294967295 with 32-bit `unsigned`).
- Practical consequence: a wrapping atomic sequence number is well-defined, but your logic must still handle the wrap.
- **Key Concept:** Atomic integer arithmetic wraps without UB, unlike plain signed arithmetic.

quick_reference.content:
#### Atomic vs non-atomic expressions on `std::atomic<int> x`
| Expression | One atomic RMW? | Lost updates possible? | Data race? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `++x`, `x++`, `x += 4` | ✅ | No | No |
| `x.fetch_add(4)` | ✅ | No | No |
| `x = x + 4` | ❌ load + store | Yes | No |
| `int v = x.load(); x.store(v + 4);` | ❌ | Yes | No |
| same on plain `int` | ❌ | Yes | **Yes (UB)** |

#### CAS in one table
| Situation | Return | Atomic after | `expected` after |
|---|---|---|---|
| current == expected | `true` | `desired` | unchanged |
| current != expected | `false` | unchanged | **current value** |
| weak, spurious failure | `false` | unchanged | current value (equal to old expected) |

#### weak vs strong
| | `compare_exchange_weak` | `compare_exchange_strong` |
|---|---|---|
| Spurious failure | allowed | never |
| Use | inside a retry loop | one-shot decision, or expensive retry |
| x86-64 | `lock cmpxchg` | same `lock cmpxchg` |
| LL/SC (ARM w/o LSE, POWER, RISC-V) | one LL/SC attempt | internal loop |

#### Lock-free queries
| API | Notes |
|---|---|
| `a.is_lock_free()` | runtime, per object |
| `std::atomic<T>::is_always_lock_free` | `constexpr`, C++17 |
| `ATOMIC_xxx_LOCK_FREE` | 0 / 1 / 2 |
| `std::atomic_flag` | the only type guaranteed lock-free |

#### Cost model (typical x86-64)
| Operation | Rough cost |
|---|---|
| load of a line shared by all readers | cheap, scales |
| uncontended `lock` RMW | ~10 to 20+ cycles, full barrier |
| contended RMW on one line | cache-line transfer per op; tens to hundreds of ns; throughput can fall as threads increase |
| seq_cst store | `xchg` (locked) |
| release store / relaxed store | plain `mov` |

#### Interview one-liners
| Question | One-liner |
|---|---|
| What does `std::atomic` guarantee? | Indivisible operations on one object, no data race, one modification order; ordering is a separate knob. |
| Is `++atomic` atomic? | Yes, it is an atomic RMW; `x = x + 1` is not. |
| Why does `load`/`store` increment fail? | The gap between two atomic operations, not the local variable. |
| What does CAS do on failure? | Returns false and writes the current value into `expected`. |
| weak vs strong? | Weak may fail spuriously; use it in loops. Strong for one-shot decisions. |
| Why the CAS loop? | Competing writers plus spurious failure; recompute `desired` each time. |
| Is a CAS loop wait-free? | No, lock-free: someone succeeds, a given thread may starve. |
| Is `std::atomic<T>` lock-free? | Not guaranteed; check `is_always_lock_free`; only `atomic_flag` is guaranteed. |
| Does atomic flush the store buffer? | Not a C++ concept; hardware mechanism varies by order and CPU. |
| Atomic or mutex? | Atomic for one independent value, mutex for multi-variable invariants; measure. |
| Can relaxed tear? | No; memory order never affects atomicity. |
| Why atomic for a bool flag? | Plain concurrent access is a data race (UB); compiler may hoist the load. |
| Why do atomics scale badly? | Every write needs exclusive cache-line ownership; the line ping-pongs. |
| `atomic<shared_ptr>`? | C++20, atomic replace/read of one `shared_ptr` object; usually not lock-free. |
