topics.topic: Memory Ordering and the C++ Memory Model

subsections.title: 1. Mental model: two separate questions
subsections.content:
- Every `std::atomic` operation answers two different questions:
  - **Atomicity:** "Can several threads touch *this variable* without a data race, torn values or lost updates?"
  - **Memory ordering:** "What does this operation guarantee about *other* memory (usually non-atomic data) around it?"
- Atomicity is always present on a `std::atomic` operation, even with `memory_order_relaxed`. The `memory_order` argument only changes the ordering answer.
- One sentence to remember: **atomic says "this operation on this variable is safe"; memory order says "how this operation relates to operations on other memory".**
- Think in three layers and never mix them in an answer:

| Layer | Vocabulary | Who defines it |
|---|---|---|
| C++ abstract machine | sequenced-before, synchronizes-with, happens-before, modification order, data race | The C++ standard (portable guarantee) |
| Compiler | instruction selection, compiler reordering, compiler barriers | Your toolchain |
| CPU / memory system | store buffers, invalidation queues, MESI, fences (`mfence`, `dmb`), `lock` prefix | The architecture (x86, ARM, POWER) |

- Interview rule: answer at the C++ level first ("release synchronizes-with an acquire that reads its value, which creates happens-before"). Mention store buffers and MESI only as *one possible implementation*, and only if asked.

subsections.title: 2. Data race and the relations that prevent it
subsections.content:
- **Data race (standard definition):** two accesses to the same memory location, from different threads, at least one is a write, at least one is non-atomic, and neither happens-before the other. Result: **undefined behaviour** for the whole program, not just "a stale value".
- Atomic operations never race with each other, whatever memory order they use.
- The relations you must use precisely:

| Relation | Scope | Created by |
|---|---|---|
| **Sequenced-before** | Within one thread | Program order of evaluations (statement order, `;`, etc.) |
| **Synchronizes-with** | Between two threads | Release op → acquire op that *reads the value written* (or a value from its release sequence); mutex unlock → next lock; thread constructor → thread start; thread end → `join()` return |
| **Happens-before** | Within and across threads | Sequenced-before and synchronizes-with chained together (transitively) |
| **Modification order** | One atomic object | Every atomic object has one total order of all its modifications, agreed on by all threads |

- The canonical chain to say out loud:
  - `data = 42` is **sequenced-before** `ready.store(true, release)`
  - that store **synchronizes-with** `ready.load(acquire)` *if the load reads `true`*
  - the load is **sequenced-before** `read(data)`
  - therefore `data = 42` **happens-before** `read(data)`: no data race, and the read must see 42.
- Execution order is not synchronization: "thread 1 ran first" proves nothing. Only a happens-before edge makes the later read safe.

subsections.title: 3. Modification order and coherence
subsections.content:
- Each atomic object (one `std::atomic<T>` instance) has **its own** single total modification order containing every store and every RMW (`fetch_add`, `exchange`, successful `compare_exchange`) from **all threads**.
- Loads are **not** part of the modification order; a load *observes* one value from that history.
- There is no combined modification order for `x` and `y`. Two different atomics can be observed "out of order" relative to each other unless you add synchronization.
- Four coherence rules hold for every memory order, including relaxed:

| Rule | Meaning |
|---|---|
| write-write | Two modifications ordered by happens-before appear in that order in the modification order |
| read-read | If a thread's load reads value from modification B, a later load in that thread cannot read a modification earlier than B |
| read-write | A load cannot read a value written by a store that happens-after it |
| write-read | After a thread writes or reads a value, it cannot later read an older value |

- Practical result: per variable, a thread's observations never go backward. If a thread reads `20`, its next relaxed load cannot return the older `10`.
- RMW operations always read the **latest** value in the modification order, which is why `fetch_add` never loses an increment even when relaxed.
- Atomic does **not** mean "every thread instantly sees the newest store". The standard only says implementations *should* make stores visible to loads "within a reasonable amount of time".

subsections.title: 4. The six memory orders
subsections.content:
| Order | Valid on | Guarantees beyond atomicity | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `relaxed` | load, store, RMW | Nothing for other memory; only atomicity and per-object coherence | Statistics counters, IDs, a stop flag that publishes no data |
| `consume` | load | Dependency ordering only (data reached through the loaded pointer). Every major compiler promotes it to acquire; discouraged since C++17, deprecated in C++26 | Do not use; write `acquire` |
| `acquire` | load, RMW | No later read/write in this thread may be reordered before it; synchronizes-with a release whose value it reads | Consumer side of publication, lock acquire |
| `release` | store, RMW | No earlier read/write in this thread may be reordered after it; publishes everything sequenced before it | Producer side of publication, lock release |
| `acq_rel` | RMW only | Acquire and release in one RMW | CAS that both claims and publishes, ref-count decrement |
| `seq_cst` (default) | all | Acquire (load) / release (store) / acq_rel (RMW) **plus** one single total order `S` of all `seq_cst` operations on all objects, consistent with each thread's order | Default; required for store-load patterns (Dekker, Peterson, flag pairs) |

- Passing an order that is invalid for the operation is a precondition violation (undefined behaviour): `store(x, acquire)`, `store(x, acq_rel)`, `load(release)`, `load(acq_rel)`. libstdc++ aborts with `-D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS`; a plain build compiles silently.
- `compare_exchange_*(expected, desired, success, failure)`: the failure order is a load, so it cannot be `release` or `acq_rel`.
- Acquire and release are **one-way** barriers ("roach motel"):
  - Operations *before* a release cannot move below it, but operations *after* it may move above it.
  - Operations *after* an acquire cannot move above it, but operations *before* it may move below it.
  - So release + acquire alone never prevents a **store followed by a load** (to different variables) from being reordered. That is exactly the gap `seq_cst` closes.

subsections.title: 5. Release sequences and transitivity
subsections.content:
- Happens-before is transitive: if T1 publishes to T2 (release/acquire on `a`), and T2 then publishes to T3 (release/acquire on `b`), everything T1 did before its release happens-before T3's reads. T3 never touched `a`.
- **Release sequence:** after a release store `A` on atomic `M`, any chain of RMW operations on `M` (from any thread, even relaxed ones) continues the release sequence. An acquire that reads a value written by one of those RMWs still synchronizes-with `A`.
  - This is why a relaxed `fetch_add` in the middle does not break publication through a counter.
  - C++20 narrowed the rule: a later plain (non-RMW) store by the same thread no longer extends the release sequence.
- An acquire synchronizes-with a release only through the value it actually reads. Reading the initial value, or a value from a different unrelated plain store, gives no synchronization.

subsections.title: 6. Fences: `std::atomic_thread_fence`
subsections.content:
- A fence is not tied to one variable; it upgrades the ordering of nearby **relaxed atomic** operations.
- Synchronization through fences always needs an atomic object to carry the value:

| Pattern | Producer | Consumer |
|---|---|---|
| fence-fence | `fence(release); flag.store(1, relaxed);` | `if (flag.load(relaxed)) { fence(acquire); use(); }` |
| fence-atomic | `fence(release); flag.store(1, relaxed);` | `flag.load(acquire)` |
| atomic-fence | `flag.store(1, release);` | `flag.load(relaxed); fence(acquire);` |

- Placement matters: the release fence goes **before** the publishing store, the acquire fence goes **after** the load that observed it.
- `atomic_thread_fence(seq_cst)` is the strongest fence and restores store-load ordering between relaxed operations.
- `std::atomic_signal_fence` orders only against a signal handler on the same thread: compiler-only, emits no CPU instruction.
- A fence with no atomic operation around it creates no synchronization at all. "Sprinkle a barrier and it works" is a myth.
- Use fences when one acquire should cover many relaxed loads (for example, only after a loop finds the slot it wants), or when implementing seqlocks and reference counting.

subsections.title: 7. Compiler reordering vs CPU reordering, x86 vs ARM
subsections.content:
- Two independent sources of reordering, and C++ orders control **both**:
  - **Compiler:** under the as-if rule it may reorder, merge, hoist out of loops or delete non-atomic accesses, assuming no other thread is watching (because a data race would be UB).
  - **CPU:** out-of-order execution, store buffers and invalidation queues make memory operations visible to other cores in an order different from program order.
- A compiler-only barrier (`asm volatile("" ::: "memory")` in GCC/Clang, or `atomic_signal_fence`) stops the compiler but not the CPU. It is not a portable inter-thread tool.
- x86-64 is **TSO** (total store order): the only visible hardware reordering is a store followed by a later load to a different address (store buffer). Loads are not reordered with loads, stores not with stores.
- ARMv8 and POWER are **weakly ordered**: load-load, load-store, store-store and store-load reorderings are all allowed without barriers.
- Typical code generation (verified for x86-64 with GCC 11; ARM is the standard published mapping):

| C++ operation | x86-64 (GCC) | ARMv8 (AArch64) |
|---|---|---|
| load relaxed / acquire / seq_cst | plain `mov` (all three) | `ldr` / `ldar` (or `ldapr`) / `ldar` |
| store relaxed / release | plain `mov` | `str` / `stlr` |
| store seq_cst | `xchg` (or `mov` + `mfence` on older compilers) | `stlr` |
| `fetch_add` (any order) | `lock xadd` | LL/SC loop (`ldxr`/`stxr`) or LSE `ldadd` with `a`/`l` variants |
| `atomic_thread_fence(acq_rel)` | nothing (compiler barrier only) | `dmb ish` |
| `atomic_thread_fence(seq_cst)` | `mfence` or `lock or [rsp], 0` | `dmb ish` |

- Consequence 1: on x86 acquire/release cost nothing at runtime but still restrict the **compiler**. Code with a relaxed flag can "work" on x86 and break on ARM, or break on x86 after the compiler reorders it.
- Consequence 2: on x86 the expensive part of `seq_cst` is the store (a locked instruction that drains the store buffer), which is why `seq_cst` stores are a known hot-path cost in low-latency code.

subsections.title: 8. Synchronization you get for free: mutexes, threads, `call_once`, statics
subsections.content:
- `mutex.lock()` is an acquire operation; `mutex.unlock()` is a release operation.
- Every mutex has a total order of lock/unlock; each unlock **synchronizes-with** the next successful lock of the same mutex. Everything written inside one critical section happens-before everything in the next one.
- Which thread locks first is **not** decided. If the reader gets the lock first it sees the old value, but there is still **no data race**: a logical race, not UB.
- A condition variable provides waiting and notification; the data visibility comes from the **mutex** it is used with.
- `std::thread` constructor completion synchronizes-with the start of the thread function; thread completion synchronizes-with the return of `join()`. That is why main can read results after `join()` without atomics.
- `std::call_once` and function-local `static` initialization (C++11 "magic statics") are thread-safe and publish the initialized object to every caller.
- C++20 `atomic::wait` / `notify_one`: blocking waits on an atomic; ordering still comes from the memory orders of the store and of the load that returns.

subsections.title: 9. `volatile` is not a threading tool
subsections.content:
- `volatile` tells the compiler: "accesses to this object are observable side effects; actually perform every read and write, do not cache or remove them".
- Valid uses: memory-mapped hardware registers (MMIO), `volatile std::sig_atomic_t` flags written by signal handlers, locals that must survive `longjmp`.
- What `volatile` does **not** provide:
  - ❌ atomicity (a `volatile int` increment is still read, add, write)
  - ❌ freedom from data races (a race on a `volatile` object is still UB)
  - ❌ any happens-before or release/acquire semantics
  - ❌ CPU ordering: the compiler keeps volatile accesses in order relative to each other, but non-volatile accesses can move across them and the CPU can still reorder.
- MSVC's `/volatile:ms` (default on x86/x64, not on ARM) gives volatile acquire/release semantics. This is a non-portable extension; never rely on it in interview answers or portable code.
- Rule: hardware or signal handler → `volatile`; another C++ thread → `std::atomic`, a mutex, or another synchronization primitive.

subsections.title: 10. Misconceptions to unlearn
subsections.content:
- ❌ "Release flushes the store buffer; acquire invalidates stale cache lines." ✅ Those are possible implementation effects. The C++ guarantee is a synchronizes-with edge when the acquire reads the released value.
- ❌ "Relaxed flushes or commits the store buffer." ✅ Relaxed adds no ordering at all; it is still fully atomic.
- ❌ "`seq_cst` stalls the pipeline / flushes every cache." ✅ It adds a single total order of `seq_cst` operations; its cost depends on the architecture (on x86, mostly the store).
- ❌ "Atomic means one indivisible CPU instruction." ✅ C++ only promises atomic semantics; the implementation may use a lock (`is_lock_free()` tells you, see topic 05).
- ❌ "Atomic means every thread immediately sees the newest value." ✅ Loads observe some value allowed by coherence and ordering rules.
- ❌ "A relaxed publication might just print 0." ✅ With non-atomic `data` it is a data race: undefined behaviour.
- ❌ "Only `data` is the problem; a plain `bool ready` flag is fine." ✅ The flag itself races if it is not atomic.
- ❌ "Making the consumer load `acquire` fixes a relaxed store." ✅ Both sides are required: release on the store, acquire on the load.
- ❌ "Acquire waits for the release." ✅ Acquire never waits; a load that runs first just reads the old value and synchronizes with nothing.
- ❌ "Modification order is per thread" or "one order for all atomics." ✅ One order **per atomic object**, across all threads.
- ❌ "Relaxed is unsafe." ✅ Relaxed is exactly right for counters and flags that publish nothing.
- ❌ "Every two `seq_cst` operations synchronize." ✅ They share one total order; synchronizes-with still needs a store whose value a load reads.
- ❌ "`seq_cst` decides which thread runs first." ✅ It constrains allowed outcomes, not scheduling.
- ❌ "Any memory barrier makes the code correct." ✅ You need a matched pair (release side and acquire side) on the same atomic object.
- ❌ "`volatile` means don't reorder, so it works for flags between threads." ✅ It gives no atomicity and no inter-thread ordering.
- ❌ "MESI is the definition of release/acquire" and ❌ "MESI is unrelated." ✅ Cache coherence is part of how hardware implements the guarantees, but it is not the guarantee.

theory.full_text:
#### 1. Mental model: two separate questions
- Every `std::atomic` operation answers two different questions:
  - **Atomicity:** "Can several threads touch *this variable* without a data race, torn values or lost updates?"
  - **Memory ordering:** "What does this operation guarantee about *other* memory (usually non-atomic data) around it?"
- Atomicity is always present on a `std::atomic` operation, even with `memory_order_relaxed`. The `memory_order` argument only changes the ordering answer.
- One sentence to remember: **atomic says "this operation on this variable is safe"; memory order says "how this operation relates to operations on other memory".**
- Think in three layers and never mix them in an answer:

| Layer | Vocabulary | Who defines it |
|---|---|---|
| C++ abstract machine | sequenced-before, synchronizes-with, happens-before, modification order, data race | The C++ standard (portable guarantee) |
| Compiler | instruction selection, compiler reordering, compiler barriers | Your toolchain |
| CPU / memory system | store buffers, invalidation queues, MESI, fences (`mfence`, `dmb`), `lock` prefix | The architecture (x86, ARM, POWER) |

- Interview rule: answer at the C++ level first ("release synchronizes-with an acquire that reads its value, which creates happens-before"). Mention store buffers and MESI only as *one possible implementation*, and only if asked.

#### 2. Data race and the relations that prevent it
- **Data race (standard definition):** two accesses to the same memory location, from different threads, at least one is a write, at least one is non-atomic, and neither happens-before the other. Result: **undefined behaviour** for the whole program, not just "a stale value".
- Atomic operations never race with each other, whatever memory order they use.
- The relations you must use precisely:

| Relation | Scope | Created by |
|---|---|---|
| **Sequenced-before** | Within one thread | Program order of evaluations (statement order, `;`, etc.) |
| **Synchronizes-with** | Between two threads | Release op → acquire op that *reads the value written* (or a value from its release sequence); mutex unlock → next lock; thread constructor → thread start; thread end → `join()` return |
| **Happens-before** | Within and across threads | Sequenced-before and synchronizes-with chained together (transitively) |
| **Modification order** | One atomic object | Every atomic object has one total order of all its modifications, agreed on by all threads |

- The canonical chain to say out loud:
  - `data = 42` is **sequenced-before** `ready.store(true, release)`
  - that store **synchronizes-with** `ready.load(acquire)` *if the load reads `true`*
  - the load is **sequenced-before** `read(data)`
  - therefore `data = 42` **happens-before** `read(data)`: no data race, and the read must see 42.
- Execution order is not synchronization: "thread 1 ran first" proves nothing. Only a happens-before edge makes the later read safe.

#### 3. Modification order and coherence
- Each atomic object (one `std::atomic<T>` instance) has **its own** single total modification order containing every store and every RMW (`fetch_add`, `exchange`, successful `compare_exchange`) from **all threads**.
- Loads are **not** part of the modification order; a load *observes* one value from that history.
- There is no combined modification order for `x` and `y`. Two different atomics can be observed "out of order" relative to each other unless you add synchronization.
- Four coherence rules hold for every memory order, including relaxed:

| Rule | Meaning |
|---|---|
| write-write | Two modifications ordered by happens-before appear in that order in the modification order |
| read-read | If a thread's load reads value from modification B, a later load in that thread cannot read a modification earlier than B |
| read-write | A load cannot read a value written by a store that happens-after it |
| write-read | After a thread writes or reads a value, it cannot later read an older value |

- Practical result: per variable, a thread's observations never go backward. If a thread reads `20`, its next relaxed load cannot return the older `10`.
- RMW operations always read the **latest** value in the modification order, which is why `fetch_add` never loses an increment even when relaxed.
- Atomic does **not** mean "every thread instantly sees the newest store". The standard only says implementations *should* make stores visible to loads "within a reasonable amount of time".

#### 4. The six memory orders

| Order | Valid on | Guarantees beyond atomicity | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `relaxed` | load, store, RMW | Nothing for other memory; only atomicity and per-object coherence | Statistics counters, IDs, a stop flag that publishes no data |
| `consume` | load | Dependency ordering only (data reached through the loaded pointer). Every major compiler promotes it to acquire; discouraged since C++17, deprecated in C++26 | Do not use; write `acquire` |
| `acquire` | load, RMW | No later read/write in this thread may be reordered before it; synchronizes-with a release whose value it reads | Consumer side of publication, lock acquire |
| `release` | store, RMW | No earlier read/write in this thread may be reordered after it; publishes everything sequenced before it | Producer side of publication, lock release |
| `acq_rel` | RMW only | Acquire and release in one RMW | CAS that both claims and publishes, ref-count decrement |
| `seq_cst` (default) | all | Acquire (load) / release (store) / acq_rel (RMW) **plus** one single total order `S` of all `seq_cst` operations on all objects, consistent with each thread's order | Default; required for store-load patterns (Dekker, Peterson, flag pairs) |

- Passing an order that is invalid for the operation is a precondition violation (undefined behaviour): `store(x, acquire)`, `store(x, acq_rel)`, `load(release)`, `load(acq_rel)`. libstdc++ aborts with `-D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS`; a plain build compiles silently.
- `compare_exchange_*(expected, desired, success, failure)`: the failure order is a load, so it cannot be `release` or `acq_rel`.
- Acquire and release are **one-way** barriers ("roach motel"):
  - Operations *before* a release cannot move below it, but operations *after* it may move above it.
  - Operations *after* an acquire cannot move above it, but operations *before* it may move below it.
  - So release + acquire alone never prevents a **store followed by a load** (to different variables) from being reordered. That is exactly the gap `seq_cst` closes.

#### 5. Release sequences and transitivity
- Happens-before is transitive: if T1 publishes to T2 (release/acquire on `a`), and T2 then publishes to T3 (release/acquire on `b`), everything T1 did before its release happens-before T3's reads. T3 never touched `a`.
- **Release sequence:** after a release store `A` on atomic `M`, any chain of RMW operations on `M` (from any thread, even relaxed ones) continues the release sequence. An acquire that reads a value written by one of those RMWs still synchronizes-with `A`.
  - This is why a relaxed `fetch_add` in the middle does not break publication through a counter.
  - C++20 narrowed the rule: a later plain (non-RMW) store by the same thread no longer extends the release sequence.
- An acquire synchronizes-with a release only through the value it actually reads. Reading the initial value, or a value from a different unrelated plain store, gives no synchronization.

#### 6. Fences: `std::atomic_thread_fence`
- A fence is not tied to one variable; it upgrades the ordering of nearby **relaxed atomic** operations.
- Synchronization through fences always needs an atomic object to carry the value:

| Pattern | Producer | Consumer |
|---|---|---|
| fence-fence | `fence(release); flag.store(1, relaxed);` | `if (flag.load(relaxed)) { fence(acquire); use(); }` |
| fence-atomic | `fence(release); flag.store(1, relaxed);` | `flag.load(acquire)` |
| atomic-fence | `flag.store(1, release);` | `flag.load(relaxed); fence(acquire);` |

- Placement matters: the release fence goes **before** the publishing store, the acquire fence goes **after** the load that observed it.
- `atomic_thread_fence(seq_cst)` is the strongest fence and restores store-load ordering between relaxed operations.
- `std::atomic_signal_fence` orders only against a signal handler on the same thread: compiler-only, emits no CPU instruction.
- A fence with no atomic operation around it creates no synchronization at all. "Sprinkle a barrier and it works" is a myth.
- Use fences when one acquire should cover many relaxed loads (for example, only after a loop finds the slot it wants), or when implementing seqlocks and reference counting.

#### 7. Compiler reordering vs CPU reordering, x86 vs ARM
- Two independent sources of reordering, and C++ orders control **both**:
  - **Compiler:** under the as-if rule it may reorder, merge, hoist out of loops or delete non-atomic accesses, assuming no other thread is watching (because a data race would be UB).
  - **CPU:** out-of-order execution, store buffers and invalidation queues make memory operations visible to other cores in an order different from program order.
- A compiler-only barrier (`asm volatile("" ::: "memory")` in GCC/Clang, or `atomic_signal_fence`) stops the compiler but not the CPU. It is not a portable inter-thread tool.
- x86-64 is **TSO** (total store order): the only visible hardware reordering is a store followed by a later load to a different address (store buffer). Loads are not reordered with loads, stores not with stores.
- ARMv8 and POWER are **weakly ordered**: load-load, load-store, store-store and store-load reorderings are all allowed without barriers.
- Typical code generation (verified for x86-64 with GCC 11; ARM is the standard published mapping):

| C++ operation | x86-64 (GCC) | ARMv8 (AArch64) |
|---|---|---|
| load relaxed / acquire / seq_cst | plain `mov` (all three) | `ldr` / `ldar` (or `ldapr`) / `ldar` |
| store relaxed / release | plain `mov` | `str` / `stlr` |
| store seq_cst | `xchg` (or `mov` + `mfence` on older compilers) | `stlr` |
| `fetch_add` (any order) | `lock xadd` | LL/SC loop (`ldxr`/`stxr`) or LSE `ldadd` with `a`/`l` variants |
| `atomic_thread_fence(acq_rel)` | nothing (compiler barrier only) | `dmb ish` |
| `atomic_thread_fence(seq_cst)` | `mfence` or `lock or [rsp], 0` | `dmb ish` |

- Consequence 1: on x86 acquire/release cost nothing at runtime but still restrict the **compiler**. Code with a relaxed flag can "work" on x86 and break on ARM, or break on x86 after the compiler reorders it.
- Consequence 2: on x86 the expensive part of `seq_cst` is the store (a locked instruction that drains the store buffer), which is why `seq_cst` stores are a known hot-path cost in low-latency code.

#### 8. Synchronization you get for free: mutexes, threads, `call_once`, statics
- `mutex.lock()` is an acquire operation; `mutex.unlock()` is a release operation.
- Every mutex has a total order of lock/unlock; each unlock **synchronizes-with** the next successful lock of the same mutex. Everything written inside one critical section happens-before everything in the next one.
- Which thread locks first is **not** decided. If the reader gets the lock first it sees the old value, but there is still **no data race**: a logical race, not UB.
- A condition variable provides waiting and notification; the data visibility comes from the **mutex** it is used with.
- `std::thread` constructor completion synchronizes-with the start of the thread function; thread completion synchronizes-with the return of `join()`. That is why main can read results after `join()` without atomics.
- `std::call_once` and function-local `static` initialization (C++11 "magic statics") are thread-safe and publish the initialized object to every caller.
- C++20 `atomic::wait` / `notify_one`: blocking waits on an atomic; ordering still comes from the memory orders of the store and of the load that returns.

#### 9. `volatile` is not a threading tool
- `volatile` tells the compiler: "accesses to this object are observable side effects; actually perform every read and write, do not cache or remove them".
- Valid uses: memory-mapped hardware registers (MMIO), `volatile std::sig_atomic_t` flags written by signal handlers, locals that must survive `longjmp`.
- What `volatile` does **not** provide:
  - ❌ atomicity (a `volatile int` increment is still read, add, write)
  - ❌ freedom from data races (a race on a `volatile` object is still UB)
  - ❌ any happens-before or release/acquire semantics
  - ❌ CPU ordering: the compiler keeps volatile accesses in order relative to each other, but non-volatile accesses can move across them and the CPU can still reorder.
- MSVC's `/volatile:ms` (default on x86/x64, not on ARM) gives volatile acquire/release semantics. This is a non-portable extension; never rely on it in interview answers or portable code.
- Rule: hardware or signal handler → `volatile`; another C++ thread → `std::atomic`, a mutex, or another synchronization primitive.

#### 10. Misconceptions to unlearn
- ❌ "Release flushes the store buffer; acquire invalidates stale cache lines." ✅ Those are possible implementation effects. The C++ guarantee is a synchronizes-with edge when the acquire reads the released value.
- ❌ "Relaxed flushes or commits the store buffer." ✅ Relaxed adds no ordering at all; it is still fully atomic.
- ❌ "`seq_cst` stalls the pipeline / flushes every cache." ✅ It adds a single total order of `seq_cst` operations; its cost depends on the architecture (on x86, mostly the store).
- ❌ "Atomic means one indivisible CPU instruction." ✅ C++ only promises atomic semantics; the implementation may use a lock (`is_lock_free()` tells you, see topic 05).
- ❌ "Atomic means every thread immediately sees the newest value." ✅ Loads observe some value allowed by coherence and ordering rules.
- ❌ "A relaxed publication might just print 0." ✅ With non-atomic `data` it is a data race: undefined behaviour.
- ❌ "Only `data` is the problem; a plain `bool ready` flag is fine." ✅ The flag itself races if it is not atomic.
- ❌ "Making the consumer load `acquire` fixes a relaxed store." ✅ Both sides are required: release on the store, acquire on the load.
- ❌ "Acquire waits for the release." ✅ Acquire never waits; a load that runs first just reads the old value and synchronizes with nothing.
- ❌ "Modification order is per thread" or "one order for all atomics." ✅ One order **per atomic object**, across all threads.
- ❌ "Relaxed is unsafe." ✅ Relaxed is exactly right for counters and flags that publish nothing.
- ❌ "Every two `seq_cst` operations synchronize." ✅ They share one total order; synchronizes-with still needs a store whose value a load reads.
- ❌ "`seq_cst` decides which thread runs first." ✅ It constrains allowed outcomes, not scheduling.
- ❌ "Any memory barrier makes the code correct." ✅ You need a matched pair (release side and acquire side) on the same atomic object.
- ❌ "`volatile` means don't reorder, so it works for flags between threads." ✅ It gives no atomicity and no inter-thread ordering.
- ❌ "MESI is the definition of release/acquire" and ❌ "MESI is unrelated." ✅ Cache coherence is part of how hardware implements the guarantees, but it is not the guarantee.

edge_cases.title: Acquire on one side only gives you nothing
An acquire load that runs before the release store
edge_cases.explanation:
- What people assume: "acquire waits until the producer releases".
- What actually happens: a load returns whatever value it observes at that point. If it reads the initial value, it synchronizes with nothing; the consumer simply sees "not ready".
- This is correct behaviour, not a bug, provided the consumer only touches the data when the flag says ready.
```cpp
// Consumer runs first
if (ready.load(std::memory_order_acquire)) {   // reads false
    use(data);                                 // not executed: no access, no race
}
// The producer's release store that happens later does not update this old load.
```
- If the consumer must wait, use a loop, C++20 `ready.wait(false)`, or a condition variable.

edge_cases.title: Release/acquire does not forbid store-then-load reordering
edge_cases.explanation:
- What people assume: "acquire/release is strong enough for any flag protocol".
- What actually happens: release keeps earlier operations above it; acquire keeps later operations below it. A release **store** followed by an acquire **load** of a different variable can still be reordered (the store can sit in the store buffer while the load executes).
- Classic store-buffering (Dekker) test, `x = y = 0` initially:
```cpp
// T1                                 // T2
x.store(1, std::memory_order_release); y.store(1, std::memory_order_release);
r1 = y.load(std::memory_order_acquire); r2 = x.load(std::memory_order_acquire);
```
- `r1 == 0 && r2 == 0` is allowed and is observed on real x86 hardware (thousands of times per 200,000 runs in Example 3).
- With `seq_cst` on all four operations it is impossible: all four must fit one total order, and whichever store comes first in that order must be seen by the other thread's later load.
- This is why Peterson's and Dekker's algorithms need `seq_cst` (or `seq_cst` fences).

edge_cases.title: Mixing `seq_cst` with weaker orders silently loses the guarantee
edge_cases.explanation:
- What people assume: "one side uses `seq_cst`, so the protocol is sequentially consistent".
- What actually happens: the single total order covers only `seq_cst` operations. If T1's load in the store-buffering test above is `acquire` instead of `seq_cst`, `r1 == r2 == 0` becomes possible again.
- Also: the default memory order is `seq_cst`, so `flag = true;` and `if (flag)` on a `std::atomic` are `seq_cst`. Optimizing one of them to `relaxed` "for speed" can break a protocol that relied on the total order.

edge_cases.title: `volatile` compiles, runs, and is still wrong
edge_cases.explanation:
- What people assume: "`volatile bool stop` forces a real memory read each iteration, so the worker eventually sees the update; that is all a stop flag needs".
- What actually happens: the program has a data race (UB). In practice on x86 it often "works", which is why the bug survives code review. It publishes nothing: data written before `stop = true` is not guaranteed visible.
- `volatile int counter; ++counter;` from two threads loses increments exactly like a plain `int`.
- `volatile` + `std::atomic` are orthogonal: `volatile std::atomic<int>` exists for atomics that live in MMIO or are shared with signal handlers, not for "extra safety".

edge_cases.title: Invalid memory order arguments are undefined behaviour, not a no-op
edge_cases.explanation:
- `store(v, memory_order_acquire)`, `store(v, memory_order_acq_rel)`, `load(memory_order_release)` and `load(memory_order_acq_rel)` violate preconditions.
- With GCC 11 and Clang a normal build compiles without a warning when the order is passed this way, and the program appears to work.
- `-D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS` (libstdc++) turns it into an assertion failure and `abort()`.
- A compare-exchange failure order of `release` or `acq_rel` is also invalid (the failure path is just a load).

edge_cases.title: A fence on the wrong side of the store does nothing useful
Two atomics written in order can be observed out of order
edge_cases.explanation:
- What people assume: "both `data` and `ready` are `std::atomic`, so the reader sees them in the order they were written".
- What actually happens: with relaxed operations each atomic has its own modification order and nothing links them. The reader may see `ready == true` and then `data == 0`.
- It is **not** a data race (everything is atomic), so the behaviour is defined: the output is simply either the old or the new value.
- Interview precision: "no happens-before, so no guarantee of 42" is correct; "data race, UB" is wrong for this all-atomic version.
- Fix: release store on `ready`, acquire load of `ready`; `data` may then stay relaxed, or even become a plain `int`.

code_examples.title: Release/acquire publication of non-atomic data
code_examples.explanation:
- The flag is atomic because it is the synchronization mechanism; the payload stays ordinary memory.

- Output is always `7 101.25 ABC`.
- The guarantee covers every write sequenced before the release, including the heap allocation inside `std::string`.

code_examples.title: Relaxed counter, and why `join()` makes the final read safe
code_examples.explanation:
- Relaxed is enough because the counter publishes no other data.

- Always prints `4000000`: each RMW reads the latest value in the counter's modification order, so no increment is lost.
- The final relaxed load is safe and complete because of `join()`, not because of the memory order.

code_examples.title: Store-buffering litmus test: release/acquire vs seq_cst on real hardware
code_examples.explanation:
- Runs the Dekker pattern many times and counts the outcome `r1 == 0 && r2 == 0`.

- Sample run on an x86-64 machine (the first count varies per run, two runs gave 3488 and 11714):

- On x86 the release/acquire version compiles to plain `mov`s, so the store buffer lets each load run before the other core sees the store. The `seq_cst` store compiles to `xchg`, which drains the store buffer.
- The `seq_cst` line is 0 by guarantee; the first line is merely *allowed* to be non-zero.
additional_code:
release/acquire: r1==0 && r2==0 in 3488 of 200000 rounds
seq_cst        : r1==0 && r2==0 in 0 of 200000 rounds

code_examples.title: Publication with fences instead of ordered operations
code_examples.explanation:
- One acquire fence covers the payload after a relaxed polling loop.

- Always prints `6`.
- Fence-fence synchronization: the release fence is sequenced before a store, the acquire fence is sequenced after a load that read that store.
- Tooling note: ThreadSanitizer (GCC 11 at least) does not model standalone `atomic_thread_fence`, so fence-based code like this can be reported as a false data race on `payload` depending on how the program is built and scheduled. Prefer ordered operations where possible so that TSan stays useful.

code_examples.title: A spinlock is just acquire on lock and release on unlock
code_examples.explanation:
- Shows that "lock = acquire, unlock = release" is literally how mutual exclusion publishes data.

- Always prints `400000`.
- Each `unlock()` (release) synchronizes-with the next successful `exchange` (acquire) that reads `false`, so every critical section happens-before the next.
- With `relaxed` on both, mutual exclusion on the flag would still hold, but `shared_total` would be a data race (see Practice Q14).

code_examples.title: Happens-before is transitive across three threads
code_examples.explanation:
- T3 never touches `stage1`, yet safely reads data written by T1.

- Always prints `30`.
- Chain: `config = 10` →sb→ release(stage1) →sw→ acquire(stage1) →sb→ release(stage2) →sw→ acquire(stage2) →sb→ read.

code_examples.title: Reference counting: relaxed increment, acq_rel decrement
code_examples.explanation:
- The pattern used by `std::shared_ptr`-style control blocks.

- Always prints `deleting, value = 99`, whichever thread drops the last reference:
  - Worker decrements last: it prints its own write.
  - Main decrements last: its `fetch_sub` reads the value written by the worker's release `fetch_sub`, so it synchronizes-with it and must see `value = 99`.
- Increment can be relaxed: a thread can only call `retain` while it already owns a reference, so the object cannot die concurrently.
- Decrement needs release (so this thread's writes are published) and the final decrement needs acquire (so the deleter sees all writes). Common optimization: `fetch_sub(1, release)` then `atomic_thread_fence(acquire)` only in the `== 1` branch.

interview_qa.question: What is the difference between atomicity and memory ordering for a std::atomic operation?
interview_qa.answer: Atomicity means operations on that one atomic object never race, tear or lose updates, whatever order is used. Memory ordering is a separate property: it says what the operation guarantees about other memory, for example whether earlier writes are published to another thread.
interview_qa.explanation:
- `x.store(42, std::memory_order_relaxed)` is fully atomic. Relaxed only removes ordering guarantees for *other* variables.
- Atomicity answers "can two threads touch this variable safely?". Ordering answers "if I see this value, what else am I guaranteed to see?".
- The memory order is not applied to the plain data. It is applied to the atomic operation that acts as the synchronization point, and that point then orders the surrounding plain accesses.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "atomic means the operation is one indivisible CPU instruction, and the memory order controls how fast it reaches other cores". C++ only promises atomic semantics (an implementation may even use a lock), and memory order is about happens-before, not speed.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the layering. C++ defines atomicity, modification order and happens-before; the compiler maps them to instructions (`lock xadd`, `ldar`/`stlr`, fences); the CPU implements them with store buffers and cache coherence. The definition lives in the first layer.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Atomic protects the variable; memory order decides what that variable can publish about other memory.

**Explanation:**

interview_qa.question: Is this flag handoff with a plain `int` and `bool` correct, and what exactly is wrong?
interview_qa.answer: No. Both `ready` and `data` are written by one thread and read by another with no happens-before relation, so there are data races on both and the behaviour is undefined. Fix: make `ready` a `std::atomic<bool>` with a release store and an acquire load.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Source order inside one thread proves nothing to another thread; only happens-before does.

interview_qa.question: What does memory_order_relaxed guarantee, and when is it the right choice?
interview_qa.answer: Relaxed guarantees atomicity and per-object coherence (one modification order, no going backward) but no ordering of other memory. It is right when the atomic carries no information about other data: statistics counters, ID generators, a stop flag that publishes nothing.
interview_qa.explanation:

  - no data race on the atomic itself

interview_qa.question: Why may the consumer read a non-atomic `data` once an acquire load of `ready` sees true? Must `data` be atomic?

```text
                                         |
                                  synchronizes-with (load reads true)
                                         v
T2:                       ready.load(acquire) --sequenced-before--> read data
=> data = 42  happens-before  read data
```

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: after the consumer has read the data, the producer must not modify it again without another synchronization round, otherwise that later write races with the consumer's reads.

interview_qa.question: What happens if the consumer's acquire load executes before the producer's release store? Does acquire wait for the release?
interview_qa.answer: Acquire never waits. The load returns whatever value it reads at that moment, usually the old one, and synchronizes with nothing. That is correct behaviour as long as the consumer only touches the published data when the loaded value says it is ready.

interview_qa.question: What is the modification order of an atomic object? Is it per thread? Are loads part of it? Do two atomics share one?
interview_qa.answer: Each atomic object has one total order of all its modifications (stores and RMWs) from all threads, and every thread agrees on it. It is per object, not per thread. Loads are not in it; they observe a value from it. Two atomics have independent orders.
interview_qa.explanation:

- `x` and `y` written as `x=10, y=20, x=30, y=40` by one thread give two orders: `x: 0→10→30`, `y: 0→20→40`. There is no combined order, so a relaxed reader can see `y == 40` and then `x == 10`.

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the four coherence rules (write-write, read-read, read-write, write-read) hold even for relaxed, and RMWs always read the last value in the order, which is why lock-free counters work.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: One modification order per atomic object, across all threads; loads only observe it.

interview_qa.question: A colleague says a flag shared by two threads needs `volatile`. Do you agree?
interview_qa.answer: No. `volatile` makes the compiler perform every access, which is meant for memory-mapped I/O and signal handlers, but it gives no atomicity, no data-race freedom and no inter-thread ordering. |---|---|---|
| Every access performed | ✅ | ✅ (in effect) |
| Atomic read-modify-write | ❌ | ✅ |
| Data-race free | ❌ | ✅ |
| Release/acquire, happens-before | ❌ | ✅ |
| Typical use | MMIO registers, `sig_atomic_t`, `longjmp` locals | Communication between threads |

interview_qa.question: What does seq_cst add over acquire/release? Does it order which thread runs first, and do seq_cst loads synchronize?
interview_qa.answer: A seq_cst load is an acquire, a store is a release, and in addition all seq_cst operations on all objects fit one single total order consistent with each thread's program order. It does not control scheduling, and two loads never synchronize with each other.

- "Participates in a total order" and "synchronizes-with" are different statements. Synchronizes-with still requires a load to read a value stored by a release (any seq_cst store is a release).

- ✅ What a strong answer adds: the guarantee covers only seq_cst operations. Mix in one acquire or release operation and the total-order reasoning no longer applies to it.

interview_qa.question: Which `(r1, r2)` results are possible here with seq_cst, and with release/acquire?

interview_qa.question: What is the difference between compiler reordering and CPU reordering, and what stops each?
interview_qa.answer: The compiler reorders, merges, hoists or deletes memory accesses under the as-if rule, assuming no data races. The CPU reorders visibility through out-of-order execution and store buffers. C++ atomics with the right memory order constrain both; a compiler-only barrier stops just the compiler.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Compiler example: `while (!flag) {}` on a plain `bool` may become `if (!flag) for (;;) {}`. Legal, because a concurrent write would be a data race.
- CPU example: on x86, `x = 1; r = y;` can complete the load before the store is visible to other cores.
- Tools:

| Tool | Stops compiler | Stops CPU | Portable |
|---|---|---|---|
| `std::atomic` op with order | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| `std::atomic_thread_fence` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| `std::atomic_signal_fence` | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ (signal handlers only) |
| `asm volatile("" ::: "memory")` | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ GCC/Clang |
| `volatile` | only among volatile accesses | ❌ | ✅ but not for threads |

interview_qa.question: How do x86 and ARM differ in memory ordering, and what do acquire, release and seq_cst compile to on each?
interview_qa.answer: x86 is TSO: only a store followed by a later load can be reordered, so acquire loads and release stores are plain `mov`, and only seq_cst stores need `xchg` or `mfence`. ARMv8 is weakly ordered (all four reorderings), so it uses `ldar`/`stlr` and `dmb` barriers.
interview_qa.explanation:
| C++ | x86-64 (GCC 11, verified) | AArch64 (standard mapping) |
|---|---|---|
| relaxed / acquire / seq_cst load | `mov` | `ldr` / `ldar` (or `ldapr`) / `ldar` |
| relaxed / release store | `mov` | `str` / `stlr` |
| seq_cst store | `xchg` | `stlr` |
| `fetch_add` | `lock xadd` | LL/SC loop or LSE `ldadd*` |
| `atomic_thread_fence(seq_cst)` | `lock or [rsp], 0` (or `mfence`) | `dmb ish` |

- Consequence: buggy code with relaxed flags often passes all tests on x86 and fails on ARM servers, Apple silicon or phones.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "x86 is sequentially consistent, so memory order does not matter on x86". x86 allows store-load reordering, and the compiler reorders regardless of CPU.
- ❌ Another wrong answer: "the store buffer on every CPU releases stores in program order". True on x86 (FIFO store buffer), false on ARM/POWER.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: neither x86 nor ARMv8 hardware lets two readers disagree on the order of two independent writes (the IRIW anomaly), but the C++ model allows it for acquire/release because it also targets POWER. Only seq_cst forbids it. Design to the C++ model, not to the CPU you test on.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: On x86 only seq_cst stores cost extra; on ARM every non-relaxed order costs something; C++ code must not care.

interview_qa.question: When do you use memory_order_acq_rel, and what happens if you pass acquire to a store or release to a load?
interview_qa.answer: acq_rel is for read-modify-write operations that must both import (acquire, via the read) and publish (release, via the write), such as a ref-count decrement or a CAS that hands work over. Passing acquire to a store or release to a load violates a precondition: undefined behaviour.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Valid orders:
  - load: `relaxed`, `consume`, `acquire`, `seq_cst`
  - store: `relaxed`, `release`, `seq_cst`
  - RMW: all six
  - CAS failure order: a load order, so not `release` or `acq_rel`
- GCC 11 and Clang compile `x.store(1, std::memory_order_acquire)` silently when the order is passed through `std::atomic`; libstdc++ with `-D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS` aborts at runtime.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "acq_rel on a load gives you both". A load has no write to attach release semantics to.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: an RMW that reads from a release store continues that store's release sequence. So a chain of relaxed `fetch_add`s between a release store and an acquire load does not break the synchronization.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: acq_rel is for RMWs; mismatched orders on loads/stores are UB, not "the strongest possible".

interview_qa.question: What is std::atomic_thread_fence, and how does fence-based synchronization differ from release/acquire operations?
interview_qa.answer: A fence is not bound to one atomic; it upgrades nearby relaxed atomic operations. A release fence sequenced before a relaxed store synchronizes with an acquire fence sequenced after a relaxed load that read that store. An atomic object must still carry the value.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Fences upgrade relaxed atomics; release fence before the store, acquire fence after the load.

interview_qa.question: What is memory_order_consume, and should you use it?
interview_qa.answer: consume was meant to be a cheaper acquire: it orders only operations that carry a data dependency on the loaded value, such as dereferencing a loaded pointer. It proved unimplementable as specified, every major compiler treats it as acquire, and C++26 deprecates it. Use acquire.
interview_qa.explanation:
- Motivation: on ARM/POWER, address dependencies are ordered by hardware for free (Linux RCU's `rcu_dereference` relies on this), so `p->field` after loading `p` would need no barrier.
- Problem: compilers optimize away dependencies (e.g. `x - x`, value speculation), and tracking them through the type system never worked. The standard discouraged it since C++17.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "consume is the right order for pointer publication in low-latency code". In practice you pay acquire cost anyway, with more fragile code.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: on x86 acquire is already free (a plain `mov`), so the only beneficiaries would be weak architectures, where `ldapr` (RCpc acquire, ARMv8.3) already narrows the gap.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: consume is effectively acquire everywhere and deprecated in C++26; write acquire.

interview_qa.question: Is a release/acquire chain through a middle thread enough for T3 to read `config` safely?
interview_qa.answer: Yes. Happens-before is transitive: T1's write is sequenced-before its release on `a`, which synchronizes-with T2's acquire, which is sequenced-before T2's release on `b`, which synchronizes-with T3's acquire. So the write to `config` happens-before T3's read.
interview_qa.explanation:
- This is what makes pipelines work: each stage only synchronizes with the previous one, yet every stage sees everything written by all earlier stages.
- Related rule, the release sequence: after a release store to `M`, RMWs on `M` by any thread (even relaxed) extend the sequence. An acquire reading the value of one of those RMWs still synchronizes-with the original release.
- C++20 change: a later plain store by the same thread no longer extends a release sequence; only RMWs do.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "T3 must also acquire `a` to see T1's data".
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: transitivity requires each link to be real. If T2's store to `b` were relaxed, or T2 stored before it acquired, the chain breaks and T3 races on `config`.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Happens-before chains across any number of threads, as long as every link is a real release/acquire pair.

- T1 writes `config`, then release-stores `a`. T2 acquires `a`, then release-stores `b`.
- T3 acquires `b` and reads `config`, but never touches `a`.

interview_qa.question: Which memory orders does a shared_ptr-style reference count need for increment and decrement, and why?
interview_qa.answer: Increment can be relaxed: a thread only adds a reference while it already holds one, so the object cannot die concurrently. Decrement needs release so each owner's writes are published, and the thread that reaches zero needs acquire before deleting. Use `fetch_sub(acq_rel)`, or release plus an acquire fence.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Relaxed to add a reference you already own; release on drop; acquire before destroy.
interview_qa.full_content:
**Answer:**
Increment can be relaxed: a thread only adds a reference while it already holds one, so the object cannot die concurrently. Decrement needs release so each owner's writes are published, and the thread that reaches zero needs acquire before deleting. Use `fetch_sub(acq_rel)`, or release plus an acquire fence.

**Explanation:**
```cpp
void release_ref(Block* b) {
    if (b->refs.fetch_sub(1, std::memory_order_release) == 1) {
        std::atomic_thread_fence(std::memory_order_acquire);  // only the last owner pays
        delete b;
    }
}
```
- Without release on every decrement, a thread's last writes to the object could be reordered after its decrement; the deleting thread then destroys an object that is still being written.
- Without acquire before `delete`, the destructor may not see other owners' writes: a data race with the destructor.
- The decrements form a release sequence (all RMWs), so the final acquire synchronizes with every earlier owner's release.
- ❌ Common wrong answer: "a counter only needs relaxed". That is true for statistics, but this counter controls object lifetime, so it publishes.
- ✅ What a strong answer adds: `std::shared_ptr` copies are not free: each copy is an atomic RMW on a shared cache line. Pass by `const&` in hot paths. `std::atomic<std::shared_ptr<T>>` (C++20) is usually not lock-free.

**Key takeaway:** Relaxed to add a reference you already own; release on drop; acquire before destroy.

interview_qa.question: Why is double-checked locking with a plain `Singleton*` broken, and how do you fix it?
interview_qa.answer: The unlocked first check reads the pointer while another thread writes it under the lock: a data race. Even ignoring that, a reader may see a non-null pointer before the object's construction is visible. Fix: an atomic pointer with acquire load and release store, or simply a function-local static.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Any lock-free fast path must carry its own release/acquire; prefer magic statics.

interview_qa.question: How would you build a seqlock for a one-writer, many-reader market-data snapshot, and which memory orders does it need?
interview_qa.answer: A sequence counter is odd while a write is in progress. Readers load it (acquire), copy the data with relaxed atomic loads, issue an acquire fence, reload the counter, and retry if it was odd or changed. The writer bumps it to odd, release fence, writes, then release-stores the even value.
interview_qa.key_takeaway: Seqlock = odd/even counter + relaxed atomic payload + fences on both sides of the data accesses.

practice_tasks.title: Question 7
practice_tasks.answer:
Data races on both `done` and `result`: undefined behaviour.
volatile gives no atomicity and no inter-thread ordering.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- `volatile` only forces the compiler to perform each access to `done`. It creates no happens-before, so `result = 123` is not published.

volatile gives no atomicity and no inter-thread ordering.

practice_tasks.title: Question 8
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Either "not ready" or "42". Never "0". No undefined behaviour.
```

**Explanation:**
- Acquire does not wait for a release. If the load runs first it reads `false`, synchronizes with nothing, and the program prints "not ready" without ever touching `data`: no access, no race.
- If the load reads `true`, it read the release store's value, so `data = 42` happens-before the read and `42` is printed.
- A later release store does not update the value already loaded; to wait, loop, use `ready.wait(false)` (C++20), or a condition variable.
- **Key Concept:** synchronization happens only when the acquire reads the released value; acquire is a filter, not a wait.

practice_tasks.title: Question 9
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
It compiles without warnings (GCC 11 / Clang, -Wall -Wextra) and normally prints 1,
but both calls violate preconditions: undefined behaviour.
With -D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS (libstdc++) the program aborts at the store.
```

**Explanation:**
- A store accepts only `relaxed`, `release` or `seq_cst`. A load accepts only `relaxed`, `consume`, `acquire` or `seq_cst`.
- Acquire is about the *read* side of synchronization and release about the *write* side; they have no meaning on the other operation.
- If you need both on one operation, it must be an RMW (`exchange`, `fetch_add`, CAS) with `acq_rel`.
- **Key Concept:** invalid memory-order arguments are UB, not "the strongest order"; enable library assertions in debug builds.

**Fixed Version:**
```cpp
#include <atomic>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::atomic<int> ready{0};
    ready.store(1, std::memory_order_release);
    std::cout << ready.load(std::memory_order_acquire) << '\n';   // prints 1
}
```

practice_tasks.title: Question 10
practice_tasks.answer: Data race on `value`: undefined behaviour. The release fence is on the wrong side of the store.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- Fence-fence synchronization requires the release fence to be **sequenced before** the store that the consumer reads. Here the store comes first, so the fence publishes nothing to that store's readers.
- The consumer side is correct: acquire fence after the relaxed load that saw `1`.
- A fence is not a "flush everything" instruction; it only upgrades the relaxed atomic operations on the correct side of it.
- Tooling note: ThreadSanitizer (GCC 11) does not model standalone fences, so it flags the fixed version too (a false positive). Fence code needs reasoning, not just TSan.
- **Key Concept:** release fence before the publishing store, acquire fence after the observing load.
practice_tasks.key_concept: release fence before the publishing store, acquire fence after the observing load.
additional_code: Data race on `value`: undefined behaviour. The release fence is on the wrong side of the store.

practice_tasks.title: Question 11
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
No data race. Prints 42 or 0, depending on which thread locks first.
```

**Explanation:**
- Lock is an acquire, unlock is a release, and each unlock synchronizes-with the next lock of the same mutex. Whichever critical section comes second sees everything the first one wrote.
- If the reader locks first it prints `0`: a well-defined outcome, a logical ordering problem, not UB.
- To force "42", the reader must wait for a state change: a condition variable with a predicate, an atomic flag, or simply joining the writer first.
- **Key Concept:** a mutex orders whole critical sections; it does not decide which thread goes first.

practice_tasks.title: Question 12
practice_tasks.answer: No. Data race on `config` in T3: undefined behaviour.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- T1 → T2 is a proper link: release on `a`, acquire that reads it.
- T2 → T3 is broken: the store to `b` is relaxed, so T3's acquire has no release to synchronize with.
- Happens-before is transitive only through real links; one relaxed hop cuts the whole chain.
- With `b.store(true, std::memory_order_release)` the chain `config = 10 → release a → acquire a → release b → acquire b → read` holds, and T3 always prints `10`, even though T3 never touches `a`.
- **Key Concept:** transitivity works through any number of threads, but every hop needs its own release/acquire pair.

additional_code: No. Data race on `config` in T3: undefined behaviour.

practice_tasks.title: Question 13
practice_tasks.full_content:
**Answer:**
```
Safe. Always prints 42.
```

**Explanation:**
- T3 reads the value `2`, written by T2's relaxed CAS, not by T1's release store. It looks like the chain is broken.
- But a successful CAS is a read-modify-write, and an RMW on the same atomic continues the **release sequence** headed by T1's release store. An acquire that reads any value in that release sequence synchronizes-with the head.
- So `data = 42` happens-before T3's read, even though T2 used `relaxed`.
- Since C++20 only RMWs extend a release sequence. If T2 had done a plain `stage.store(2, relaxed)` instead, T3 would race on `data`.
- **Key Concept:** RMWs in the middle (counters, CAS) do not break a release/acquire publication; plain stores do.

practice_tasks.title: Question 14
practice_tasks.answer:
Data race on `total`: undefined behaviour. On x86 it usually still prints 400000,
because the locked xchg is a full barrier there; on ARM, or after compiler reordering, increments can be lost.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- Mutual exclusion on the flag works (the `exchange` is atomic), but relaxed ordering means the critical section's accesses to `total` are not ordered with the lock operations.
- The compiler may move `++total` outside the lock/unlock pair, and a weak CPU may make the store to `total` visible after the unlock.
- Lock must be acquire (later accesses stay below it), unlock must be release (earlier accesses stay above it). Then unlock synchronizes-with the next successful lock.
- Bonus improvement: spin on a plain load (test-and-test-and-set) so waiting cores do not keep stealing the cache line with RMWs.
- **Key Concept:** a lock is mutual exclusion plus acquire/release; relaxed gives only the first.

practice_tasks.title: Question 15
practice_tasks.answer:
Data race on `instance`: undefined behaviour.
A thread can see a non-null pointer before the Config constructor's writes are visible.
practice_tasks.explanation:
- The first check reads `instance` without the mutex while another thread writes it under the mutex. The mutex only orders threads that both lock it.
- `instance = new Config` is allocation, construction, then pointer store. Nothing stops the compiler or CPU from making the pointer store visible before `port = 8080`, so the fast path can read `port == 0`.
- `volatile Config*` would not fix either problem.
- Fix 1: `std::atomic<Config*>` with an acquire load on the fast path and a release store after construction.
- Fix 2 (preferred): a function-local static. Its initialization is thread-safe since C++11, and compilers implement it with an acquire-load fast path.
- **Key Concept:** an unlocked fast path must carry its own release/acquire publication.
practice_tasks.key_concept: an unlocked fast path must carry its own release/acquire publication.

A thread can see a non-null pointer before the Config constructor's writes are visible.

quick_reference.content:
#### Choosing a memory order

| You need | Use |
|---|---|
| A counter / statistic / unique ID nobody uses to publish data | `relaxed` |
| A stop flag that publishes no data | `relaxed` is enough (`seq_cst` is fine and simpler) |
| Publish data written before a flag/pointer/index | `release` store + `acquire` load on the **same** atomic |
| RMW that both claims and publishes (CAS on a lock, ref-count decrement) | `acq_rel` |
| Store-then-load protocols (Dekker, Peterson), several flags read by several readers | `seq_cst` |
| One acquire for many relaxed loads | relaxed loads + `atomic_thread_fence(acquire)` |
| Not sure | `seq_cst` (default), then optimize with a proof |

#### Relations

| Term | One line |
|---|---|
| Data race | Conflicting accesses, at least one non-atomic, no happens-before → UB |
| Sequenced-before | Program order inside one thread |
| Synchronizes-with | Release → acquire that reads its value; unlock → next lock; thread start/join |
| Happens-before | Transitive chain of sequenced-before + synchronizes-with |
| Modification order | One total order of all writes/RMWs per atomic object; loads only observe |
| Release sequence | Release store + following RMWs on that object; acquire reading any of them syncs with the release |
| SC total order | One order of all `seq_cst` ops on all objects; not scheduling, not synchronization |

#### Hardware cheat sheet

| | x86-64 (TSO) | ARMv8 (weak) |
|---|---|---|
| Visible reorderings | store → later load only | all four (LL, LS, SL, SS) |
| acquire load / release store | plain `mov` | `ldar` / `stlr` |
| seq_cst store | `xchg` (or `mov; mfence`) | `stlr` |
| seq_cst fence | `mfence` / `lock or` | `dmb ish` |
| "Works on x86" with relaxed flag? | Often, until the compiler reorders | Breaks |

#### Interview one-liners

| Question | One-liner |
|---|---|
| Atomic vs ordering? | Atomicity protects the variable; memory order defines what it publishes about other memory. |
| What does release do? | Makes every earlier write in the thread visible to any thread whose acquire reads this store's value. |
| What does acquire do? | If it reads a value from a release, everything before that release happens-before everything after this acquire. |
| Does acquire wait? | No. It reads whatever is there; only reading the released value synchronizes. |
| Relaxed publication with plain data? | Data race on the payload: undefined behaviour, not "maybe prints 0". |
| Why is relaxed fine for counters? | RMWs read the latest value in the modification order; nothing else is published. |
| What does seq_cst add? | A single total order of all seq_cst ops, which forbids store-load reordering. |
| Does seq_cst pick which thread runs first? | No, it restricts allowed outcomes, not scheduling. |
| Does release flush the store buffer? | C++ does not say; it defines happens-before. Hardware chooses the mechanism. |
| volatile vs atomic? | volatile = perform every access (MMIO, signals); atomic = atomicity + inter-thread ordering. |
| How does a mutex order memory? | Lock is acquire, unlock is release; unlock synchronizes-with the next lock. |
| x86 vs ARM? | x86 only reorders store→load; ARM reorders everything; C++ orders hide the difference. |
| consume? | Promoted to acquire by every compiler, deprecated in C++26; just use acquire. |
| Fences? | Upgrade nearby relaxed atomics; need an atomic carrying the value; release fence before the store, acquire fence after the load. |


## TOPIC: Memory Ordering and the C++ Memory Model
